title: UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham
description: The prime minister says "defensive air-to-air refuelling" is to be provided following a request from Saudi Arabia, after it faced attacks from the Houthis in Yemen.
body: A single British aircraft, an RAF Voyager, is believed to be involved in the operation. Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, in response to attacks the country has faced from the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. It is understood this is likely to begin in the coming days and will involve a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. The prime minister said it follows a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. Government officials said the offer is "time limited" and likely, in the first instance, to last "for weeks". Houthi militants are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. In recent days, the Houthis in Yemen say they have carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast. Defensive support is described by UK officials as that which aides Saudi air force jets shooting down incoming Houthi missiles and drones. Speaking to reporters travelling with him on the way to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Burnham linked cost of living pressures to the decision. "I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region," he said. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request." Shipping routes through the Red Sea are a vital artery of the world economy. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to the Red Sea - a key shipping route used by Saudi Arabia. In a BBC interview last week, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte hinted that European support for Saudi Arabia was likely. He said: "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'. "Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful." Energy Minister Martin McCluskey last week told MPs that the UK was "providing air defence support" to Saudi Arabia through the defence partnership that they have, although would not be drawn on questions of operational military activity. In January 2024, the UK joined the US in launching air strikes against Houthi targets across Yemen. Then-Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the UK "acted in self-defence" following the Houthis' targeting of ships, including a Royal Navy warship. He also said the strikes were "necessary, proportionate, and targeted" to protect lives and commercial shipping. Further joint air strikes from the UK and US followed in 2024, external. title: Driver jailed after killing 'devoted' mum while fleeing police
description: Lydia La Polla's life was "needlessly cut short, not far from her 25th wedding anniversary", the judge said.
body: Michael Connors, 28, admitted causing death by dangerous driving A dangerous driver has been jailed for 13 years after causing the death of a "devoted" mum while he fled police. Michael Connors went on the run to Ireland after killing Lydia La Polla, 47, in Wrexham in March 2025. He was extradited on an international arrest warrant. Connors, 28, had been driving at 71mph in a 20mph zone seconds before the crash, which also seriously injured the victim's husband Robert La Polla, 44, and a 16-year-old girl who was a passenger in the car driven by the defendant. Judge Simon Mills told Mold Crown Court that Lydia's "excellent life was needlessly cut short at the age of 47, not far from her 25th wedding anniversary". Connors did not have insurance or a driving licence when he killed Lydia La Polla Judge Mills said Connors, who was driving a silver Mercedes, fled the scene in a "cowardly fashion". "If the defendant has any sense of decency at all, he will carry the weight of what he did until the end of his days," he said. Judge Mills said Connors should not have been driving the vehicle, as he did not have insurance or a driving licence. He added: "We don't know whether you were under the influence of cannabis or not. I don't assume you were although four wraps of it were found in the vehicle." Connors, who was on licence from jail at the time of the crash, had driven across two junctions in two "highly dangerous" manoeuvres. Judge Mills said it was "simply by chance" that "more people were not killed" as a result of his "dangerous" and "completely selfish actions". Prosecutor David Mainstone said on 24 March 2025, a police officer spotted the Mercedes and decided to follow it. Lydia La Polla had been driving a Toyota Yaris when the Mercedes ploughed into the passenger side, causing it to become airborne, roll over and hit a wall. The Mercedes was still travelling at 63mph at the time of the crash and three passengers were inside. Connors' DNA was found on an airbag and his fingerprint on a can of Red Bull. In a victim impact statement read out to the court, Robert La Polla said the death of his wife had left him with a "profound sense of loss". "My life will never be the same again," he wrote. "To say I am heartbroken is an understatement. "Lydia was a wonderful mother to our children and they absolutely adored her. It breaks my heart to know that their mother won't be there for their weddings, and she won't be there to see them grow up and have children of their own. "Our close family unit has been shattered into a thousand pieces, and it will never be the same again without Lydia." Connors, of Landen Road, Ballyfermot, Dublin, admitted causing death by dangerous driving. He also pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving. As well as his prison sentence, he received an eight-year driving ban with an extended re-test, to run after his release from prison. Mainstone said Connors had a record for 64 offences, including nine dangerous driving allegations in Ireland. He had nine offences for being uninsured and, in 2021, in Britain, had been sentenced to six years for conspiracy to burgle. Jane Miller, defending, said: "The defendant appears genuine in his remorse. He's had time to reflect upon his conduct." title: Settling old scores with royals drives Spencer's book, but Diana steals focus
description: What more revelations are going to appear now the full details of his Diana book are published?
body: Earl Spencer talked about his memoir of Diana with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg A slanging match doesn't usually do either side much good. Unless you're selling books, when a controversy can be extremely helpful. Earl Spencer's book about his sister, Diana, has had six days of public accusations and counter-claims, with extensive news coverage. So perhaps it's not surprising that even before it's officially published, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is racing up the Amazon best-seller chart. It's likely to be the most significant royal book since Prince Harry's startling 2023 memoir, Spare, and Andrew Lownie's 2025 book Entitled, which doomed Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's reputation. Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should we believe the unusually robust denial from Buckingham Palace? But when you read further through the book, there's a more complicated story being told. Earl Spencer is the brother watching events unfolding in the strange and ultimately doomed life of his sister, who has stepped from being his childhood companion to become one of the most famous women in the world. He describes a kind of grief and irritation as Diana becomes public property and then royal property, which irks him even more, disliking the "nonsense of fawning" around the monarchy. It's a stark reminder that Diana was only just 20 years old when she married - becoming a global superstar - and was dead 16 years later. Earl Spencer depicts her as a caring, generous character who was haunted by self-doubt, dogged by eating disorders, lacking in warmth from her new royal family and then ultimately dragged down by the tabloid media. "She craved acceptance, admiration, kindness, and - perhaps above all - love," writes Charles Spencer about Diana. "She got stuck into gritty, controversial, but crucial causes partly because she had a fine, natural social conscience, but also to assuage nagging feelings of worthlessness." And with a memoir like this it will be the extra details that will fascinate people. The stepmother to Diana and Charles, Raine Spencer, is painted in an unflattering light, and Diana is described as getting so angry once that she pushed Raine down the staircase at their home in Althorp. "Raine fortunately landed flush on her buttocks, rather than on bone, and got up, leaving the saloon without a backwards glance," he writes. It was in response, says the book, to Raine telling Diana: "I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you." There's not a single mention of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, even though she was talked about in the TV interviews We're told that a "nephew" wanted Earl Spencer to be in a documentary about Diana, which will raise speculation about Prince Harry's plans for his mother's 30th anniversary next year The book recounts that she disliked Dodi Fayed's father, Mohammed Fayed, accusing him of crudely groping her Diana's preferences included the soap opera Crossroads and the music of David Bowie. She'd watched The Sound of Music 16 times and the paper she read was the Daily Mail Earl Spencer and the then-Prince Charles opening a memorial to Diana in 2004 Earl Spencer will ultimately be remembered by the passionate eulogy he delivered at Diana's funeral in Westminster Abbey. He reveals how he had pretended to have lost his copy of his speech at the rehearsal, so no one could hear it in advance and try to tone down his stinging criticism of the press and the royals. After the hounding of Diana by the paparazzi, he says he personally rang tabloid newspaper editors to disinvite them from the Abbey funeral, after their invitations had already been sent out. She was buried on an island in the Spencers' Althorp estate, rather than a graveyard - and the book describes how a bishop was brought to consecrate the ground to make it possible. Much of the interest in this book has been driven by its settling of old scores with the Royal Family. It can feel like medieval barons jousting. References to King Charles are almost all negative, including the suggestion that he was jealous of his wife's public popularity. The book reports a conversation in which it's claimed the then-Prince Charles complained: "I mean, I'm 43,' he said, 'and I employ fifty people' – he was flushed in the face now – 'but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!'" The King is portrayed as resentful, with a "senior courtier" reporting an alleged comment by the late Queen: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet." There's a bizarre account of discussions in the Royal Family about whether the then-Prince Charles's ears should have been pinned back. And there's the allegation that Diana had said the King was in love with his valet, which the author himself says seemed improbable. What comes across is how close the Spencers were to the royals - but without being friends. Charles and Diana Spencer went to the same children's parties as the young royals. The royals are depicted as the type of children who come round, break your toys and then disappear, in what might be an extended metaphor for how he saw Diana's story. There's also a story about a teenage Prince Andrew smirking in a church service because the priest used the word "womb". title: Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teeside
description: Cleveland Police carried out one of their biggest raids in years, following the A66 crash that left two officers dead.
body: This video can not be played Cleveland Police have carried out one of their biggest raids on organised crime targets in years. About 130 officers were involved in the operation which saw 17 people arrested in the Middlesborough area. The raids are part of a response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month, which resulted in the death of two officers in a police pursuit. The BBC's Stuart Whincup was with the police as they carried out the arrests. Read more about the raids in this story. Watch: Police raid organised crime targets in Teeside. title: Infantino says he is open to Fifa reform
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of the governance of world football's governing body.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform. In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino said the process would "recommend potential improvements". Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened". This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives". Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash. In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you." He then insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!" His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not." Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be". He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together". Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company. Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football. "We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association. What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided. "The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead." Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan. The 56-year-old Swiss-Italian Fifa leader will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents. Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation. title: 'Real fear Littler could walk away' - darts would be loser in booing row
description: Could Luke Littler walk away from darts completely if the booing he has suffered at European tournaments continues?
body: This video can not be played Why does Luke Littler keep getting booed? At just 19, Luke Littler has won almost every major trophy in darts. He is a multi-millionaire with lucrative sponsorship deals and his own TV show. But has his rapid rise turned some against him? This past weekend the teenager was once again subjected to boos and whistles from sections of the crowd as he took to the stage at the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam. What is surprising though is that it came as 'The Nuke' was on a quest to complete a darts clean sweep by becoming the first player to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year. Littler suggested afterwards that, if the booing continues, he will not attend events held in the Netherlands. But Samuel Gill, editor of Dartnews.com, suggests Littler's future in the sport could be at stake. "There's a real fear that within a few years he'll just turn around and walk away from the sport," Gill told BBC Sport. "So, I think for fans, 'Don't bite the hand that feeds you'. If people keep taunting him and don't want him to win, he might end up just walking away and not bothering anymore." Amsterdam was the latest tournament where Littler has faced what some might describe as an overly hostile reaction from fans. A vibrant pantomime-style atmosphere is part and parcel of the darts experience and Dutch and German crowds are amongs the most raucous - but it is clear Littler believes he has been unfairly targeted. The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last-16 on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed. It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday. The teenager's quarter-final defeat to Jonny Clayton ended Littler's quest for the clean sweep, but the Warrington native clearly felt fans had been unduly harsh towards him. Littler has now withdrawn from a series of upcoming events. "Just no point in me travelling, wasting my time while I'm getting booed," said Littler. Littler has also been jeered at numerous events in the UK. His phenomenal rise saw him reach the PDC World Darts Championship aged just 16 in his debut year as a professional. He captured the title the following year and the trophies, sponsorship deals and six-figure winners' cheques have continued to flow. But increasingly so have whistles and boos during his performances. "I don't think people expected him to reach the heights that he has so quickly," Gill said. The darts journalist - who became aware of Littler when the sport star was 14 - says this level of attention is not just unique to the British player. "Michael van Gerwen was the same for a long time when he dominated the sport. He barely lost a game in about five years, and he was hoovering up titles for fun and it was similar," said Gill. "Everyone wanted to boo him and even me as a viewer before I got into this role, growing up watching Van Gerwen, I wanted him to lose because it's something different for the sport every single week." Currently ranked number one in the world, Littler is so far ahead of his closest rivals that he already has the advantage of only having to play in selective tournaments. His boycott threat could end up being a blow to tournament organisers. "They don't like him because he's that good. And he's got a bit of swagger to him," said Karl Holden secretary of St Helen's Darts Academy - where Littler honed his skills from the age of nine. "Luke's got a bit of a character to him. For me, he's the ultimate professional. He might give a little bit of the large sometimes, but you need that, otherwise darts would be totally boring." This video can not be played How the teenager became a dart sensation It seems remarkable that the future of Littler's career in the sport is even being debated. More so when you consider his age and the fact he only turned professional two years ago. However, Gill believes that Littler's rapid haul of trophies, coupled with the huge amounts of money now in the sport, could result in the teenager leaving in the next "four to five years" should the boos and whistles continue. Gill believes Littler's impact on the darting world is immeasurable. Tickets to events featuring him are often sold out, applications to darting academies are reported to be at an all-time high and the Briton has transcended the sport. Gill therefore feels that, if Littler was to walk away, the sport would be the real loser. "He's the one who is bringing this sport to a completely different level. Nowadays, he is back-page news wherever you go," Gill said. "He might just decide 'I just want a quiet life now and just live off his money'." Littler has barely known anything other than winning. His challenged now is maintaining that victorious streak while keeping fans - whose interest helps fund his prize money - happy. Tricky when some are paying with the hope of seeing him lose. "If he was on that stage, everybody liked him and he just threw darts, I think I'd get bored of watching him," Holden said. title: Drunk council leader accused of drinking bottle of gin and vowing to 'wipe out' Plaid Cymru quits
description: Steve Hunt apologised and blamed "personal" reasons for his behaviour and "banter".
body: Steve Hunt will continue to serve as an independent councillor in his constituency A council leader who fell over while drunk after allegations he drank a "whole bottle of gin" and then threatened to "wipe out" the Welsh party Plaid Cymru has quit. Steve Hunt, from Neath Port Talbot Council, said he "should have exercised better judgement" after becoming "intoxicated" at a Welsh Local Government Association conference. Hunt said he was a strong supporter of the Welsh language, but admitted saying he wanted to "wipe out" Plaid Cymru politically as "banter". He denied drinking a bottle of gin. Hunt will continue to serve as an independent councillor, but a council spokesperson said a new leader would be appointed on 14 October. A source who attended the conference told the Local Democracy Reporting Service the independent councillor for the Crynant, Onllwyn and Seven Sisters ward was loudly bragging about drinking heavily. Hunt said the comment about Plaid Cymru "should be understood in the context of political banter and disagreement at the end of a long evening, rather than as a threat or anything other than a political statement". The councillor also said there were "personal circumstances" that contributed to his behaviour which were "relevant". His role as council leader had carried a "significant level of pressure and responsibility", he said, and he saw the event as an opportunity to "switch off" from those pressures. "Regrettably, I drank far beyond what was sensible," he said. Hunt said it did not excuse his behaviour and that he apologised to the Plaid Cymru group leader the following morning. Hunt has led the council's Independent and Plaid Cymru coalition since local elections took place in 2022. It was the first time in Neath Port Talbot's history that the Labour Party lost control of the council. Following his decision to step down, Hunt said he had done what he believed was in the "best interests" of the council and residents and communities that it represents. "I will continue to serve as an Independent councillor and will continue to work for the residents and communities I represent," he said. title: Paramount settles lawsuit with US states, helping clear way for $110bn merger with Warner Bros
description: Paramount has reached a settlement with the US states in a lawsuit challenging its $110bn merger with Warner Bros
body: A coalition of states led by California had challenged the deal, raising concerns over competition across film and television. Paramount Skydance has settled a lawsuit with dozens of US states, removing a major hurdle to its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told a news conference that state officials agreed to terms after securing commitments to protect competition across film and television, and broadcasting. Still, "the settlement is not a vote of support for this merger," Bonta said. "I don't think these two companies should merge." Paramount chief executive David Ellison hailed the resolution, saying: "Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and - most importantly -the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling." In a statement, Ellison said that now the state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America concerns had been addressed, "we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action". Ellison had previously threatened to move studio operations out of California. The settlement will help boost film production in the US, Bonta said, adding that under the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. Bonta stressed the agreement guarantees a massive boost to domestic output, "$300m to $1.5bn more, at minimum, for film and TV production right here in our country". "Importantly, that is the baseline. That is the minimum," Bonta said, noting that production commitments could surge by up to 700% if Congress passes a federal film tax credit. Under the deal's initial terms, Paramount must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising over 30% over the following three years. While mergers typically lead to corporate overlap and redundancies, Bonta maintained that it would be a "job creator" that will put people back to work across the industry. title: Atletico hit back at Mourinho over referee complaints
description: Atletico Madrid hit back at Jose Mourinho after he complained about the refereeing in the Madrid derby.
body: Mourinho arrived at his news conference with screenshots of incidents he believed should have resulted in red cards for Atletico Atletico Madrid have hit back at Jose Mourinho after the Real Madrid boss arrived at his post-derby news conference on Sunday carrying printouts of screenshots displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in red cards for Atletico. Mourinho accused the officials of making key errors after Real were beaten 2-1 by Atletico, claiming the hosts should have been handed two red cards in the first half. On Monday, Atletico posted twice on their X account, the first being a video showing a sheet of paper coming out of a printer with the words #StopAcosoArbitralYA, meaning "stop referee harassment now". A second post showed a picture of Mourinho at the news conference with the same message. The response from Atletico, whose team are coached by Diego Simeone, received two million views on X within two hours of it being posted. Atletico often use their social media accounts to respond to rivals, repeatedly posting on X this summer to ridicule Barcelona over their pursuit of Atletico's talisman Julian Alvarez. Alongside Mourinho's post‑match claims, the match report published on Real's website said that the derby loss was decided because of "dreadful refereeing", external by Ortiz Arias. The posts has more than two million views on X Mourinho's side had defender Dean Huijsen sent off early in the second half, when the game was goalless, for pulling down Atletico's Giuliano Simeone just inside the penalty area. The match outcome was Real's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September. "We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images on sheets of A4 paper on Sunday. "Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like. "So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half." Simeone, when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions. "I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Barcelona manager Hansi] Flick, [Real Betis boss Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said. "We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line." title: First UK charges brought over 1994 Rwanda genocide
description: Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday charged with seven offences.
body: The Metropolitan Police said the charges follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation" A Rwandan man, who has been living in north London, has become the first person charged in the UK with offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, has been charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Brown "is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others". Brown will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday. Ferguson said the decision to charge Brown was made "after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the War Crimes Team at the Metropolitan Police". "We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met," he added. The War Crimes Team began their investigation in September 2019 after a formal request from the Rwandan government to investigate people allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994. Over the course of 100 days in 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed in Rwanda by Hutu extremists. They were targeting members of the minority Tutsi community, as well as their political opponents, irrespective of their ethnic origin. The mainly Tutsi forces who took power following the genocide were alleged to have killed thousands of Hutu people in Rwanda in retaliation. The Metropolitan Police said the charges against Brown follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation". Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes. "The War Crimes Teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process. "A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda." title: Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out
description: Blackburn Rovers midfielder Kristi Montgomery gets a first call-up for Scotland as Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean drop out of the Nations League squad.
body: Montgomery made his Scotland Under-21 debut last year Kristi Montgomery has been given a first call-up for Scotland after Kieran Tierney and Kenny McLean dropped out of the Nations League squad. The Blackburn Rovers midfielder has been promoted from the under-21s by new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli for the games against Slovenia (twice), Switzerland and North Macedonia. The 22-year-old has started all eight Championship matches for Tony Mowbray's side this season. Celtic defender Tierney and Norwich midfielder McLean have 119 international caps between them, while experienced trio Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland were unavailable before Pocognoli made his picks. Montgomery is the eighth uncapped player in the 27-strong group, joining Luke Graham, Robbie Ure, Luis Binks, Colby Donovan, Jon McCracken, Josh McPake and Stephen Welsh. Oli McBurnie, Scott Bain, Kieron Bowie, Josh Doig, Lennon Miller and James Wilson were recalled and Napoli midfielder Billy Gilmour returns after missing the World Cup through injury. Dominic Hyam, Lyndon Dykes, George Hirst, Grant Hanley, Anthony Ralston and Ross Stewart are among those overlooked by Pocognoli, with Manchester United teenager Tyler Fletcher in the under-21s after taking Gilmour's place in the USA. title: F1 reduces maximum distance of races by 15km
description: F1 announces the maximum race distance for grands prix will be reduced by 15km from 305km to 290km for the 2027 season.
body: New rules will cover F1 races delayed or disrupted by rain or incidents from 2027 Formula 1 has announced the maximum race distance for grands prix will be reduced by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season. Grands prix are limited to a maximum of two hours of racing, but when there are interruptions caused by rain or accidents, a "hard stop time" will replace the current maximum three-hour duration to finish the event. This will allow for greater flexibility to complete disrupted races. A statement from governing body the FIA said: "These changes were introduced to ensure that the spectators have the best possible chance to enjoy a full race if disruptions occur." The hard stop time will vary from race to race, depending on local conditions. At night races, for example, there will be more flexibility to allow the race to run later than at a daytime race when there is a relatively early sunset. The reduction in race distance has been introduced because the ratio of internal combustion to electrical power is changing from 53-47 this year to 58-42 next year, before becoming 60-40 in 2028. This means that the cars will use more fuel, and that became a concern when it emerged that some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money. As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks. Another change agreed at a meeting of the F1 Commission, a rule-making body composed of the teams, the FIA and commercial rights holder F1, was to introduce "greater flexibility to extend free practice sessions should they be interrupted". Under current rules, the clock does not stop in practice sessions in the event of a red flag caused by an incident, unlike in qualifying and races when the competition is suspended. title: Invitation for men to 'experience hot flushes'
description: A MenoVest will allow people at an event in Hull to experience one of the symptoms of the menopause.
body: A common symptom of the menopause is a hot flush Partners of women going through the menopause are being invited to experience one of the symptoms at a forthcoming support event. At the Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Hull next month, health group Over The Bloody Moon will be taking one of its MenoVests, allowing people to experience a hot flush – one of the symptoms of the menopause. Sarah Weichardt, who co-manages the project, said: "We're particularly interested in getting men along to come and experience the MenoVest, just so that they can understand what women go through." The event will be at Princes Quay shopping centre on 17 October, from 10:30 until 14:30 BST. "It's not just a hot flush, it's what the hot flush brings with it," said Weichardt. "So it could be panic, it could be anxiety. It's experiencing it all at the same time." She said she hoped the vest would give people a "better understanding of what women are going through". "The more people we can get to experience it, the better," she added. Treatment for the menopause can include HRT patches The menopause describes the end of a woman's reproductive years, and often happens at about the age of 50. The period leading up to this is called the perimenopause, which is when many women notice their periods becoming unpredictable. Other symptoms can include mood shifts, difficulty sleeping, and discomfort during sex. Weichardt said her organisation had a banner with nearly 40 symptoms on it. Many women "don't necessarily know that they're going into the menopause or they're perimenopausal" until they see the banner – and then they sometimes have a "lightbulb moment", she said. Once women have "accepted it and are happy" they are menopausal or peri-menopausal, they can seek the support they need, she added. There is also a Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Beverley on 10 October between 10:30 and 13:30 BST at the Toll Gavel Church. title: First look at The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special revealed
description: Filming wrapped on the BBC Christmas special in October, as fans eagerly await its return.
body: The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn The first image from The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special has been revealed, teasing a romantic picnic scene. Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks. The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn. Filming wrapped on the BBC three-part Christmas special at the end of October, as fans eagerly await its return. The first series focused on Mary, the couple's seemingly unremarkable middle daughter as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England. It was primarily filmed in south Wales, at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys. The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, primarily in Wales. Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones will return to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter Mary. Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as Mr Ryder. Also resuming their roles are Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins. Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy. The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of October. He posted a short but sweet message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!" The first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 7.3 million UK viewers in its first four weeks Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming Christmas special, however, the BBC has teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" The three additional episodes, announced in June, will run for 30 minutes each and continue to be based on storylines from the original novel by Janice Hadlow. It has been written by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, with Asim Abbasi returning to direct the special. It will air in the UK on BBC iPlayer and BBC One, while in the US and Canada, it will also be available on BritBox. Sony Pictures Television will distribute The Other Bennet Sister internationally. title: Man charged with causing death by dangerous driving over crash that killed 6
description: Four members of the same family and a married couple on a motorbike died in the 2024 collision.
body: Shannen Morgan, Shane Roller and their daughters Rubie and Lillie died in the collision with husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving over a crash that killed six people, including two children. Shannen Morgan and Shane Roller died along with two of their daughters, nine-year-old Rubie, and Lillie, four, when the family's car collided with a motorbike on the A61 between Barnsley and Wakefield on 21 July 2024. Husband and wife Christopher and Janine Barton, from Barnsley, who were both travelling on the motorcycle, also died in the crash. Christopher Cockell, 50, is due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court in October charged with six counts of causing death by dangerous driving. An inquest previously heard that the silver Ford Focus being driven by Mr Roller, 33, collided head on with the BMW motorcycle being driven by Mr Barton, 56, at about 15:50 BST between Staincross and Newmillerdam. Wakefield Coroner's Court heard the collision happened as the motorcycle was overtaking another vehicle on the single-carriageway road, which had a 50mph (80 km/h) speed limit. Coroner's support officer Phil Marr told the hearing: "As a result of a head-on impact, the car was spun to the side of the road, where it caught fire. "It was not possible to release any of the occupants and all four were pronounced dead by paramedics at the scene." Floral tributes were left at the scene of the collision on the A61 Marr said a pathologist concluded Mr Barton's provisional cause of death was due to head and chest injuries. He said Mrs Barton was "thrown onto the adjacent golf course" in the collision, with her death due to chest injuries. Ms Morgan and van driver Mr Roller, who lived in Athersley, Barnsley, had another daughter, aged 11, who was not with them at the time of the crash. An online fundraising page, set up by a family friend in the wake of the tragedy, raised more than £400,000 for her. In a social media post at the time, Mr Roller's father, Graham, paid tribute to the couple, who he described as an "amazing" mum and dad. "Shane wasn't just a son but an amazing father and he had a heart of gold," he wrote. "Shannen, our daughter-in-law, was funny and was also an amazing mum and they thought the world of their little family." The A61 was closed while forensic teams inspected the scene Co-head teachers of Athersley North Primary School, which Rubie and Lillie had attended, said the girls had been "a delight to teach". In a statement, Clare Storr and Kirsty Wordsworth, said: "The girls were a credit to their parents, who were always incredibly supportive and who will also be greatly missed." Mr and Mrs Barton, 48, who had lived in Barnsley, had recently celebrated their 25th wedding anniversary. In a tribute issued via West Yorkshire Police in 2024, their son described his parents as "a loving, caring mum and dad who always put me before everything else". A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said Cockell had been summoned following an investigation by the force's Major Collision Enquiry Team and would appear before magistrates on 28 October. Cockell, of Gresford Close, Woolley Grange, had already been facing a charge of failing to stop at the scene of a collision. title: Two pilot whales dead after mass stranding
description: Attempts to refloat the whales off the Northumberland coast are unsuccessful due to the tides.
body: The pod contained about 40 pilot whales Two pilot whales have died after a distressed pod was spotted off the Northumberland coast. British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR) said it had been alerted to a group of about 40 whales near to the shore at Amble at 15:00 BST on Sunday. It said the whales had been "behaving in a distressed manner typically seen prior to a stranding event". Due to the tides, attempts to refloat the animals had been unsuccessful, the charity said, and rescue teams were forced to withdraw. Whales are highly social mammals and are well known for stranding in groups because they travel in large, close-knit communities which rely on constant communication. There are a range of theories for why beachings occur. Some experts say the animals can become disorientated after following fish they hunt to the shore. Others believe that one individual can mistakenly lead whole groups to shore. The BDMLR said it was not the same pod of whales which was herded out of the River Thames at the weekend as the distance between the locations was further than the species could swim in 24 hours. Local boats were launched with medics on board to try to herd the whales offshore to stop them from stranding. But the animals remained tightly packed around one of the largest, which was lying motionless on its side. The teams were stood down after losing the light on Sunday. Earlier on Monday, the BDMLR said about a dozen had been stranded on Coquet Island around rocky terrain. On investigation, six animals were found - five ashore and one afloat. Two of the stranded whales were confirmed to have died, the BDMLR said. Due to the tides and limited access to the island, attempts to refloat the live animals were not possible and the teams withdrew once again. The BDMLR said it would remain along the coast, ready to provide care and attempt to refloat those which were healthy enough. The RSPB said its staff from nearby Coquet Island were continuing to support the BDMLR's response to the incident. "This is a distressing situation and our thoughts are with all those involved in the response," a spokesperson said. title: Repeated air traffic control failures leave us in worrying territory
description: The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic.
body: To have one air traffic control failure in a fortnight may be regarded as a misfortune, to have two looks like carelessness. The UK's air traffic services provider is coming in for a wave of criticism at the moment, so where is it all leading? The incident at the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) main control centre in Swanwick earlier this month was extremely serious. It caused more than 2,000 flight cancellations over two days, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. Some were left sleeping on airport floors, others were stranded in foreign airports. Monday's failure at the Prestwick centre, which looks after air traffic in Scotland, northern England and northern Ireland was not as dramatic. But according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, it still led to about 150 flights being cancelled and many other delays affecting tens of thousands of travellers. The first failure this month was attributed to a previously undetected software flaw, which had an impact due to a very specific set of circumstances combining in a millisecond. Today's issue was blamed on a "connectivity issue" specific to the system used in Scotland. The two, Nats says, were unrelated. But this is becoming worryingly familiar territory. In August 2023, on a bank holiday weekend, a problem with a single aircraft's flight plan caused a key system at Swanwick to break down, leading to cancellations and delays that affected 700,000 passengers. Two years later, a smaller "radar-related issue" disrupted air traffic for four hours, and led to the cancellation of 150 flights. The question is whether all of these incidents were isolated and unavoidable, or whether they point to something more systemic. Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption UK flight delays continue after issue with air traffic control in Scotland is fixed There is no question that the job Nats has to do is fiendishly complicated, looking after some of the busiest airspace in Europe - including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick - which means handling up to 8,000 flights a day. Visiting the Swanwick centre, it's hard not to be impressed by the sheer scale of the place, where hundreds of staff sit behind an array of large radar screens, calmly making sense of what looks to the untrained eye like utter chaos. But these controllers need reliable equipment, and the concern is that they aren't getting it. Steve Heapy, chief executive of Jet2 made the point: "It is simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down." Easyjet said the latest incident "calls into question the resilience of Nats' systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures." A Nats spokesperson, apologising for the latest issue, said technology "can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible." They continued: "What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority." Sources say that behind the scenes, airlines are "furious" that disruption keeps on happening, and that they have to bear the costs of refunding passengers and looking after those who are affected by delays. There are deep concerns that not enough resources are being put into ensuring the air traffic control system has the resilience it needs. Some have gone further. Ryanair, for example, has repeatedly called for the Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign, or failing that for the Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander to remove him from his post. But although Alexander has described the disruption in early September as "completely unacceptable", there seems little appetite to force through a change of leadership at Nats. The government has asked the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) to carry out an independent review of the first incident from this month, which is expected to take six months to complete. Action is unlikely before the CAA's report appears, and today's events do not appear to have changed that. Meanwhile, Rolfe made it clear on Friday that he has no plans to resign. He emphasised that in systems of such complexity, obscure faults are extremely hard to prevent. "We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said. Nevertheless, it is clear that impatience with the Nats failures is growing, both among the airlines that pay for air traffic services and among passengers who bear the brunt when systems do not work as they should. title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
description: As London Fashion Week comes to a close, here are the biggest trends for your wardrobe.
body: Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fused severe tailoring with dark romanticism This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs. The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us". Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses. Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers. Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth". Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026: Rejecting "quiet luxury" uniforms, Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey, and Conner Ives led London Fashion Week's embrace of the "messy girl" aesthetic by championing deliberate chaos, pairing intentionally undone tailoring and messy updos "The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season. She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year. Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion. She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy". This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives. Erdem, Yuhan Wang, and Bora Aksu channelled a "gardencore" vibe, trading quiet luxury for unpolished, allotment-ready chaos - pairing parkas and structured trench outerwear with kitchen-garden details According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world. A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower. "There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats. It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu. Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show. Dujancourt's free-spirited aesthetic, organic draping, trailing ribbons, and delicately hitched slip skirts Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film. Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer. Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes". Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics. Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide. "Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in thier shows Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year. Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits , externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days. A school sports hall is transformed into a ballet stage for Edeline Lee's latest collection which drew inspiration from the intense discipline, repetition, and physical toll of classical dance Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet. After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year. Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall. "Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel. "Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

title: I've got no ceiling on Lib Dem ambitions, says leader Ed Davey
description: The Lib Dem leader also backed the controversial Jackdaw gas field, which the government is expected to approve.
body: Sir Ed Davey and Lib Dem MPs visited a wind farm off the south coast of England Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey has insisted he is not just aiming to be a junior partner in a coalition government, saying: "I am a candidate to be prime minister." He also backed the controversial Jackdaw gas field, which the government is expected to green light later this month, saying it had "passed the climate test" and was compatible with a transition to renewables. Sir Ed has faced criticism from some in his party that he lacks ambition and the vision needed to cut through in a crowded political field. He acknowledged the "frustration" felt by some of his MPs that the party was not making a bigger impact - and vowed to set out bold policies in his conference speech on Tuesday. Sir Ed led the Lib Dems to a record 72 MPs at the 2024 election, making big gains at the expense of the Conservatives in southern England, but the party has since slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind Labour, the Tories, the Greens and Reform UK. Despite this, the Lib Dem leader claimed his party had an "historic opportunity to do far better than anyone imagines at the moment" at the next general election. "Because the right wing is split," he said, "and fragmented like it's never happened before in over 200 years of British parliamentary elections. "If we take that opportunity, and I believe we're showing how we can, we'll be a massive force in the next parliament." Asked if he wanted to be the kingmaker in the next government, providing support for a party falling short of the 326 MPs needed for a majority, Sir Ed said: "I've got no ceiling on our ambitions. "I'm a candidate to be prime minister, but what we need to do is make sure that we build on that [election success], area by area, constituency by constituency." He made clear he will not go into a coalition government with Reform UK and has dismissed suggestions he could do a deal with the Conservatives. "We've got a moral responsibility to stop Nigel Farage - and indeed stop Kemi Badenoch giving the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage - I think there could be that sort of coalition on the right and we've got to stop that," he told the BBC. Asked if he would form a coalition with Labour, he said he did not deal in "hypotheticals". He said he wanted the Lib Dems to win support across the UK, but the BBC has been told his party's strategy is focused on the 27 seats where they came second in 2024. Of those 27, 20 are held by the Conservatives. Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth Sir Ed was speaking just before he headed out to visit the wind farm off the coast of Brighton, which he said he had signed off on when he was energy secretary in the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government a decade ago. He set out why supporting Jackdaw was not in conflict with his party's stance on tackling climate change, saying: "We're going to need gas for a long, long time as part of our transition, and when I was secretary of state for climate change, I always thought that we were going to need gas, and [Jackdaw] has passed the climate change test." Sir Ed explained the alternative was shipping in liquified natural gas (LNG) from across the globe, which would be more problematic than using gas from the North Sea, about 150 miles northeast of Aberdeen. "There's a lot of energy produced in both putting the gas into liquid and then taking it out into gas," he said. "The carbon footprint of that is far bigger, a lot more damaging for our climate, so this way, not only is it better for the climate, but also tax revenues come to the Exchequer." However, he told the BBC "the jury is very much out" on the Rosebank oil field, not least because that may not pass the same test on reducing carbon emissions. And he insisted the Lib Dems were still committed to a transition away from oil and gas, for the climate and also to lower people's energy bills. "Thanks to President Trump's mad war in Iran, people are paying far higher," he said. "We are paying far higher for that fossil fuel energy, and you've seen over the years how fossil fuels, oil and gas, can be extremely expensive. "So, the way to get energy bills down, get the economy growing, is to be less dependent on fossil fuels and we want to be." title: Seventeen arrested in Teesside police raids
description: The raids across Teesside follow the A66 crash which killed two police officers and five men.
body: About 130 officers were involved in the raids across parts of Teesside Police have carried out a series of early morning raids targeting those suspected of being involved in organised crime. Cleveland Police said 17 people had been arrested during the operation - involving about 130 officers including some from the National Crime Agency - across South Bank, Grangetown and Eston, near Middlesbrough, on Monday. It is part of a high-profile response to a crash on the nearby A66 last month which came at the end of a police pursuit and left two officers dead. Five men died also died when their Volkswagen Passat went the wrong way down the road and hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle heading in the opposite direction. The force said Monday's raids had seen people arrested on suspicion of various offences including drugs and assault. A convoy of about a dozen vans started the operation shortly after 08:00 BST, with roads temporarily blocked by patrol cars. Officers used battering rams to force entry to several properties as parents walked past with their children on the school run. Cleveland Police said much of the information behind the raids had come from the local community Assistant Chief Constable Mark Hall said public support after the crash had been ''absolutely phenomenal". "It's clear criminality of any sort is not welcome on these estates and we are here to tell those people we've heard their concerns and we will act," he said. Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, along with all five occupants of the Passat died at the scene of the A66 crash. Cleveland's Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said it was important for people to see officers on the streets targeting those responsible for crime. He said: "This makes people more reassured about what is really going in their communities. They see people arrested, charged and taken off the streets. "It shows the public good work is happening, despite the problems we have." Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external. title: Was Neville right to call out Man Utd for a 'lack of effort'?
description: Was Gary Neville right to call out Manchester United for a "lack of effort" in their 1-1 draw at Fulham on Sunday?
body: Gary Neville started for Sky Sports as a pundit and co-commentator in 2011 "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic." Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of the Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham. The players had just laboured through the opening period of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead. "I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?" Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position. This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints. But does that tell the whole story? How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season? And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United? This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism. After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins". He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game. In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints. It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games. So is this down to the running and the effort? Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager. Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games. Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints. There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season. Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners. Then there is the comparison to rival teams. Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches, but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division. Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints. Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough? Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing. The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions. Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side which saw Ralf Rangnick's side trail 1-0 at the break. "They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything. "There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game." Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines. You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw. Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue. But the die was cast. "Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph. "15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star. "United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express. It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece. This video can not be played Carrick impressed Man Utd 'kept belief' to earn draw at Fulham When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight. In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club". Amorim was dismissed the following day. There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era. For example throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation. It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media. But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company. How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief 'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict "When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?" It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast. While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry. After co-founding the sports entertainment production company Buzz16 in 2016, Neville launched YouTube platform 'The Overlap' in 2021. 'The Overlap' produces 'Stick to Football' - one of the UK&#x

title: Scotland's 32 councils could be cut to six under government plan
description: Between six and 10 regional bodies would replace local authorities under proposals submitted by ministers.
body: Scotland's 32 councils could be replaced by as few as six regional authorities under proposals published by the government. Under the reforms, external, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth. They would also be responsible for supporting between 120 and 160 community authorities, which would oversee some local issues. The proposals have been shared with Holyrood's committees and council umbrella body Cosla ahead of a public consultation. Scotland's councils face budget shortfalls. How bad is it in your area? How will Swinney 'rewire' local government and public services? The proposals suggest that the regional bodies would be given powers over larger planning decisions, education and economic development. They would also oversee the delivery of key services such as waste management, cleaning and early learning. The smaller community authorities would contribute to local planning decisions, town centre regeneration, licensing and the historic environment. Separate set-ups for Scotland's islands would also be required, according to the paper. Councillors would be elected to the existing wards across Scotland and serve on both the local and regional authorities. However, the document suggests the increased time commitment may require a boost in pay. The proposals do not outline how the reforms would be financed. Scotland's current council set-up, with 32 local authorities, was introduced by the UK government in 1996. Before then, the country had a two-tier system of nine regional councils and 53 district councils. Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth said: "We need to ensure investment is focused on frontline delivery, with the right staff in the right roles to empower communities and deliver real improvements in public services." She added: "Existing local government responsibilities could also be extended, including enhanced roles in economic development and business support so that individual areas can reflect local strengths and ambitions. "These proposals are intended to provide a starting point to facilitate debate and discussion as we work to deliver reforms that strengthen public services and improve outcomes for the people and communities we serve." Scottish Labour local government spokesman Joe Fagan said: "The Scottish government must not blunder into another reorganisation. "Any reforms must be made in partnership with local government and backed up with fair funding for local services." Earlier this month, First Minister John Swinney announced plans to cut the number of health boards in Scotland from 14 to 2. He described the reforms, designed to cut costs and improve efficiency, as "the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era". Separate plans are also being considered for the three island groups - Shetland, Orkney, and the Western Isles. title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption
description: EasyJet says the latest incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the system.
body: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of how the service works, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic. The technical problem at Prestwick in Ayrshire caused disruption at airports across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, delaying dozens of flights. Nats said a "connectivity issue" was to blame for the disruption, and that it had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights earlier in September. The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects. A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal". According to aviation analytics company Cirium, as of 13:45 BST, at least 200 flights had been cancelled or did not fly on Monday. This includes 100 flights scheduled to arrive in the UK and 99 that were due to depart from the UK. Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 47 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 11 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures. The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation. It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident". Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure". Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership. When asked by BBC Radio 4's World at One programme whether Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?" Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure. Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers. British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing". Airlines criticise air traffic control after second glitch this month causes more disruption A Nats spokesperson apologised for the disruption, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible. "What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority." They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the problems with flights were "deeply frustrating" for passengers. Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot". He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their easyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning. Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled. She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived. Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time". Nicole McCloskey and her daughters have had their flight to Disneyland cancelled This is the second failure at Nats, the company that looks after UK airspace, in less than a fortnight. Not much is known about what happened on this occasion, except that there was a technical failure at Nats' control centre in Prestwick. Nats has two main centres. The first, at Swanwick in Hampshire, looks after airspace in the southern part of the UK, including the approaches to Heathrow and Gatwick. Nats says the latest failure at Prestwick was different - Prestwick in Ayrshire looks after traffic across northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, catering for about 42% of the UK's air traffic. The Swanwick incident last month affected hundreds of thousands of passengers, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas earlier this month. That disruption was much more severe as it affected intercontinental and long-haul travel via UK airspace. Nats said in a report last week that the software glitch happened "in the space of a millisecond" leading to the system producing corrupted data. However, the fact that the UK's air traffic control system has suffered two significant issues in a short space of time has attracted a great deal of criticism, and the pressure on Nats boss Martin Rolfe - who insisted last week he would not resign - is only likely to mount. Rolfe told the BBC at the time he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure". "My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he said.
