title: Two arrested over major fire at Kent hotel
description: A 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were arrested on suspicion of arson, police say.
body: The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement Two people have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire at a seaside hotel which led to hundreds of people being evacuated. Kent Police said a 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were held after the blaze at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone on Saturday. The fire broke out at the hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours and about 280 people were evacuated from the building. A total of 90 people were relocated from neighbouring Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said. The pair who were arrested have been released while inquiries continue, a police spokesperson said. Police say road closures remain in place for investigation work following the blaze, which started at about 01:20 BST. The blaze is being treated as suspicious and police are appealing for witnesses. Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said at the weekend it was fully cooperating with police and supporting the investigation. The group said engineers and building inspectors had been at the site to carry out structural assessments, and its team was working to assist guests. Twenty six fire engines were sent to the hotel and Kent Fire and Rescue Service said it was believed the fire had started in the basement of the building. The council has been working to arrange alternative housing for affected residents while the hotel undergoes assessments and any required works to make it safe. Kent Police said the fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel was being treated as suspicious On Saturday, a welfare centre was set up for hotel residents. Other businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected. Ross Honeycombe, who was staying at the hotel with his family, described how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00, adding: "We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. "Later we started hearing explosions." A resident at Pavilion Court, John Dighton, said he "grabbed stuff for a couple of days" and was staying at a nearby hotel. He said the worst thing was not knowing how long they would be away from their homes. title: Council leader found guilty of fraud and tax evasion
description: Jason Zadrozny, leader of Ashfield District Council in Nottinghamshire, is convicted of 13 offences.
body: Jason Zadrozny was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion Ashfield District Council leader Jason Zadrozny has been found guilty of fraud and tax evasion. Zadrozny, of Stanton Hill, was accused of setting up a fake heritage group to defraud Nottinghamshire County Council out of thousands of pounds. Prosecutors also alleged he failed to pay tax on four rental properties. The 46-year-old, who served as an Ashfield Independents councillor on the county council, was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and four counts of tax evasion. The verdicts came after a jury at Northampton Crown Court had deliberated for nearly 11 hours. Zadrozny was told by the judge he will be sentenced on 27 November, and was "at risk of an immediate custodial sentence". Thanking jury members for their "care and attention" during the trial, judge David Herbert KC added the council leader would be given unconditional bail until his sentencing hearing. Zadrozny denied any wrongdoing at Northampton Crown Court During the trial, jurors were told Zadrozny had set up the Ashfield Heritage Society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council, which he then transferred into his personal account. This included £7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny - who was a county councillor at the time - claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield". The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March. Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends. They said the fraud came to light in March 2021, when Catherine Mason, who was hoping to stand for election in Ashfield, was looking into the council's expenditure and investigated the setting up of the heritage society. The county council launched an investigation and subsequently passed the details on to the police. Zadrozny denied the offences and told the trial all the funds he had received were spent on the community. He told jurors he gave the cash from the Ashfield Heritage Society to Tony Brewer - a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020 - to carry out the repair and maintenance of war memorials in the area. The defendant told jurors his paperwork for funding applications was "terrible", adding: "I wouldn't be sitting in the dock if I filled it out much more clearly." He also said the wrong address on the application form for the heritage society was "clearly an error" and he cannot remember why he wrote it down. Jurors found him not guilty of three of the 12 counts of fraud. Addressing Zadrozny, the judge said: "You have been convicted by the jury. Please understand in my mind is an immediate custodial sentence, given the nature of these offences. The breach of trust element makes them particularly serious. "Please don't think because the sentencing is not today that it won't be an immediate custodial sentence." A spokesperson for Ashfield District Council said the authority was aware of the verdict. "The council will now follow the appropriate legal and democratic processes," they said. "We will continue to deliver our services and undertake our responsibilities for residents, businesses and communities." title: Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'
description: The chancellor has come under increasing pressure after resounding state election defeats, but says the results "go far beyond my own person"
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections. "We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing even to reach the threshold to stay in the state parliament. Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains. Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-left CDU. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged. Merz said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats. "I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me." "We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world." There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings. Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave." This video can not be played AfD co-leader Alice Weidel predicts Friedrich Merz will be out of government soon The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster". While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it was far short of a majority and is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it. Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition. title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
description: The BBC's Frank Gardner speaks to some of those who have fled the war by crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti
body: This video can not be played Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. "How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised UN-recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. "We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. "What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically. "It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. "Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first,

title: Driver, 20, jailed after dashcam filmed 'horrific' head-on crash which left victim with PTSD
description: Martin Howells was left unable to work for 10 months after Ethan Loveridge crashed into him.
body: This video can not be played Head on collision captured on dash cam A 20-year-old man who lost control of his car and crashed head-on into another driver has been jailed. Ethan Loveridge, from Llanbradach, Caerphilly county, seriously injured Martin Howells in the "horrific" crash in August 2024. Howells, 50, suffered suffered eight broken ribs, a broken nose, a detached bicep, injury to his left shoulder and a rotator cuff, and nerve damage to his neck and shoulder. He was off work for 10 months. Dashcam footage showed Loveridge's Kia Sorento clip another car on the A468 in Caerphilly before hitting Howells' car. At Newport Crown Court, Loveridge admitted causing serious injury by dangerous driving and a string of drugs offences and jailed for five years. "It was a horrific crash that has changed my life forever," Howells said. Loveridge's car ended up on its side, while Howells remained injured inside his vehicle as passers-by attempted to help him. In a victim personal statement read to the jury, Paul Hewitt, prosecuting, said: "It was a horrific crash and it changed my life forever. "I had 18 months of physical therapy. "My injuries left me with weakness in my arms and I am unable to lift anything above shoulder height, which I will live with for the rest of my life." He said difficulties with his fingers had prevented him from playing guitar, which he described as something he loved. "I have been diagnosed with PTSD and underwent eight months of psychological therapy," he said. Howells said his grandson was born six weeks after the crash, but he was unable to fully enjoy his arrival because of his injuries. He said he was unable to sleep properly and would wake during the night thinking about what could have happened. Ethan Loveridge pleaded guilty to multiple charges Loveridge was also sentenced for drug offences after he and his then partner Elise Humphreys, 21, were stopped in a Ford Mondeo on 26 June 2025. They were seen discarding items from the car and a search found cannabis and cash. Their phones were seized and messages revealed they had been involved in supplying cocaine and cannabis for six months. A search of Loveridge's property found 810g of cannabis worth £8,000. Loveridge later pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, possession with intent to supply a class B drug, being concerned in the supply of class A and B drugs, and possession of criminal property. Recorder John Philpotts said: "You are well aware of the potential consequences of a head on collision of the sort you caused. "In fact you are fortunate there was no fatality in this case." Humphreys was given a 12-month community order, a 15-day rehabilitation activity requirement and a six-month trail monitoring requirement. Loveridge was sentenced to five years in prison and disqualified from driving for four years. title: Millions urged to evacuate as powerful Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
description: The country's meteorological agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life," but this has now been downgraded in most areas.
body: Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures. Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several warnings have now been downgraded, with the danger to life warning remaining in place in Oshima Town. Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended. Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h. It is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms. Pedestrians caught in the rain at the Shibuya crossing in Tokyo The level three warnings, for heavy rain, and the level four warnings, for landslides have now been either downgraded or lifted by the Japan Meteorological Agency in most areas. The level four warnings remain in Shinagawa Ward, Toshima Village, and Niijima Village. Authorities have advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, has hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events. Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival have been cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, has also cancelled Monday's programme. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has reportedly delayed her trip to the United States this week to monitor the effects of the typhoon. She had been due in New York on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump and speak at the UN General Assembly. Passengers waiting for updates at Haneda Airport The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman who lived in the house, aged in her 60s, may have been swept away and is believed to have been buried alive. Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site. The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital. Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture said they received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide. A woman struggles with her umbrella outside Shinjuku station Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions. As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall. A satellite view shows Typhoon Dujuan approaching Japan This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor. El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit. Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example. The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday. title: Cate Blanchett asks theatre audience to stop filming during show
description: The A-list actress is the latest star to ask fans to put their phones away during performances.
body: The actress is appearing at London's National Theatre in Electra/Persona A-list actress Cate Blanchett has become the latest star to make a plea for theatre audiences to put their phones away during performances. The Australian film and stage actor and producer was appearing at London's National Theatre in Electra/Persona. During the curtain call on Friday, Blanchett said: "There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present. "I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way – but for anyone who is filming the show, please don't, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much." The two-time Oscar winner's words were greeted with cheers and clapping from the audience. One audience member explained what had happened earlier in the performance, saying that the filming took place between two acts: "I was there on Friday, so just to clarify what happened: after the first act, while they were changing and preparing for the second, latecomers were being let in, the staff were cleaning the stage, and the cast were doing their makeup on stage. "Cate noticed someone recording during that break. She came towards the front of the stage and gestured "no, no, no" with her finger for them to stop. She also mentioned it to the audience at the very end before they left," the theatre-goer wrote on Instagram, external. "The person wasn't filming the actual performance, but the interval between the two acts while the cast were still on stage. To be fair, people do this quite often and the staff usually don't say anything. It was my third time seeing the play, and I've seen people film during that break every time. Friday was simply the first time I saw Cate notice it herself, just after she had finished doing her makeup." Electra/Persona is a new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman's film Persona. The play, which is on until 10 October, sees Blanchett sharing the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma with her co-star Nina Hoss, determined by a coin toss live on stage every night ahead of each performance. Rosamund Pike calls out audience member for texting during show Loud eaters and phones nearly spoiled my cinema trip - and it's not just me Actors rage at World Cup fans on phones Many theatres, like cinemas, ask audiences to switch off their mobile phones during performances. Rosamund Pike called out an audience member for texting during an emotional moment from her performance in West End play Inter Alia earlier this year, saying: "When I feel that and see it, it's hard." Cynthia Erivo interrupted her recent performance of Dracula after spotting an audience member filming. And Andrew Scott halted his "to be or not to be" soliloquy in Hamlet, a few years back, after someone started using a laptop. Other stars including Daniel Craig, Hugh Jackman and Patti LuPone have all made similar criticisms, while Lesley Manville told BBC Radio 4 earlier this year that she found it "insulting" when punters took photos, even of curtain calls. title: Man guilty of murdering partner in frenzied flat attack
description: Alexander Brennan, 54, killed Brodie MacGregor, 23, at her flat in Glasgow's Springburn on 26 August 2024.
body: Brodie MacGregor was found dead in her home on Elmvale Street in Springburn on 26 August 2024 A man who attacked his partner with broken glass bottles has been found guilty of murder. Alexander Brennan, 54, killed Brodie MacGregor, 23, at her flat in Glasgow's Springburn on 26 August 2024. A post-mortem examination found MacGregor suffered a total of 78 injuries to her head and body after she was repeatedly punched, slapped and struck with glass bottles and a microwave plate. Brennan was convicted and jailed for a minimum of 22 years following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. This story contains details which some readers may find distressing. Judge Lord Scott told the killer he had left a child without a mother. He said: "You brutally murdered a woman who offered no serious physical threat to you. "A doctor described her injuries as ones seen in high velocity impacts or falling from a building. "As she lay there for around an hour, conscious or unconscious, you took no steps to seek medical assistance which would have offered a slight chance that she would survive. "You showed complete disregard to whether she lived or died." The judge told Brennan he had showed 'complete disregard' for MacGregor The court previously heard Brennan had fallen out with MacGregor when he travelled from Stirling to her home in Glasgow, at about 01:35 on the day of the murder. MacGregor dialled 999 at about 04:35, where she was heard to say on the call: "You attacked me". Officers showed up at the property but MacGregor told them the call was a mistake and she was safe in Brennan's company. CCTV later showed the pair separately leaving the flat and walking in the surrounding area before returning. About 09:41, footage showed Brennan putting his blood stained trousers in a clothing bin near MacGregor's flat. He called 999 at about 09:55 and told the call handler he did not think MacGregor was breathing. Brennan did not respond to the handler when he was asked what happened. Emergency services arrived at the scene and the door lock was forced open. Witnesses found MacGregor lying face down on the living room floor, surrounded by fragments of broken glass bottles. Det Sgt David White told the court: "It looks like her mouth has been severed completely. "Her face more or less was hanging off." The court heard there was blood in the living room, including on the ceiling. White added: "This was one that stood out for me and will stay with me forever." MacGregor was pronounced dead at the scene at 10:15. After the attack, Brennan got on a train to Camelon, in the Falkirk area, where he visited the home of friend Robert McCallum. McCallum's then partner Tina Marie Hatton, 46, told jurors Brennan had "blood all over him" and she cleaned him up. When she asked what had happened Brennan replied he "couldn't stop" and he was "done". Hatton added he had injuries to his hands and above his eyebrow. The blood stained jumper was seized from a washing machine and the trousers were recovered from the clothing bin. The blood on the garments was found to have come from MacGregor. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Dr Julie McAdam, 54, told the court MacGregor's cause of death was "extensive facial injuries" She said a post-mortem examination found the victim had suffered a series of "blunt force injuries, bruises, abrasions and lacerations". MacGregor was described as having two "bilateral black eyes", which McAdam said was seen in "high velocity injuries, people in road traffic injuries or seriously assaulted". The trial was also told MacGregor had swallowed a lot of blood which filled her lungs and airways. McAdam added MacGregor would have been alive for an hour after suffering her injuries and could have survived had medical assistance been sought sooner. Brian McConnachie KC, defending, stated after the verdict: "As far as events are concerned, he has very little recollection. "As I understand it, he has some recollection of an argument taking place but has unable through proceedings to accept total responsibility for what took place." It was revealed that Brennan has previous convictions for assaults which include to injury. Det Supt Lynsey Watters said: "My thoughts remain with Brodie's family and friends as they continue to come to terms with what happened. "No verdict can bring her back, but I hope this sentence will bring them come comfort. "Brennan now faces the consequences of his reprehensible actions." She added violence against women and girls was "an absolute priority" for Police Scotland. title: Celtic can't sack manager O'Neill, says Lambert
description: Martin O'Neill leaving Celtic would not surprise Paul Lambert, but the former club captain would be "shocked and disappointed" if the veteran manager was to be sacked.
body: While Celtic are two points clear at the top of the Premiership, Martin O'Neill has said he will consider his future Martin O'Neill leaving Celtic would not surprise Paul Lambert, but the former club captain would be "shocked and disappointed" if the manager was to be sacked. The 74-year-old said he would use the international break to take stock following back-to-back defeats by Rangers. Those Old Firm setbacks came either side of a home loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League, while there was a shock Champions League collapse to LASK in August, with a 4-0 aggregate lead surrendered. "I will reflect on the games," said O'Neill, who was made permanent manager for a second time in the summer after two stints as interim boss last season resulted in a league and Scottish Cup double. O'Neill, who won another seven trophies with Celtic from 2000-05, when Lambert was playing, added: "I'm not immune from criticism. Absolutely and utterly far from it. "I think there's every reason to ask 'can you turn this round? Can you change the whole thing?' I have to kind of look at the bigger picture at this minute." Lambert insists O'Neill is Celtic's best manager since the great Jock Stein, but the 57-year-old added: "It wouldn't surprise me if he left. I don't think he needs it. "I'd be shocked and disappointed if Celtic sacked him. "I think they give him the option, if that's what's on his mind, if he did want to walk away. "He's got enough credit in the bank. It wasn't that long ago people were shouting for a statue for him, so I don't think you can go from one extreme to the other. "If he wants to go, then he goes himself." 'It might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill ponders Celtic future after defeat Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost O'Neill steadied the Celtic ship twice last term following the departures of Brendan Rodgers and Wilfried Nancy. "They were hanging on by a thread and he turned that around," is how former Ipswich Town and Norwich City manager Lambert described the impact of his former boss. "There was only one person who could rescue Celtic last season and he did that. "I'd bet any money that he hasn't changed anything from how he was then." Lambert was critical of individual performances in the defeats by Rangers as well as the remarks of defender Cameron Carter-Vickers, who spoke of playing "too random" and "getting a script and sticking to it". "The players need to take responsibility," he told BBC Radio Scotland. "I watched the game and dear oh dear... "That was cringeworthy, the stuff from Carter-Vickers. I thought 'hang on, you're not making a movie'. "Solve the problem yourselves. When something is not going right, you look to rectify it, you don't look to a manager to say 'do this or do that'. "I thought that was bang out of order, coming from someone who's been a decent player for Celtic." title: Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay
description: The ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her.
body: This video can not be played In an interview with CBS, the BBC's US news partner, Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths. Clancy also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children. The Clancy trial was declared a mistrial earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict. Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay. title: How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut?
description: Sebastien Pocognoli's faces his first test as Scotland head coach against Slovenia on Saturday, but how are his squad shaping up for his debut?
body: Billy Gilmour (left) scored for Napoli against Fiorentina Sometimes luck can be the difference between success and failure as a manager and Sebastien Pocognoli appears to have it with him for his first Scotland squad - at least before a ball is kicked. Scott McTominay was obviously a notable miss from the new head coach's original selection, the 29-year-old Napoli midfielder having to undergo what he described as minor heart surgery that should only keep him sidelined for a few weeks. Rangers' Lawrence Shankland and Torino's Che Adams are also absentees from the frontline options through injury. But, of the 28 players named in Pocognoli's extended squad for Scotland's opening four Nations League fixtures, none have so far pulled out through injury. So how are they shaping up after their latest round of club games? Pocognoli Facetime helps Miller over summer of discontent Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate Scottish Football Podcast: Belief is back for Rangers as Celtic in turmoil The goalkeeping position was a problem for some time under predecessor Steve Clarke, exacerbated by 84-cap Craig Gordon coming to the end of his career and with playing time often limited for the alternatives. But current first-choice Angus Gunn is now a regular starter with San Jose Earthquakes after his summer switch from Nottingham Forest. Scott Bain is also performing well for Falkirk, while Jon McCracken has helped Bradford City to the top of League One after his move from Dundee, making Rangers' Liam Kelly the only goalkeeper not playing for his club. The absence of Shankland and Adams gave Pocognoli the opportunity to bring in some fresh blood among the forwards, and the recalled Oli McBurnie continues to start for Hull City on their return to the Premier League. Meanwhile, Robbie Ure was back in the starting line-up for new club Sevilla as they lost 3-1 to La Liga leaders Barcelona on Saturday, while James Wilson has cemented a first-team place since returning to Heart of Midlothian from his loan to Tottenham Hotspur. In saying that, striker Kieron Bowie and wingers Findlay Curtis and Ben Gannon-Doak had to make do with being substitutes over the weekend for Sassuolo, Rangers and Bournemouth respectively. John McGinn (centre) set up Aston Villa's third goal against Tottenham Hotspur While 20-year-old Gannon-Doak's continued lack of minutes is not ideal considering he has proved to be a key provider of pace to Scotland's play, club-mate Ryan Christie will have received a boost by being handed only his second start of the season, albeit the midfielder came off after 75 minutes of a 1-0 home defeat by Liverpool. Indeed, all seven of Pocognoli's central midfield options started at the weekend. That includes Lennon Miller in Udinese's 1-0 home defeat by Cagliari. Also in Serie A, Billy Gilmour scored only his second senior goal with a fine strike in Napoli's 1-1 draw at Fiorentina, as well as being named man of the match. Meanwhile, Lewis Ferguson is back starting every game as Bologna captain, including their 1-1 draw with Torino. For visitors Torino, Nathan Patterson made his second appearance as a substitute since his loan move from Everton as right-back continues to be a problem area for Scotland. Aaron Hickey also had to make do with coming off the bench in Brentford's fine 3-0 win over Chelsea. Colby Donovan did start again for Celtic, albeit as the Scottish champions suffered a third straight defeat, while all three left-backs - Donovan's club-mate Kieran Tierney, Tottenham Hotspur's Andy Robertson and Sassuolo's Josh Doig suffered losses after starting. Only Scott McKenna - an unused sub as Croatian league leaders Dinamo Zagreb beat Lokomotiva - did not play in his club side's latest game among Pocognoli's defensive options. With Gilmour the only weekend goalscorer and Robertson and Aston Villa midfielder John McGinn providing an assist each in Spurs' 3-2 defeat, Pocognoli could look to that experienced trio to provide the creative spark for the Nations League matches starting away to Slovenia on Saturday. title: Best not to underestimate us - GB plan BJK Cup upset against all-star Czechs
description: Great Britain face the Czech Republic at the Billie Jean King Cup Finals on Tuesday - and know full well the size of the challenge facing them.
body: Great Britain play the Czech Republic in the BJK Cup on Tuesday from 10:00 BST - live on the BBC "It's best not to underestimate us," says a defiant Harriet Dart. But Great Britain's Billie Jean King Cup squad know full well the enormity of the challenge that awaits them. On Tuesday, the tight-knit British team - Dart, Katie Boulter, Sonay Kartal, Mika Stojsavljevic and Jodie Burrage - take on the Czech Republic in their BJK Cup quarter-final in Shenzhen, China. GB have reached the semi-finals in three of the past four seasons, but in the Czechs they face the 11-time champions and an eye-watering line-up - the only team boasting two top-10 players at the Finals tournament. In Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova, they have the current Wimbledon champion and her beaten opponent from this summer's all-Czech final. While Marie Bouzkova has not yet hit such heights in reaching a major final, the 28-year-old has won two WTA titles this year, including on the Nottingham grass, and team-mate Sara Bejlek, 20, has enjoyed a breakthrough season featuring a first title and victories against the likes of Aryna Sabalenka and Madison Keys. In doubles, Bouzkova and Noskova teamed up to triumph in Cincinnati in August, though Katerina Siniakova is likely to feature in the BJK Cup as the current top-ranked women's doubles player with 12 Grand Slams to her name. All five members of the Czech team are ranked higher in the singles rankings than any of the British squad. "I think naturally we are definite underdogs," Boulter, the current world number 54, told BBC Sport. "We are the ones that are going to have to make something happen, something special. But that being said, a lot of pressure is on them, and we've seen in this tournament before that people can make upsets, and I think that's what we'll be looking to do. "I think we have no pressure ourselves, and we're just going to go out there with no expectations." The tie will be shown on the BBC Sport website and app and on BBC iPlayer, with coverage beginning from 10:00 BST. Billie Jean King Cup: Czech Republic v Great Britain Coverage from 10:00 BST on BBC Sport website and app and BBC iPlayer By her own reckoning, the 2026 season has brought "an improvement" for Boulter, winning her fourth WTA title in Ostrava and beating new world number one Elena Rybakina at Queen's in a year in which the Kazakh won the Australian and US Open crowns. But the British number one has repeatedly come unstuck against Czech players. Boulter lost 6-3 7-5 to Muchova in Miami back in March but fell to a more emphatic defeat to her in the US Open second round earlier this month, winning just one game in a "bad day at the office". She faced Noskova in Cincinnati in August and lost 6-3 6-3, but Boulter can take confidence from the fact she beat the Czech in straight sets in Osaka in October 2025. "They are both incredible players, both extremely good at what they do," Boulter, 30, said. "They have been in places that I've never been before. So I think for me, it's about taking it to them. "Their base level is so high, you can't play the same way that you would normally play if you were to play someone ranked a lot lower. "I think you have to give them respect, but also play the ball that's coming at you at the same time. That's my challenge, to focus on the ball coming at me and try and impose my own game. "I think there are ways I'm going to try and win points, and that's through what I'm doing, not what they're doing." Dart, who lost 6-2 6-2 to Bouzkova in the US Open second round, said: "I think even though the match-up on paper here is pretty rough for us, at the same time I know how well this team can play. "We have strong belief within ourselves and within our own team that we can do well in this competition." Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter return to the GB squad having missed the win over Australia in April Great Britain qualified for Shenzhen - their fourth BJK Cup Finals in five years - by shocking Australia in Melbourne in April. Boulter and Kartal were among a list of absentees from that squad - including Emma Raducanu, who is again missing through injury - but the pair's return to the line-up strengthens captain Anne Keothavong's side. Should they pull off an upset and beat the Czechs, GB would next play the winner of the quarter-final between Kazakhstan - who are without Rybakina - and Spain on Friday. "I think pressure is a privilege, isn't it? I think whoever you're drawn against in this competition, particularly when you've made it through to the Finals, there are no easy matches," said Keothavong. "We've seen over the years how people are able to rise to the occasion when they represent their nation. I've seen it from the players here beside me. title: Katya Adler: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
description: Political shifts in Germany are being watched closely in Europe and beyond, Katya Adler writes.
body: The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeats Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker. The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them. The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield. At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems. He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament. Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist. The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past. The AfD, led by Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, has surged in national opinion polls The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want. Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party. The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets. High time for political change, says the AfD. Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party. I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted. Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed. He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required. This video can not be played Why Merz is staying on as German chancellor after election 'disaster' But German patience is running thin. Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future. Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people. Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive". Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect. Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy. As the AfD squeezes the CDU on the right, the left wing Die Linke party attracts voters elsewhere Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget. When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable. Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example. This comes

title: How will clubs train during three-week international break?
description: BBC Sport looks at how clubs are planning to deal with the extended three-week international break.
body: Keith Andrews will give his remaining Brentford players the week off before they return to the training ground on Saturday The first international break of the season is under way - and this one is longer than fans will have become accustomed to. For the first time, the Premier League and the Championship will come to a halt for three weeks rather than the usual two. Football fans tend not to love international breaks, but this change has been done with good intentions. It merges the four games played in the old September and October breaks into one slot. So the domestic game stops for three weeks, rather than four weeks across two windows. Club football is actually getting a week back. But for players not on international duty, three weeks is a long time for finely tuned athletes not to play competitively. So how are clubs going to deal with this change? Here's how different teams plan to balance the international break. Most squads in the Premier League these days are packed with international players, and Brentford are no different. Most of the Bees' squad are away, with about 12 players - including Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago - left at their training facility, including five who are coming back from injury. Brentford have a longer break than almost every other team, given they hosted Chelsea on Friday evening. Boss Keith Andrews has given his first-team players a week off with individual training programmes to follow. Those players will not have restrictions on leaving the country, but it is unlikely long-haul flights would be sanctioned. The squad will reconvene on Saturday, 26 September to begin training again, before playing a behind-closed-doors game against another English club on the weekend of 3 October. That friendly could potentially give the likes of Nathan Collins and Sepp van den Berg a chance to return to action, with the rest of the squad made up of under-21 players. The second international break will look very different, with the Bees playing Brighton on Sunday, 8 November and back in action against Everton on Saturday, 21 November. Players may be given the odd day off, but in general it will be a normal training programme with no friendly before the usual preparation for the fixture against the Toffees. Liverpool, meanwhile, will carry on training with the small number of players that remain, with a few days off. Manager Andoni Iraola says he will be left with "no more than three days probably to prepare" for the home game with Manchester City on 11 October. Aston Villa have a very different international break planned. Unai Emery will return to former club Sevilla, where he won the Europa League three times on the bounce. Sevilla and Villa will face off in the 15th edition of the Antonio Puerta Trophy on Friday, 2 October. The game is played in memory of the 22-year-old Sevilla wing-back, who died on 28 August 2007 after having multiple cardiac arrests on the pitch during a La Liga game against Getafe. Tony Mowbray was appointed Blackburn Rovers manager for a second time in June While Premier League teams see their squads decimated by international call-ups, it is not quite as dramatic in the Championship. Many clubs will only have a handful, such as Blackburn Rovers with just four call-ups. For Rovers boss Tony Mowbray this break will be a positive for a couple of reasons. Mowbray has had to contend with an injury crisis in the early part of the season, with more than 10 players ruled out in the opening weeks. The break gives Rovers the chance to ease some of those players back into action, such as Gady Beyuku and Moussa Baradji who recently made their comebacks, and others close to a return like Scott Wharton. After the trip to Portsmouth on Saturday, Rovers headed back to Lancashire and will have a few days on the training ground this week. After such a busy start to the campaign, with league fixtures and the Carabao Cup, it also gives Mowbray - who returned to the club in the summer - a chance to properly work with his players. But it will not all be training. Mowbray intends to give the players a few days off from the end of the week. Players such as Yuri Ribeiro will be able to return home to Portugal, if they so wish. The cycle will then be repeated the following week, training the first half with a short break over the weekend. Then for week three, it is back to the usual pre-match routine before the home game against Cardiff. Mowbray is also looking to find a Premier League or League One team to play in a behind-closed-doors friendly. It will help those returning from injury to get minutes in the bank, and keep other members of the squad ticking over. In the two-week break in November, players may still get a short spell off while matches are more likely to be in-house affairs with teams made up of senior and under-21 players. The three-week international break might have posed a unique situation for a couple of clubs, whereby they could have a full squad and no games to play. League One carries on playing unless clubs get three call-ups which meet the EFL's criteria, then a postponement can be requested. Only four of the 12 matches have survived on each of the two weekends. Yet many clubs prepared in advance by scheduling Football League Trophy fixtures during these three weeks. Clubs tend to rotate in this competition anyway, so the games still go ahead even if league games are postponed. Twelve teams will play two trophy ties, with 10 clubs playing once. That left just Leyton Orient and Reading at risk at not having a game to play. Both have only had one league match called off, so will not have all three weeks vacant. title: Fourteen people linked to evidential activity at time of Omagh bomb, inquiry told
description: Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles.
body: The bombing exploded during a busy Saturday in Omagh, County Tyrone in 1998 Fourteen people have been linked to evidential activity in the days leading up to and on the day of the Omagh bombing, the inquiry into the explosion has heard. Twenty-nine people, including a woman pregnant with twins, died in the bombing in the County Tyrone town on 15 August 1998 - the biggest single atrocity in the Troubles. It came less than three months after the people of Northern Ireland had voted yes to the Good Friday Agreement. The inquiry, which opened last year with 14 days of testimony from bereaved families and survivors, was established to determine if the bombing could have been prevented by UK state authorities. Paul Greaney KC outlined the "working hypothesis" of the inquiry when it resumed its latest phase on Monday. In 2009, a judge ruled that four men - Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all liable for the Omagh bomb. A fifth man, Seamus McKenna, was acquitted in the civil action and later died in a roofing accident in 2013. In a statement to the inquiry, sitting at Bradford Court in Belfast, Greaney named McKenna, Daly and Murphy as among the 14 people linked to evidential activity. Greaney told the inquiry: "The evidence suggests Colm Murphy sat like a spider in the centre of the web of the plan to detonate a bomb in Omagh." Referring to the civil case, Greaney said that the fact that McKenna "was not found liable is not an outcome which binds this inquiry". "Our working hypothesis is that, contrary to that finding, he played a key role," he said. The use of telecommunications is a key part of the evidence in front of the inquiry and some of the most frequently referred to mobile phones have been assigned colours for ease of following their links. The inquiry heard how it was "likely" that the Vauxhall Cavalier car used in the bombing was "stolen to order" in the days before the bombing. Evidence was outlined that on 14 August 1998, the day before the bombing, a "test run" of the journey to the bomb site was carried out in a Volkswagen Golf car. This video can not be played The principal objective of this chapter of the inquiry is to understand how the bombing was carried out and by whom. Among the witnesses this week will be a senior garda officer who is expected to provide initial evidence about the theft of the car used in the explosion. It was stolen in Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, two days before the explosion. The inquiry was established to determine if the bombing could have been prevented by UK state authorities. The third phase is expected to last about four weeks. The Omagh bomb exploded on 15 August 1998, killing 29 people including a woman pregnant with twins. More than 200 people were injured in the blast. No-one has ever been convicted of the atrocity. The bomb devastated Omagh town centre in August 1998 Three days after the attack, the Real IRA released a statement claiming responsibility for the explosion. It apologised to "civilian" victims and said its targets had been commercial. No-one has been convicted of carrying out the murders by a criminal court. In 2009, Michael McKevitt, Liam Campbell, Colm Murphy and Seamus Daly were all ordered to pay a total of £1.6m in damages to the relatives, but appeals against the ruling delayed the compensation process. title: Google hit with €403m fine by Irish data watchdog over GDPR violations
description: The penalty follows an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations.
body: Google say they have improved data protection practices in recent years Google has been fined €403m (£345m) by the Republic of Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) over its handling of location data. The penalty - one of the largest of its kind imposed by the Irish watchdog authority - followed an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations. On Monday the DPC said its investigation found Google had processed data in a manner that was not "lawful", "fair" or "transparent". The inquiry concerned Google's processing of location data in three specific features - Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy between 25 May 2018 to 4 February 2020. Location data is any kind of data which can be used to infer a person's location. It can "reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private", said DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle in a statement released on Monday. The report said Google's practices "infringed" General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) - legislation that came into effect on 25 May, 2018, creating strict data privacy and security law within the European Union (EU). Doyle added: "The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA (European Economic Area), and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner." He continued: "As a result of Google's failures... individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data. "The retention of users' location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control." In addition to being fined, Google has also been ordered to bring its data processing into compliance within six months. In a statement, Google said: "This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we've significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple." They also said they have made data protection improvements in recent years, including "industry-first auto-delete controls", which enables all users to "set your account to automatically delete your data on a rolling three, 18, or 36-month basis". Other measures to safeguard personal data have also been introduced, they said, such as "simple ads management", which allows you "to turn off personalized ads entirely", and "increased transparency", including "consolidated detailed information about our location data practices and account settings". title: Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate
description: Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is being investigated over an issue with his Covid-19 vaccination certificate.
body: Granit Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate. The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad. The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate. The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty". He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way. "Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry. "I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities." The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one. These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad. The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement. It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window. Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October. Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday. "It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good." Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina. title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
description: Visitors stopping to take pictures of the 68m medieval embroidery were holding up others, prompting the rule change.
body: The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work. Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition. The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction. But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors. A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible. "In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry." The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027. British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux. The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries. Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government. The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London. Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses. Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October. Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum. title: 'Other generations just buried it' - Youths share their mental health concerns
description: The BBC's Catherine Burns spoke to some young mental health ambassadors who called for an increase in mental health support.
body: This video can not be played Accusations that those growing up today are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has said. Prof Peter Fonagy told the BBC that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common. His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off". The BBC's Catherine Burns spoke to some young mental health ambassadors who echoed the report's findings and called for an increase in mental health support. title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
description: A report says the attacks, of which there have been at least 68, were not self-defence.
body: The report comes two days after the US military released these pictures of an attack on alleged traffickers in the Caribbean A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity. The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people. Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law. The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video. But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law". "There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded. BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people". The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September. However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking. Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted. However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year. Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election. title: Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac buy historic Wrexham football pub
description: The Turf is a regular feature on the Welcome to Wrexham Disney documentary series.
body: Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought The Turf pub to "protect its future" Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought the pub next door to the football club's Racecourse home ground to "protect the future of the club". Wrexham AFC was founded at the then-named Turf Hotel in October 1864 and is the oldest football club in Wales. A club statement announcing the purchase from Admiral Taverns said it hoped to "help protect the historic pub" by "incorporating the club, the Racecourse Ground and The Turf under a single ownership". The pub and its landlord, Wayne Jones, have become regular features on the award-winning "Welcome to Wrexham" Disney documentary series, and Jones described the buy as "great news for all Wrexham fans". Celebrities have been spotted visiting The Turf since Reynolds and Mac took over the club in 2021, including Paul Rudd, Channing Tatum and Will Ferrell. Prince William even pulled a pint behind the bar with Mac to mark St David's Day in 2024. This video can not be played Prince William pulled a pint at the Turf pub alongside Rob Mac The club statement continued: "The acquisition allows for the preservation of the history and traditions of the historic public house that is inexorably linked to the Racecourse Ground and Wrexham AFC Football Club since its foundation in 1864. "This will include opportunities to enhance the current fan zone and other fan-related activities in the area next to The Turf on the Mold Road. "The acquisition of The Turf is a continuation of the strategy to protect the future of the club and its interests by ring fencing key areas related to the life of the club." Channing Tatum and Ryan Reynolds dropped by the Deadpool sculpture at the Turf pub in Febuary last year "The Turf Tavern, as it was then, predates the club and records suggest that the club itself was founded in the pub," said Jones, who has been landlord of The Turf for the past 20 years." "It has played a key part of the club's history ever since, with the players changing in the pub before running out onto the Racecourse Ground as recently as the 1940s. "It continues to be a focal point for fans on matchdays and non-matchdays," Jones added. Jones will continue running the pub as part of the purchase deal, and said he was looking forward to bringing its "unique mix of history, atmosphere and sometimes Hollywood stardust" to the next generation of Wrexham fans and locals alike. The club said the purchase of The Turf pub will allow for "further investment into the fan experience in and around matchdays" The Racecourse Ground staged its first Wales fixture in March 1877 and is the world's oldest football stadium still hosting international matches. Eric Allyn, on behalf of minority investors the Allyn family, said: "Ever since we invested in Wrexham AFC through Red Dragon Ventures in 2024, the town, the community and the football club have become a second home. "By bringing The Turf into the group, we are securing the long-term future of the pub and with it preserving its history and that of the club." title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
description: The US media outlets say they are defending "the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".
body: Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House. President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the three organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his government. The companies said their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized when attempting to access the building on Saturday. In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes". The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the CNN, Politico and MS NOW statement continued. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." BBC News has asked the White House for comment. Announcing the ban last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years". The US president added that there "may be others to join them". When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news." CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally slated to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday. But the pool slot has remained vacant and instead the staunchly conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on the trip. The pool acts as a representative for the media, sharing material with other outlets to save on finance and space when covering presidential events. In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the BBC. Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.
