title: Chiefs back in business as star QBs go down - five things from NFL week two
description: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs look back to their best but Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels suffer serious injuries. Here's what you need to know from week two in the NFL.
body: Caleb Williams (l) and Jayden Daniels (r) suffered serious injuries while Patrick Mahomes looked back to his best in week two After a feast of points in week one, defences hit back in week two of the NFL. The Chicago Bears came crashing back down to earth after a flying start - and they suffered one of the two worrying injuries to two of the league's top young quarterbacks. The Kansas City Chiefs were back doing what they do best but the Baltimore Ravens were surprisingly beaten, while two games were settled in overtime and one decided with just nine seconds on the clock. Here's our pick from Sunday's week two action. Allen stars as Bills open new stadium in style The Chicago Bears hope Caleb Williams' hamstring injury is not as bad as first feared The Chicago Bears scored 59 points last week but just three this time in an ugly 9-3 home loss to the Vikings, as Minnesota won their seventh straight game at Soldier Field. The 56-point drop-off is the second most in NFL history as the Bears saw two touchdowns lost with a dropped catch and a fumble, had a field goal blocked but worst of all lost their star quarterback Caleb Williams. The first pick of the 2024 draft was carried off the field in the fourth quarter looking in serious pain, but initial reports are that his hamstring injury may not be as serious as first feared. Jayden Daniels was the second pick of that 2024 draft behind Williams and he left Washington's defeat at Dallas with a serious injury to the same elbow he dislocated last season. Daniels, who seems certain to be out for some time, would still have struggled to keep up with Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott who threw four touchdowns in their 37-20 victory. Prescott surpassed Tony Romo's team record of 248 touchdown passes by taking his tally to 249. Patrick Mahomes showed no signs of his surgically repaired knee troubling him as he recorded his most passing yards for three years The Kansas City Chiefs gave another ominous sign that they were back in business with a 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts. Winning tight games was a hallmark of the Patrick Mahomes dynasty during three recent Super Bowl wins, so there was a familiar feeling when Harrison Butker kicked the winning field goal right at the death. Mahomes threw three touchdowns and his 382 passing yards was his most for three years. Travis Kelce had 101 yards and a touchdown and summer signing Kenneth Walker had another huge game. The Super Bowl MVP had 178 total yards and was crucial in overtime to help overcome a strong challenge from Daniel Jones and the Colts - who may have lost their first two games but look to have plenty to build on. The Green Bay Packers also triumphed in overtime by erasing a 10-point deficit in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets to win 20-17 - and snap a six-game losing streak. Super Bowl champions Seattle look the real deal again after beating the Arizona Cardinals 31-7 for a 12th straight win. Drew Lock showed he is no ordinary back-up quarterback with three touchdown passes to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, including an 82 yarder that is the longest of the talented receiver's career. The Seahawks lost Walker to the Chiefs but have retained a remarkable 17 of 22 starters and 44 of their 53-man roster from last season's title win. That consistency should see them go close again, but they'll face a rejuvenated San Francisco 49ers in their division, who are also 2-0 after beating the Miami Dolphins 35-15. Showing no signs of jet leg from their victory over the Los Angeles Rams in Australia, the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five possessions to blow Miami away - Christian McCaffrey scored twice, George Kittle also found the end zone and Brock Purdy accounted for three scores. With the 49ers having their defensive stars back from injury Kyle Shanahan's squad look the total package once again. The Cincinnati Bengals also look more well rounded this season after winning a 20-6 battle in Houston, thanks to an early touchdown of the season contender catch from Ja'Marr Chase. We expect fireworks from Chase and Joe Burrow, but having a defence capable of keeping CJ Stroud out of the end zone, and sacking him four times in a road game is the biggest reason for optimism among Bengals fans. The Philadelphia Eagles were on the ropes against the Tennessee Titans until Jalen Hurts threw the winning touchdown pass to Darius Cooper with just nine seconds left in the game. Although not as impressive overall as other 2-0 sides, that ability to win games at the death is a familiar trait with Philly - and will make them dangerous all season again. The New Orleans Saints just fell short after a monster comeback in Detroit last week, but went one better this week by upsetting Lamar Jackson's Baltimore Ravens 24-17 in their home opener. Tyler Shough bundled over in a big crowd for a slightly controversial touchdown given the ball was largely unsighted, before two-time MVP Jackson then threw a late interception when trying to salvage the game. The Saints may just surprise a few more teams this season. Surprising everyone right now are the Las Vegas Raiders, who sit on 2-0 after winning 26-14 at the hapless Chargers. The Chargers have lost by double digits to two of last season's biggest strugglers and with away games at Buffalo and Seattle, things look likely to get much worse. DeShaun Watson threw a fourth quarter touchdown as the Cleveland Browns also sprung an upset win on the road in Tampa Bay, with a weather delay meaning they had to wait an extra two hours to seal the deal. Perhaps the biggest surprise so far though is just how bad the Atlanta Falcons are. They were beaten 34-3 by the Carolina Panthers to become just the fourth team since 1978 to fail to get into an opponents red zone in their first two games. title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband explains why he forgave her over children's killings
description: The husband of the US mother who strangled her three young children discusses his grief in an interview with CBS News.
body: This video can not be played 'It's painful to see,' Patrick Clancy says about online hate Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths. In an interview with CBS, he also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children. Lindsay has not disputed that she killed them but her lawyers argued she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness. A judge declared a mistrial in the case earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty of murder. The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. Clancy, now 36, was then left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. She attended the trial in a wheelchair. Lindsay Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis after birth Patrick Clancy testified during the trial about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth. Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both. "I didn't know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he told CBS, the BBC's US news partner. It was her mental health that led to Patrick Clancy deciding later to forgive her. "I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom', and 'Baby Murderer', 'Monster'. And none of them were accurate," he said in the interview. "I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever." Asked if he felt he had failed in some way in this period leading up to the killings, he said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day." Living with his grief in the weeks after the tragedy became a struggle and he admitted having suicidal thoughts. "I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he said. This video can not be played Watch: Patrick Clancy's new wife describes him as "selfless father" During the seven week trial, Patrick was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations. There were claims he was to blame for the murders in some way. Thrust into the limelight, tabloids snapped photos of him travelling and with his new wife Rachel Danis. The 36-year-old said the speculation was "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health". It was also "painful to see" for him personally. "And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said. The intense scrutiny prompted him to move from Duxbury to New York City in a bid to seek anonymity. Now he is starting a family with Danis and looking forward to telling his future children about their siblings. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids. And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external. A list of UK organisations that can help is available here. title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
description: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's Vice Premier He Lifeng Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday. Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach. "We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks. He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade. A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November. The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment. Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI. Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people." The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries. In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity. Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China. He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins." title: Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, dies aged 27
description: His family asked for privacy during a "very difficult and painful time" following the model's death.
body: Presley Gerber became a model like his mother and sister Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, has died at the age of 27. Gerber, a model, passed away at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to records filed by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. The cause of death was not listed. Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US news partner CBS: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time." Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16. He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta. His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney. In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use. In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do." And in this month's American Vogue, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone. "I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help." title: 'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict
description: As Southampton manager Tonda Eckert awaits the FA hearing into his 'Spygate' misconduct conduct charge BBC sports editor Dan Roan speaks to him and club chief executive Phil Parsons on what happens next.
body: This video can not be played I've asked for forgiveness and apologised publicly - Eckert More than four months since the Spygate scandal erupted, Southampton manager Tonda Eckert's wait to discover his fate for authorising an espionage campaign is almost over. In the coming days, a decisive Football Association hearing will take place, after the German coach was charged with misconduct in July. Spying on three clubs has already cost Southampton the chance of promotion to the Premier League (worth £200m), after they were expelled from the Championship play-off final. An EFL panel also docked the club four points for this season. Now Eckert could be banned. As the club prepared for the latest twist in the saga, BBC Sport spoke exclusively to both Eckert and Southampton chief executive Phil Parsons, who - in his first interview on the case - insists any further punishment would be "really tough to take". But how are the club and their coach dealing with the prospect of more turmoil? What is at stake? And why have Southampton given a permanent role to the intern who was caught spying on Middlesbrough in May? "I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothing that prepares you for that. There just isn't." Eckert speaks slowly and with an intense gaze when asked to reflect on being at the centre of one of the biggest controversies in English football history. The 33-year-old apologised in June after an EFL independent disciplinary commission found he had orchestrated a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich Town, then Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final. Having insisted he was unaware it breached EFL rules, and that the spying had no impact on performances, Eckert was backed by Southampton. His team have made an encouraging start to the new season. Without the four-point deduction, they would be fourth in the table, rather than 13th. "We've talked a lot over the summer of how we want to go through that process of addressing everything, giving everyone the chance to put questions out that are still there, to put out what they feel and have gone through, and then also close the door and move on," he says. "Because the reality is it's a new season. We have big ambitions as a football club, and in order to reach them, we need to move on." That is easier said than done, with Eckert in limbo while he awaits the outcome of the FA's disciplinary process. "I've had the chance to sit down and just talk the FA through everything that happened," he says. "And now it's up to them to make a decision. I don't really have any emotions towards that." So does he feel the FA has listened to him during its investigation? "That was my impression," he says. "We sat for almost four hours, so it's been quite a long conversation." When asked whether he feels the club has been punished enough, and if a suspension for him would be excessive, Eckert chooses his words carefully. "It's been a big, big punishment," he says. "Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports. "And it's tough for me to say that because it concerns me. I'm judging on myself, not an outside situation. But I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly. "I think the punishment has been very hard on the club for the last season. And to go into a new season on minus four. And the rest is not for me to decide." Southampton owner will not sack head coach Eckert This video can not be played We don't know what the FA will hand out - Parsons Parsons is more forthright on whether the club has been punished enough. "We don't know what the FA will actually hand out," he says. "It could be a long ban. It could be a short ban. It could be a suspended sentence. "What we hope as a club is they actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account. I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history. "This isn't just about the club, this is about people. We lose money not being in the Premier League, but [local] businesses lose money. We had to spend a huge amount on legal fees, and it really impacts the club even further. We don't want to be seen as a victim of this. We need to get on. We've had our cards dealt." When it is put to Parsons that the EFL's punishments applied to the club - rather than Eckert himself - he says: "I think it's impossible to sanction the manager without the club getting hurt even more." The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year, after opponents New Zealand were spied on. Parsons insists "the Canadian case is very different" but if Eckert , who is only contracted until the end of the season, is also banned, how long would it have to be for the club to look elsewhere for a new coach? "We don't know," he says, firmly denying having approached other coaches in case Eckert has to leave. Parsons also says the club may appeal if the ruling goes against them. "We can't worry about something we can't control at the moment," he says. "We have to deal with it when we get there but we're hoping that they look at it sensibly." Parsons says the club's ownership "want" to back Eckert. "We've been through an entire transfer window when it comes to recruiting players for Tonda, and that's another challenge. title: 'Constant bombardment' - fans shown 65,000 junk food ads at World Cup
description: New data shows fans were shown more than 28 hours of adverts for unhealthy food and drinks during World Cup matches this summer.
body: This summer's World Cup featured ads promoting an official beverage partner (Coca-Cola), official snack food partner (Lay's), and an official quick-service restaurant sponsor (McDonald's) Football fans were shown a "constant bombardment" of advertisements promoting junk food and drinks during matches at the 2026 Fifa World Cup, according to a new study. Researchers at the University of Bristol and University of Oxford created an AI tool to analyse ads which were visible to television viewers during live play in the tournament's 104 matches, mostly displayed on pitchside advertising boards and around stadiums in the USA, Canada, and Mexico. They found that logos and products for brands that produce junk food and drinks - defined by the UK government as being high in fat, salt or sugar - were displayed 65,722 times in total. And the study also found that those adverts were visible for 28.1 hours' time across the tournament, or just over 16% of the total time that matches were being played. The ads were all shown on the international feed of matches during play - meaning they were visible to every viewer in every country broadcasting matches - and do not include ads shown during pre-match coverage, half-time commercial breaks, or the controversial in-match hydration breaks. The model used by the researchers estimated that there were an average of 576 visible ads for junk food and drink shown during each individual match. Coca-Cola had the highest number (21,893), followed by McDonald's (13,915), Powerade (12,777), and Lay's - the crisps manufacturer known as Walkers in the UK - (12,087). All four brands are official partners of world football governing body Fifa, with the Powerade energy drink owned by the Coca-Cola company. In response to the findings, Fifa argued that the vast majority of its revenue is put back into football, including on projects promoting health and wellbeing in which thousands of people participate. A Fifa spokesperson said: "Fifa works with a broad, global portfolio of partners, all of which are subject to its governance and compliance frameworks. "Fifa's social impact campaigns, including Be Active, delivered messages of unity, inclusion, health and friendship to audiences on an unprecedented scale throughout the World Cup". BBC Sport also contacted Coca Cola, McDonald's and PepsiCo - which owns Lay's - but did not receive a reply. The report also analysed other forms of "potentially harmful" advertising, and found that junk food and drink promotion was far more prevalent. Junk food and drink logos were recorded around seven times more often than those for alcohol and prediction market brands, 10 times more often than those of gambling firms, and almost 25 times more often than cryptocurrency. "Repeatedly connecting unhealthy food and drink brands with football, excitement and national identity can make these brands familiar and normalise their consumption," the researchers argue. McDonald's advertisements were displayed frequently throughout Spain's victory over Argentina in the World Cup final Since October 2025, foods such as burgers, chips, crisps and drinks with added sugar have been included in a ban on junk food advertising on TV before 9pm in the UK. But because the advertising shown during matches appears on hoardings, and is at an international event, it falls outside the legislation. That means viewers seeing ads for burgers, crisps and fizzy drinks during the hours they are theoretically banned, and calls have grown for a more global approach. "It is definitely a loophole," Greg Fell, president of the Association of Directors of Public Health, told BBC Sport. "There is acres of evidence demonstrating that governments around the world are legislating very hard at the moment to limit advertising of junk food. "It requires worldwide collaboration because obesity is a problem everywhere. Advertising is one of the key mechanisms by which harm from obesity happens. "Obesity is almost the new tobacco - there isn't much difference with the methods the tobacco industry used before they were excluded from advertising. "A lot of this is targeted at children, because these companies want to grow their markets, and children are the future market." The UK government recently announced sweeping changes to school dinner rules, banning deep-fried food and increasing the inclusion of fruit, vegetables, fibre and wholegrains, in attempt to tackle childhood obesity. According to the NHS, data from 2024 showed that 15% of children in the UK were obese, and 26% were overweight. "We are facing a global crisis of childhood obesity and diet-related disease, yet the world's biggest sporting event is saturated with marketing for unhealthy food and drinks", said Dr Elisa Becker, one of the report's co-authors. "Sport should be part of the solution to poor health – not one of the world's most powerful advertising platforms for the products driving it." title: Portrait of George Mitchell will not be removed from Hillsborough Castle
description: The picture will remain as part of the castle's "important story" in the peace process".
body: The portrait is on display in Lady Grey's study A portrait of former US Senator George Mitchell on display at Hillsborough Castle, Northern Ireland's official residence of the Royal family, will remain in place as part of the castle's "important story" in the peace process. The former US envoy played a key role in the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, external, which ended decades of violence in Northern Ireland. In 2026, a number of institutions had severed ties with George Mitchell over his links with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. It followed the release of millions of files relating to Epstein by the US Department of Justice, including further references to an earlier claim George Mitchell had sex with Epstein victim, Virginia Giuffre. A bust of Mitchell was removed from Queen's University Belfast last year Mitchell has previously said allegations contained in released documents are false, saying "I have never met, spoken with or had any contact with Ms. Giuffre." As a result of the files, the US-Ireland Alliance said the George J Mitchell Scholarship Program would no longer bear his name. Queen's University Belfast also removed a £35,000 bust from its grounds. BBC News NI has been told there are no plans to move a portrait of Mitchell from Hillsborough Castle, which is also the UK's official residence of the Secretary of State. It is on display in Lady Grey's study, a room open to the public for guided tours which features a number of figures from the Northern Ireland peace process. The study features a number of figures from the Northern Ireland peace process Portraits of high-profile figures are displayed, including former prime ministers, taoisigh (Irish prime ministers), US presidents, secretaries of state and local politicians. The space often hosted small one-to one discussions or bilateral talks during the peace negotiations. The room is described as a "calm, cosy place for contemplation" by the independent charity which looks after six royal sites and palaces. The Historic Royal Palaces has the responsibility for the curation of exhibitions and art hanging at Hillsborough Castle. The Royal Household is not involved in the process. The charity has told BBC News NI there are no immediate plans to change the display. "The 'Preparing the Peace' display is the means through which we share the story of the peace process, and the role that the castle played in negotiations, with our visitors. "The display is situated in a room at the castle where many important negotiations and bilateral talks between the individuals involved took place. "It does not seek to promote or endorse the contribution of any one individual and the works on display have been selected solely because the sitters featured attended peace talks at Hillsborough Castle. "We maintain that the castle's role in the peace process is an important story to share, and we will continue to do so." Hillsborough Castle is the official residence of the Royal family and the UK's official residence of the Secretary of State in NI In response to a question from BBC News NI about whether there has been any consideration of the portrait's place, a Northern Ireland Office spokesperson said the running of the castle is not their responsibility. "In March 2017, the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) granted Historic Royal Palaces a 25-year lease to manage Hillsborough Castle and Gardens. NIO Ministers have use of the castle, but responsibility for its day-to-day running, including the collections and art on display, rests with Historic Royal Palaces." In 2019, a court document contained claims that Virginia Giuffre had been directed to have sex with a number of high-profile people, including former US Senator George Mitchell. Mitchell has previously said the allegation contained in the released documents is false. "I have never met, spoken with or had any contact with Ms. Giuffre." The latest release of documents indicated a continued relationship between Mitchell and Epstein, following Epstein's first conviction. Earlier this year, Mitchell's spokesperson said "he never met, spoken to or had any contact with Giuffre or any underage women". A spokesperson said Mitchell "profoundly regrets ever having known Jeffrey Epstein and condemns, without reservation, the horrific harm Epstein inflicted on so many women". The spokesperson added that he did not observe, suspect or have any knowledge of Epstein engaging in "illegal or inappropriate conduct with underage women". Epstein, a well-connected financier and convicted sex offender, was found dead by suicide in 2019 while awaiting a trial on sex trafficking charges. Trafficking victim Virginia Giuffre took her own life at the age of 41. Being named or pictured in the Epstein files is not an indication of wrongdoing. Many of those identified in other releases have denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein. title: Quadruple amputee enters the Big Brother house
description: Charlotte lost her arms and legs to meningitis as a toddler and is now a contestant on Big Brother.
body: Charlotte Nott, 18, from Oxford, lost her arms and legs to meningitis as a toddler Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back. The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was just two years old. Now 18, Charlotte is a contestant in the latest series of Big Brother, something she has dreamed about for most of her life. Her dad, Alex, told BBC Radio Oxford he was anxious about her appearance on the show, but said there had never been much point telling his daughter not to do something she had her sights on. That resilience was on full display within seconds of Charlotte's arrival on the show. During the launch, her shoe broke as she stepped out to be introduced, and she had to remove her prosthetic legs on stage before entering the house. "Maybe it was my fate to walk in with no legs," she told the diary room. "Maybe that was just what was meant to happen." She added that she was used to going without her prosthetics at home. "When I'm at home, I have my legs off all the time," she said. "When I'm cooking, I have my legs off. I like to be four foot. I like to be tiny, like a little tiny doll." Alex said the moment had summed up his daughter's unstoppable nature perfectly. Charlotte applied for the show earlier this year - the first time she had been old enough to enter - and made it through a process her dad said involved around 50,000 applicants. "She's wanted to go in there since she was about five or six," he said. "I think she used to watch it religiously with her mum." Charlotte had applied without telling her dad and had already completed several interviews with producers before he found out. He admitted he had struggled to come to terms with her decision to apply. "I thought she was on a wind-up to start with," he said. "She was dead serious. I've been in bits for about three months." But Alex said there was little point trying to stand in her way. Charlotte, pictured as a child, lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis at the age of two "You try telling someone like Charlotte that she's not allowed to do something," he said. "We've gone her whole life trying to tell her that she can't do stuff, and she's just taken on that mantle." Since she turned 16, he said she had taken charge of every decision relating to her own care and prosthetics. Alex said his daughter had the resilience to handle whatever reaction she received from the public. "Every day is a struggle for her, more than for anybody else," he said. "But she's got skin as thick as a rhino's. I take my hat off to her." Charlotte said she expected viewers watching her around the clock to be surprised by how ordinary her daily life actually was. Charlotte's dad said she had wanted to go in the Big Brother house since she was young Watch the latest episode of South Today Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire "People are surprised at anything I do, even normal things like cooking, doing my makeup, getting dressed," she said. "They're probably going to be surprised at the most normal things for me." Asked what she would do with the prize money if she won, Charlotte said her prosthetic legs cost around £25,000 each. "I probably would put a lot of it into savings," she said. "My prosthetic legs are about £25,000 per leg, so probably put half in savings and then the other half... just go on a nice holiday, just kind of spend it." Caroline Hughes, senior support services Manager for Meningitis Research Foundation, said the long term consequences of the disease "remain widely misunderstood". "Every day, we support people navigating the physical, emotional and practical challenges that can follow a meningitis diagnosis," she said. "That's why it is so powerful to see people like Charlotte sharing their experience on a platform like Big Brother. "By speaking so openly about her story, she is helping bring greater understanding of the long-term impact meningitis can have, while also enabling others affected by the disease to feel seen, heard and less alone." The 23rd series of Big Brother began on 13 September and will last 54 days, making it the longest series since 2017. ITV said the series had been "reimagined as a house of surprises" and viewers could expect "ambitious tasks, high-stakes nominations and dramatic live evictions". title: University staff begin five-week strike on day one of new term
description: UCU members at the university will not take part in lectures, seminars or tutorials until the end of October.
body: UCU staff voted in June for the five week industrial action Lecturers at the University of Dundee are beginning an unprecedented five-week strike over the threat of compulsory redundancies. Members of the UCU union will not take part in lectures, seminars or tutorials until after 23 October. The vote for "last resort" industrial action was the latest move in a long-running dispute which started almost two years ago when the university announced a £30m deficit. Since then, 675 jobs have been lost through voluntary redundancy, and the university has received bailouts of £40m from the Scottish government and £22m from the Scottish Funding Council. The university said it "anticipates the majority of classes will run as normal" from Monday and that it would seek to minimise the impact of strike action on students. UCU staff at Dundee University went on strike for three weeks last year The latest of wave of cuts was announced in June proposing to close 187 posts, however that figure fell to 154 job losses by August. Since the announcement, UCU bosses said there had been 149 applications for voluntary redundancies, which should now rule out the need for compulsory redundancies. Dr. Melissa D'Ascenzio, co-president of the Dundee UCU branch told BBC News: "None of our members want to go on strike for five weeks, this is absolutely last resort that we've come to. "The university is still refusing to remove the threat of compulsory redundancy. "There has been no attempt from the university to try to find common ground and try to avoid five weeks of disruption." Dundee UCU will stage five weeks of strike action from 21 September Lecturers previously went on strike for three weeks in February last year. Two voluntary severance schemes have now run at the institution, with previous rounds focused on professional services staff who work alongside academics. But the latest round of redundancies over the summer was aimed at lecturers and researchers. Union officials said they were keen to highlight the impact of previous cuts to student services and the student experience. BBC News understands that while lecturers are not required to notify the university in advance of taking strike action, some academics told students during freshers week that their classes might not be on. Iain Ellis, co-president said, "New and returning students will be impacted at the start of term, which is hugely regretful, but we're also clear that university management cutting more jobs and more staff leaving will have a major and long-term impact on students' education and the university." Tom Christisen, president of the students' association (DUSA), said he recognised that the action could have a significant impact on students. He said, "At the same time, we recognise why staff have reached this point. The prospect of compulsory redundancy has created significant uncertainty for colleagues about their jobs and futures at Dundee. "Our responsibility is to stand up for students throughout this period, while continuing to press the university to address the circumstances that have led to industrial action. UCU members at the campus are already working to contract, refusing to carry out "extra" unpaid tasks, such as attending weekend open days. This is unlikely to stop unless the dispute is resolved. It does not currently include a marking or assessment boycott. In previous strikes, a "no-detriment" policy was applied to prevent students being penalised and removing untaught topics from assessments. UCU officials told the BBC they would expect this to apply again now. More than 100 people lobbied the university's governing body, which was meeting at the Bonar Hall A spokesman for the university said: "We recognise the right of trade union members to take industrial action and will strive to work constructively with the University and College Union during the dispute. At the same time, the university will seek to minimise the effects of strike action on students, particularly at a time when they are starting the new academic year. "We anticipate the majority of classes, student contact time, and other activity across the university will proceed as normal. Any impacts will most likely be varied across different areas of the university, reflecting UCU membership." UCU members are now striking each weekday for over a month, as the university refuses to rule out compulsory redundancies. A Scottish government spokesperson said: "Industrial action is in no-one's best interests – least of all students' – so while the Scottish government cannot intervene directly, we encourage universities and trades unions to engage constructively and seek resolution to these disputes." title: Oxford grooming gang survivors tell BBC 'hundreds' of abusers still free
description: Men who sexually abused them as underage girls are still walking around the city, they say.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'I see my abusers in the supermarket' - survivors of Oxford gang tell of ongoing torment Warning: This story contains details of sexual violence Survivors of an Oxford grooming gang say they still see men who sexually abused them, and who have not been brought to justice, walking around the city. "A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant - everywhere you can imagine - you'll see a man that's done something," one survivor, Sarah, tells BBC Panorama. Sarah and two other survivors believe "hundreds" of perpetrators are still free. An ex-police detective who led the initial investigation into grooming gangs in Oxford agrees. It is the first time that Sarah (whose name we have changed) and one of the other women have spoken out publicly about what they were subjected to. Sarah says she was sexually abused and plied with heroin from the age of 11. More than two decades later, three men were found guilty of abusing her after she testified against them in court. They were jailed for between five and 24 years in 2020. But it was too little, too late for Sarah, who has battled drug addiction for most her life and has spent time in jail. "I think they should stay in there forever, because obviously they've taken my life," she says. Chloe, another survivor whose name we have changed, says she also sees some of her abusers in her local area. Like many survivors, she chose not to go through a police investigation. "It's difficult because this is where I live, it's where I grew up. There is a few of them that I've seen a few times, even just in the supermarket, driving around," she explains. She feels "sick, cold" when she sees them, she says. Sarah, whose image is blurred to protect her identity, said the gang had "taken her life" A third woman, Rachel - again, whose name we have changed - was abused between the ages of 12 to 15 and says many of those men are still free. She was a key witness in the first trial of Oxford grooming gang members, in 2013, when seven men were convicted. That trial revealed the grooming, trafficking and rape of six girls over an eight year-period in the city. But subsequent prosecutions have identified many more victims, and it was estimated in 2015 that more than 370 children were affected. Rachel says, for years, police did not believe her when she told them what was happening to her. She and the other women say the investigations have not gone far enough. Thames Valley Police works tirelessly to investigate offenders involved in these horrific crimes and bring them to justice, a spokesperson said. "It is never too late to come forward", the spokesperson continued, and the force will listen and do everything it can to support victims, survivors and their families. Panorama - Grooming Gangs: Why Were We Ignored? For years, organised gangs of abusers, mostly of Pakistani heritage, preyed on girls in Oxford while authorities looked the other way. Panorama examines the devastating legacy for three survivors. Watch now on iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST. Gangs of men were found to have sexually exploited and abused underage girls in several towns and cities - including Rotherham, Rochdale and Telford, as well as Oxford - between the 1990s and 2010s. Oxford was one of the places where most of the perpetrators were identified as older men of Pakistani heritage. In some cases, such as in Rotherham, police were accused of hesitating to act out of fear of being seen as racist. But in Oxford a serious case review found no evidence that this had been a factor. Now, the government has launched a national inquiry to address why vulnerable children were not protected in England and Wales - including whether attitudes to the girls or the ethnicity of the perpetrators contributed to the failings. Sarah says the cigarettes she was given by her groomers were laced with heroin. "My addiction through my whole life now has resulted from them giving us those cigarettes," she says. She agreed not to take drugs before speaking to Panorama and received support from her case worker. Sarah says the men who gave her the cigarettes - and alcohol - then told her she was in debt and needed to have sex with them in order to pay them back. "They're like, 'well you know, you owe me this money now, so you're going to have to do this'," she says. "They used to say 'drink this, drink that' to the point where I'm throwing up and sick. Having to be in them houses and feeling trapped. They used to just lock us in. "Then before you know it, there's one, two, six, seven people turning up. You're just outnumbered, basically." Rachel, from the age of 12, also found herself in a cycle of sexual abuse and drug addiction. She was trafficked to other towns and cities where men paid the gang for sex with her. Rachel says she was not believed for years and that investigations have not gone far enough A police officer even tried to take advantage of her in Oxford, she says, but she never reported the incident. "I was put in the back of a police van on the Cowley Road and there was two male officers and one of them said, 'Well, we know what you're about.'" He then asked her to perform oral sex on him, she says. Despite a total of 21 men now having been convicted in connection with the Oxford grooming gang, Rachel says there are many perpetrators who have never faced consequences. "There are a lot of people out there who have been involved in this to some degree or another, that have just been allowed to get on with their lives that were involved in the sexual abuse of children." Many of the girls were targeted in the Cowley area of the city, pictured here in 2015 As one of the hidden victims of the Oxford grooming gang, none of Chloe's abusers have faced justice for the crimes committed against her. title: Baby bank helping more parents in full-time work
description: The couple who run the bank say they are in "desperate need" of baby formula as demand is so high.
body: Kavita and Karvinder Dhillon say more people in full-time work are using their baby bank A Birmingham baby bank says it is helping a growing number of people in full-time work who are struggling to afford essentials for their children. Kavita Kaur Dhillon and her husband Karvinder run the Handsworth Baby and Family Bank on Soho Road, which provides free items including nappies, baby formula, clothes and toys. The couple said the majority of people they first helped were from low-income households, but they were now seeing more working families needing support with everyday costs. "We don't need any more clothing, it's the everyday essentials, formula, nappies, wipes, toiletries," said Kavita. Karvinder said demand had shifted in recent years. "Before, we mainly needed nappies," he said. "As the daily cost of living has gone up, people need help with more day-to-day things." The couple said they were currently in desperate need of baby formula and often had only a handful of tubs left in stock. "Just because you dress nice, or drive a nice car, doesn't mean you don't need help," Kavita said. "Nobody knows people's circumstances. People can judge, but the reality is people are struggling." The bank provides free essentials including nappies, clothing, toys and baby formula The bank, which operates from inside the couple's Dhillons Boutique store, has been helping families since 2024. Kavita believed sharing a space with the shop helped remove some of the stigma that can come with asking for support. "You go out of our shop and people think you have purchased something, but in fact you've just used our baby bank," she said. She described it as a "warm and welcoming space" and said demand had continued to grow since it opened. For the couple, supporting families remains the most rewarding part of the project. "For me it is fulfilling, knowing I've been able to support or help someone else be okay and smile," Kavita said. She urged anyone who was struggling not to suffer in silence. "It's nothing to be ashamed of or to be scared of. There's no shame in asking for help." title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister tells BBC
description: It comes after European Commission President proposed "opening the door" for Canada to become an associate member of the EU.
body: The UK should "team up" with a proposed economic alliance between Canada and Europe, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said. "This is all about the substance, to build an alliance of the future," he told the BBC. "The world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change." Champagne also gave a frank assessment of the Canada-US trade war after a deal collapsed last month, saying the country had "stood up for our industries, our workers, our country" by imposing tariffs. His comments come after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to an associate EU membership for Canada, an unprecedented move for the bloc. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the European Union in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the alliance of the future", Champagne said. Carney, the former Governor of the Bank of England, has previously talked about an alliance of "middle powers" working together on economic growth, resilience and security. Speaking to the BBC, Champagne said the UK and Canada had shared values. "We need to look at partnership in a different way, and the great thing is that when you look at Canada, and I would say the United Kingdom, we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?" he said. "We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together." After his return to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs, including on long-standing trade allies such as the UK. While the UK renegotiated a trade deal with the US in June last year, the new Canada-EU alliance does raise questions for the UK's post Brexit positioning with Europe, as well as its position with the US, after some changes of presidential rhetoric over the Falklands and Irish unity in recent weeks. Carney met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool in the middle of his trip to Brussels and Strasbourg last week, while Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday, alongside the Chancellor John Healey. The developing discussions around closer ties between the EU and Canada come as Canada remains locked in an escalating trade war with the US, with both sides imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after talks broke down at the last moment in August. President Trump has also threatened further tariffs on the EU if the associate membership plan proved "hostile" to the US, calling the idea laughable and labelling Canada a "terrible trading partner". Champagne said the trade war was not a conflict chosen by Canada. "We responded because at some stage you have to say 'Enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty… the world took notice," he said. The minister said Canada does not seek escalation after its "measured, targeted and strategic… dollar for dollar, tariff for tariff" response, and the country would "reengage at the right time" with its southern neighbour. Affected industries would be supported "as long as it takes and whatever it takes", he added. Champagne argued that Canada's strong fiscal position helped underpin its resilience, and the dispute with the US provided a "golden opportunity" to diversify. This is the backdrop to the promise of an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the EU, and the idea of "teaming up" with the UK too. Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, in New York at the UN General Assembly. Last year, after his election, Carney invited King Charles to open the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa, a move widely seen as a rebuff to Trump's repeated suggestion that Commonwealth Canada could become part of the US. The detail of the offer made by the EU to negotiate "associate membership" for Canada is yet to be formalised. Champagne said this was "a moment of great opportunities" and to strengthen the existing relationship between Canada and the EU. Carney last week pointed to Canadian membership of EU university, scientific research, AI and defence funding schemes, as well as for young Canadians and Europeans to "cross the ocean and be able to study and live". He said Canada could supply critical minerals and gas and would seek access to European advanced technologies. It is understood that both Canada and the EU see the opportunity for a process for like-minded nations which might not ever be full members, for example Australia. title: Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review
description: Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Prof Fonagy says being young is much harder now than it was.
body: Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC. Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common. He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media. His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off". It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training. Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health. Some have argued greater awareness and misattributing normal life stresses to mental illness were factors in the increase in cases. Fonagy said his personal battle with mental health when he was young was a driving factor in his desire to help young people. He experienced suicidal thoughts as a teenager after moving to London from Hungary without his parents. But he says he was fortunate to get therapy from a local service that "saved his life". "It's harder to be young now," the 74-year-old said, adding that his review "dismisses the idea of a snowflake generation". "I'm in awe of the way they have adjusted to an environment that is far more difficult than I ever had to face." He said economic and employment uncertainty, as well as the pressures of social media, had created a "very toxic" environment for young people. "They are a generation that has real serious challenges that I would not wish to have had when I was their age. "Adults have let them down. We're the first generation that probably collectively feels we had a better life than our children will have. "So, to the person who says it's a snowflake generation, just try living 24 hours as a 16-year-old." Prof Peter Fonagy believes the youth of today face a much more challenging childhood than previous generations More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England. He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling. The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward. Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives – giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with. Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised. Child mental health crisis: Is better resilience the solution? Teen mental health: When to seek help and what parents can do Fonagy, however, is adamant that what young people are experiencing represents a real rise in mental health problems. But he also accepted that greater awareness was leading to more people seeking medical help. The trend is affecting both boys and girls, but becomes particularly pronounced in girls from about the age of 12. Sexual aggression from boys was a big concern, he said, but added that the expectations society placed on girls and young women was a factor. "It's very difficult to be a young woman now in secondary school." Fonagy said young people were struggling with a range of different conditions from eating disorders and anxiety "that's so powerful people avoid going to school", through to depression that was "so strong people cannot sleep at night and lose their appetite and feel their life is not worth living". His report will say these problems were exacerbated by the pandemic because of the disruption it caused to their lives. Young people the BBC spoke to who have struggled with their mental health say it is important that the government acts on the findings of Fonagy's report when it comes out. "It's all very well having this flashy report, but it's useless if they don't put that into practice," Omari, 22, said. He had a tough time at school, but said his teachers did not listen. "I made an attempt on my life because I was really struggling with bullying. I was 15. "Suddenly, when I did end up in hospital, they all wanted to care. But it's like you're a bit too little, too late here." Others expressed concern about their futures. Mattea, 17, is in temporary social housing and has struggled with anxiety and depression. "I don't know what's going to happen to my life," she said, adding that she felt like adults had let her down. "No one's going to come and sort my life out for me. I have to do it on my own." Mattea feels let down and is concerned about her future Fonagy said the support being provided to young people needed to be improved. The NHS, he said, was simply "not fit for purpose". He said too many people were being left on waiting lists, pointing to figures that show one in three people referred to mental health services were still waiting for help after a year. There were some positives steps being taken, he said, including the rollout of mental health teams to work closely with schools. However, he said tackling the problem will require action across society – in education, employment, housing and families themselves. title: What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales?
description: The return of former captain Ashley Williams to the Wales coaching team excites boss Craig Bellamy before their Nations League fixtures.
body: Ashley Williams made his Wales debut in 2008 Wales go into their Nations League openers aiming to shut out Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland. With that kind of challenge, Craig Bellamy's squad might need all the defensive help they can get for games against Portugal, Denmark and Norway. Cue Ashley Williams, the centre-back described by Bellamy as Wales' "greatest captain" of the modern era. Williams was skipper as Wales reached the semi-finals of Euro 2016 against Ronaldo and Portugal, the peak of an international career that earned him 86 caps, wearing the armband for more than half of those appearances. Now 42, the former Everton and Swansea City defender will not be adding to those appearances. Instead, he will form part of a new-look Bellamy backroom team that the Football Association of Wales (FAW) hopes will add a missing ingredient in the bid to reach Euro 2028. Bellamy says Williams, and fellow new coach Alan Sheehan, will help provide "a different dynamic". But what exactly will they bring? Colwill's 'surreal' Ronaldo and Haaland ambition Wilson major Wales injury concern for Nations League With Bellamy losing two key assistants just weeks after it seemed the Wales boss himself would walk away from the job amid interest from Burnley, Williams' arrival was something of a surprise. His coaching experience has been limited to informal roles and fans are accustomed to seeing the much-admired ex-captain in the Match of the Day studio. Sheehan, too, was not an expected announcement, with the former Leeds, Leicester and Luton full-back out of work since November 2025 when he was sacked by Swansea City following a relatively unsuccessful seven-month stint. They replace James Rowberry, who has opted to focus on his role with Mark Robins at Stoke City, and Piet Cremers, a man whose analytical work Bellamy said meant "everything" but left to join Belgium's Club NXT in July. Cremers spent time under Pep Guardiola at Manchester City and worked with Bellamy and Vincent Kompany during their successful period at Burnley. He was often the person Bellamy turned to mid-match, but Bellamy says he was already keen to take on more of the tasks that Cremers performed. "I loved this summer interviewing people, seeing who could add to us," said the 47-year-old, who has seen former Wales midfielder and now Tottenham assistant Andrew Crofts remain part of the setup. "It freshens you up, gives you a different eye. Different strengths coming in means a different dynamic to how you work, which leaves me quite excited." This video can not be played Craig Bellamy on Match of the Day pundit Ashley Williams joining Wales staff The obvious strength Williams brings is his personality. Past team-mates for club and country will queue up to attest to his character as a player and a person. With Bellamy's Wales a young side, it mirrors the role the more experienced Williams played while on the field. As senior to the likes of Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey, he was a leader among equals. "I played underneath Ash as a captain, and he was a great leader in the dressing room and led by example in the way he conducted himself on and off the pitch," says Euro 2016 colleague Sam Vokes. "He can be someone who speaks from experience and [will] go into that dressing room and immediately command respect. "Portugal and Denmark away, he has played in those environments. "He will be able to speak to the lads that are going out in those environments because he led by example, and led in the trenches many times." Bellamy agrees, having retained a friendship with the former Swansea skipper after sharing a dressing room with Wales. "In my time he's been our greatest captain," says Bellamy. "Some ex-players with a certain presence can really add something, but also his knowledge of the game is really high, his football IQ is really high." Craig Bellamy and Ashley Williams first played together for Wales under John Toshack Wales might need it at the back. The appointments come against the backdrop of Wales' failure to reach the World Cup and the beginnings of criticism around the side's openness. "He'll bring some unique skills, particularly when you play Nations League A games when you have to defend a lot," said FAW chief football officer Dave Adams of Williams' appointment on the Feast of Football podcast. "Some of the dark arts of defending, he'll bring some interesting things for the players to think about." There is the thought that Williams would also be prepared to challenge Bellamy's thinking – seen as healthy part of a management team. But while Bellamy says he is keen to lean on Williams' defensive know-how, it will still be the former Liverpool, Manchester City and Newcastle forward's managerial message. "With his position, sometimes it's easier coming from a player who's been in there," said Bellamy - a former Wales captain himself. "Now, I'll lead a lot on the information, but it's nice for me to be able to ask 'What would you see with this? If you played there, how did you feel when I asked you to do that? Is that possible? Is that not possible?' I believe he'll be a huge asset to me." Sheehan's appointment also suggested a more defensive focus. The former Republic of Ireland Under-21 international was seen to have a pragmatic style at Swansea. But it appears Wales will look to benefit from the 40-year-old's eye for set-piece work, something he has also been responsible for during previous coaching roles at Luton and Southampton. "We really want someone who is in tune with restarts and set-pieces," added Adams. "In these sorts of games they could be the factor that give us a chance to win the game, because they are going to be very hard games to play in. "We realise the importance of attacking and defending set-pieces in these next six games, and feel Alan and [goalkeeping coach] Martyn Margets

title: Watch: Dramatic moment a cargo ship crashes into another vessel
description: Verified footage appears to show a cargo ship colliding with a fishing boat near Singapore, with investigators still working to establish exactly when and how the crash happened.
body: This video can not be played Two videos circulating on social media appear to show the moment a cargo ship crashes into a fishing vessel, with dramatic footage capturing the impact. BBC Verify authenticated the clips, identified the ships involved and traced the collision to waters near Singapore, with evidence suggesting it likely happened on 17 September. It remains unclear is whether anyone was injured or killed and why the collision occurred. Watch: Dramatic moment a cargo ship crashes into another vessel. title: The Papers: 'Russia to test Nato pact' and 'Labour eye tax raid'
description: Potential threats from Russia to Nato and speculation over Labour's tax plans ahead of the Budget lead Monday's papers.
body: The Guardian reports that European intelligence officials are raising the possibility of an imminent Russian attack on Nato territory, with one telling the paper it could happen within "months not years". The paper also carries comments from Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who has said intelligence reports suggest it would be part of Moscow's efforts to test whether Article 5 - which holds that Nato members will come to the defence of an ally under attack - is "more theoretical than practical". The "flames of war" are pictured on the front page of the Financial Times following Ukraine's latest drone attack on Moscow, described by the city's mayor as the largest attack to date on the Russian capital. The FT also reports that big tech firms have issued up to $300bn in "guarantees to back debt for AI data centres and chips" in the past year, but are "recording little of that exposure on their balance sheets." The Daily Telegraph, like several of Monday's papers, leads with speculation Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are eyeing up a "tax raid" in the upcoming Budget. The paper reports they are reviewing proposals to raise Capital Gains Tax to 45% in order to increase the personal allowance on income tax. The latest set of German state elections also make the front page, as the paper notes Chancellor Friedrich Merz is on course for a "humiliating double defeat". More than half of Labour MPs have a greater number of disability benefit claimants than their majorities in their respective constituencies, according to analysis by the Times, which says they are at risk of a backlash from their constituents over possible cuts to Personal Independence Payments at the Budget. The Daily Mail leads with a pledge from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to restore tax-free shopping for tourists in the UK, reversing a post-Brexit rule. The Mail agrees with her as it campaigns to "scrap the tourist tax". The Daily Express also quotes Badenoch, who is urging the government to end the "hammering" of Britain's shops and pubs. Metro carries comments made by Earl Spencer in a BBC interview ahead of his book launch. The earl has denied siding with the Duke of Sussex over his brother, the Prince of Wales. Former England footballer Andros Townsend has avoided serious injury after being run over by a pitch roller during the warm-up for a league match in Thailand, the Daily Star reports. The paper also pictures singer Ed Sheeran, who became emotional while addressing crowds at his first concert since the decision to drop a support act for making pro-Palestinian comments. "We women are all at risk from men" reads the headline of the i Paper, summarising comments from Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Philipson. Her comments follow concerns from female villagers about living near proposed housing for asylum seekers in Piddington. The Independent highlights its Climate 100 - the "changemakers and innovators helping turn the time on our climate crisis". Among them are activist Erin Brockovich and Prince William. title: Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
description: Jensen Huang's comments come after warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction.
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives". "2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible." Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models. His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade". Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down. Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly. "Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished." Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause. "Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem." Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Nvidia is a key player in the industry, developing cutting edge computer chips that are crucial for making AI models. The firm's most powerful chips face restrictions in China due to measures imposed by both Washington and Beijing. US export controls aim to slow China's military and AI progress, while Chinese regulations are designed to encourage reliance on domestically produced technology. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held talks in New York on Sunday as they try to strike deals on AI, tariffs and critical minerals. The meeting came as President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. Last week, Huang appeared at a UK summit hosted by King Charles, who warned tech leaders of the "existential dangers" of AI. "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," the King told the group. In the US, President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks. Trump made a surprise phone call to Huang while the Nvidia boss was speaking on stage at a tech conference in Los Angeles on 14 September. During the call, Trump criticised calls to slow the pace of AI development and dismissed fears as a "hoax". title: Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results is far from clear
description: Vladimir Putin will likely use the result to claim most Russians back the so-called special military operation in Ukraine, writes the BBC's Steve Rosenberg.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation for the Ukraine war Many things about Russia are hard to predict. The result of this election wasn't one of them. In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia – had been widely expected to maintain its grip on parliament. There was no upset. No surprises. No other party came close. Preliminary results suggest that United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma. And that's after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, which have resulted in huge battlefield losses for the Russian army, sparked economic hardship, as well as petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. It appears that those parties which have crossed the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma are the same ones that were in the last parliament. And that Duma was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation. Members of a local electoral commission empty a ballot box before counting votes One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko. Yabloko had been the only anti-war party allowed to run in this election. But just 12 days after being registered it was removed from the ballot by the Supreme Court. That seemed to be a sign of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public. The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as compliant as the previous one. "What other result can there be if there were 10 parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of [Russian President Vladimir] Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me. "I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did." Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around 100 of its candidates remained in individual constituency races, although the party continued to face sustained pressure. "Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says. Members of an electoral commission count votes after polls close at a polling station in Belgorod, Russia Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine had launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. The city's oil refinery was hit. At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack. Here, too, there was little surprise at what had transpired. More than four and a half years into Russia's war on Ukraine, Muscovites had grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line. Instead of astonishment, there was quiet resignation. "People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," says a voter called Viktor, who has exited the polling station. "They just get on with their lives." If the outcome of this election was predictable, what happens next is less clear. The Kremlin will likely use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the war. President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation. "There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared. Not today. But what about tomorrow? Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety over the possibility of a new mobilisation. At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a "mandate from the people" to continue the war. War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
