title: German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
description: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
body: Merz delivered a statement shortly after exit polls were announced from Berlin and Mecklenburg- Vorpommern Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party. In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left). Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap. Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms. "The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward". "I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added. As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration. This is a party that knows it's in trouble. Friedrich Merz is going on the offensive, quickly declaring he is going nowhere. He has long coveted the top job in German politics and likely won't give it up easily. Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours. According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It was followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%. However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it. For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%. Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved. Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months. While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular. The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left. title: Last-minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
description: Last minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
body: Manchester United's Marcus Rashford tries to beat Fulham pair Timothy Castagne and Josh King at Craven Cottage Matheus Cunha's deflected last-minute equaliser spared Manchester United more misery after Lisandro Martinez's own goal had threatened to give Fulham victory at Craven Cottage. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Cunha rescues point for Man Utd at Fulham Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeumo with full-length save. 7 Timothy Castagne: Booked for bringing Marcus Rashford down as Manchester United broke in the second half. 6 David Affengruber: Excellent defence-splitting pass to release Josh King, but he couldn't finish. Exceptionally fortunate to escape after being outwitted by Cunha close to the goalline but stepped in to take the ball off Mbeumo as he looked to counter. 7 Calvin Bassey: Not the easiest game positionally as Manchester United played without an orthodox centre-forward. Got forward to create Fulham's goal. 7 Antonee Robinson: Pushed into advanced areas in the inside forward position, which caused the visitors a defensive issue. 7 Sander Berge (Off, Larsson 76): Shot from the edge of the area turned away by Senne Lammens. 7 Shea Charles: Midfield partnership with Berge was key in protecting the Fulham defence when the visitors had extended spells of possession around the home area. Passing let him down on occasion. 6 Oscar Bobb (off Kevin, 70): Rolled an effort just wide of the post and probably should have done better. 6 Josh King (off Andersen, 79): Always looking to get on the ball and threaten. Took a good save from Lammens to deny him at the far post and his shot across goal was going in without the visitors' keeper kicking it away. Blotted his copybook by getting booked for diving. 8 Alex Iwobi (off Palacios, 70): Also tried to exploit the inside left channel when Fulham went forward. Low cross almost created a chance for Gonzalo Garcia and another deep one did for King. 7 Gonzalo Garcia (off Muniz, 79): Half a stride away from having a tap-in from an Iwobi cross from the left. 6 Palacios (on 70, Iwobi): Kept Fulham ticking over. 6 Kevin (on 70, Bobb): Settled in well. 6 Larsson (on 76, Berge): 6 Muniz (on 79, Garcia): 6 Andersen (on 79, King): 6 Subs not used: Lecomte, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe. Senne Lammens: Key first-half saves to keep Manchester United level and came out bravely at Iwobi's feet to prevent another Fulham chance. Distribution could have been better and he didn't cover himself in glory with the Fulham goal. 6 Diogo Dalot: Tidy spin and dash into space to create a chance for Rashford but had too much work to do defensively as he lacked cover far too often. 6 Harry Maguire: Used his experience to draw a foul out of King as United tried to deal with Fulham pressure near their own goal. 7 Lisandro Martinez: Well-struck half-volley drew an excellent save out of Leno. He did eventually find the net - at the wrong end. 5 Luke Shaw (off Dorgu, 83): Returned from a three-match absence. Carrick's side are far more balanced when he is there. 7 Youri Tielemans: Wasted an excellent opportunity when he got no power behind his effort as he ran on to Rashford's short pass. 5 Kobbie Mainoo (off 79, Mount): Usual tidy game in possession without making the key passes. Never looks flustered. 7 Bryan Mbeumo: A lot of strong runs but, like many Man Utd forwards, nowhere near his best. Tough ask, but did he give Dalot enough defensive support? 6 Bruno Fernandes: Low shot against the post from Cunha cut-back but once more not at last season's levels. 6 Marcus Rashford (off 76, Zirkzee): Tried to set up Tielemans with a short pass but the Belgian couldn't finish. An attempt of his own before the break was saved by Leno and another, better opportunity flew way over the bar. 6 Matheus Cunha: Again started in the number nine role he doesn't seem suited to but created an excellent opportunity for Fernandes. Deflected shot hit the post and spun wide. Probably the visitors' most dangerous forward. 7 Zirkzee (on 76, Rashford): 6 Mount (on 79, Mainoo): 6 Dorgu (on 83, Shaw): 7 Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Baleba, Lacey. After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Danny Dyer and Becky Hill join water industry protest
description: Activists are calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership.
body: Danny Dyer and his daughter Dani Dyer joined a protest calling for public ownership of water companies in Leysdown Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry. Activists from Surfers Against Sewage descended on Leysdown on Sunday after 315,000 signed a petition calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership. Rivals and EastEnders star Dyer, who has been running a caravan park on Isle of Sheppey as part of a new TV series, told the BBC: "Sometimes when you look out to the sea, you can smell the twang in the air." Water UK said that "no sewage spill is ever acceptable", while Southern Water said it was committed to reducing storm overflows. Dyer said that the quality of the water was "a disgrace". "It's a very dangerous thing," he told the BBC. Meanwhile Hill said that she loved swimming in the open water but found it "disgusting" to find human waste in the sea. She said that she was campaigning for her family and other families for a cleaner sea. "We can stand up and make a difference," she added. Singer Becky Hill said that she would like to see improved water quality in the sea Ed Acteson, co-founder of the protest organisers SOS Whitstable, said: "The public has had enough of being asked to accept polluted waterways, failing infrastructure and rising bills. "Water is an essential public service, not a vehicle for private profit. "We want an industry run in the interests of people and the environment, with its income reinvested in the system rather than extracted from it." Meanwhile Cliff Roney, a GMB activist who has worked in the water industry for more than 40 years, said: "I have seen this industry at its very best and now at its very worst. "If the industry is not brought back into public ownership quickly, we are heading towards a national catastrophe." Water UK said it was working to end sewage spills "as fast as we physically can". "That's why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works," a spokesperson said. "This is part of a record £104bn investment programme – the largest in the industry's history – to stop sewage entering our rivers and seas, secure our water supplies and support economic growth." Southern Water's director for environment and innovation, Nick Mills, said its 10-year, £1.5bn Clean Rivers and Seas Plan was "already starting to make a difference". "In Whitstable, we're harnessing both AI and nature-based solutions, and we're investing £90m in improvements to Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works. Together, these measures will dramatically reduce storm overflows in the area." According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025. There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
description: While Burnham praised the agreement, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory for Trump.
body: Andy Burnham has hailed a deal between Denmark and the US to "strengthen security in the Arctic" after the two countries resolved a months-long feud over Greenland. The UK prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region" in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said. Nato previously said the agreement would help stabilise the region, as Trump declared Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic. Burnham's comments come as he is expected to meet Trump for the first time at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week. Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control' The agreement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes as well as its mineral wealth. No text of the agreement has been released, but Trump said in a Truth Social post the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and meant it could "do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland". He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval". In a readout of Sunday's phone call, a No 10 spokesperson said Burnham and Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security". The spokesperson added: "The Prime Minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump." While Burnham praised the agreement, Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory and a near carbon copy of the existing agreement. Greenlanders protested against Trump's ambitions for the territory in the country's capital, Nuuk, earlier this year "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference. "So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won." Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week. The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen. The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted. Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine. Why does Trump want Greenland and what could it mean for Nato and the EU? title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
description: The widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker has given birth after last year announcing the "devastating" loss of a stillborn baby.
body: Kelsey Parker attended the VIP screening of Disney's Moana at Leicester Square in July Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth. The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix. On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said. Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media. "Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote. "Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said. Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx". Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope". Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby. It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight". Kelsey (right), pictured here in 2016, married her former partner Tom Parker (left) in July 2018 In 2023, she published a book titled With And Without You, about the first year after the death of her former partner Tom. The couple married in 2018 and had a daughter, Aurelia Rose, and a son, Bodhi. In a post after his death she wrote "thank you to everyone who has supported in his care throughout, he fought until the very end. I'm forever proud of you". Her latest pregnancy was announced in May in an Instagram post that said "somehow, through all the heartbreak, it feels like Tom and Phoenix have sent us another little gift from heaven, our little rainbow baby". title: Impressive defence seals solid start at Liverpool for Iraola
description: Liverpool are looking good defensively but Andoni Iraola needs more from his attackers after a hard-fought win at Bournemouth.
body: Liverpool have kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League for the first time since September 2024. It was third time lucky for Alexander Isak after a wayward first-half effort and a second-half cross that ballooned over the bar to much amusement from the home crowd, but Liverpool's win at Bournemouth was built as much on their increasingly solid defence. The Swedish forward took his fourth goal this season well and the chants of "Isak's a Red" from the travelling supporters, long after the final whistle, told you all you needed to know. Yet it is the lack of goals Liverpool are conceding that really deserves highlighting. They were far from perfect on Andoni Iraola's Cherries return but were solid defensively. His side have now kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League - the first time Liverpool have done so since September 2024 - and did not give up an xG of more than 0.76 in any of those. For all the talk of a front three who all cost in excess of £100m, Liverpool are becoming a harder side to beat under Iraola. "The more times they play together, the more solid the defensive line becomes," said Iraola, whose side remain unbeaten in all competitions. "Virgil [van Dijk], Jeremy [Jacquet], Ronald [Araujo] and Milos [Kerkez] - they're getting the connections and becoming more solid." Two reliable campaigners, goalkeeper Alisson and centre-back Van Dijk, were superb, with Alisson making a great first-half save to deny Evanilson. But arguably the biggest positive of Liverpool's campaign so far has been the emergence of Jacquet. "I think he has showed a lot of good things so far this season. Still so young, a lot to learn and a lot to give. Let's keep it going," said Van Dijk. Jacquet, 21, has started every Premier League game since making the £60m move from Rennes in the summer and is poised to make his France debut over the international break after getting the call-up from boss Zinedine Zidane. "I'm happy for him as he also received his first international call-up. He's also very young and adapted really well to the Premier League," said Iraola. "The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to substitute him. "Today has been a step forward. He looked solid until the end. I think he's in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development." Iraola was business-like on his return to Bournemouth, saying pre-match the time for talks would be after the game. He cut a frustrated figure for much of the match as Liverpool struggled to get a hold on the game but they improved after the break and deserved the win, according to Iraola, who held true to his word. After his post-match news conference, Iraola spent time talking about San Sebastian with some of the local journalists, who travelled there with Bournemouth earlier in the week for their Europa League bow. With nine points from a possible 15 in the Premier League and wins at Anfield in the Champions League and Carabao Cup, Iraola has had a largely positive start to life at Liverpool. The 44-year-old is the first manager to remain unbeaten in his first five league games in charge of Liverpool - winning two and drawing three - since Joe Fagan in September 1983. "Overall, we have definitely improved since the first games," he said. "Some of the things we still need to improve. I'm happy that it is the third league clean sheet in the row. "Today is a difficult game - you never play comfortable here, Bournemouth does not allow you to play comfortably, they put you under pressure and you have to adapt and you have to win these kind of games." The need to adapt and find ways to win games was stressed after last week's goalless draw against Fulham - but Iraola's side are learning. "We we still have to get ready because the schedule we have now is very difficult," he said. "I think we play against the top four teams and then in between there is Champions League and Chelsea in the Carabao Cup, every two or three days. So we have to be ready because this month after the break is very demanding for us." After the international break, Iraola will also need more from his attackers. Cody Gakpo was impressive again but Florian Wirtz struggled, while Bradley Barcola is still awaiting his first goal or assist for Liverpool. "It was a slow start but after the first phase Florian helped us to improve and I am much happier with his performance in the second half," said Iraola. On Isak, he said: "A striker's job is like this. He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control but in the end he has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition's half and have more meaningful possession. "And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goal." Latest Liverpool news, analysis and fan views Ask about Liverpool - what do you want to know? title: Perfect 24 hours for Maresca as Man City put pressure on Arsenal
description: Manchester City head into the international break in a jubilant mood after enjoying the perfect 24 hours this weekend.
body: Manchester City are three points clear at the top of the Premier League heading into the international break Manchester City head into the international break in a jubilant mood after enjoying the perfect 24 hours this weekend. City saw champions Arsenal thumped 3-0 by Brighton on Saturday and they capitalised the following day by beating Sunderland 5-3 in a thriller at Etihad Stadium. Manager Enzo Maresca said before Sunday's game this was his side's "toughest" test of the season so far, but the end result cements an ideal start to his role at City, where he faced the unenviable task of replacing Pep Guardiola in the summer. The knives were being sharpened on Maresca after a Community Shield humbling by Mikel Arteta's Gunners in August but City have responded in superb fashion with seven straight victories in all competitions. "To be honest, I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3 but I expected a very difficult game," said Maresca. "I knew how they good are, off the ball very aggressive and on the ball they have different weapons, set-pieces and [Brian] Brobbey. "I know it was a difficult game but [I'm] happy because we found a way to win the game and the good thing also is that these seven official games we played, they are all different, we experienced different things. "In the last one with 10 men and today was a complicated one - the Bournemouth one we were losing 1-0 so also a chance to learn from the game." Hat-trick hero Brobbey on losing side - player ratings for Man City v Sunderland Man City battle past Sunderland in eight-goal thriller Arsenal's stunning loss on the south coast opened the door for City and they took full advantage. They are the only side in England's top four divisions with a 100% winning record intact, going three points clear at the top of the Premier League. Such has been the brilliant start that Maresca becomes only the sixth Premier League manager to win his first five games in charge at a club after Carlo Ancelotti, Craig Shakespeare, Maurizio Sarri and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. The other name? Predecessor Guardiola when he took over at City in 2016. On the pitch there were plenty of positives to take too, including the return to form of Antoine Semenyo with two goals and an assist, Rayan Cherki's delightful performance and Enzo Fernandez scoring his first goal for the club. Meanwhile, striker Erling Haaland's late effort means the Norwegian ticked off Sunderland from his scoring list - he has now netted against all 25 Premier League teams he has faced. It means City have put pressure on Arsenal in the early stages of the campaign, with the Gunners previously being tipped as heavy favourites to retain their crown. City, though, will undergo a stern examination upon their return to action after the three-week international hiatus, facing a trip to unbeaten Liverpool on Sunday, 11 October. Former Reds midfielder Charlie Adam described it as a "brilliant start to the season" for City, adding on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A lot to work on but [positive] to score five goals at home and have shown that level of performance. "With Arsenal losing on Saturday, [City] could have gone into the break top of the table and they have done that today." Before facing the Black Cats, City had only conceded two goals in their first four Premier League games. On Sunday, they ended up shipping three in 90 minutes and the way the side lost control will be of some concern to Maresca. Sunderland striker Brobbey ran captain Ruben Dias ragged all game and managed the rare feat of scoring a Premier League hat-trick and ending up on the losing side - the Dutchman becoming just the sixth player to achieve that unwanted statistic. Regis le Bris' side could have scored more and their expected goals (xG) of 4.25 was the most by any visiting side on record at Etihad Stadium in a Premier League game. Maresca said: "I am always concerned, always trying to see what we can do better. For sure, two of the three goals we conceded were too easy. "The second coming from a quick [Granit] Xhaka free-kick and that cannot happen. The third goal comes from another free-kick, too easy in that way. "We concede more chances but we scored five, created [more] and could score two or three more." Adam said: "Maresca will be delighted in terms of how it has gone, the new players coming in and how he has adapted to being the Manchester City manager. "In terms of things to improve on, they can't go through a season playing like that, they need to be able to control spaces at times, instead of getting dragged everywhere man against man." He added for Marseca this will provide a "real positive feeling" and that City "can go into this international break with real pride". title: Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost
description: Tom English reflects on the first Old Firm league game of the season, in which Rangers repeated their League Cup win over Celtic.
body: Ryan Naderi's goal was enough to give Rangers victory At the end, every fibre of Derek McInnes' being must have wanted to have one of those Steven Gerrard moments, a scream of delight and relief into a Celtic Park camera lens, a human reaction to a significant victory on hostile terrain. McInnes, though, showed little emotion. He shook hands with a now beleaguered Martin O'Neill and pretty much got out of there. Later, the first words he uttered on radio were about not going "overboard" after back-to-back wins against their city rivals. "Just three points." he said. "Three points closer to Celtic." That's true, of course, but it was also the first time a Rangers manager has won his first two games against Celtic since Graeme Souness in 1986. McInnes was 15 years old at the time. So there was historical context but also deep relevance in the here and now. Rangers were good, and clearly deserving of the win, but they didn't quite hit the levels of ruthlessness of a week ago at Ibrox. They can be better and yet they won as comfortably as it's possible to win when the margin at the end is just a single goal. Their superiority would have been better reflected had they won by two. Naderi goal gives Rangers second derby win over Celtic in week 'It might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill ponders Celtic future after defeat Rangers flip narrative as McInnes makes mark Watch: Scott Brown & Andy Halliday discuss Old Firm game on YouTube O'Neill said there was "not much between the sides" but nobody was really buying that, Celtic folk chief among them. The Celtic manager has problems and they're mounting game-by-game. His team is physically weak and mentally substandard. They have lost the elan they had in a few games in early season. They were out-played, out-muscled and out-coached. Again. O'Neill has time to pause now, time to reassess. Time, perhaps, to question whether he's got the answers to the myriad ills of his team. He doesn't have robust players in midfield because his board has not delivered them. He doesn't have the kind of wingers the club had when Daizen Maeda, Liel Abada, the still unfit Jota and Nicolas Kuhn were knocking around. In Yang Hyun-jun's absence - and week on week he appears to be spoken about as an absent world beater - James Forrest is the best winger they have. So says former captain Scott Brown, who knows Celtic players. Forrest is 35-years-old. This video can not be played 'M8 motorway between teams' - Halliday Neither does O'Neill, at present, have good instincts. Starting Sebastian Tounekti at Ibrox last week was an odd call and he changed it at half-time. Going with Sam Johnstone in goal at Rangers back-fired. Giving Luke McCowan his first start of the season on Sunday was another curious decision that didn't work. The midfielder was off the pace and never came out for the second half. O'Neill's famed ability to problem-solve and inspire has deserted him, for now. When set against the newfound organisation and vigour of this Rangers set-up then Celtic look jaded. Their supporters are being cast into a scenario that none of them want to be a part of - wondering aloud, or just quietly, if the icon still has it in him. He sounds like he does. If that is the case then he needs more from his assistants - or just better ones. From board level to coaching and playing, the whole operation looks humdrum and in need of a mighty shake. It's as if the 5-1 Champions League disintegration against LASK has removed not just confidence but heart and soul. There was little gumption at Ibrox in the 3-0 League Cup loss, there was only a brief early reaction against Ferencvaros in the Europa League before another beating, and now there's a third poor loss in a row and a fourth inside a month. This video can not be played O'Neill on back-to-back defeats by Rangers How quickly things turn. A few short weeks ago, as Rangers exited Europe to the sound of booing, McInnes didn't hold back when assessing the problems in his team. Not a possession team, not a pressing team, not a counter-attacking team, he said. They were also too young and too inexperienced, a collection of individuals but not a unit - no identity, no discernible style of play. What were weaknesses then are, in the blink of an eye, strengths now. Callowness has become youthful excellence. For the second straight week, Olwethu Makhanya was the most dominant and classy defender on the pitch. He's 22. For the second straight week the hardest-working and most effective attacking player was Ryan Naderi. He's 23. Dan Neil and Nico Raskin, aged 24 and 25, were once again hugely influential in the middle of the park. Neil looked fairly ordinary not that long ago. Now he's growing fast as Rangers captain. The oldest Rangers player from the start was James Penrice, who is 27. Celtic had six guys who were older than him in their team. The average age of the line-ups was 26.7 versus 24.4. McInnes has moulded them all into a group of players who have, against Celtic, shown maturity and togetherness. He has really hit on something. This video can not be played 'We’ve come a long way from Jablonec' Certain things stood out. At half-time, Rangers were not just ahead thanks to Naderi's goal, they were winning battles all over the pitch, just as they had done last Sunday. They were winning aerial duels by 67.6% to 32.4%, they had eight shots to Celtic's one, six on target to Celtic's zero. Camilo Duran had eight touches of the ball, Kevin Kelsy had 13 and Naderi 23. All the individual match-ups were more or less Rangers victories. Even when Celtic's club record-signing Kasper Hogh came on, not a lot changed. Rangers had more chances in the second half. Hogh got no service again, but he's beginning to look like a player so devoid of belief that even if service did come

title: Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe - him or the King?
description: Princess Diana's brother has caused a storm with his new memoir - the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg describes how she put his claims to the test.
body: Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buried When I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library. It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm. That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe? This video can not be played 'There was a lightness in his tone', says Earl Spencer about Charles' reaction to Diana's death That's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock. Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough"? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago? Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement. Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said. Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer. There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches. Princess Diana: My Sister's Story Watch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg. After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn. We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds". Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory. This video can not be played Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister Diana In the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said. Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past. Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book

title: No criminality in death of three sisters who died in sea
description: An investigation by Sussex Police into the deaths off the coast of Brighton has concluded.
body: The three sisters, here as teenagers with their father, died in the sea. From left to right, Jane Adetoro, Joseph, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters A police investigation into the deaths of three sisters in the sea off the coast of Brighton has concluded, with no evidence found of criminality or third-party involvement. The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, were recovered from the water near Black Rock on 13 May. A post-mortem examination found that all three women died by drowning, Sussex Police said. An inquest will aim to establish the facts of where, when and how the sisters died, the force added. The police investigation found that the sisters were dropped off by a taxi in Madeira Drive at about 22:20 BST on 12 May. No evidence was found to suggest that they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time, police said. Up to the point of discovery of their bodies, there was "no evidence the women came to harm by any individuals", the force added. Ch Supt Adam Hays said: "From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public's unanswered questions and their desire for answers. "Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident's core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss. "However, our inquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light." The bodies of the three sisters were recovered off Brighton beach in the early hours of 13 May An inquest opened into the deaths in May at Brighton & Hove Coroner's Court and is set to continue early October. The father of the sisters, who were all living together in Greenford, London, formally identified their bodies. In a moving tribute, their father previously said that "no words can truly describe the pain of losing three daughters in the prime of their lives". He described the three as "my joy, my strength, and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love". title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: Earl Spencer speaks to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the publication of his book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.
body: Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history". In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true". Among claims made in Swan Song: Diana, My Sister about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession. In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car. He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death." Describing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me." In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'." He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'." "I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffin Responding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?" On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers. He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. Talking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties. "I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained. "This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant." When put to him that the statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality." Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied. "It's a brother

title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he felt Charles had 'giddy tone' during call after Diana's death
description: Princess Diana's brother has been interviewed by the BBC ahead of the release of his book on the late Princess of Wales.
body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer has said he felt there was a "lightness" in the tone of the then-Prince Charles during a phone call following the death of his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Charles, who told him how he had broken the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," Earl Spencer told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me." Buckingham Palace released a rare statement on Wednesday in response to claims made by Earl Spencer in his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published on Tuesday. It said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday. title: Watch: Emotional Earl Spencer says he misses sister Diana every day
description: "This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her", Earl Spencer told presenter Laura Kuenssberg.
body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, said he misses his sister every day during an interview with the BBC. "That's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it," he told Laura Kuenssberg. His book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. He said one of the reasons the book is called Swan Song is because it is his "sign off" as Diana's brother and "final take on the situation". "This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her," he added. The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday. title: Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader
description: Devon County Council leader Julian Brazil tells the BBC Ed Davey is not the right person to lead the party.
body: Julian Brazil is leader of Devon County Council A Liberal Democrat council leader has said the party is "sleepwalking into irrelevance" and questioned whether Sir Ed Davey was the right leader. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon County Council, told the BBC the party was "lacking ambition" and "not saying the things that people can relate to". Asked whether Sir Ed was the right leader for the party, Brazil said "I wish he was" but "all the evidence is no". A Lib Dem spokesperson said the party was in "an incredibly strong position" under Sir Ed's leadership because he was focused on the "issues that really matter" such as the cost of living and the health service. "Under Ed's leadership we had our best result for a century, and achieved a record breaking streak of remarkable local election results," they added. "We are the most united party in Westminster and with Ed as leader we will stop Reform and the Conservatives and change our country after a decade of failing governments." Sir Ed led the party to record 72 MPs in the 2024 general election, but it has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK. Brazil told the BBC the Lib Dems had "allowed other parties to go steaming past us," adding that "something has to change within the party if we're going to move to the next level and it's not happening at the moment". He added: "I think there is a fantastic opportunity now for us to be right in the middle of politics and we don't seem to be. We seem to be peripheral. "We're lacking ambition, we're lacking courage of our convictions. We're not saying the things that people can relate to." He said the party was asking people to "vote for us because we're not somebody else". Brazil became the leader of Devon County Council in May last year after the Lib Dems overtook the Tories to become the largest party, but without overall control. His comments are echoed privately by some Lib Dem MPs, as they gather for their annual conference in Brighton. In an essay, written ahead of the conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?" She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless". Sir Ed, who was elected leader in 2020, told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg he shared the "frustration" of some of his MPs that they could not bring about "real change," blaming the UK's political system. But he insisted the party was gaining ground in council elections. "It's the most successful period that we've had," he said. "But outside elections, in terms of changing the law, which is what my MPs rightly want to do, and they're a very talented bunch, and they've actually had more success than all the other smaller parties, but they want to have more." Sir Ed was asked directly about Brazil's complaints during a conference Q+A session on Sunday. "I have know Julian for many years and he is good councillor," he said. "In Devon the party doing better than it has for decades - six MPs and local councils all across the area and in parts of Devon we are showing how to beat Reform. "I'm really proud of what we have been doing in Devon." Sir Ed got a vote of confidence from former coalition cabinet colleague Sir Vince Cable, who told a fringe meeting that he was the most successful leader in the party's history and "you can't argue with success". Speaking at another fringe meeting, pollster Luke Tryl said the Lib Dems were not cutting through nationally and needed a more compelling message. The executive director of More in Common said it was possible the party could take more seats in traditional Tory heartlands at the next election, potentially putting Sir Ed in a position to be deputy prime minister in a Labour-led government. But the risk for the party, he added, was the Tories saying "if you vote Lib Dem you will get Labour". title: Justice minister 'deeply concerned' over temporary release of convicted killer
description: Gary Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral of his father but absconded and remains at large.
body: The department of justice said minister Naomi Long "remains deeply concerned surrounding compassionate temporary release of Gary Anderson and his subsequent absconding" The justice minister remains "deeply concerned" about the circumstances surrounding the temporary release of a convicted murderer. The NI Prison Service (NIPS) refused Gary Anderson permission to attend his father's funeral but that decision was quashed by the courts. Anderson was released on Monday from Maghaberry Prison to attend the funeral but absconded and remains at large. He is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the 2018 murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry. The court service has now published the full 15 page judgement from the judicial review. It reveals the decision to refuse Anderson's request to attend the funeral was taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison. But the judge found that that decision "was based upon inaccurate information which was material to the key issue of the potential risks posed by the applicant". "The information which was considered was also materially disadvantageous to the applicant." That's a reference to an internal assessment of the likelihood of Anderson reoffending, which was wrongly recorded at a higher level than recorded in the internal system. A legal representative for the prison service admitted to the court that "information containing an increased score came, not from the duty governor's personal knowledge, but from a colleague. When the system was checked, the score was sitting at 27 (medium likelihood) and not 32 (high likelihood) as stated in the decision letter." The judge, Mr Justice Rooney, found "the duty governor clearly took account of this incorrect information when making his own risk assessment and when conducting a proportionality assessment". He invited the duty governor to review the decision but that offer was declined, in a move the judge described as "somewhat surprising". Gary Anderson, who is serving a 15-year sentence for the murder of Karol Kelly, remains on the run In a statement, the Justice department said that "this opportunity was not communicated by legal representatives to those within NIPS who held responsibility for the decision". "Updates provided to NIPS following the hearing, including legal readouts, did not indicate such an opportunity had been offered." Mr Justice Rooney granted Anderson temporary release with a number of conditions attached after finding that the prison service's decision was "flawed" and took into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors". He added "the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment is unlawful". The department said Minister Naomi Long "remains deeply concerned surrounding compassionate temporary release of Gary Anderson and his subsequent absconding". Following a review of the case, further information emerged regarding the handling of the case. "As soon as the minister was made aware of these issues, she instructed the director general of the Northern Ireland Prison Service to undertake an urgent investigation into these matters." "The minister is clear that it is important that all relevant facts are established and considered carefully, and she intends to update the assembly at the earliest opportunity as to the actions she will be taking to ensure that this happens." UUP leader Jon Burrows called the judgement "damning" Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader, Jon Burrows described the judgement as "damning" adding "it exposes catastrophic and inexplicable failures in senior decision-making, procedure and record-keeping at Maghaberry Prison". "The substantive decision to refuse Gary Anderson compassionate temporary release was, in my view, clearly correct. His subsequent absconding has only underlined the serious risk he presented. "However, that decision was catastrophically undermined by incorrect information, missing records and an extraordinary refusal to reconsider it when the court provided an opportunity to do so. "This was not a minor administrative error. The incorrect information went directly to the assessment of the risk posed by a convicted murderer and was expressly relied upon in refusing his release. "The decision collapsed because it relied upon materially incorrect information, the assessment supposedly supporting it could not be produced and the duty governor refused the opportunity to reconsider. "The family of Karol Kelly and the wider public deserve the full truth, urgent accountability and firm action to ensure that this can never happen again." title: Top Gear star Richard Hammond thanks emergency crews 20 years on from crash
description: Richard Hammond was seriously injured in a jet dragster crash at Elvington in September 2006.
body: In his post on Instagram, Hammond, pictured in 2023, thanked all those involved in saving him Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed. Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show. In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart". In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash. He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die." He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate". "Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said. Richard Hammond crashed in a jet-powered dragster at Elvington airfield near York in September 2006 A front tyre had blown on the car and Hammond said in his post that he did not scream during the ensuing crash. He explained that while "it wasn't frightening", it had "simply occurred to me that the next thing on my to do list was to die". The Top Gear star spent two weeks in a coma after the crash and returned to the show in early 2007. In 2023, he spoke of how he believed his memory may have been affected by the accident. In his post on social media marking the anniversary of the crash, Hammond said: "I am only here today to note this anniversary and write these words because of the work of the many people involved in rescuing me from the shattered car, flying me to hospital and treating me there." Hammond, pictured with Clarkson (centre) and May (right) presented Top Gear until 2015 Hammond went on to name members of the Yorkshire Air Ambulance and aftercare teams who helped him, saying he would be "forever grateful" to them. He said he would not have had the lucky career breaks, amazing adventures around the world and two of the "happiest, kindest, most wonderfully talented and loving daughters" if he had not been helped that day. "Thank you all from the bottom of my heart," he added. Hammond was also injured in a serious crash during a practice run for an electric car race 11 years later in Switzerland in June 2017, when his vehicle left the road, tumbled down a hillside and burst into flames close to a house. After leaving Top Gear with co-hosts Jeremy Clarkson and James May in 2015, the trio reunited for The Grand Tour, which they presented until 2024. title: Trump says his planned triumphal arch will double as a military complex to store ammunition
description: Trump said the updated plans were at the request of the US military and for national security purposes.
body: This video can not be played A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in April US President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones. In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes". The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said. He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility. "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are. Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue. At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument. Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles. The BBC has contacted the Department of Defence for more information on the updated plans. Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on. title: Man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
description: The remains of mother-of-three Joanne Sheen were found almost seven years after she went missing.
body: Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 A 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three. Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019. Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier. The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. The human remains were found at Padstow Walk in Feltham, south-west London Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force said led to more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, more than 300 statements taken and detailed searches at more than 10 addresses carried out using numerous vessels. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020, two months after she was last seen. An investigation led to a number of arrests on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no-one was charged and the case remained unsolved. Officers previously said she had no fixed address and did not own a vehicle or hold a bank account. The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the public London Fire Brigade attended a fire at Bedfont Pits on 5 August that damaged about two hectares of shrubland. The Metropolitan Police said human remains were found by a member of the public at the site near Bedfont Lakes Country Park a week later. Detectives in London handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen. title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
description: Residents living near Folkestone’s Grand Burstin Hotel relocated after safety inspectors' concerns.
body: Kent Police said the fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel was being treated as suspicious Residents living near to a fire-damaged seaside hotel in Folkestone have been evacuated over safety fears that the intensity of the basement blaze weakened the building's structure, the council has said. The blaze broke out at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours of Saturday, with about 280 people evacuated. Folkestone and Hythe District Council said 90 people were relocated from Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors. Kent Police said the blaze was being treated as suspicious and has appealed for witnesses. The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement A council spokesperson said the Pavilion Court residents had been given hotel accommodation in the town, adding that it was "working to arrange alternative housing for all affected residents while the Grand Burstin undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe". In a statement, Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "fully cooperating with Kent Police and supporting their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fire". It added: "We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and will provide any assistance or information required as their enquiries continue. "In the meantime, the safety and wellbeing of our guests and team members remains our priority." A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the hotel at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said, adding: "It's believed the fire started in the basement of the property." On Sunday, a fire service spokesperson said the firefighting operation had ended, and the scene had been handed over to Kent Police. Station manager Lawrence Pater said the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building and that the fire service was seeking advice from inspectors. Folkestone & Hythe District Council set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park for hotel residents evacuated on Saturday. Other local businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected. John Dighton said he was told to leave his Pavilion Court flat on Saturday evening Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday. The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days. "The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats." Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00. He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying. "We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions." Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel. The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm. "We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin. "We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was." The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks. "This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes." title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
description: The billionaire businessman told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.
body: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile. Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt". Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration. He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return. When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile". Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects". Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos. But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do." "Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said. Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules. Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK UK's third-biggest taxpayer to leave for Greece Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be about £15bn, also criticised the government for failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas, claiming it amounted to "insanity". "You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down. "If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening," he added. Sir Jim's company, Ineos, operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil. The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses." title: Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth
description: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper also proposes a Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU in a speech to her party conference.
body: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper says she has a plan for growth Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper has warned the UK's economic growth is being held back by a "computer says no" approach. She unveiled a 30-page growth plan aimed at removing barriers to business as part of her speech to the Lib Dem conference in Brighton. Cooper, who is also the party's Treasury spokesperson, said too many ideas, start-ups and research started in Britain but ended up being taken overseas. She also outlined a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU to reverse the economic damage of Brexit, that she claimed is currently costing the UK £90bn a year in lost tax revenue. Speaking on stage in Brighton, she said: "We build brilliant start-ups, and watch too many leave to scale somewhere else. We produce world-class research, and too little of it becomes a British product." "Britain has the potential," she went on. "The system holds it back. The computer says no. "This plan tears down the barriers to investment, to innovation, and to skills." Cooper called for the creation of a digital one-stop-shop service for businesses and investors, combining tax, regulatory, legal, Companies House, and general business services. Creating this within a new Department for Growth would simplify red tape and help small and medium-sized businesses compete and grow, she said. Cooper said a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU, would be the "single biggest growth lever we could pull" by deepening ties with Europe. "It could turbo-charge our economy and start to reverse the economic damage of Brexit which is currently costing us £90bn a year in lost tax revenue," she said. "In power, we will strike the deal on the single market, we will strike the deal on a customs union, we will strike the deal on defence." She claimed the Lib Dems would say "what no other party dares to say" that Britain "belongs at the heart of Europe, and we will take her there." Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime but he respected the result of the 2016 referendum and had no plans to "re-run" Brexit arguments. On Friday, Chancellor John Healey met EU ministers and asked them to let the UK into its Made in Europe scheme, aimed at protecting industries from unfair Chinese competition. Healey also pushed for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin the same day, as Burnham held his first official meeting with Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin in No 10 North. Seeking to differentiate the Liberal Democrats from rival parties, she said her party would avoid "more punishing tax hikes from Labour or painful spending cuts by the Conservatives and Reform UK". She attacked Healey for his speech earlier this month, which "contained no vision, no ideas, and absolutely no mention of Europe". Cooper also attacked Reform and the Conservatives for being "locked in a race to the bottom without a single credible costing between them". She highlighted how the new Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith had helped to deliver and defend the Liz Truss mini-budget, which she said "crashed the pound, it spiked your mortgage, it cost the country billions", and Nigel Farage defended the move. "But the worst could be yet to come: Farage is modelling himself on Trump," she said. "A President who has used the presidency to enrich himself, dismantled anti-corruption safeguards and pardoned crypto criminals. "We cannot allow that kind of politics to take hold in our country -- We cannot afford to allow Nigel Farage to win the keys to No 10 or let the Tories put him there."
