title: Chiltern Railways renationalised after 30 years
description: It joins Great British Railways as part of government plans to save money and improve services.
body: Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, has become part of the Great British Railways Chiltern Railways has been brought into public ownership after 30 years as a private company. It is the 10th rail company now under the Great British Railways (GBR), the government's programme of public ownership, which it says will save money and improve services. Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, operates services from London Marylebone to Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Warwickshire, as well as destinations in the West Midlands. The government said the transfer into public ownership would tackle overcrowding by introducing 25 additional daily services from December. The start of the first day of public ownership saw some disruption, with Chiltern warning the line between Birmingham and Marylebone, external was "expected to be much busier" due to the late notice of the West Coast Main Line closure affecting services at London Euston. The operator said it would run more trains than usual between the stations with significantly enhanced capacity. The Department for Transport (DfT) said the additional weekday services under GBR would provide 10,000 extra seats. They would include half hourly services during weekdays on the Chiltern Main Line between London and Birmingham, as well as more weekend services. Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy met staff at Marylebone Station on Thursday alongside the first Chiltern train in the GBR livery. "The most difficult thing on Chiltern is that it's shorter capacity and those extra trains and those extra seats will make a real difference to people travelling on this line up here from Marylebone every day," he said. Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy said the government hoped to "build a railway the country can trust and rely on" The rollout of the new trains would also improve accessibility and provide better Wi-Fi on board, the rail operator said. From Sunday, passengers whose train had been cancelled can use another operator's service two hours either side of their train to get to their destination at no extra cost, it added. Chiltern's interim managing director Tony Baxter said: "Sunday is a significant milestone for Chiltern Railways and we look forward to working together with the wider rail industry to deliver a better railway for everyone in Great Britain." The aim is for GBR to operate all passenger services by the end of 2027. Great Western Railway's services will be the next operator to be brought into public ownership, on 13 December. Lord Henry said: "Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time. "As we set up Great British Railways (GBR), we're putting passengers first. "It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes." title: MP calls for Yorkshire to get its own parliament
description: Harrogate Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon says Yorkshire devolution should go further than elected mayors.
body: Harrogate and Knaresborough Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon would like to see devolution go further A Liberal Democrat MP has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to go further with his devolution plans and give Yorkshire its own parliament. Harrogate and Knaresborough MP Tom Gordon said too much power was currently in the hands of elected mayors and a Yorkshire parliament would better reflect the region. Burnham has recently set out plans to give elected mayors more power over planning and tackling fly-tipping and said he would give them a share of income tax and business rates. But Gordon told BBC Politics North he believed that giving more money and powers to four separate Yorkshire mayoralties actually deepened divides in the county and a Yorkshire parliament would be "a good thing". Yorkshire currently has three Labour mayors - Oliver Coppard for South Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin for West Yorkshire and David Skaith for York and North Yorkshire - as well as Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire. The MP said if Wales, Scotland and London could have a parliament, then so should Yorkshire Gordon said Yorkshire had a population larger than Scotland and an economy larger than Wales, and, as such, it should have a parliament with a broader spectrum of views represented, rather than so much power resting with the four elected mayors. The Lib Dem said that while people had been told the recent local government reorganisation in North Yorkshire would "simplify" the situation, he believed that was not the case. "We've ended up with a new North Yorkshire Council at a higher tier and a Harrogate town council below it, so we've ended up with two tiers. In fact, there's a third tier when you throw in the regional mayor," he said. "So we've ended up with more tiers, but those powers have been moved upwards rather than down to people. "I think we owe it to have everyone have a seat at that table, not just all that power put in one person's hands." Gordon said he believed a Yorkshire parliament was the way forward "if it's good enough for Scotland, if it's good enough for Wales, if it's good enough for London". "We should have a model where we have broader people elected to it who can feed in all those issues into a Yorkshire-wide parliament. That, to me, is only a good thing," he said. The idea of a Yorkshire parliament has previously been advocated by the Yorkshire Party. Since 2014, the party has argued that it would create a more "engaged, democratic society". Meanwhile, when devolution deals were first being discussed, a proposal was put forward for one mayor for all of Yorkshire. The so-called "One Yorkshire" plan was backed by 18 of the region's 20 local councils, while Sheffield and Rotherham opted for a separate South Yorkshire solution. However, the then Conservative Communities Secretary James Brokenshire rejected the proposal and said the plan did "not meet our criteria". Deals were later done for the four counties within Yorkshire In a speech earlier this year, Burnham said decision-making needed to be "pushed to regions and local communities", adding that it would see "good growth in every postcode". David Skaith says Yorkshire's mayors work "collectively" Responding to Gordon's comments, Skaith said the Greater Manchester and Liverpool City Region, which has had devolved powers for longer, had worked "really well". But Skaith also said he believed that all views were represented within the current system. "It's not just four mayors who sit in Yorkshire, all our combined authorities are made up of those local authorities as well," he said. "So, I'm not making decisions sat in York and North Yorkshire on my own. It's in partnership with the two local authorities." Skaith pointed to the so-called "White Rose Agreement", signed by himself and the mayors of South and West Yorkshire, pledging to work closer on things like transport. “Rail is a classic case - Northern Powerhouse Rail - where we got particularly the working around York station and the wider area of North Yorkshire," he said. "We have got that collective buy-in as to what we want for Yorkshire for rail. "That's why we've got so far with government, because we work collectively as mayors, because we know our transport is so interconnected." When he was prime minister, David Cameron, together with Chancellor George Osborne, previously introduced "devolution deals". Successive Conservative governments have extended those deals and powers for regional mayors. However, York Conservative councillor Chris Steward warned that a parliament for Yorkshire would be "an absurd, costly and bureaucratic nonsense". "I am a proud Yorkshireman, having lived here all my life," he said. "But while it is a county for so much - from the scenery to county cricket to all the things making it famous - as we saw in the discussions about devolution, it is not a functional economic geography and politics viewed across the region would not work. "People do not want yet another layer of politicians and the related expenses." Reform UK has been approached for comment. title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
description: Sir Ed blamed Donald Trump's war with Iran for damaging the UK economy and pushing fuel prices up.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living. The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump. Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy. "Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding." In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%. He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs. Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already. "Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them." title: Family shares hidden cost of cancer care
description: Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma when she was three.
body: The family of Maya, 13, from Hythe, say they have faced an increased financial burden while they care for her after she was diagnosed with neuroblastoma The parents of a teenage girl with a rare form of childhood cancer say the hidden costs of caring for their daughter have left them in fear of losing their home. Maya, 13, from Hythe in Kent, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma at three years old, but relapsed in 2023 having been in remission for five years. Her mother, Dellanie, said the pressure of paying a mortgage and bills whilst she and her husband, Terry, are working less to care for Maya is continuing to take its toll on their family of five. Dellanie, an NHS nurse, said: "Whilst your child is poorly and you are fighting for her life, the bills don't stop coming." She added: "My husband has lost his income as he is caring for Maya, and these days you need two people working just to keep your head above water. "It has been very, very difficult but our aim has always been to to look after our child as well as each other. "I always put a brave face on - of course I'm hurting, but I can't be in the corner crying." Maya, who her mother described as a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music, was first diagnosed with neuroblastoma near her adrenal gland when she was three-years-old. Dellanie says Maya is a "larger than life person" who loves animals and music Neuroblastoma is a rare cancer which mainly affects children under five-years-old and around 100 children are diagnosed with it a year in the UK, according to Cancer Research UK. After initially going into remission, Maya's neuroblastoma returned three years ago, and has since been cared for by specialist teams including at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, and Great Ormond Street Hospital. In 2025, during a clinical trial of CAR T-cell therapy, a technique currently used to treat some types of leukaemia and lymphoma, Maya developed a brain injury which Dellanie said left her "profoundly disabled". Her disability meant Terry had to leave his job to care for Maya full time, while Dellanie reduced her working hours to care for her, and support her husband. Dellanie said: "I just have to be grateful for what we have got. "At the moment, Maya is a fighter and there is so much fight in her." Charity Young Lives vs Cancer says families of children with cancer face average extra costs of around £700 a month, and an average loss of income of about £6,000 per household. Sonia Malik, the charity's associate policy director, said: "We find people are having to dip into savings, and most of these costs are immediate. "It impacts the whole family and their lives are thrown into chaos. "The financial stress should be the last thing families have to think about." Malik said that some support is available for cancer patients and their carers, such as financial support from charities, disability benefits and carer's allowance, but it can take time for families to receive benefits support. title: Townsend run over by pitch roller in Thailand
description: Former England winger Andros Townsend jokes that playing Stoke away "wasn't so bad after all" following a bizarre incident before a game in Thailand.
body: Andros Townsend moved to Thailand in 2025 when he joined Kanchanaburi Power Former England winger Andros Townsend joked that playing Stoke away "wasn't so bad after all" following a bizarre incident in Thailand in which he was run over by a pitch roller. The 35-year-old former Tottenham, Luton and Crystal Palace forward plays for PT Prachuap in Thai League 1. Townsend was warming up before a match at Pattani on Saturday when a member of staff appeared to lose control of a heavy pitch roller. Townsend's left leg briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he was unhurt. He came off the bench late on in a 3-0 win., external Townsend, who won 13 caps for England, made light of the incident on Instagram, referencing one of his recent posts in which he compared a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke's Bet365 Stadium. He wrote:, external "It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all. Swipe to see why." title: Littler could boycott Dutch events over booing
description: Luke Littler threatens a boycott of playing in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
body: Littler has won back-to-back PDC World Championship titles World champion Luke Littler has threatened to stop playing in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. The referee stopped the match during his narrow win against Nathan Aspinall in the last eight on Saturday to warn the hostile crowd about its behaviour, before play resumed. It followed Littler also being booed during his win against home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday. Littler has faced similar treatment in Germany and has stopped playing in European Tour events in the country. Asked if he was prepared to take a similar stance for Dutch events, the 19-year-old told Online Darts: "100%." Littler, who is expected to play at the European Championship in Dortmund in October, added: "With the Germans, I haven't been for a long time, we will have to see in Dortmund whether it changes or stays the same. "If the Dutch stay like this, then I'm not going to do any Euro tours over there. There's just no point in me travelling, wasting my time whilst I'm getting booed. "I just want to play my darts, obviously sign autographs. "The past two nights, I've done nothing, I've just walked off stage and not thanked anyone. There's no point thanking everyone when they are booing me." Littler was also booed during a win over Rob Cross at the PDC World Championship in December. After the match, he said: "I'm not bothered [by the booing]. Really not bothered. You guys pay for tickets and you pay for my prize so thanks for booing me." title: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
description: The chancellor is facing intense political pressure which will increase if his party struggles in Sunday's polls.
body: Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future. These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved. There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve. He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external. According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place. Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election. How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise. Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig. Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours. But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU. Reinhart thinks the chancellor is out of touch with the German public In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away. "Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down." He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him. "He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public." Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited. But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him. The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left. His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave. Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it. But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom. Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restorting trust in the CDU lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel". But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder. Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons". Rohloff believes there are people with "better feelings" towards the public than the chancellor "Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well". Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public." Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn. But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time. The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis. A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression. How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? title: 'Beat the Aussies' - new England coach Fleming's key aim
description: New Test coach Stephen Fleming says he shares English cricket’s “obsession” with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to “beat the Aussies”.
body: This video can not be played England job one of the most prestigious in cricket - Fleming New Test coach Stephen Fleming said he shared English cricket's "obsession" with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to "beat the Aussies". Fleming was speaking to the media for the first time since being appointed in July and ahead of taking charge for the tour of South Africa in December. Like his predecessor Brendon McCullum, Fleming is from New Zealand, the "little cousin" to Australia, in his words. The next Ashes series is in the UK next summer, when England will look to defeat the Australians for the first time since 2015 and avenge a dismal 4-1 defeat down under last winter. Asked if England are too obsessed with beating Australia, Fleming told BBC Sport: "No, because I have an obsession with it as well. New Zealand has an obsession with it, we love it. "We want to beat the Aussies. We're heavily linked to England performances. We have a deep desire to beat Australia in everything, as the little cousin. We are linked, and I'm incredibly excited about being part of it. "You don't think you're ever going to get that opportunity. To have that opportunity and be part of it, I can't wait. "I want to be my best self and have a team that represents itself in the best possible way. I've got a vision of that and it's aspirational. It will be brilliant." Listen to the full Stephen Fleming interview on the TMS podcast Fleming on England discipline, Stokes, late arrival and coaching styles Fleming, the former New Zealand captain, did not taste victory in any of the 14 Tests he played against Australia. He succeeds his former team-mate McCullum, who was sacked as Test coach earlier this summer, but remains as boss of the white-ball team. England won only two of McCullum's final 10 Tests in charge, including the hammering in Australia. Part of the criticism of England under McCullum and former captain Ben Stokes was their inability to adapt to the changing situations of Test cricket, as well as a lack of attention to detail. Fleming is a great friend of McCullum – the pair are business partners. He described the difference between the two as being: "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible." On whether a Test team should have a brand or style, Fleming said: "I don't think so. The greatest thing for a team to do is to be able to play conditions and situations. "I'd love people to say we are well-planned, there's a discipline and a really strong basic structure to what we're doing, but there's also a bit of flair." Stephen Fleming, left, and Brendon McCullum, right, played 32 Tests together between 2004 and 2008 The final months of McCullum's reign were dogged by late-night drinking controversies, which continued after England changed the Test coach. On Friday, Derbyshire Police announced they had closed an investigation involving England pace bowler Brydon Carse following allegations of an assault last month. Though Carse will face no action from the police, he now faces an investigation from the Cricket Regulator. He remains available for England selection, albeit has not been part of a squad in any format since the Derby incident. "There are standards," said Fleming. "We pick on runs and wickets primarily, but I think it's foolish not to also say there are standards that need to be set. "You need to behave in accordance with your position. We're in a very privileged position, and it's understanding that privilege and what goes along with it. It can't be convenient. You can't be when it suits you to do the right things, then when you don't want it to suit you, not. "You've got to live it every day. If we can create something when you want to live it every day and better, then that's really powerful." Fleming was at Old Trafford for England's defeat of Sri Lanka in the third T20 on Saturday. Earlier in the week he visited a number of counties and met Stokes during Durham's draw against Worcestershire. Stokes abruptly retired from international cricket in July and has a previous relationship with Fleming from their time together with Chennai Super Kings at the Indian Premier League. But Fleming said he had too much "respect" for Stokes' decision to attempt to coax him out of retirement. "He was in a great space, really happy, enjoying his time with Durham," said Fleming. "He's got a good winter planned with the family and is very much at peace with his decision. When a player makes that decision to retire, I respect that decision 100%. "To try to turn that around and question that is wrong. I know how much goes into that type of decision, and I respect that." Almost two months after being appointed Test coach, Stephen Fleming outlined what the England team may look like under his stewardship. He was calm, measured and authoritative, perhaps showing he is exactly the sort of leader England need after a chaotic period on and off the pitch. There were also signs of Fleming's character and sense of humour. He joked he has a "stress fracture of the left ear" after all the phone calls he has had with those connected with the England team, then laughed about occasionally turning up in fancy dress to relax the environment of his Chennai Super Kings team. Most revealing was the description of his relationship with Brendon McCullum – "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible". There were plenty of times during McCullum's reign as Test coach where those long-odds bets were placed, while Fleming seems much more likely to play the percentages. The two are great friends, which should help with a split-coaching dynamic that has not always served England well in the past. "Big brother" was one way the Fleming-McCullum dynamic was referred to, and there was a sense that England now have a grown-up in charge

title: New £1m grant to help groups protect green spaces
description: The cash can be used by local communities to protect threatened green spaces and wildlife sites.
body: The grant from the Summerfield Charitable Trust aims to help protect woodland and green spaces A £1m fund has been set up to help local communities protect threatened green spaces. The Summerfield Charitable Trust said the money would help groups buy and safeguard local woodlands and wildlife sites when they come up for sale. It is part of a new initiative from the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund and the Gloucestershire Local Nature Partnership. "We need an initiative like this now more than ever," said Diane Hill, chair of the Gloucestershire Nature and Climate Fund. "Once an important green space is lost, it can be lost for good." Under pressure council 'seeking second bailout' Granddad, 82, to take on 10k as part of family team Fans line street for EMF star's final farewell Hill said: "We know there are people across Gloucestershire who desperately want to protect woodland or wildlife sites in their community but when that land comes up for sale, they simply don't have the time or resources to compete with a private buyer. "This funding means we can help them when it really matters. "We can provide money to act quickly, bring in the legal and ecological expertise they need." Recent examples of communities taking action to protect land include Daisybank, Lott Meadow and Southcourt Green, in Cheltenham, as well as Juniper Hill Field and Heavens Valley in Stroud. Another was Rodborough Fields, near Stroud, where a public campaign to protect the woodland from development led to it being brought into community ownership. John Bloxsom, chair of the Rodborough Fields and Frome Banks Preservation Group, said: "It's good news that a fund like this has been set up." The group successfully bought nine acres of Rodborough Fields thanks to a Crowdfunding campaign that raised £200,000 but now the future of a further 30 acres is uncertain after it was put on the market this summer. Bloxsom said that their latest bid had been rejected in favour of a rival bid from an unknown party, which was "causing concern in the community". Rodborough Fields Preservation Group said it wanted to maintain the area's biodiversity Angela France, one of the directors at Daisybank CIC, which helped to saved the field in Cheltenham from development last year, said she was "delighted" to hear about the new fund. "Local green spaces are so important to us now," she said. "I see more and more local communities getting together to protect them." She said since buying the land, the group had organised litter picking, butterfly counts and an ecological survey in order to plan how best to maintain the field so that local wildlife could thrive. A community event is also organised for 24 October to gather views on the future of the field. The new fund has also been designed to contribute to nature recovery across the county, while addressing unequal access to nature. David Owen, chair of trustees at The Summerfield Charitable Trust, said the initiative "has the potential to create a lasting legacy for nature, communities and future generations across Gloucestershire". He added: "Through this investment, we hope to enable communities to act quickly when opportunities arise, protect important natural assets and create benefits for wildlife, health and wellbeing that will endure for many years to come." title: Wembley welcomes 'rabid' college football fans
description: Wembley hosted its first American college football game on Saturday, but did the event meet expectations?
body: Tate Nagy of Kansas scored the opening touchdown with a 72-yard punt return It wasn't even gameday in London but the rivalry had already begun. Fans of the Kansas Jayhawks and Arizona State Sun Devils gathered at a pre-game party in Waterloo on Friday. Kansas fans shouted their rallying cry "Rock Chalk, Jayhawk", while their rivals replied with "ASU, ASU". After hosting 42 NFL games since 2007, this was London's introduction to a different kind of American football and a different kind of fandom. Wembley hosted its first American college football game on Saturday, with 46,523 fans attending the inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC). UJC organisers vowed to create an authentic college gameday in London, and they began with tailgate parties. Fans enjoy food, drink and music for hours before the game, and they are far bigger for college games than in the NFL. One American fan told BBC Sport she prefers the tailgate to the game itself. The main tailgate at Wembley opened at 10am - seven hours before kick-off - with Kansas City rapper Tech N9ne helping to entertain the crowd. Arizona State alumni held their own party, with nearly 2,000 fans packed in, while ASU's marching band and cheerleaders performed on stage. But the wildest party was on Wembley Way, where Fox Sports had an outdoor studio for its live pre-game show. It was surrounded by fans and the Fox crew kept trying to stoke the rivalry, while the Kansas and ASU bands battled it out on Wembley Way and on the pitch before kick-off. This video can not be played American college football comes to London The pageantry and passion of college football is what makes it different. NFL fans often choose their team, whereas college teams tend to be passed down through families. "You feel a loyalty to your lineage," said Kansas fan Hannah, who added that college football fans are not just fanatical but "rabid". BBC Sport spoke to families at Wembley who have had multiple generations attend the same school and alumni who now live all over the US but travel thousands of miles to watch their alma mater. Current ASU student Sophie said her family "bleeds maroon and gold". Her friend Amelia has ASU merchandise all over the house. She just got a car that's maroon too. About 15,000 fans travelled from the US for Saturday's game - 9,000 rooting for ASU and 6,000 Kansas. College games in the US rarely have away fans but, with both teams having a sizable contingent at Wembley, as well as playing at a neutral venue, some visitors said the atmosphere was like a play-off game. The Arizona State Sun Devils went into Saturday's game as favourites Fans from 35 countries bought tickets and, as with NFL games in London, they represented several teams, not just those playing. Neutrals wore NFL jerseys and college jerseys, of bigger schools such as Oklahoma, Miami and Texas. There were even some British university jerseys. More than 100 universities in the UK have American football teams, and UJC organisers targeted those players, partly because, as students, they often find college football more relatable than the NFL. They formed partnerships with the British American Football Association, British Universities and Colleges Sport and the Jacksonville Jaguars to establish links with the grassroots game in the UK. The UJC has helped to train more than 1,050 British coaches and referees this year, some of whom were at Saturday's game. Cambridge University player Alex said it has been "cool" to learn the stories of Kansas and ASU and he would probably go to more college games in future "if they're teams we can rally behind". Jaren Hamilton made the game's best play with a 100-yard kick-off return at the start of the second half to help ASU to a 17-7 lead After planning for an attendance of 60,000, Wembley was about half full at 46,523, with some ticketholders moved to the bottom tier to keep the top tier empty. Although there were some big plays, the game was not as entertaining as anticipated as ASU claimed a 24-17 win that flattered Kansas. Music acts played throughout the game and there was a light show in the third quarter. It gave UK fans a flavour of college football, but it lacked the pomp and circumstance of regular games in the US. There were fewer band members and cheerleaders than normal, and the crowd was not as loud as during ASU home games – they averaged 54,000 last season. Both teams took 105 players (or student-athletes), 90% of which did not have a passport before this trip. Many fans and members of the coaches' families also visited London for the first time, and ASU head coach Kenny Dillingham said they had "an experience they will remember for the rest of their lives". Kansas head coach Lance Leipold added that the hospitality was outstanding, while the hotel and practice facility "was a win". Both teams are part of the Big 12 Conference, whose commissioner Brett Yormark said: "It exceeded my expectations, from the crowd to the logistics to how the local community has embraced us. It's been fantastic, so we want more." UJC organisers have signed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley, and Yormark says other Big 12 colleges are interested in playing in London. Big 12 teams also played two games in Dublin over the past 13 months, and the conference could expand to another international market. Yormark said: "There's not a two-week period where I don't get a call to say 'take some of your product to this country or that country', so we're exploring that right now." He said there will be an announcement about next year's London game "within the next month or two". That will give UK fans plenty of time to swot up on the next two teams who will make their presence known across the pond. Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? title: 'You never quite know what you're going to pull out'
description: The group is marking a decade of fishing everything from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo out of the harbour.
body: Volunteers are celebrating a decade of cleaning up Bristol Harbour A voluntary clean-up group is marking a decade of finding unusual items in Bristol Harbour, ranging from an inflatable doll to a Nintendo Switch. Clean Up Bristol Harbour was launched in September 2016 in a bid to remove plastic pollution from in and around Bristol's waterways. The group has fished out some unusual items from the harbour in the past 10 years, including a message in a bottle containing a note in Spanish, a kettle, tennis balls, glasses and single shoes as well as the inflatable doll and Nintendo Switch. "You never quite know what you're going to pull out of Bristol Harbour," said founder and Bristol resident Chloe Juyon. Volunteers have fished out a whole range of unusual items from the harbour over the years "Some of the things we've found over the years have definitely made us laugh but there is a serious point behind it. "So much floating rubbish simply can't be reached from the harbourside. "Getting volunteers onto the water was always a big part of what I wanted Clean Up Bristol Harbour to become." However, the future of the project remains uncertain because funding was coming to an end, Juyon said. Volunteers found a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper Juyon founded the group after she was struck by the amount of rubbish floating around her boat while she was coxing on the River Avon at high tide. The group has since been taken on by adventure sports centre All Aboard Watersports. During recorded monitoring between 2021 and 2023, some 236 volunteers removed more than 880kg (1940lb) of waste from Bristol Harbour with almost 390kg (859lbs) sent for recycling. Nipple tattooist 'frustrated' by online censorship Dealer jailed for firearms and drug offences 'Helping people with music is my mission' Much of the rubbish includes everyday waste, such as plastic packaging, bottles, cans, polystyrene and takeaway rubbish. But over the years, volunteers have fished out some unusual items, such as a Nespresso capsules, alcohol bottles, plastic cones, clothing - including thermals still in their packaging - and even a packet of butcher's tripe mix. One particularly unusual find was a Marathon-branded chocolate wrapper - the UK name for Snickers until 1990 - found during a clean-up several years ago. Reflecting on the anniversary, Juyon said: "There were just five of us at that first clean-up in 2016. "I stepped away from running the project several years ago, so seeing it reach its tenth birthday is quite amazing. "For me, it really demonstrates the power of community." To mark the 10th anniversary, the group will hold a community clean-up event later to mark World Cleanup Day., external Members of the public can take part in a self-guided litter pick from 10:00 to 12:00 BST, either on foot around the harbourside or using their own craft. With its current funding coming to an end, All Aboard Watersports has launched a Crowdfunder bid aiming to raise an initial £5,000 to help continue the project. Charley Peak-Payne, from All Aboard Watersports, said having a clean harbour has had a positive impact on people who use the harbourside for waters sports and boating. "The direct effect it has had on wildlife has been a gradual but noticeable change," he said. "The water that they are swimming in is considerably cleaner - to the point that we are now running swimming events in the harbour too, something that due to pollution would never have happened 10 years ago." title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
description: Suppliers tell the government that Britain's manufacturing future lies beyond car production.
body: JLR suppliers say skills and factories could be redirected into aerospace and defence Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline. In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market". The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs. The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production. JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood. Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs. David Roberts said large-scale car production in the UK faced long-term decline The group, which includes Coventry-based Evtec, Solihull-based Artifex and the Confederation of British Metal Forming, said suppliers faced rising energy costs, growing overseas competition and increasing pressure from vehicle manufacturers sourcing components abroad. David Roberts, chairman of Evtec, said manufacturers believed high-volume car production in the UK was entering a decade of decline. Speaking on BBC Politics Midlands, he said: "We want to take action today rather than wait for that to happen." Roberts argued there was a "very big opportunity" for manufacturers to redirect skills, factories and investment into the UK's expanding aerospace and defence sectors. The letter said automotive suppliers already possessed many of the capabilities needed to support aircraft, defence equipment and military vehicles, but warned firms needed help to make the transition. "The capacity exists. The people exist. What is missing is the bridge," it said. The open letter calls for support to help automotive firms enter aerospace and defence The manufacturers called for lower industrial energy costs, support to help firms qualify for aerospace and defence contracts, and a West Midlands programme to accelerate the shift into those sectors. The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metal Forming, which represents about 75,000 workers. According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, Chinese-owned brands accounted for about 15% of new car registrations in the UK in 2025 and 2026. The suppliers argued that competitors overseas benefited from lower energy costs, greater automation and, in some cases, government subsidies. A Treasury spokesperson said Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds had met JLR and trade union representatives following the redundancy announcement and pointed to government backing for electric vehicle production through the £2.5bn DRIVE35 programme. The government said manufacturers were also expected to benefit from measures to reduce industrial electricity costs and support investment in the sector. title: An arrest, a defection and a new leader - how Reform's 'challenging' week unfolded
description: How an extraordinary seven days that rocked the party unfolded.
body: Dan Thomas made his last appearance as Reform Wales leader on the BBC's Politics Wales "It's been challenging but we've come through it," said Reform's chief whip in the Senedd, Llŷr Powell, as he reflected on the past seven days. The week began with the party's leader in Wales being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Dan Thomas said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong". Confirmation of his arrest was swiftly followed by news of a Reform Senedd member's defection to Plaid Cymru. This is the story of how that "challenging" week unfolded. Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice Last Sunday morning, Thomas was at the BBC's offices in Cardiff to appear as a guest on the Politics Wales programme. Later that day, he was arrested before being released on bail. Journalists got wind of the arrest on Monday evening, which is also when senior Reform figures in Wales began to find out. A few people at Reform HQ in London, including Nigel Farage, had already been told. Helen Jenner filled in for Dan Thomas at First Minister's Questions and is expected to replace Thomas On Tuesday morning, Reform Members of the Senedd (MSs) gathered for their weekly group meeting. With the "rumour mill going wild" there was "confusion" within the group. Dan Thomas was not present, and the MSs were not given the full picture, but they were warned that the party faced "a tough few days". It was soon announced that Thomas would not take his usual spot in the chamber for First Minister's Questions and would be replaced by his deputy, Helen Jenner. At that point Reform said his absence was due to "personal reasons". But as time went on it became clear that the story was about to break. A legal letter sent to media organisations by a Reform barrister would not be enough to block the reporting of Thomas's arrest. BBC Wales and others had secured confirmation that Thomas had been arrested and so the party needed to act. That's when Thomas sent a WhatsApp message to his party's MSs explaining the situation. Some of them were in the chamber at the time. In his media statement Thomas said he was standing down as leader. He remains a Reform MS for Casnewydd Islwyn. Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's defection emerged soon after Dan Thomas stood down as leader Then came the next bombshell as it emerged that Reform MS for Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was defecting to Plaid Cymru. Reform only found out about it after BBC Wales asked the party for a response to the story. Moments earlier she had been sitting on the Reform benches and had been due to speak for the party in the chamber. Most of Plaid Cymru's MSs - including some government ministers - were only told about the defection plan at their group meeting earlier in the day. The defection needed the group's approval and some Plaid MSs wanted assurances that Cooper-Lesadd fully understood what it meant to be a Plaid Cymru member. The defection was approved with the necessary two thirds majority. But it wasn't backed by everyone. At a hastily arranged news conference in the Senedd, Cooper-Lesadd said her switch to Plaid followed "a period of reflection and deliberation" and that she had found "the right political home". The move was completely unconnected to Dan Thomas's arrest. Neither Cooper-Lesadd nor Plaid will say how or when the talks over the defection began, only that the process had gone on for "a while" and she had been on a "journey". The defection, just four months on from May's Senedd election, has raised fresh questions about the electoral process where voters were required to back a party rather than an individual. Jess Blair, from the Electoral Reform Society, said that while defections were "nothing new" there was more of an "accountability gap" given the Welsh voting system. "When this electoral system was put in place a review mechanism was also built into that process and what we need now is to really see that review take place," she said. By Wednesday, Reform's focus was on appointing a new leader. A party official from London came to explain the process to MSs, and Dan Thomas was also at that meeting. As is the case when a new leader is needed, various names were being discussed. James Evans was seen as one obvious contender. When it was announced that he would make a media statement reporters scrambled to hear what he had to say. "Having consulted with my family...I will not be putting my name forward," he said, despite "a majority" of the party's MSs backing him to take over. By Thursday morning it was looking increasingly likely that Helen Jenner would be the next leader. While Reform UK bosses in London have not had any formal input to the process, sources say there have been "signals" that Jenner - a Farage ally since the UKIP days - would be seen as a good choice in HQ. Confirmation of Jenner's appointment is expected as soon as Monday. "I feel we're more united than ever," said Llŷr Powell. "For us it's a new start next week and that's what we're building on." title: When did grey squirrels start posing a threat to reds?
description: A pair of grey squirrels was reportedly brought to the United Kingdom by a Cheshire banker in 1876.
body: Grey squirrels, native to North America, carry a virus which is deadly to red squirrels Endangered red squirrel populations have plummeted from about 3.5 million to less than 300,000 in the UK, with their grey-haired rivals continuing to thrive. But when exactly did the squirrel stand-off begin and how bad has the situation become? In England, the situation is particularly dire for reds. The Woodland Trust reckons there are only 39,000 of them left, while the Save Our Reds campaign thinks just 15,000 remain, including in conservation areas such as Formby on Merseyside. In May the group warned that red squirrels, which "still cling on" in parts of northern England, could disappear entirely within 25 years. In stark contrast, since their introduction from North America in the 19th Century, greys have thrived at the expense of their distant cousins, which compete for habitats and carry lethal viruses. The first verifiable importation of greys, external is widely understood to have come 150 years ago, when a Victorian banker named Thomas V. Brocklehurst is said to have released a pair of greys into Henbury Park, near Macclesfield in Cheshire, that he had brought back from a business trip to the United States. The rest, they say, is history and nobody back then would have realised the unintended lasting consequences of his actions. According to Graham Paskett from the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, there are now between 2.5 million and 2.7 million greys in the UK. A petition earlier this year calling for urgent action to conserve red squirrels attracted more than 75,000 signatures Jackie Foott, from the British Red Squirrel conservation group, told the BBC that reds and greys cannot coexist in the same location and that to protect the reds you have to "get rid of the greys - we realised that a while ago". She explained: "The grey squirrel is a pest, non-native, invasive species. "People don't realise just how much damage they are doing to trees, crops and properties - they cause at least £40m damage to forests and forestry services each year." But why can reds and greys not live cheek by jowl? "Greys outcompete reds for habitat and food - they don't actually physically attack them but they do bother them," said Foott. "Secondly, greys have squirrel pox - it doesn't affect them but they transmit it to red squirrels and it's fatal for them. It's a horrible disease and causes them ulcers and blindness." So what solutions are available? "Fertility control isn't available now - and has the effect of affecting other species, including reds," said Foott. "Gene therapy is probably at least 10 years away. "For now, the only way is lethal control - by shooting or trapping." The collapse of the native red squirrel population over the past 150 years Paskett, though, thinks there could be an effective additional way to control grey squirrel numbers within the next five years. He said the Red Squirrel Survival Trust was jointly funding a field trial by the government's Animal and Plant Health Agency. Beginning "later this year or early next year" Paskett said his organisation had "developed the means to deliver oral contraceptives to grey squirrels using a 'hopper' which sees the squirrel lift up a lid" to access them. Because greys typically weigh 500g - approximately twice that of reds, only they can access the contraceptive. If the field trial is successful, Paskett hopes landowners and forest rangers will be able to sign up to the scheme. For now, though, Foott said shooting and trapping were the main options. However, she said: "The reintroduction of pine martens can help. Because they are a native species in the UK, they evolved together with red squirrels. "They do eat red squirrels but the reds know to quickly get out of their way and will send out the alarm signal to the rest of the colony. "The greys are a little bit stupid and will say 'hello, I haven't seen you before' and the pine marten will get them!" When asked about the grey squirrels' UK origin story, Foott said: "Nobody really knows - there are several records but it doesn't really matter." So why were greys imported in the first place? Foott said: "Somebody said 'Wouldn't they look cute running around my garden?' More than a century later, she said experienced British Red Squirrel volunteers were now working with farmers and landowners to control grey squirrel populations near red colonies. In May, a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the government was protecting endangered red squirrels by tackling the threat of non-native grey squirrels. title: Families missing out on NHS money for healthy food
description: Figures show as few as 64% of eligible families are claiming NHS money to buy milk, fruit and veg.
body: NHS money is available to help families on the lowest incomes with young children to pay for healthy food and milk Charities are warning that thousands of low income families are missing out on money they are eligible to claim to buy fresh fruit, vegetables, and milk. Families earning less than £400 a week are entitled to weekly NHS Health Start payments including pregnant women and those with children under four years old who are entitled to £4.65 a week. Figures found take-up of the scheme is as low as 64% in some parts of the North East and Cumbria. Newcastle-based charity Feeding Britain said hikes in food prices meant "every layer of protection possible" was needed for families on the lowest incomes. The government has been approached for comment. Amelia, from Sunderland, has a two-year-old son and does not qualify for the scheme, but said she understood the struggle families face. "It's expensive to feed the whole family. It's getting ridiculous really. It's not just food, it's the nappies and wipes and days out." She said she tries to batch cook to save money and eat the same meals as her son. Amy, a working mother with a toddler, said: "He was on formula and it was expensive for the tins. They never had offers or promotions." She said she often eats less so her son can have more food. Amelia from Sunderland said food prices were "ridiculous" Families with a baby under 12 months old can claim £9.30 a week as part of the NHS Health Start scheme. However, figures suggest thousands of eligible families have not enrolled. The latest NHS figures on the take-up are from 2022. Redcar and Cleveland Council had the highest enrolment - 87% of entitled families were claiming the weekly payments. In the former Eden Council area, only 64% of those eligible were enrolled and in the former Copeland Council area, take-up was 68%. In Sunderland and Stockton, 81% of eligible families were enrolled. Take-up was lower in Newcastle and Middlesbrough, where just 77% of those entitled to payments received them. Across the region that meant 6,149 eligible families were missing out. Penny Walters works for the charity Feeding Britain and said the value of the healthy start scheme was "worthless" Penny Walters works for Feeding Britain which supports some of the most deprived families in the North East. She said Healthy Start payments were not increasing in line with inflation. "£4.65 - what can you buy with that?" she said. "If you've got a baby you get £9.30 and you can buy one tin of formula with that. "But how many tins have you got to go through a week with a baby? It's worthless." She said professionals were still finding stark levels of poverty in the region, including a malnourished baby admitted to hospital in Newcastle. "The only thing the mam could afford to give the baby was sugar water," she said. "That's not right. We're not in Dickensian England. Where was the support? Why is this happening?" Director of Feeding Britain, Andrew Forsey, wants the Healthy Start scheme to have an auto-enrollment system Several national charities are calling for the Healthy Start scheme to be updated, including Sustain, The Food Foundation, and Feeding Britain. Newcastle-based Feeding Britain director Andrew Forsey said: "Given the increases in food prices that are coming our way in the months ahead we need every layer of protection possible for families on the lowest incomes." He said the government should make Healthy Start an auto-enrollment scheme for eligible families. "The government can use the data and the technology at its disposal to register parents automatically, just to lift some of the burden off parents' shoulders," he said. Labour MP for South Shields, Emma Lewell, said she had been campaigning to try and ensure the allocated money does not return to the Treasury if unclaimed. "It just feels like such a no brainer," she said. "The money is there, the government have it, it's not going to the people who need it and there's things we can do to make sure it does, but they're not being done. Charities are also calling on the Department for Health and Social Care to release updated figures on enrollment on the scheme. The NHS stopped publishing data in January 2023 due to an inaccuracy that was discovered and this has not since been rectified. It means charities and local authorities cannot track who might be missing out. The department has been approached for comment. title: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, says Russia
description: An oil refinery was also reportedly hit in Moscow, and flights were suspended at two capital airports.
body: Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery in Moscow after reports of an overnight Ukrainian drone attack At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said. Vorobyev said 249 drones had been shot down, and he reported fires in several residential houses. A local warehouse was also ablaze. In the capital Moscow, an oil refinery was damaged, and flight restrictions were in place at two airports. Earlier, a Ukraine official said seven people, including two children, were killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday. Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs. In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Vorobyev said a 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino after a drone hit a three-storey residential building. Another five people - including two children - were injured, he said. In the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, an elderly man died after a private house was hit, the regional governor said. Videos have emerged on social media purportedly showing explosions in the night skies in the Moscow region, and of a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC. Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said a drone struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged. He said on social media that 450 drones heading for Moscow had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". Sheremetyevo - Moscow's biggest airport - warned passengers about "temporary restrictions" in place, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. In Ukraine, a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in Saturday's Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko said. He added that several private houses were also damaged. In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said. Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. title: Will the three-week break put more pressure on managers?
description: So far this season two coaches have lost their jobs, but plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break.
body: Fulham coach Alvaro Arbeloa and Manchester United boss Michael Carrick have endured difficult starts to the season Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results. So far this season two coaches have lost their jobs - Paul Heckingbottom at Preston North End and Michael Duff at Wycombe Wanderers. But plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break. That includes the managers of Fulham and Manchester United, who on Sunday meet at Craven Cottage in the final fixture before players jet off around the world with their countries. It will all be pretty new to Alvaro Arbeloa, appointed as Fulham's manager in the summer after taking charge of just 28 games as Real Madrid boss in the second half of last season. But with no wins and three defeats in his first four Premier League matches, and speculation of unrest among the squad due to players' social media activity, the pressure is already on Arbeloa. Likewise Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, especially after the 3-2 EFL Cup exit to Brighton on Wednesday. It was the first time United had led at home by two goals and lost since they were beaten 3-2 by Tottenham in 1976, half a century ago. Coming on the back of the 1-0 loss to 10-man Manchester City, and with their only victories this season against Ipswich Town and Sabah, Carrick needs results. But they are not the only managers who might have cause for concern. Over the past 10 years, it has been rare for a Premier League manager to be replaced this early in the campaign. Even more so in the international break. But could it be different this year? The first break is longer, three weeks rather than two, and comes later. The September slot used to come at the start of the month when clubs had only played three league fixtures. In the past 10 years only two managers - Watford's Javi Gracia in 2019 and Nottingham Forest's Nuno Espirito Santo last year - moved on during this break. What about the October stoppage? Again, only two managers have previously lost their jobs during the same period - Francesco Guidolin at Swansea in 2016, and Xisco Munoz at Watford in 2021. This suggests clubs do not tend to use an international break to change manager. It is, though, far more likely to happen in November, with six bosses replaced in the past 10 years. That does not mean managers are safe, though. The changes simply were not made during the breaks. In the past 10 campaigns, nine coaches had left their jobs by the time the second international break came along - which is where we are in the number of games. With no manager to move on yet, could it come in the next three weeks? Former Stoke, West Brom and Middlesbrough boss Tony Pulis explains when the pressure can build for a football manager. With the first international break upon us, rumblings around certain clubs that have started the season poorly have surfaced. In my time, the October/November international breaks, the pause just after the Christmas period, and then early March would be the three sticking points for any manager who was struggling with results. Why these breaks are used for clubs to make changes is plain to see. The pause in the season gives football clubs the chance to appoint a new manager with time for them to settle into their new role, to take stock of the surroundings, staff and time to prepare for their first game in charge. After Christmas, usually the first game is an FA Cup match, which again gives the new boss a chance close up to see what they have to work with. First impressions can be a vital starting point, so again the manager has time to prepare and deliver their principles to the lads. Personally, I've joined quite a few of my clubs midway through seasons, and have left a few clubs going the other way, but I do honestly believe that those international breaks, for the reasons I've given, definitely heighten the chances of struggling managers getting the sack. I don't see this September break as a flashing light, it is too early in the season, but from then on in, the dates I have mentioned really do come into play. But this early international break doesn't help any managers. Whether your team is winning or losing, on both accounts, it's a nightmare. If you're winning you want to keep playing, and yet if you've started badly as a manager you want more time to put it right. Players travelling and the chance of injuries at such an early stage of the season is completely bonkers in my opinion. Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham are yet to win a Premier League game this season While the evidence suggests things have to get pretty bad for a club to change manager early in the season, a few bosses are feeling the heat. There are ways of losing games of course, but I don't see the trip to Fulham as being 'make or break' for Carrick in the sense of his job. Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to think that way - and I agree. He got enough credit in the bank last season by steering Manchester United into the Champions League to ride out a poor start to the season. I think the issue is United generate so much debate that a loss at Craven Cottage, which would be United's first since 2009, against a team that has only one point and is bottom of the table, would lead to numerous external inquests - which in turn puts a laser focus on the club when they resume their campaign against Tottenham on 10 October. It is unclear exactly how much danger Arbeloa is in, but there appears to be some substance to reports of disgruntlement among elements of Fulham's squad early in the campaign. His significant tactical changes since replacing Marco Silva have left the Cottagers vulnerable at the back, although they produced a more solid display in a goalless draw away to Liverpool last weekend. Silva spent five years at Craven Cottage. However, owner Shahid Khan

title: Artist, 94, thrilled by House of Commons exhibition
description: Eric Fawley says that the chance to have his artwork displayed has made him "very happy".
body: Eric Fawley said he had been drawing since he was five years old A 94-year-old man with dementia said he was "very happy" to be given the opportunity to have his artwork exhibited in the House of Commons. Eric Fawley, from Blackpool, has produced hundreds of drawings since arriving at Greenbanks Care Home in Watford, Hertfordshire, over a year ago, after a fire at his home. His drawings and paintings depict the world around him, as well as his former bosses at BT. Nirmala Singhvi, the lifestyle coordinator at the home, said: "Eric's story offers a warm and thoughtful look at creativity in later life, as well as the individuality and imagination that remain after a dementia diagnosis." Fawley's work is due to go on display in the Upper Waiting Hall at the Houses of Parliament in October. The exhibition was facilitated by the Watford Labour MP Matt Turmaine after he saw Fawley's work at the care home. This is one of the few drawings Fawley has produced in colour, as he prefers to sketch in black and white Fawley said he began creating artworks from an early age, encouraged by his mother, a violinist, and his father, a gifted amateur painter. His family were unable to support his ambition to attend art school. He left school at the age of 14 and worked in a variety of jobs, including electrical work for the famous Blackpool illuminations, before going on to become a Post Office engineer with BT. Singhvi ensures Fawley's artwork is framed and displayed for residents and staff at the care home Fawley relocated to London, after he married his wife Olive, and he continued to work for the telecoms company. From there, he rose through the ranks of the company, taking charge of an office where his portraits and keenly observed caricatures of colleagues were prominently displayed. Fawley said he enjoyed "sending up colleagues" and that they "secretly used to like it". When drawing someone, he said it was important to start with their hair. "If the hair is wrong, then everything is wrong," he added. Fawley's sketches of former colleagues at BT won him several art competitions. One of Fawley's wartime sketches features his sister, Charlotte, who regularly visits him at the care home Since moving to Greenbanks in March last year, Fawley has continued to sketch. He said being creative helped to focus his mind and "ensures that every day is different". He has held exhibitions across Essex and also performed a ceremonial ribbon-cutting at an exhibition at Harlow Library. Staff at the care home are "super proud of him" and are "excited" to see his artwork gain wider recognition, with Fawley challenging perceptions of what people can achieve in care. title: Watch: Diana's brother says press has 'cancerous influence' on Harry and Meghan's lives
description: Earl Spencer says that he can see echoes of Princess Diana's treatment from the press in the way Harry and Meghan are scrutinised.
body: This video can not be played Earl Spencer has told the BBC that there are similarities between the way his sister Diana, Princess of Wales and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been treated by the press. He said Princess Diana was "brought low" by press criticism of her and that it is a "pity" to see echoes of that in Harry and Meghan's lives now. He added that people should learn from Princess Diana's example, and that for anyone being "destroyed daily" by the tabloid press, it must be a "cancerous influence" on their lives. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, will be available on iPlayer from 16:00 and broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday. title: Watch: Fans cheer as Ed Sheeran speaks out over Macklemore controversy at show
description: Ed Sheeran told the crowd he had made mistakes after Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks.
body: This video can not be played Ed Sheeran told his fans that he had made mistakes after Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage this month. Earlier, pro-Palestinian protesters had gathered near the stadium to express solidarity with Macklemore. The British singer's backing band and opening acts boycotted the event – leaving Sheeran alone on stage to address the crowd. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division," Sheeran said. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." The BBC's Carl Nasman was at the concert. title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
description: Princess Diana's brother says she was "really brought low by all that criticism" and he saw her in "tears of despair".
body: This video can not be played Diana's brother says Harry and Meghan face 'cancerous' press like his sister Earl Spencer has told the BBC the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's treatment at the hands of the media has "echoes" of what happened to his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. He described press coverage of Prince Harry and Meghan as a "cancerous influence in their life" and said it would be "beholden on people to learn from Diana's example". The Sussexes, who recently returned to the UK from California six years after stepping back from royal duties, have been repeatedly critical of the media. It comes after the BBC reported on Friday how Earl Spencer says he was "telling the truth" when he claimed King Charles said people would forget Diana "soon enough" in a phone call in the days after her death. Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face. "If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied. "And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. "I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life." He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism". Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan. He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them." Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness". Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK. They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK. Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear". Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me". In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m. In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology. Harry and Meghan seen during a visit to Australia earlier this year Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles. That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous". In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary." When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth." Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".
