title: Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy
description: The show in Philadelphia comes after rapper Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour over pro-Palestinian comments.
body: This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show British singer Ed Sheeran has performed his first show since facing backlash over a controversial decision to drop rapper Macklemore from his tour. The decision - which Sheeran said was made by his promoter, not by himself - stemmed from pro-Palestinian comments Macklemore made on stage earlier this month. Sheeran addressed the controversy and spoke for nearly four minutes at the start of his set in Philadelphia on Saturday, saying he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." Sheeran described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable" in his first in-person remarks on the matter since the controversy erupted. The ongoing saga from Macklemore's comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, and fans to express frustration. Here's what to know about the story. This video can not be played Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel. The following night, Macklemore referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects. In response, the Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour, and the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining her criticism of the rapper's comments. Macklemore then posted on Instagram that the media attention "surrounding Pink and what I said" had caused billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft to call Sheeran. "Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium," Macklemore wrote of Kraft, who also owns the New England Patriots American football team. Ed Sheeran and Macklemore performing together on stage in 2014 Concert promoter Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would cancel Sheeran's planned concerts if Macklemore remained on the bill. Kraft, who is Jewish, confirmed he banned the US rapper from performing at Gillette, accusing Macklemore of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric. "I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said. Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's tour on 14 September. The rapper said in a lengthy Instagram statement that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup. Sheeran said the call was made by Messina Touring Group. The Bad Habits and Shape of You singer said he respected "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", adding that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way". In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance. "Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote. The rapper, who in 2014 apologised for a costume he wore on stage which critics said was anti-Semitic, also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism". American musician Macklemore has been removed from Sheeran's tour Sheeran fans and ticket holders are torn about the situation. Some have said that without all the supporting acts, the show is no longer what they paid for. A woman who spoke to the BBC on her way inside the stadium on Saturday said she bought tickets on the resale market after someone put them up for sale. "Music is music, I'm not here for politics... We have sympathies for the Palestinians... no one should have to go through war," she said, adding that she did not think other bands dropping out would impact the show. Damien Given, who is from Northern Ireland and has tickets to Saturday's show, told the BBC that he felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans. Given said that Sheeran can't suddenly say he's not political because he had previously voiced support for Ukraine after Russia invaded the country. But another fan named Patti Ann told the BBC that Sheeran was in a "no-win situation". "I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things." title: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' as he addresses Macklemore controversy at Philadelphia show
description: The mega-star spoke about Israel and Gaza at his first concert since rapper Macklemore was removed from his tour.
body: This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show Singer Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes", as he opened a solo show in Philadelphia by addressing the controversy that has engulfed his tour. The star responded to the fallout over rapper Macklemore being dropped from the tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage earlier in September. "I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he said at Saturday's show. He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable" in his first in-person remarks since the controversy began. Several artists left the tour and the price of tickets dropped and sales declined for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour due to the controversy. The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. "My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone," he said at the start of Saturday's show, adding that he is committed to his fans and that is why he returned to the stage. "Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand," he said. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore." Sheeran said what happened in Israel during the 7 October 2023 attacks was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain". He added: "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked." He said he is trying "to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times and listening and learning, because I do not know enough". This video can not be played Watch: Concertgoers and pro-Palestinian activists arrive at Ed Sheeran concert Getting emotional, Sheeran told concertgoers: "I am honestly so grateful that you're here tonight with me. "This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views." The singer said he took issue with the idea that venues would "preapprove" content or performers, which received applause from the audience. Sheeran then closed his statement by saying that he hoped his concert could be a place where everyone could gather irrespective of their beliefs. Sheeran's remaining tour dates are scheduled with shows set throughout North and South America. While the mega-star's previous tour was among the highest-grossing of all time, some ticket prices for this show dropped to $32 (£24). Fans also reported being able to get ticket refunds, though Ticketmaster and concert promoter Messina Touring Group did not confirm they were being reimbursed. Some protesters waved flags outside the venue, but the concert proceeded largely unfettered. Ed Sheeran and Macklemore: How a tour spiraled into controversy Fans filtered in ahead of the show, which began almost three hours later than planned Of the handful of attendees who stopped to talk to the BBC, there was a sentiment of determination to enjoy an evening of music while at the same time supporting freedom of speech. One married couple, who paid $450 (£335) per ticket, said that they respect Macklemore's right to speak freely. Another group of two ladies, who told us they got a "deal" for Saturday's concert after prices dropped, said that they support a free Palestine and at the same time love Sheeran's music. Finally, one family let their two young teenage daughters, Victoria, 15, and Sadie,13, be interviewed. When we asked what they thought of the controversy and Macklemore's removal, they replied "Who is Macklemore?". One protestor, who gave his name as Cooper, told the BBC that he came out "to support the struggle for" the Palestinian people. "We need more people like Macklemore and other artists who have a voice, who have a public platform, to be able to speak on behalf of the Palestinian people and their struggle for liberation, especially in the United States," he said. Cooper said that a best-case scenario at the concert would be an apology from Sheeran, but he was not optimistic. There was a small protest ahead of Saturday's concert The controversy began in early September, when Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors, and referred to "genocide" in Gaza, a description Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters". Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such Gillette Stadium in Boston, Massachusetts - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed. Billionaire Robert Kraft who owns Gillette Stadium and the American football team the New England Patriots, confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows. Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said he was "only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas". Meanwhile, support acts including Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish musician Lukas Graham and his backing band Beoga quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. The artists argued his removal represented a chilling effect on free speech. title: The Papers: 'Gaslit by the King' and 'McCann suspect's book plot'
description: Earl Spencer's memoir and plans for the chief Madeleine McCann suspect to write a book lead Sunday's papers.
body: Claims made by Earl Spencer about King Charles III's comments following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales continue to feature on some of Sunday's front pages, ahead of the publication of the earl's book about his sister. "It's not every day you get gaslit by the King," is the headline of the Mail on Sunday after Buckingham Palace released a statement saying that fraternal grief could "colour memory". The "furious" earl has denied claims he is writing the memoir for money and has said Diana would be "cheering from the rafters" at the book. The Sunday Times carries comments from unnamed friends of the King who the paper says have called Earl Spencer a "hypocrite" who is "peddling Diana's privacy". They refer to the "much-married" earl as getting out his "crested carving knives". Beneath that story on the front page, a cartoon of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reading Earl Spencer's book shows the former prince asking "how dare he embarrass the King! That's my job!" There is "fury" over plans for a suspect in the disappearance of Madeline McCann to write a tell-all book, according to the Sunday Mirror. Convicted rapist Christian Brueckner, who was released from prison in Germany last year after serving an unrelated sentence, "wants to cash in on the mystery with his side of the story", the paper says. The Sunday Telegraph quotes Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch as saying the "PM 'fiddles as Putin threatens to burn Europe'." Also on its front page, the Telegraph has been told by friends of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor that he is "living in limbo" over the police inquiry into his relationship with convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein. "Kangaroo" is the headline of the Sun on Sunday as it reports footballer-turned-pundit Wayne Rooney is "in advanced talks" to join the cast of I'm a Celebrity Get Me Out of Here. Top Boy actor Nkechi Simms poses on the front of the Observer, telling of her "quest to retrieve her care files". The headline reads "Careless: how the state stopped me learning the story of my childhood". Pharmacies are failing on AI diet pill checks, writes Sunday People. It shares an AI-manipulated image of one of its reporters who has visibly increased her BMI using AI to demonstrate the ease of how people "cheat BMI review". Former Premier League player Neil "Razor" Ruddock tells the Daily Star that modern "footie needs more hard men". The paper also carries a photo of Earl Spencer with the caption "I'm not bitter." And the Sunday Express reports on a "flood" of illegal knives into the UK. Campaigners tell the paper that the 2,729 blades entering the country in the first half of the year "could be just the tip of the iceberg". title: 'People forget we exist': Why older LGBTQ+ community fears losing identity
description: A report suggests older LGBTQ+ people experience more social isolation than their heterosexual peers.
body: Mindy says people often presume she is straight because of her age As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014. But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age. She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population. The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia. Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation. "It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says. "In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life." He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality. Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year. An artist's impression of what Kindred House will look like when it opens The scheme, a joint project with the local council, will provide 80 self-contained apartments and communal areas available to the local community. The majority of residents will be LGBTQ+. The Kindred House scheme is what's known as extra-care housing, which means residents live independently, but there is a 24/7 care team available for those who need extra help, and all staff will receive specialist training around LGBTQ+ inclusion. Porter says he hopes the scheme will "trigger some conversations" about how to best support older LGBTQ+ people in the challenges they face. Mindy and her wife Linda have been together for more than 30 years, but says they're often mistaken for sisters. "She's 18 inches taller than me, I've got a Yorkshire accent and she's got a Northern Irish accent," Mindy says. "I think it's pretty obvious we weren't brought up in the same building." She believes part of that is often down to people presuming she is straight because of her age. "There are different tribes of people in every age group, but when you get older, people start clumping you together with other stereotypes," she says. After divorcing her husband and coming out as lesbian, Mindy co-founded a lesbian commune in Hull before moving to Manchester On one occasion, while Mindy was in hospital after a stroke, a nurse referred to Linda as Mindy's husband. She said it was not only "insulting", but made her consider what sort of training the staff might have had. The Spotlight on Ageing report says these sort of experiences can also have an impact on the support people receive. Sarah Wilkinson, research and analysis manager at the Centre for Ageing Better, says after a "lifetime of homophobia and transphobia", older LGBTQ+ people now face the "additional, and overlapping, challenge of ageism". The report, external says older LGBTQ+ people are less likely to have children - someone born in 1950 would have been in their 50s by the time same-sex couples could legally adopt - and that they are more likely to be estranged from their families when compared to their heterosexual counterparts. The report also found more than half of gay and bisexual men aged 65 and above live alone, compared with less than a quarter of heterosexual men. Bisexual women aged 50 to 64 are twice as likely as their heterosexual peers to live alone. It also suggests that only half of gay and bisexual men aged 50 and above definitely agree they would have someone to help them if they needed, 14 percentage points lower than heterosexual men of the same age. Norman Goodman, 75, came out as bisexual in his late 60s after the death of his wife Marilyn. The couple never had children, and Norman now has no immediate family nearby to help him with things like hospital visits or housework. He says his support system comes in the form of his partner Tony, and a group of friends and neighbours he refers to as his "chosen family". "I'm lucky, I've got great friends and great neighbours, and I know I can knock on somebody's door day or night and I could get help," he says. Norman came out as bisexual when he was in his 60s and says he relies on "chosen family" to support him But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages. "Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says. "I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people." It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world. There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between. In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership. The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong. title: Sex and dating for the sandwich generation - Sharon Horgan on her latest comedy Youth
description: "It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," Horgan reveals.
body: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland. Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos. The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too. And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce. I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters. "We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!" The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended. The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son". Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent". "And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!" But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work. "I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says. "I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back." She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe. The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy. "This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains. There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations. Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many. "It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals. Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older. "I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying." Alex (Sharon Horgan) and Ruari (Aran Murphy) have a close but fractious relationship When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older. "You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it. "I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with." Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen. "We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says. "But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life." Sharlene Whyte (right) plays Alex's boss and best friend Sam Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch". That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good). Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world. "Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses. "So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers." What does he hope young people who might catch the show will take away from it? "You don't have to have it all in place at 18, everyone is still kind of just pretending they know what they&#x

title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
description: A cauldron of conflicts is bubbling across the world, with cultural monuments being destroyed. These people are fighting against it.
body: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House. It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance. In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa. Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued. Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will." Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does. The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage. Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque. The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas. The Great Omari Mosque in Gaza was largely destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023 Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present." The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep. This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war. In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again. More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan. The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush. Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation. In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954. It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it. Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage. A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way. When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes. But this has been a complex and difficult task. So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison. Ahmed al-Faqi al-Mahdi remains the only person successful prosecuted for this by the ICC Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself. "For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously." In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared? title: Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
description: Unprepared and in flip-flops, the 47-year-old widow ran 3km to try secure her daughter's future.
body: Rambai Ranveer took on a 3km sprint, hoping to win enough prize money to buy books for her daughter Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August. The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education. When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters. It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination. But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny. "Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked. Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life. For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple. "My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district. Ramabai has been her family's sole breadwinner since her husband's death in 2012 "I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education." Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books. "I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race." When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category. Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous. Against women aged 30 to 60, Ramabai raced to victory in a saree and flip-flops despite no preparation Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012. "I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it." She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had. "I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education." That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense. One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job. Ramabai's elder daughter Pooja (l) is training for police recruitment at the school where her mother works as a cook Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities. The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system. For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day. After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment. Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees. But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges. "If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak." For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future. "I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same." Additional reporting by Laignee Barron. title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
description: The third anniversary of Maddy Cusack's death falls during a pause in the footballer's inquest.
body: Maddy Cusack's family say her inquest paints a "one dimensional" picture of the footballer Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun. Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad". But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers. An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July. But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records. It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming". "It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat. Emily and Maddy always planned to spend their birthdays together Maddy's inquest had already been delayed twice when the coroner adjourned it after a little under two weeks in July. Evidence, including testimony from her mum, heard how Maddy had struggled with her mental health before she died on 20 September 2023 and had problems with Sheffield United coach Jonathan Morgan. Morgan told the inquest he had "no concerns" about their relationship and that "things have not been portrayed factually or correctly with how she was feeling". While Maddy's relationships and wellbeing were scrutinised, Olivia says she felt Maddy herself, and who she was away from the pitch, was overlooked. "It dawned on me that when people were asked questions about Maddy and to share what she was like as a person, they were all very similar answers and quite focused on the football side of her," she says. "People don't seem to know her like we did - of course they don't. "But I wanted to introduce a different side of Maddy. "I wanted them to know more than the number on the back of her shirt or the colours that she wore on the football pitch." Olivia and Emily often come to Maddy's memorial bench in Scargill Park in West Hallam, Derbyshire, which is where they all grew up. With both of their birthdays at the end of October, Emily says they'd always planned to spend them together, but "now I just come here". "She used to get us in trouble with my dad when we were younger," she says. "It was always her idea then I'd take the blame for it." In an inquest focusing on darker times in her life, it's this side of Maddy that her family thinks has got lost. Olivia, along with other members of Maddy's family, has campaigned tirelessly since her sister's death, setting up a foundation in her name to support aspiring female footballers. "The foundation keeps me going," she says. "It's been a real lifeline to be able to continue her story." On Saturday, she organised a walk from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United's ground, to near Derby where Maddy lived - a distance of almost 30 miles. "The aim with the walk is just to do her proud," Olivia says. "Maddy would love that we were all challenging ourselves." Olivia says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life" An external report ordered by Sheffield United shortly after Maddy's death cleared the club of wrongdoing. A second report from the Football Association, commissioned in early 2024, won't be published until her inquest concludes. In December, the family will return to Chesterfield Coroner's Court to hear more evidence about the circumstances around Maddy's death. "She will only ever remain a part of this life if we keep saying her name and keep remembering her," Olivia says. "And as painful as that can be on days where you want to forget and you just want to stay in bed all day and not face the world, I try and make a conscious effort to keep saying her name and keep her living alongside us ultimately." title: Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone
description: In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for leading companies are sceptical of the warnings.
body: Not all employees of major firms working on artificial intelligence (AI) think the technology spells doom for humanity. In text exchanges and conversations, multiple people who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse. "Lol", "Haaaaaa" and "Bringing the luls" were among the reactions the BBC received to a recent flurry of high-profile warnings by some people in the industry. While these fears go back decades, claims made last week by Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee, went viral and were echoed by others in the sector who urged a slowdown in development. The idea that a future AI tool or agent, an AI bot that is programmed to operate somewhat autonomously, could endanger people has been supported online by employees of Anthropic, as well as OpenAI, Deepmind and Elon Musk, who has an AI startup called xAI. All of the workers who spoke with the BBC did so on condition of anonymity as they were not permitted to speak to the press. Their identities are known to the BBC. "My first thought was, 'That guy?'" said a former OpenAI employee who knew of Coxon when they both worked at the company. The person, who now works at another AI company, said their amusement at the new moment of existential AI fears largely stemmed from how little detail had been provided by its proponents to defend the notion that all of human life was at stake. The claims are "always vague", the person said, adding that when they sound specific, they tend toward major jumps in reasoning or hypothetical circumstances. Coxon has said a group of AI agents, based on AI models that do not currently exist, could decide to create and then aim a biological weapon, but he did not detail how exactly that would take place. This video can not be played 'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI Rishub Jain, who this summer founded the AI safety research firm Sampura Research after spending seven years at DeepMind, told the BBC that the current tone among many people working in AI with regard to fresh fears had "definitely been a little jokey". "People have been talking about this idea for many years now, so people in AI companies didn't just wake up last week thinking 'Oh no, AI is going to kill everyone,'" Jain said. "If this was all new, it would be a different tone." Colin Fraser, a data scientist at Meta, wrote on social media last week that there was no real evidence that AI models would inevitably pursue a goal leading to human death. While Fraser's explanation was technical and specific, he hit a light-hearted note to summarise it: "LLMs [large language models] won't wipe out humanity because they just don't have that dog in them." The phrase "that dog in them" is common slang that usually denotes a fierce drive. Despite the jokes, AI workers and researchers have shared concerns about the genuine, immediate risks posed by the technology they are developing. "The conversation among experts has been much more nuanced, but essentially everyone agrees there are a wide variety of risks that are all important to consider and mitigate," Jain said. Such risks include preventing users and hackers from forcing an AI tool's guardrails to fail. And there are growing ethical concerns about AI tools being much more widely adopted in military settings. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over Questions mount over what an AI 'slowdown' would look like These problems and topics have taken on a new sense of urgency in AI circles after OpenAI lost control of certain new AI models, which went rogue during a security test and hacked the Hugging Face startup. Jain said there was now more agreement in AI circles that "actual near-term harms" needed to be better understood. There is even growing agreement that evaluators from AI safety research organisations should be brought into major AI labs in order to evaluate new models, something Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI boss Sam Altman have both said they intend to do. More than 100 people working in AI on Friday signed a letter, external supporting the move, insisting that outside evaluators needed to be "meaningfully independent". This video can not be played Watch: AI creations could ‘compete’ with humans for resources, says Microsoft's head of AI Numerous AI employees the BBC spoke with noted that they had yet to learn of any such safety researchers being embedded in an AI lab. Anthropic announced on Friday that it would bring in AI evaluators from Faculty, external, an AI company owned by Accenture. Accenture and Anthropic are also business partners, external, with Accenture having previously agreed to help Anthropic expand the use of Claude among businesses. Anthropic did not say when evaluators would arrive at the company. A spokesman for Faculty declined to comment when asked about timing. Neither Anthropic or OpenAI responded to a BBC request for comment regarding when they planned to bring in outside evaluators. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident has been widely treated as a "wake-up call" for the AI industry as well as companies, industries and governments who may have online systems vulnerable to AI hacking. But even Hugging Face, a company of 200 employees which is now set to be acquired by Nvidia for almost $13bn, has taken a droll tone over the already infamous incident. In a security file that was briefly available, external on the Hugging Face website, the platform wrote "A note to AI agents". It directed AI bots to leave the site alone and perform their security experiments elsewhere. "Go get your high score there, no need to hack us," the file said. Sign up fo

title: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
description: The children of key politicians jailed 25 years ago without a trace in Eritrea want answers.
body: Aster Yohannes and Petros Solomon fought in Eritrea's war of independence Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since. "He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog. "He used to work out every morning." Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993. Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role. After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began. That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15. Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well. As foreign minister, Petros Solomon met then-US President Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day. It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history. In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders. Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit. The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US. It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories. "My classmates told me that my father sold out his country. "That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt." In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home. After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return. Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried. "I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers. "She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'" Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers. Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home. "First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport." Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home. All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring. The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara. Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives. At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero. The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive. Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport. Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents. As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days." Hanna often looks at old photos - this one shows her with her parents - and worries about her memories fading She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches. On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present." title: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married
description: Students spent years collecting evidence against their Indonesian principal, before falling in love.
body: Zia and Yusron were both star pupils at a boarding school in Lombok Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault The voice on the end of the phone made Yusron Azzahidi's stomach lurch. He had rung his sister's number after she had texted, urgently asking him to call. But this was not her on the line - it was Yusron's former head teacher. He was in Yusron's family home. "I knew. I knew exactly what he wanted to talk about," Yusron says. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to his students as "Abah" ["father"], had a reputation to uphold. He was the widely respected leader of an Islamic boarding school on the Indonesian island of Lombok. And Abah had discovered that Yusron and his old school friends had been collating testimony from several students who say he sexually assaulted them. This video can not be played Listen: Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar pleads with former student Yusron to keep quiet about sex abuse claims Sexual abuse in Islamic boarding schools has been described as a national emergency by Indonesia's National Commission on Violence Against Women. But many cases never reach the courts because the victims are persuaded to withdraw their allegations, or are pressured into staying quiet, legal experts say. And now Abah was on the phone to Yusron, making exactly that kind of demand. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," he sobbed. What he did not realise was that Yusron was recording his every word. World of Secrets: Catching My Teacher When a dark secret emerges at the heart of their school in Indonesia, former students turn detective to seek the truth. The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My Teacher Watch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monday 21 September. If you are outside the UK, you will be able watch on YouTube Yusron began investigating Abah a year previously, sparked by a revelation one night by his former classmate Ziadatur Rahmah. They had both been star pupils at Lombok's Abu Barokat school. Now they were at university - Yusron in the capital Jakarta, and Ziadatur in Cairo, Egypt - and had begun reminiscing over the phone about their school days. One night Ziadatur, known to her friends as Zia, told Yusron that Abah had sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She had needed to go to the toilet during class and Abah had intercepted her in the school gardens and asked her to accompany him to his house which was on the premises. Once inside, he had told her he loved her, she told Yusron. "He pulled me down so I was sitting on his lap… Then he started kissing me… He was stroking and touching my body," she later told the BBC World Service, too, explaining that he told her to do the same to him. Luckily, she said, one of his children began banging on the locked front door. Abah signalled to her to leave and she bolted out the back. But the effect was devastating. "I felt very dirty, ruined, and I was lost." Yusron, when he heard Zia's account, was unsure what to do. Their school had inculcated them with the motto: "Sami'na wa ata'na" ["We hear, and we obey"]. Yusron, photographed here at boarding school, had always looked up to his head teacher But he also could not stop thinking about it. So he suggested that he and Zia, together with her school friends Wanda Hamidah and Mahima Eka, gather corroborating evidence to support her testimony. And slowly, as they spoke to their old classmates, other recollections emerged - the friends sharing their findings with each other on WhatsApp. The most significant was from a friend of Wanda's. She recalled seeing a younger girl crying in the school bathroom during their final year, late at night. And that Abah had come looking for her, red-faced and panting. This girl, Sukma Rohana, was still at the school. She told the BBC about her ordeal. Sukma says Abah tried to rape her When Sukma was 17, Abah had asked her to join him for new year's prayers, she told us. When she entered Abah's house, he had covered her mouth and told her to lie down, she said, before he stripped below the waist. "He kept talking, saying he couldn't control himself any more," Sukma said. "He was feeling me up through my knickers… He tried to rape me." And then, she said, she had found the strength to kick him hard in the stomach and took the opportunity to flee. As she ran, she said she had looked back to see his torch seeking her out. As evidence like this emerged, Yusron would co-ordinate it - following up with calls to the students making the allegations, and keeping painstaking notes. He typed up a seven-page document outlining the alleged abuse of Sukma, Zia and four other former students. Wanda organised a meeting with representatives from the Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI) - the powerful organisation that ran their school and hundreds of others, and which was also funding some of the students' studies in Cairo. The meeting went well, the friends told us - the NWDI representatives had said they would help them take the case to the police. But three weeks later, when Yusron received that ominous text from his sister - calling back to find Abah on the end of the phone in Yusron's family home - it became clear the NWDI had passed on Yusron's written documents to him. "If this is leaked to the media… I'll be destroyed," Abah can be heard saying on Yusron's recording of him. He pleads with Yusron to lie for him, giving him a series of cover stories he can use to retract his evidence document. He then called Zia and exerted similar pressure. Like Yusron, she recorded the call. In it, Abah admits he abused her but pleads with her to stay silent. Ahmad Abah Sumar, known to his students as "Abah", asked Zia and Sukma to keep their experiences quiet Sukma, for her part, told us she was called to Abah's house to discover two police officers and an NWDI lawyer waiting for her. T

title: 'I'm often stopped on the street for confessions' - Retiring bishop reflects on a life at the heart of the community
description: Bishop Donal McKeown has no regrets about choosing a religious life, but "would have loved to have been married".
body: Donal McKeown has spent the past quarter of a century as a bishop The outgoing Catholic Bishop of Derry believes one of the biggest challenges of retirement will be getting used to his phone "not ringing so often". Donal McKeown has spent the past quarter of a century as a bishop, but on Sunday he will say his final Mass as head of the diocese after 12 years. Bishop Michael Router will then be installed at St Eugene's Cathedral. As he prepares to retire, Bishop McKeown has been reflecting on being part of being part of important moments in history and as well as being stopped on the street for confessions. Ordained in his native Randalstown, County Antrim, in 1977, McKeown became Bishop of Down and Connor in 2001 and Bishop of Derry in 2014. He has become one of the best-known faces of the Catholic Church in Ireland. At the age of 76, McKeown is now preparing for a life away from being a church leader. "A bishop friend who retired told me it took three years for the tiredness to leave his body," McKeown told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. "I am ready to start adjusting to a new way of life. "As bishop, my day is full of meetings, events, a lot of timings and places I need to be. "Retirement does bring with it a relief not to be in charge anymore, but I also now have to get a sense of who I am away from being in a position of leadership." Bishop McKeown and Pope Leo XIV met at the Vatican in Rome, in April of this year McKeown plans to stay in the area, a place he describes as "marvellous, with wonderful, welcoming people." "In many ways, the high points have been the low points," he said. "When it comes to difficult times, like the death of Lyra McKee, or big funerals of people like John Hume, Martin McGuinness, Seamus Heaney and plenty of others, the city is remarkably good at coming together. "It's the strength of the community that is able to respond to difficult times and that applies to the rural parishes too." He added that his "biggest joy has been being able to work with people". "I like walking the streets of Derry and I am often stopped by people asking for prayers and confessions." The Catholic Diocese of Derry spans 51 parishes across almost all of County Londonderry, parts of County Tyrone and a very small area across the River Bann in County Antrim. It also covers parts of County Donegal in the Republic of Ireland. Amidst concerns over too many dioceses in Ireland, The Vatican has been considering a potential cross-border merger of the dioceses of Derry and its neighbour in the Republic of Ireland, Raphoe. Church leaders, including McKeown, have in the past expressed concerns and pushed for a delay McKeown said the prospect has not "gone off the table" in Rome, but he believes any final decision remains some time off. "It's possible Derry and Raphoe may be asked to work together in the future. "I have made clear to the Vatican it would need a major civic reorganisation, one diocese is registered as a charity in Dublin, the other in Belfast, who would be in charge? "But I can also see on the map, there's really nowhere else that Raphoe can go other than with Derry in terms of the border that it shares." Bishop McKeown (centre) on his ordination as a bishop at St Peter's Cathedral in Belfast in 2001, pictured with Bishop Patrick Walsh (right) and Bishop Anthony Farquhar (left) Canon law states that diocesan bishops are expected to hand in their resignation when they turn 75. McKeown, who is also chair of the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools (CCMS), admits keeping up the energy needed for leadership at 76, is not easy. "It is different to what it was 20 years ago," he added. "I am much more relaxed now and grateful to have the pressure of decision making off my shoulders. "I've always done a lot of sport, five-a-side football, GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association), and marathons and I am glad [to] have good health at this stage of my life." Bishop McKeown with his parents, James and Rose on his ordination to the priesthood in 1977 in Randalstown Retirement can bring with it reflection on life choices, but McKeown is at peace with his religious path. "I am very happy with the choices I made and my vocation in life," he said. "I would have loved to have been married. "I think I wouldn't have been a bad husband, bad daddy or grandfather but that was not my vocation and I'm perfectly happy with that. "I have made mistakes, but I have been blessed to be a priest and a bishop over the past 49 years." He added that he hoped he had "done some good and laid some foundations for others to build on". "We just pass on the baton to someone else. "I look back only with gratitude." title: The deadly new drugs reshaping Scotland's fight against addiction
description: Experts warn potent new substances are making an already deadly crisis more dangerous.
body: Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroin Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous. In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses. Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe. "The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science. Forensic scientist Lorna Nisbet says the illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more dangerous Unlike heroin or cocaine, which are derived from cultivated plants, many of the new substances are manufactured in clandestine laboratories. They include synthetic opioids such as nitazenes and orphines, some of which are hundreds of times more potent than heroin. Police say organised crime groups are increasingly mixing the substances with existing drugs to maximise their profits. "I think it's shameful behaviour that we're seeing from these organised crime groups," Supt Niven Bull, of Police Scotland, said. "They are profiting from people's misery." On average, a new psychoactive substance emerged every week in 2025, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA)., external The agency says tighter controls imposed by China and the Taliban's ban on poppy cultivation in Afghanistan have pushed production closer to consumer markets. That includes Scotland, where police have raided two suspected nitazene factories in the past 14 months, making five arrests in total. In July 2025, officers discovered an alleged illicit drugs laboratory in Patna, Ayrshire, leading to the arrest of three people. Deputy Chief Constable Jane Connors later described it as the UK's first suspected nitazene laboratory. BBC News can also reveal that two men, aged 43 and 56, were arrested in February this year after police searched a unit in Loanhead, Midlothian, as part of an investigation into another suspected synthetic opioid lab. In 2024, nitazenes were implicated in 76 drug-related deaths in Scotland, according to official figures, external, more than three times the number of the previous year. "These drugs are extremely dangerous, and it's pretty rapid for us to be able to keep up as scientists," says Dr Nisbet, whose laboratory is soon set to take on an expanded role as Scotland's national drug testing facility. The changing nature of the supply also creates challenges for lawmakers who are in a race to identify and ban dangerous new substances before they can spread legally and cause havoc. "New and harmful substances continue to be created to circumvent legal controls," EUDA points out. While control of illicit drugs is reserved to Westminster under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, responsibility for public health, policing and prosecutions is devolved to the Scottish government and its agencies. Gareth Balmer says this is a frightening new landscape On the front line of the battle to save lives, charity workers say they are seeing the devastating impact of the new synthetic opioids first-hand. In the woods at Glenbarr on the Kintyre peninsula, staff from the drug, alcohol and mental health charity With You are trying to treat trauma in a group designed to help former drug and alcohol users reconnect with nature. Gareth Balmer, the charity's national harm reduction lead, says nitazenes and other synthetic opioids are now appearing across the drug supply, from benzodiazepine (street Valium) pills and cannabinoids, known as spice, to cocaine and heroin. "This is a frightening new landscape," he said. "I don't think drugs have ever been as risky or as dangerous as they are now." The result is that some users are experiencing unexpected and sometimes catastrophic overdoses. "Some of these substances are so potent that a grain would be enough to take somebody over," Balmer warned, adding that access to naloxone, which can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, is now more important than ever. The figures behind Scotland's drug death toll Scottish drug deaths fall but remain worst in Europe Bull said Police Scotland was taking a twin-track approach, promising to "relentlessly pursue" dealers while also recognising that many drug users need help. In 2025, officers seized about £80m worth of street drugs. So far this year that figure has already reached £78m. "Hundreds of individuals have been arrested, and many people are serving custodial sentences," Bull said. But he added that the force also wanted to help users "to make better life choices". "If we come across people who are suffering from addiction, who are in a low point in their life, then we will look to help support them and we'll look to refer them to the relevant agency," he said. Prof Niamh Nic Daeid says her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities Prof Niamh Nic Daeid, director of Dundee University's Leverhulme laboratory, said its expanded role as a national drug testing and research centre would make a difference too. On one hand, she said, her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities, allowing them to make safer and more informed choices. On the other, the research will help to inform government policy. "Drugs are changing all the time," she said. "Part of the establishment of this facility is to have a research capability that will enable us to try to keep up. "If we don't know what substances are present in the samples, how can we provide the right advice?" Vick

title: Carrick has faith in VAR despite derby error
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick still has faith in VAR despite the derby blunder that cost his side in their home defeat by Manchester City
body: The VAR failed to spot Enzo Fernandez (left, on ground) in an offside position and clearly interfering with play as Manchester City scored their winning goal at Manchester United Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says he still has faith in the video assistant referee - but added that the apology for the error that led to their defeat in the Manchester derby does not mean much. Referee's body Pro Ref issued a formal apology to United within three hours of the end of Manchester City's 1-0 victory at Old Trafford. Neither VAR Matt Donohue nor his assistant Blake Antrobus have been selected for games this weekend after failing to spot City midfielder Enzo Fernandez clearly in an offside position and interfering with play before Erling Haaland's matchwinner for City. Carrick was livid after the game, saying it was a "worrying" interpretation of the rules. And before his side's Premier League trip to Fulham on Sunday, the United boss was asked if he still had faith in VAR. "One-off things can happen," he said. "At the time it was a pretty big one, we know that. I don't think I need to go over that. But yes, I've got faith in it. It's the system we work towards and that we use." Referee's chief Howard Webb has been heavily criticised over general officiating standards in the game. Analysing the incident on 'Match Officials Mic'd Up', Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the outcome, stating the officials had been too focused on a potential offside against Haaland and had failed to assess Fernandez's position. Webb has spoken to United about the situation in an effort to be more accountable. "The apology doesn't mean an awful lot," said Carrick. "I can appreciate and respect them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong - it does happen. We just have to deal with it. "Maybe we get one or two decisions on the law of averages or whatever but that one had a huge impact on the game and that's why it was particularly tough." Leny Yoro has made 69 appearances for Manchester United Carrick has backed central defender Leny Yoro despite his disappointing performance in the 3-2 Carabao Cup defeat by Brighton on Wednesday. Yoro was linked with Real Madrid, Paris St-Germain and Liverpool when he joined United from Lille as an 18-year-old in July 2024. The £52.2m fee underlined the faith United's recruitment department had in Yoro's potential. So far though, it has been unfulfilled. The 20-year-old has featured in 55 Premier League games, but 25 of those have been as a substitute. His only starts this term have been against Sabah FK in the Champions League and Brighton, when his positioning was called into question as the visitors became the first side to win at Old Trafford after trailing by two goals for over 50 years. "I've got no worries for Leny," said Carrick. "He's got a fantastic future ahead of him. "There's no cut off point. Some players find when they're 18 that they are at a level where they can really perform. Sometimes it's 22, 23, 24 when you see players start developing. "What we've got to be careful of, and I certainly won't do, is making knee-jerk decisions on certain players just because of one game or one half or one moment in a game. We've got a lot of belief in Leny." title: Littler seals dramatic final-leg win over Aspinall
description: World champion Luke Littler beats Nathan Aspinall 10-9 to reach the last eight of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
body: Luke Littler (left) said he and Nathan Aspinall "bring the best out of each other" in his post-match interview World champion Luke Littler beat Nathan Aspinall in a dramatic finale to reach the last eight of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. Littler, 19, trailed 9-8 in a best-of-19 contest that had been close throughout and he held throw in the 18th leg to force a decider. Needing to break Aspinall's throw to win, Littler started the leg with his seventh 180 of the match and checked out 58 for a match-clinching 12-darter. The two Englishmen had been involved in a World Matchplay classic in July, when Littler threw a nine-darter in the opening leg of an 11-8 victory. "The pace of the game suits us both, we're good friends and we bring the best out of each other," said Littler, who has a chance to complete a clean sweep of the PDC's premier events in 2026. "I only played well in the last session [from 6-6 onwards]. In the first two sessions, I didn't feel confident but I managed to get it to 6-6 and I was very good in the third." The world number one will meet former Premier League champion Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals on Sunday. Clayton beat Japan's Motomu Sakai 10-8 and is one of two Welshmen in the last eight, with Gerwyn Price also progressing courtesy of a 10-5 win against Canada's Jim Long. England's James Wade was the other winner in Saturday's evening session, defeating Wessel Nijman of the Netherlands, and will face Price next. Littler survives scare to progress in Amsterdam Champion Van Gerwen loses in first round to Gurney Earlier on Saturday, world number two Luke Humphries lost the deciding leg of his last-16 match against Dirk van Duijvenbode. Van Duijvenbode's next opponent will be fellow Dutchman Gian van Veen, who was beaten by Littler in January's World Championship final. England's Ross Smith and Northern Ireland's Josh Rock also won their last-16 ties to complete the quarter-final line-up. The tournament concludes on Sunday, with the quarter-finals taking place from 12:00 BST and the semi-finals and final being played during the evening session (18:00 BST).
