title: CNN and MS NOW say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
description: The reporters' badges were confiscated, the outlets reported.
body: CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets. An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported. CNN also said Saturday morning that one of its reporters was denied access and had her badge seized. Trump said on Friday he was barring MS NOW, CNN, and Politico - three major US media outlets - from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. Press freedom advocates called the move "unconstitutional". "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him." Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked. CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated. An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars". "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy." It was not clear whether Politico reporter were at the White House on Saturday. Following Trump's ban, all three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right," CNN said. In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years". Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news." Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called out Trump's White House ban as illegal and unconstitutional. A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional". "The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media. It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC. Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing. Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza. title: Smoke seen near Riyadh airport after air raid alerts in Saudi capital
description: The King Khalid International Airport incident caused hours of flight disruptions and comes amid an escalating conflict with Houthi rebels in Yemen.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Thick black plumes of smoke rise from near Riyadh's international airport A column of black smoke has been seen near Riyadh's international airport hours after air raid alerts were issued in the Saudi capital. It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighbouring Yemen. A number of apparent explosions were heard in the capital and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations earlier in the day, external. One report suggested a fuel tank had been set on fire near the airport. There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities. How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks An AFP news agency journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to state oil and gas company Aramco. The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts. "I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this." On Friday, the Houthis announced that they had thwarted Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sanaa which they said bore the hallmarks of an Islamic State operation. Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said Saudi Arabia had carried out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week. He warned the reported attacks on Sanaa would "not go unanswered". The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen. According to an unconfirmed report from AFP, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday. The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency. On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame". title: Nature reserve to double in size, thanks to gift
description: Staffordshire Wildlife Trust acquires an area of wet woodland, marsh and pastureland due to the will.
body: Staffordshire Wildlife Trust has secured more land on the reserve due to the gift in will A nature reserve will double in size due to a generous gift left in a will, a wildlife trust has said. The donation has secured more land at Jackson's Coppice and Marsh Nature Reserve near Eccleshall, Staffordshire. An area of wet woodland and marsh has been acquired alongside pastureland south of the River Sow. Public footpaths and a scheme to slow the flow of the river in heavy rainfall are being planned. "This is fantastic news for wildlife and a wonderful example of how gifts in wills can create lasting change for nature," Jeff Sim of Staffordshire Wildlife Trust said. The donation was made by trust supporter David Aldred. Plans for the floodplain land include coppicing mature alder trees and managing willow growth to support a greater diversity of plants and wildlife. Under the trust's ownership, the floodplain will enable the river to flow slower during heavy rainfall and will alleviate flooding downstream. The reserve's expansion provides public footpaths over the new land, so visitors will be able to explore different trails, the trust said. "We can restore habitats on a much bigger scale, making more of a difference to the wildlife that relies on these places to live, feed and breed," Sim added. title: Converse pulls 'deeply upsetting' advert after backlash
description: Social media users say an image from the brand's Instagram account resembled a KKK hood and hanging.
body: A photo posted on Converse's Instagram account was described as evoking KKK imagery American footwear brand Converse has pulled an advert that social media users said evoked Ku Klux Klan imagery, saying it recognised "that we got this wrong". The photo, posted to the company's Instagram account, received backlash online after critics described lighting in the image as looking like a white pointed hood. A pair of shoes, dangling in the picture, were also likened to an image of a lynching victim by social media users. In an apology, first issued on Friday, Converse said the photo had been removed from its social media channels and it was working to remove it elsewhere. "This should not have happened and we will do better," it said. The statement also said: "We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong". The image has since been removed from Converse's social media accounts The photo was part of a campaign promoting its Chuck 70 X trainer, launched internationally on 27 August. The campaign features the South Korean singer Karina, of the K-pop group Aespa, who is pictured in a series of advertisements for the shoes. Founded in Massachusetts in the early 1900s, the popularity of Converse has skyrocketed since its Chuck Taylor sneaker was first introduced to US basketball courts in 1917. The global brand has been a subsidiary of Nike since 2003. title: DUP will 'not be found wanting' when it comes to unionist co-operation, says Robinson
description: Gavin Robinson was speaking at his annual conference ahead of highly anticipated assembly and council elections next May.
body: Gavin Robinson was speaking at his party's annual conference ahead of highly anticipated assembly and council elections next May The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) will "not be found wanting" when it comes to co-operating with other unionist parties to maximise the pro-union vote in next year's elections, Gavin Robinson has said. The DUP leader was giving his annual conference speech ahead of highly anticipated assembly and council elections next May. Robinson told his conference that the party "must not gift wrap seats to Sinn Féin, the SDLP or Alliance that we could otherwise win". The DUP believes that in constituencies like Lagan Valley and North Antrim a split unionist vote handed seats to its opponents unnecessarily in the 2022 assembly election. He told delegates at a hotel in greater Belfast on Saturday: "I am committed to constructively work and actively engage again with other unionist parties, as we have before, to get the largest number of pro-union candidates elected to the assembly and to our councils. "I am not asking anyone to give up what they believe." He appealed to the unionist electorate and others: "Staying at home, or voting for parties that spend more time attacking fellow unionists, and who have no plan, will deliver a weakened and divided unionism - and that is exactly what Sinn Féin hope for. "They know what split votes and lost seats will mean for unionism and the union. "More power for them to take Northern Ireland in the wrong direction. That is the danger." While not ruling out co-operation with other unionist parties the new Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows has often spoken of his ambition to return his party to its former position as the largest unionist party. Traditonal Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister has frequently said he is open to co-operation, but he also accused the DUP of betraying unionism by returning to Stormont and accepting post-Brexit trading arrangements that effectively partition the United Kingdom. It is not clear what any discussions between the parties could ultimately amount to. It was Gavin Robinson's third conference speech as party leader In his speech, Robinson also addressed what he called "appalling" crimes committed by the party's former leader Jeffrey Donaldson. The former MP was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children. Donaldson is seeking to appeal. Robinson said he understood that many delegates felt "deceived and deeply let down by a life of lies", but he added that the party would "face the past honestly". "We will not let the vile actions of one man define our values and our integrity," he added. The conference was also told that the DUP would "never" support reform of Stormont that he claimed were "designed to strip unionists of their consent for our governing arrangements". Alliance, the SDLP and Sinn Féin have called on the government to engage in a process to amend the current structures, in a bid to remove vetoes and prevent future collapses of the institutions. Robinson said his party backed reforms that "improve delivery", but insisted that calls for institutional reform were "not designed to advance the cause of everyday issues". "No self-respecting unionist can allow themselves to naively fall into the trap of lining up with those who are determined to weaken the consent mechanisms at Stormont," he added. Friday night's entertainment at this year's DUP conference dinner was an ABBA tribute act. And if the winner takes it all - then the DUP knows the high stakes in next year's assembly and council elections, having lost its lead at Stormont four years ago. Gavin Robinson issued the SOS to his unionist rivals to set aside their relative divisions and unite next May to maximise their vote. But such calls have in the recent past amounted to little and with an energised UUP under its new leader, and the TUV posing its own threat in various constituencies, it is hard to predict what this latest plea will amount to. Robinson also addressed head on, early in his speech, the ongoing shadow cast over the party by Jeffrey Donaldson's conviction for child sex offences, which could well cost it votes among the unionist electorate. Two-and-a-half years ago, Robinson was thrust into the leadership position because of the most shocking and sudden news the party had ever faced. His biggest challenge as leader is approaching, and when all is said and done next year, he desperately needs something to show for it. title: Police release CCTV of missing Lillia's last sighting
description: Lillia went missing from Bolton on 11 September and has not been seen by her family since.
body: Lillia was last seen by her family over a week ago CCTV footage showing the last known sighting of a missing 13-year-old girl has been released by Greater Manchester Police (GMP). Lillia, from Bolton, was last seen by her family on 11 September. Officers said further inquiries identified a sighting of her at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10:36 BST on 14 September. Police have handed out hundreds of leaflets and used an advertising van displaying her photograph in Piccadilly Gardens as they continue efforts to find her. She is described as white, slim, about 5ft 5in (1.65m) tall, with light brown hair and glasses. CCTV shows Lillia at Manchester Piccadilly bus station on 14 September The latest sighting at 10:36 at Piccadilly bus station on Monday follows a previous one earlier that morning when Lillia was seen boarding the number 36 bus from Salford. Ch Supt Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her. "I can now confirm that our last known current sighting was of Lillia at Manchester Piccadilly bus station at 10.36am on the morning of Monday 14 September. "We can also share that she exited the number 36 bus at Piccadilly, with her boarding it in Salford. "That bus service travels from Bolton through Salford and into Manchester city centre. "If anyone has any information regarding Lillia's whereabouts or movements from this bus – or you were on the bus at the time she was also on there or when she got on in Salford or off in Piccadilly – please contact us via 101 or the Major Incident Portal below." Police officers have handed out hundreds of leaflets and a van has a huge poster of the missing appeal in a bid to find Lillia She continued: "We are also still keen to hear from anyone who may have been in Piccadilly Gardens on Sunday 13 September around 8.20pm, or saw her in McDonald's at that time." She said its investigation currently covers the whole of Greater Manchester but added: "We are also mindful that Lillia could have travelled outside of the Manchester area and are keeping an open mind regarding this possibility." "If you have any information that could help us find Lillia, I would urge you to come forward. Her family just want her home." title: 'Enough is enough': Vigils held for murdered women in South Africa
description: The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
body: This video can not be played Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg. She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July. The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run. Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely. "This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo. In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act. The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas". title: Shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia as victim named
description: Greg O'Neill "loved the ocean", his family say, as police boats and helicopters patrol Perth's beaches in search of his body and the shark that attacked him.
body: Greg O'Neill, 63, was killed in a shark attack at Sorrento Beach on Friday A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was killed at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found. Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues. It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year. The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia. In a statement, Greg O'Neill's family said they were "deeply shocked and devastated by the terrible tragedy." "Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy." On Saturday, his family visited the scene, where locals have been laying flowers. Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water. Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish". Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time. Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday. Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter. A police boat and helicopter are being used to search Perth's beaches Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species. WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident". The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark". It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past. The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers. Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks. The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC. There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year. A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland. title: How Queen perfected trademark harmonies in a cave
description: Drummer Roger Taylor says Queen perfected their singing in a cave on a beach in Cornwall.
body: Queen pictured before an awards ceremony in London in 1976 Queen drummer Roger Taylor has recalled how his mum organised the band's first ever concert to raise funds for the British Red Cross. The show in Truro in June 1970 featured Taylor on drums, Brian May on guitar and vocals by Freddie Mercury, then known as Fred Bulsara. Taylor also revealed how the group perfected their trademark harmonies by singing in a cave on a Cornish beach because they loved the "big sound". The musician was speaking ahead of the release of his latest solo album, Violence Insane in a Beautiful World. The Truro gig was Mercury's first live performance with Taylor and May and he used the occasion to announce their new name, Queen. The set consisted of songs they had written themselves, including Stone Cold Crazy and Son and Daughter, as well as rock 'n' roll covers. Taylor was born in King's Lynn, Norfolk and moved to Cornwall with his family when he was seven years old Queen went on to become one of the most successful rock bands in history, selling more than 300 million records worldwide. They also gained a reputation as a formidable live act, filling stadiums around the world. Taylor was born in King's Lynn, Norfolk, and was drawn to drumming from an early age. "I got all my mother's saucepans and turned them upside down. She had some big wooden knitting needles, which I used to use to sort of play them. And I would pretend I was playing the drums, but I was playing the saucepans." Taylor moved to Cornwall with his family when he was seven. He sang in the Truro Cathedral Choir for about a year and played drums with various local bands as a teenager. "We lived by the sea at first, but just a few months. Then we moved to Truro which, of course, is in the middle [of Cornwall] and is kind of the capital really. It was a nice place to grow up. Cornwall's beautiful, you know." A newspaper advert for the first ever gig by Queen but they were billed under their former name, Smile More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall At the age of 18, Roger Taylor headed to London to study dentistry, later switching to biology. But his heart was set on music. He answered an advert on a college noticeboard for a drummer to join a band called Smile that included Brian May. Smile broke up in the spring of 1970 but the group still had a booking to fulfill at Truro City Hall, now known as the Hall for Cornwall. With Freddie Mercury on board, Smile became Queen and the Truro gig marked their live debut. "I think we were paid £50, which was an enormous amount in those days. "We had just started Queen then and Freddie hadn't really developed his voice, his vocal capacities, to the full. "He sounded quite alarming some of the time. He sounded a little bit like a strangled sheep at times with a very fast falsetto. But of course he kind of invented himself out of it all. "We didn't realise at the time what a great musician he was. A great piano player. A fantastic songwriter. We didn't know what a gem we had at first." Queen in 1973 after a show at the County Ballroom in Taunton, Somerset Taylor admitted his mum was "rather alarmed" by their performance but she admired Freddie's courtesy and style. "She could never believe how Freddie had such beautiful manners and he was always so deferential and polite and how his trousers were always immaculately creased," he said. "We found out he was putting his trousers under the mattress and pressing them as he slept." Taylor said calling the group Queen was Freddie's idea. "We were discussing daft names. One was Build Your Own Boat, which is a sort of prog name, I suppose. "There were various things, you know. But it [Queen] was a good name. It was simple. It was easy to remember and direct." Taylor recalled practising harmonies with May and Mercury in the caves at Chapel Porth beach in St Agnes. "I think we must have been in caves because of the nice reverberation, echo in there. So it sounds bigger," he said. "It would have been a nice place to sing. Bit like singing in a big church or something. The sound rattles around everywhere." It was an early hint of the powerhouse vocals that became a hallmark of hits like Bohemian Rhapsody and Somebody to Love. "We had a great blend between the three of us. The three voices had different characteristics. But they went together to make a very good sound when we harmonised." Posters advertising Queen's first outdoor show in August 1971. Queen feature towards the bottom of the bill In the summer of 1971, Queen played a dozen gigs in Cornwall over six weeks, with John Deacon on bass completing their classic line-up. Many of the shows were organised by Taylor, using his contacts in the county, including dates at Hayle Rugby Club, the Driftwood Spars pub in St Agnes and the band's first open-air concert at the Carnon Downs Festival. There was also an unlikely appearance at the Royal Navy airbase RNAS Culdrose where the group performed for service personnel in the Warrant Officers and Senior Rates Mess. Taylor said: "We would play anywhere that would give us a gig. "We all lived in a nice little cottage in a tiny village called Devoran. I was getting up every morning and working on a farm which was very hard but we were broke, we didn't have any money so it was tough." Taylor said he still has a house on the Helford River in Cornwall and his son Rufus - who's the drummer for The Darkness - has a pub on the other side of the water. "I love to get down there. Don't get down enough," he said. Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external. title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
description: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.
body: Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout. The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said. Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said. It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation. UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba. Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday. Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages. Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close. "Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday. "Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again." "It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy." Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days". The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed. Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership. Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January. US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US. Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year. Trump is putting pressure on Cuba - why and to what end? title: About 280 people evacuated after fire at seaside hotel
description: The blaze is believed to have broken out in the basement of the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone.
body: A seaside hotel in Folkestone has been evacuated after a fire in the basement in the early hours About 280 people have been evacuated from a seaside hotel after a fire broke out overnight. Kent Fire and Rescue Service said 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST. In an update at 08:30, it said 10 fire engines remained at the scene "dampening down any remaining hotspots". The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement of the building, adding that the cause was not yet known. No fire-related injuries have been reported. Folkestone and Hythe District Council has set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park and nearby residents have been advised to avoid the area of the fire and close windows and doors. "We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety", said the council. A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "taking immediate action to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all guests and team members". "Emergency services are on site and we are fully cooperating with the authorities to support those affected and assist with the ongoing response", it added. title: We've been transatlantic pen pals for 70 years and are now more like sisters
description: Kathleen Bonthron and Shirley Hedtke were age 10 and 11 when their friendship began to blossom in letters sent between Scotland and the US.
body: Kathleen (left) and Shirley have built a strong friendship over the past 70 years Two women who became transatlantic pen pals when they were in the Brownies say they now feel "more like family", having written to each other regularly for 70 years. Kathleen Bonthron (now Wilson) from Drumchapel in Glasgow was 10 when her group leader gave her the Wisconsin address for 11-year-old Shirley Hedtke (now Yaeger) in 1956. The pair - now 80 and 81 - began writing to each other and soon built up a rapport, with regular letters going back and forth between Scotland and the United States. The girls kept in touch throughout their childhood, then their teenage years, and as they settled down and had families - and are still in contact now they are pensioners. In the 50s, the only way they could communicate was by writing letters through air mail but this later progressed to emails and now their method of choice is WhatsApp. The bond between the two women is so strong that 55 years ago Kathleen named her daughter after Shirley. They are now known in their families as Shirley America and Shirley Scotland. Shirley (left) and Kathleen (right) first became pen pals as Brownies in 1956 Kathleen's first letter to Shirley in 1956 which talks about her family and interests "When Shirley was born, as I had a friend in America I just thought we'll have Shirley," Kathleen said. "And her dad was quite happy with that. "Shirley was chuffed to bits." Her daughter Shirley added: "Shirley has actually gifted me her childhood mug with her name on it." Speaking from her home in Wisconsin, Shirley (America) said: "My mother named me after Shirley Temple and I was so honoured that Shirley was named after me. It was just wonderful, especially once I met her." Shirley, a former nurse, recalled being given Kathleen's address in 1956. "My Brownie leader came in with a cigar box full of names and asked if anyone would like a pen pal from Scotland," she said. "I grabbed a name and it was Kathleen Bonthron. "We just wrote a few times a year at first but then we started writing more and it just got to be fun. "I got to learn about her culture and she learned about ours. And I learned new words. I loved her from the minute I started writing to her. "We told each other about our families, Brownies and school and then later, of course, we got into the dating which was exciting." Kathleen, who now lives in Lenzie, said: "You didn't know what America was at that age. I think we just used to write about school and going out with our mums and dads. "It was just all chit chat, as it is now. It's just bigger chit chat now." Bill Haley and Elvis Presley were big rock 'n' roll stars in 1956 - the year the two women started writing to each other The Suez Crisis - Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal, threatening British shipping and economic interests, leading to British and French forces invading Egypt to retake the canal, alongside Israel. Facing severe financial pressure and opposition from the US, British troops withdrew in defeat Rock 'n' roll is on the rise with Elvis Presley releasing Heartbreak Hotel and Bill Haley and His Comets starring in Rock Around the Clock The US Supreme Court ruled that Alabama laws requiring segregated buses were unconstitutional, officially ending a historic boycott Hollywood star Marilyn Monroe married playwright Arthur Miller in New York Queen Elizabeth II opened the world's first full-scale commercial nuclear power station at Calder Hall in Cumberland The Duke of Edinburgh's Award was launched to help young people build life skills The beginnings of homegrown rock and pop, with artists like Tommy Steele beginning to chart, while Skiffle bands inspired teenagers to pick up washboards and tea chest basses Dundee Corporation Tramways and Edinburgh Corporation Tramways operated their final tram services, ending an era of streetcar transit in those cities The National Library of Scotland opened its first purpose-built premises on George IV Bridge in Edinburgh Scotland's first commercial ski centre opened in Glencoe Shirley Yaeger (left) said she felt honoured that Kathleen named her daughter Shirley (right) after her Kathleen and Shirley have met three times - twice in Scotland in 2007 and 2019 and then once in the US a few weeks ago. "The first time we met, Shirley was just what she is," Kathleen said. "She's as friendly as me and can talk. We both can talk. "It just felt natural. We just slotted right in with each other. "I'm quite happy now that I've seen her in her house. I feel a bit closer to her, she's more like family now. "But we don't stop talking. We do not stop talking. We never get to the end of the stories because we're talking so much. "We will never not be in touch." Kathleen, who was formerly a punch card operator at IBM and then a doctor's receptionist, added: "She's just a good friend now, more like family. I mean, it's been 70 years. We speak on the phone every now and then but mostly message on WhatsApp." Shirley said: "When we were in Scotland we only got to see Kathleen for a few hours because we had a schedule but when they came to the US we lived together and really got to know each other. "It was just wonderful. She's like a sister to me. We have discussed everything - our pregnancies, our kids when they were little - she was always there for me." Shirley and Kathleen spent a week together at Shirley's home in Wisconsin a few weeks ago Both women have a son and a daughter. As well as Shirley, Kathleen had her son Andrew with her late husband Eric and now has two grandchildren. Shirley has been married to Daniel for 61 years and has a daughter Christine and son Jon. And now the women's children have vowed to keep in touch with each other. "The plan is for Christine - Shirley's daughter - and I, to keep in touch," Shirley (Scotland) said. title: Politician who switched from Reform to Plaid 'lied about her beliefs', says Richard Tice
description: Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who left Reform this week, also revealed she had voted Remain in the 2016 EU referendum.
body: Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was elected as a Member of the Senedd for Reform in May Reform UK's deputy leader has accused the party's former Senedd Member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd of lying to them about her political beliefs before she defected to Plaid Cymru. Richard Tice was speaking after a chaotic week for his party in which its Welsh leader resigned after being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Helen Jenner, the party's deputy leader in Wales, is favourite to take over next week. Tice insisted the events had not distracted the party from the issues it was tackling, saying there were good days and bad days in politics. Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been "honest about her political beliefs" and had acknowledged her views had changed. Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, made the dramatic political move to Plaid Cymru, claiming Reform UK was "far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions". As well as saying she was now a supporter of Welsh independence, she also revealed she had voted to Remain in the EU referendum a decade ago. Richard Tice said the "whole thing" around Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's defection is "absurd" When asked how she had got through the vetting process as a Remain voter, Tice said: "If someone deliberately misleads you, and fibs to you, and lies to you, then it doesn't matter how much vetting you do. "So, why don't you ask her that question? How can you turn from being a unionist to a separatist? "How can you turn from being someone who believes in defending our borders to want to open the borders and become a nation of sanctuary? The whole thing's absurd. "I'm not in charge of vetting. Look, we make lots of brilliant, fast-moving decisions and judgements. "That's why we've grown to be the second-largest party in Wales so quickly from a standing start. We never claim that we're perfect. You know, we're real people." Tice refused to confirm whether Helen Jenner would take over from Thomas next week other than to say that whoever becomes leader will get the seal of approval from him and the UK leader Nigel Farage. Thomas, who was released on bail after his arrest, stood down saying he had done nothing wrong but did not want to be a distraction to the party. He has not been suspended from the party - which would have effectively left him as an independent MS - while Gwent Police continues its investigation. Senedd member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd quits Reform to join Plaid Cymru Helen Jenner likely to take over as Reform Wales leader, sources tell BBC Tice said the events had not distracted Reform Senedd Members from focusing on issues such as the housing of illegal migrants, small boats crossing the English Channel and the 20mph speed limit. He said: "Life is work in progress. But the bottom line is that we've got a group of 33 elected representatives, and they're the second largest party by a considerable margin, and we're raising issues that are absolutely vital to the residents of Wales. "Life moves at different paces, and you have sometimes good days, you have sometimes bad days. "The reality is that very shortly, we'll have a new leader. But our representatives are getting on with the job of representing their constituents and raising issues they want raised." A Plaid Cymru spokesperson said: "Sarah has been honest about her political journey and has acknowledged that her views have changed since she first entered politics." You can see more of the interview on Politics Wales on BBC One Wales at 10:00 on Sunday and on BBC iPlayer. title: 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?
description: James Schaife and his partner are among the many Londoners struggling to sell their flat.
body: James and his partner have been unable to sell their one-bedroom flat in London and say they are on the verge of bankruptcy In 2015, thousands of people queued overnight in the rain to reserve and buy studio apartments selling for under £200,000 in Hounslow, west London. It's in stark contrast to today's appetite for flats, with property portals reporting a slump in sales. But why, when the country is in a housing crisis with a desperate need for affordable homes, are flats now struggling to sell? According to the property site Zoopla, 88% of flats listed for sale in inner London on its website in 2025 did not find a buyer within six months. The company also says the gap between the value of a flat and a house is the widest it has been for 30 years. Executive director Richard Donnell points to post-pandemic social changes with "people looking for space, prioritising houses, working from home". He also points to higher mortgage rates, people concerned about "all the costs and liabilities of owning a property" including service charges and ground rents. In September, nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK announced increases in the cost of home loans. Donnell says flats in inner London are struggling in particular as they are more expensive, the service charges are higher, and "there's greater complexity - it's highly likely it's a bigger building, maybe more of a complex building, so less are selling within six months". This is a message echoed by property platform Rightmove, which says as of August, only 50% of flats listed for sale nationally successfully find a buyer, compared to 65% of houses. Nationally, as of August, the average price for a flat is down 2% from 12 months prior. That is the largest drop seen over the period by any type of property. Compared with August 2021, flats have only risen in price by 4% nationally, the least of all property types. Colleen Babcock, Rightmove's head of partner marketing, says London faces additional challenges because its market is heavily weighted towards flats, and "affordability more broadly remains a key challenge". She points to higher borrowing costs, increased stamp duty costs, and the limitations of the Lifetime ISA in higher-priced areas, which mean both first-time buyers and home-movers in London can face additional hurdles when buying a home. Flats aren't becoming unsellable for one single reason. Higher borrowing costs, service charges, leasehold and shared ownership complications have made them more expensive and complicated to own, damaging their reputation. James Schaife, 36, says he and his partner are "on the verge of bankruptcy" after struggling to sell their one-bedroom north London flat for the past four years. He bought a 35% share of the £585,000 flat - run by Newlon Housing Trust - in 2017, but after his partner got a new job, James moved out of London in 2022 and relocated north, putting the flat on the market. Within an initial "nomination period" - a set window of time where the association has the exclusive right to find an eligible buyer - the flat generated next to no interest. The housing association gave them permission to sell it on the open market - but James claims they have been "forced to use a narrow selection of valuers chosen by Newlon", despite estate agents telling him the flat has been overvalued. They have been forced to rent out the property with a special "consent-to-let" agreement with their housing association - although this is due to expire imminently and James claims Newlon will not renew it. James said the situation has affected their plans to start a family, pushing them back to an age "where it's probably unlikely that we'll have children". "It's just ruined our lives." A spokesperson for Newlon Housing Trust said that "this is not a picture we recognise", adding that they were bound by "strict rules about resales to protect the public purse". The spokesperson said that "strict rules to limit subletting... prevent the risk of people profiting by letting subsidised affordable housing". "As is well reported, the sales market is flat. The saleability of a home at any time is subject to variation in the property market, which we have no control over, and is part of the risk taken on by anyone who buys a home." Sophie Bishener is unable to move to a bigger property as her building needs a second wave of fire safety repairs Some flat-owners living in homes with building safety concerns have also found their properties impossible to sell. It may be a more extreme example, but many find themselves in this position. As of July 2026, there are 4,697 residential buildings 11m and over in height being monitored due to unsafe cladding, external, but work still isn't complete on 61% of them. Sophie Bishener, leaseholder and campaigner with the End our Cladding Scandal group, said that flats with unsafe cladding left unremediated were like "prisons", and this is having a "devastating" impact on people's lives. She bought her one-bedroom flat in Hertfordshire in 2017 but nine years later, now with a young family, she is unable to move to a bigger property as her building needs a second wave of fire safety repairs. "Being trapped means that you can't move on with your life." She points out that even buildings which have been remediated are affected by a market that is "so distrusting" at the moment. "If you're in a position where you can get to market, there are so many hurdles... management packs costing hundreds of pounds, conveyancing solicitors not willing to take on buildings covered by the Building Safety Act." Sophie thinks there should be a building safety register, "where you've got all the buildings noted, and we know what they're made of" to help boost buyer confidence. The BBC has also investigated problems with new-build properties, including people living in brand-new flats. Their stories come as the number

title: The man who would be king - the rise and fall of 'the next Prince Naseem'
description: Touted as the king to Naseem Hamed's prince, Daniel Teasdale's story is instead a cautionary tale.
body: Daniel Teasdale, pictured, was tipped for the top from an early age Boxer Daniel Teasdale was hailed as the heir to the legendary Prince Naseem Hamed, but his promise never materialised into fame, fortune and films. "He's better than Naz at the same age," said trainer Brendan Ingle. Hamed had won his first world title aged 21. Teasdale was still a teenager. Ingle, from his gym in Sheffield, moulded the careers of a conveyor belt of world-beaters and title winners. He guided both of the fighters from childhood. Before super-middleweight Teasdale's first professional bout, the Rotherham fighter had been featured in national newspapers, books and was being documented by photographers and film-makers. He won a succession of national titles, establishing himself as the next contender to emerge from the Ingle gym. Photographer Simon Roberts travelled to the Ingle gym in 1997 hoping to photograph Hamed. "Brendan said 'don't worry about Naz, start photographing that kid in the corner. He's going to be bigger than Naz'. That was Daniel," Roberts said. Roberts began to follow the young sensation, hoping to capture his rise on camera. Teasdale's early promise earned him plenty of headlines and column inches Filmmaker Stuart Mitchell had a similar brief. "We were selling the documentary as 'who's the next Prince Naseem?'," says Mitchell. He recalls Teasdale being the subject of similar headlines in national newspapers, and later accompanying him to an event gathering together the best British prospects from every sport for the new Millennium. Attention on Ingle's latest protégé was more than just hype. "He was like Oscar de la Hoya," recalls former stablemate Amer Khan. "Teasdale was exceptional as a junior, he was stopping everyone." Teasdale learnt both ballet and gymnastics to develop his footwork and skills in the ring and was seemingly set for stardom. "I was very teachable, could talk, had the looks and could box," says Teasdale, who took up the sport aged six. Prince Naseem's star quality brought plenty of media attention to the Ingle gym and its fighters The bitterness of Hamed's split from trainer Ingle in 1998 has been well-documented, with both sides seemingly losing. "Brendan lost the focus with the up-and-comers," Teasdale says. He followed Naz in leaving the gym, linking up with one of its greatest exports, three-time world title challenger Herol 'Bomber' Graham. The exit was said to have been spearheaded by Teasdale's father who "essentially gave up his career" to help his son fulfil his potential, Roberts says. It was funded by a businessman with no prior experience in boxing, but a thirst to be part of Teasdale's rise to the top. Teasdale remembers Graham's influence as "a breath of fresh air", but the presence of others was less helpful. "People started to try and feed off Daniel," says Roberts. "I photographed [Mike] Tyson and Lennox [Lewis], I have seen all of this stuff before." Mitchell was also filming future Olympic bronze medallist Darren Sutherland when he arrived at the Ingle gym from Ireland. "Daniel was probably more talented than Darren, the trouble with Daniel was he was always being wooed," reveals Mitchell. Teasdale's tag as the next Prince Naseem also hung heavy. "I was like catnip for cats, everybody wanted a piece," Teasdale explains. While the career of some talented prospects is carefully nurtured, Teasdale may not have been as well protected. "To some extent Daniel was used because he was seen as a big potential and was a good scalp for somebody who wanted to get through the ranks," Roberts says. Different trainers, managers and promoters followed, but Teasdale admits instability harmed his progress. His debut had been a disaster - abandoned due to rioting in the crowd - while the following year he received death threats before a bout. Despite undeniable talent, those early misfortunes could now be seen as an omen of what was to come. Daniel with his then trainer Glyn Rhodes in 2004 following death threats. He won the fight After filming Teasdale across five years, Mitchell shelved his documentary when commissioners lost interest. He too lost faith after a training session in Graham's garage. "It felt very small and I didn't think this was going anywhere," he says bluntly. Many have since raised doubts over whether the "pretty boy" was made for a career getting punched in the face. "Everybody has a weakness and mine was women," Teasdale confesses. "I lost the edge and my focus wasn't where it should be." He walked away from the sport in 2005 after he was stopped in the first round of a light-heavyweight contest - his first professional defeat. He returned in 2010 and reunited with Ingle, winning his one and only comeback fight. Teasdale and Ingle reunited ahead of his brief comeback in 2010 "After that I just gave it up, I thought 'I'm not going to be second best to the first me," says Teasdale, whose professional career ended after just five fights over a seven-year period. "At 27 I should have been a world champion defending my title." Roberts continued to photograph Teasdale. "There were a lot of unfortunate circumstances with him which meant he didn't fulfil his potential," Roberts says. "There was a lot of bad advice and a lot of people wanting something from him, and not necessarily for the good." Mitchell did some "soul searching" over his role in Teasdale's journey. "There was so much clamour around him - then it just evaporated," he recalls. "That must be very difficult to deal with when expectations are that you are going to be a successful and famous boxer." Teasdale says "everything went up in the air" as a professional, in contrast to the stability of his early years. title: Hummingbird hawk moths and ivy bees: The insects thriving as temperatures rise
description: Hummingbird hawk moths - often mistaken for small birds - are being spotted in the West Midlands.
body: The hummingbird hawk moth hovers as it feeds from flowers, much like its feathered namesake As parts of the West Midlands baked in warmer temperatures this summer, species once considered unusual in the region, such as hummingbird hawk moths, ivy bees and the wasp spider have been spotted in growing numbers. The hummingbird hawk moth, known for its furry grey body, orange hindwings and long proboscis, migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, said 2026 was a "record year" for sightings of the species, which was often mistaken for a small bird. The moth, which can be seen hovering over flowers, has wings that beat about 80 times per second, external, according to Benwell. "They've had a really good year this year," he said. "Normally they would come in small numbers. We'd normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we've seen loads of records of them. "They're absolutely amazing but I somehow haven't seen one this year, so I'm jealous of anybody else that has." The moth migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months Ivy bees, which feed mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers, had also become more prevalent in the Midlands, Benwell said, adding they were easy to find on buildings. The bees, first recorded in the UK in 2001, are slowly spreading north, after first being recorded in the region in Stourbridge in 2015. "There's nothing that distinguishes them from other bees really, they're not that kind of attention-grabbing species, but, you know, were you to look for them, go to ivy and you'll see them," Benwell said. The ivy bee was first recorded on British shores in 2001 Other insects that had seen an increase in their numbers locally included the clouded yellow butterfly, a European migratory species known to have "peak" years during unusually hot summers. "Most individuals are unable to survive the British winter, but if temperatures continue to rise as a result of climate change, we may well see them becoming permanent residents," Benwell said. "There's numerous species that we could point out that weren't here 20 years ago... and now they're quite abundant." The clouded yellow butterfly was a regular visitor to Britain and Ireland, the Butterfly Conservation said Others once more commonly associated with southern England have also spread further north. The trust said the hornet hoverfly, with yellow markings that mimic a hornet to protect against predators, although it cannot sting, had become really common after it was first recorded in Birmingham and the Black Country in 2004. Another species, the cricket bat spider, which gets its name from its cricket bat-like markings, has also become more common in grassland since it was first spotted in the region in 2019. The sightings come as one of the UK's largest spider species, the wasp spider, was spotted in the Midlands as warmer temperatures pushed it more than 100 miles away from its usual habitat. The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, said the Worcestershire Wildlife Trust. The wasp spider is known for its distinctive yellow, black and white stripes Rosemary Winnall, from the Wyre Forest Study Group, which maps the wildlife and ecology of the forest in Worcestershire, said the arrival of the wasp spider was to be celebrated. She said the group was always on the lookout for new arrivals and had already recorded the willow emerald damselfly, the southern oak bush cricket and the purple emperor butterfly, as more species travelled north. "The impressive western conifer seed bug is here as is the box bug," she added. Hot weather had also benefited butterflies that loved sunshine, such as the holly blue and the pearl-bordered fritillary, which the Butterfly Conservation charity, external said was once "very widespread" but had rapidly declined in recent decades. However, despite an increase in some species appearing in the region, there were others whose numbers were dwindling. "The once-common small tortoiseshell butterfly is now rarely seen for example, and there are far fewer records of the two-spot ladybird," Winnall explained. "We are encouraging folk to record the common species of today as they may be the rarities of the future." title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
description: Videos show groups of riders weaving through busy city centre traffic in Birmingham.
body: This video can not be played Several videos showed riders around the Stephenson Street area of the city Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them. The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city. "It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said. Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates. One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre. "I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said. "People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check. "They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens." Residents say groups of riders have become a familiar sight in the city centre The resident, who did not want to reveal their name, said the groups were not a daily occurrence but had become a familiar sight over the past year. "The one I filmed the other day was at six o'clock and they were coming back around at nine," he said. "It goes on for hours by the look of it." Birmingham-based content creator GB Street Stories has also encountered and filmed riders in the city. "It might just be a hobby or for fun for them, but they have absolutely no right to put other people's lives at risk or damage public property," he said. "I've personally witnessed them breaking traffic laws, driving down the wrong side of the road and speeding straight through stop signs at tram tracks without pausing even for a second. "Riding in this manner is extremely dangerous and puts both their own lives and the safety of everyone else in serious jeopardy." Residents say riders have been seen performing wheelies in busy parts of Birmingham city centre Residents say the issue is not solely about road safety. The noise created by the bikes is also a source of frustration, particularly in busy pedestrian areas. "For people in and around the city, not just residents but visitors too, if you've got young children walking around, you don't want to hear all that," the resident said. "It's fast, furious and dangerous." Witnesses said some riders ignored red lights and weaved through moving traffic The riders have also been seen by street wardens working across Birmingham city centre. A spokesperson for Colmore and Southside Business Improvement Districts said wardens had, on occasion, witnessed groups of riders while carrying out patrols and had shared information with relevant agencies where appropriate. The organisation said wardens did not have powers to stop or detain individuals, but continued to work alongside partners including West Midlands Police and Birmingham City Council. Residents say concerns extend beyond road safety to noise and disruption The issue is not unique to Birmingham. Cleveland Police has used drones in efforts to tackle off-road bikes, while Metropolitan Police officers have deployed electric bikes to pursue riders through areas difficult to access with patrol cars. Elsewhere, new measures allowing police to order people to remove face coverings have been introduced in Nottingham and are due to be introduced in Stafford, as authorities look at different ways of tackling anti-social behaviour. West Midlands Police said it was aware of the issues in Birmingham city centre. "We are aware of concerns around the use of e-scooters and off-road bikes being ridden antisocially in the city centre," a spokesperson said. "Officers are working to crack down on their use locally and, as a result, we are encouraging the public to report any incidents to us. "If a rider is caught using any type of off-road motorbike or quad bike and causing a nuisance to others, they are liable to prosecution, and the vehicle will be seized." Most quad bikes cannot legally be ridden on public road Vehicles used on roads must be registered, taxed and insured Riders must hold the appropriate driving licence Police can seize vehicles being used illegally or antisocially Riders causing a nuisance can be prosecuted (Source: Department for Transport), external Tell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country Follow BBC Birmingham on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: RNLI video receives 'pure hatred' after anti-migrant protests
description: Elizabeth Evans, who shared a video of an RNLI training exercise, says the comments were "really, really bad".
body: Elizabeth Evans said people "spread hatred" in the Facebook comments A woman who shared an RNLI video on social media says she has received "pure hatred" following anti-migrant protests in England. Councillor Elizabeth Evans, who represents Aberaeron and Aberarth in Ceredigion, shared a video on Facebook which showed New Quay's RNLI lifeboat leaving the station on a training day. According to Evans, the post - which attracted 30,000 views - drew comments of hatred, some of which she described as "really, really bad". It comes after RNLI volunteers in Portsmouth were targeted by protesters following the charity's role in helping to bring migrants on a small boat to shore earlier this month. The RNLI said it existed "to save lives at sea". Evans said she was "really shocked" by the reaction to the video. "I couldn't believe it," she said. "And it wasn't a few. It took me a good half hour to get rid of those comments, just one after the other. With that thread of hatred." Describing the comments, Evans continued: "The comment thread was 'traitors', 'taxis for migrants', they were some of the politest ones." She said one of the comments was suggestive of violence, adding: "I don't want to go on because I don't want to give those comments oxygen but they were really, really bad." Evans said she deleted the comments but was subsequently criticised for "shutting down discussion". "I wasn't shutting down discussion because there was no discussion available to be had," she said. "I was shutting down hatred." The video showed an RNLI lifeboat leave the station at New Quay Peter Sparkes, chief executive of the RNLI, said recent events had "generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI". "Our mission, and our tasking is to rescue those women, children and men in danger of drowning. "Anyone rescued from a small boat by the RNLI is immediately handed over to the UK's immigration authorities. "Illegal immigration is a political issue; the RNLI exists to save lives at sea." Small boat protest explained: How a Channel crossing sparked unrest Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats A total of 16,513 people arrived in the UK in small boats in the year to 1 September, 43% lower than the same period the previous year. UK net migration has meanwhile dropped to its lowest level outside of the Covid pandemic since 2012. Evans said social media platforms should do more to crackdown on online abuse and urged the UK government to help. "They need to enforce through legislation that these companies have an absolute responsibility to make sure that they keep their users safe but also, that it's not used as a platform for hatred… We must not allow it to be normalised," said Evans. The UK government said those who dedicated themselves to the service of others should be able to do their work without fear of harassment or abuse online, adding that Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy expected social media companies to be more proactive and rigorous in removing harmful content. A spokesperson for Meta, which owns several social media platforms including Facebook, said "no one should be subjected to abuse of any kind" adding that it removes harmful content when it finds it. title: The man who's been walking around the world for 28 years
description: The BBC heads to Belgium as the adventurer from Hull nears the end of his 28-year expedition.
body: Karl Bushby, right, with the BBC's Kevin Shoesmith as they approach Mons, Belgium Adventurer Karl Bushby has been walking around the world for 28 years and now the end of his journey is in sight. I have been writing about him for most of that time, but although we have spoken frequently and exchanged hundreds of emails we have never met. We are in the village of Havré and I am joining Karl on a five-mile (8km) stretch to Mons. It is part of the final march to Calais, from where he plans to swim across the English Channel in October. Dressed in shorts and a T-shirt which bears evidence of a roadside repair, Karl - sporting a grey beard - appears in the car park of a Belgian railway station. He is pushing a trolley laden with camping equipment and other essentials. Karl set off from Chile, heading back home to Hull, with two self-imposed rules: he cannot use transport to advance and he cannot return to the UK until the walk is complete. Karl arrives in Mons as his adventure nears its end Sweat is seeping through his T-shirt, forming wing-like patches over his shoulder blades. The former paratrooper set off in November 1998, expecting his walk back to his childhood home, where his mother still lives, to take about 12 years. Some 28 years on, he is still going, with visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash which cost him sponsors, Covid-19 and geopolitics having slowed his progress. The 57-year-old has covered more than 30,000 miles (more than 48,000km) and a swim across the English Channel now beckons after Channel Tunnel bosses vetoed his request for access to a service tunnel. Karl ducks into a shop and comes out with a bottle of water, flinging it under a bungee cord attached to his trolley, which he had made in Nicaragua early in the adventure. The Beast, as he calls it, is his lifeline. Karl battling through ice as he crosses the Bering Strait to cross into Russia in 2006 We maintain a fast pace. In 30C heat, I am finding it hard to keep up, with Karl showing no sign of fatigue, despite having trekked 10 miles before lunch. We talk about how he crossed the frozen Bering Strait in 2006 with French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer and his 186-mile swim across the Caspian Sea. Discussing his crossing of the Darién Gap, which links Colombia and Panama, Karl says: "You're having to push through a dense jungle. "You've got these river systems and lots of swamps. Laid over the top of that you've got the fact that it's a warzone." Faced with the threat of kidnap, Karl sought to look as though he was homeless. "Homeless people are pretty much invisible, nobody pays attention to them, so that was our intent. "I did not want to be the blond-haired, blue-eyed gringo with the latest North Face equipment. "I dyed my hair and skin and reduced my clothing to tatters. I carried my stuff in sacks." Karl pictured in Chile at the start of his adventure A woman peers out of a window and looks bemused at the sight of two men and a trolley. Karl invites me to push The Beast for a short while. The black fabric tape covering the handle is worn and peeling. With each passing mile, our conversation becomes more philosophical. I ask him what the biggest lessons have been on the walk. "Tenacity is emperor," he replies. Karl struggles to weave The Beast past a row of parked cars. "These towns can be fun assault courses," he sighs. Returning to the question, he adds: "Coming from a military background, you don't necessarily see the best in people, so it has really been an eye-opener. "From day one, I have been received with open arms from the rest of the world." Karl says he has been out to prove to himself and others what he can do Karl talks about the "kindness of strangers", noting how one family in Chile became "almost like a second family". "They were driving out for eight hours at a time to find me and feed me on the side of the road," he recalls. I reach into my rucksack and retrieve a letter from Karl's mother, Angela Bushby. Also in the bag are packets of his favourite sweets. "Mother remembers," he laughs, selecting the caramel wafers. The pair last met in 2015. "You're still her little boy, aren't you?" I ask. "Apparently so," says Karl. "A very happy little boy with all that chocolate." In the letter, Angela asks if he really must swim the Channel. Both mother and son know the answer. And then comes a line that speaks volumes. "You used to think you were useless. Well, you have proven you're not," Angela has written. I have always known Karl to be self-deprecating, but this leaps from the page. Angela Bushby writes a note to her son, which I handed to him on his approach into Mons He tells me he never felt as fit as his fellow comrades during his Army days. Karl, whose father served in the SAS, says the Army helped build his confidence, but the "damage was done" in his early childhood, with undiagnosed dyslexia making him a target for bullies. "I had no confidence," he says. "I was an underachiever. My dyslexia was not identified until my last year in school." Karl, though, has never doubted he could finish his journey. "There is definitely this sense of wanting to prove myself," he says. "To myself and others. We're talking about doing something other people couldn't even dream of doing." Karl in Colombia in 2001, when he was three years into his trek home For years, Karl has been relaxed about the end date. Not now. There is a real urgency. "It's definitely time to call it a day," he says. "I don't want to keep this going for much longer." We reach Mons and the impressive Grand-Place, where several young people, recognising him from his Instagram account, make a beeline for him. "Oh my God, you are a legend," one excited young man tells Karl. Karl says he is now recognised everywhere because of social media Does the future scare Karl? "Yes," he admits. "One day I'm going to wake up in my mother's house – 57 years old with noth

title: Bluebird at centre of new legal dispute
description: The claim for nearly £150,000 revolves around whether items provided were donated or not.
body: The restored Bluebird ran on Coniston Water earlier this year Donald Campbell's Bluebird is at the centre of a legal battle worth nearly £150,000. Paul Kinghan is seeking £147,162 from the museum which houses the world-famous hydroplane – the Ruskin Museum in Coniston. He said this was the value of the items and cash he had provided to the museum in recent years which had not been repaid. But museum director Tracey Hodgson said everything Kinghan had provided to the museum had been given as donations. Kinghan's claim, issued through a statutory demand, centres upon three engines he bought for the museum as part of its plans to run Bluebird in the Lake District earlier this year. Two of the engines ended up being sold with Kinghan giving the proceeds of the sales to the Ruskin Museum. The museum still owns the third engine. Kinghan said the engines, as well other items and services he had supplied, had been delivered with the understanding that those running the museum were the "right people to be the trustees of the boat". But he said he now wanted his money back because he felt "deceived and let down". "They weren't the people they told me they were," he said. "I was misled". But Hodgson said: "You cannot just donate something and then ask for it back. That's the whole point of a donation." She said the museum had documentation for everything Kinghan had provided and that the forms did not offer any stipulations for the items and services provided. Hodgson said Kinghan's claim had been passed on to the museum's legal representatives, and that it was up him whether to pursue it further in court. Campbell, pictured here at Coniston Water in November 1966, was killed two months later The museum had previously faced a long-running legal dispute with the Tyneside engineer Bill Smith who recovered and restored Bluebird. Smith went on to stake a claim in its ownership, which was disputed by Campbell's daughter, Gina Campbell, and the museum. Smith eventually walked away and handed the hydroplane to the Ruskin Museum. Crowds lined Coniston's streets when Bluebird was handed over to the Ruskin Museum in 2024 Bluebird was recovered from Coniston Water in 2001 after its pilot was killed in a crash in 1967. Donald Campbell died aged 45 when the hydroplane flipped into the air and disintegrated as he attempted a water speed record.
