title: 'I will be a WWE champion': Meet the young wrestlers dreaming big
description: With a new generation of talent setting their sights on some of wrestling's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce its next big star?
body: Among those hoping to make it to the top is 16-year-old Eva For many wrestling fans growing up meant watching stars like The Rock, Stone Cold Steve Austin and John Cena on television. But for anyone who dreamed of following in their footsteps, making it into the industry could feel a world away. Now, those involved in the sport say opportunities are growing closer to home, giving aspiring wrestlers a chance to train, perform and begin building a career. With a new generation setting their sights on some of the sport's biggest stages, could Northern Ireland produce the next big wrestling star? Among those hoping to make it to the top is 16-year-old Eva, who only began training in January. A lifelong wrestling fan, she grew up watching WWE with her family. Discovering she could train locally turned something she watched on television into a realistic ambition. "The reason I joined is because it's so local, it was a great opportunity because I always wanted to do something like this," she said. Eva hopes to study performing arts after leaving school, which she believes could help develop the character and performance side of her wrestling. Eva's wrestling ambitions stretch well beyond Northern Ireland She also points to Irish WWE star Becky Lynch as an inspiration, saying her success gives her "hope and motivation" that where someone comes from does not have to limit them. Despite being only months into her wrestling journey, she has already set herself the biggest possible target. "In the future I will be a WWE champion," she said. Eva is one of a growing number of people turning an interest in wrestling into action by stepping into the ring. And she isn't on her own, with one coach saying the number of people interested in the sport has "grown exponentially" in recent years. Five years ago, the number of people training in professional wrestling across Northern Ireland was believed to be in the 30s. Today it is more than 150. Amira Blair moved to London to pursue her dream For Lisburn's Amira Blair, who appeared in the ring at Wembley Stadium last month, the route into wrestling looked very different when she was growing up. She first dreamed of becoming a wrestler at the age of 11, but pursuing it as a career from Northern Ireland seemed a very distant prospect. "I never thought this was a goal that you could have. It seemed like something on the TV you see Americans doing," she said. Blair is now a full-time professional wrestler, but growing it was such a "niche thing" that she did not feel able to talk about her ambition with others. Following that dream also meant moving from Northern Ireland to London - a decision some people struggled to understand. "They thought I was just losing the plot and why would I not go get a normal job with stability," she added. "Why am I moving to London on a whim and pursuing something that's just so out there?" She says the industry has also changed significantly for women, going "from having three minutes of time in matches to getting main events". Damien Corvin opened a professional wrestling academy in Larne last year Damien Corvin believes the gap between starting out in Northern Ireland and building a career is beginning to narrow. He is a full-time professional wrestler and head coach at the Relentless Pro Wrestling Academy in Larne. Corvin says aspiring wrestlers no longer necessarily have to move away to turn wrestling into a career: "It's very, very possible to be a full-time pro wrestler, for this to be your full-time job while still living in Northern Ireland. "You can travel the world as an independent pro wrestler." Corvin has done that himself, wrestling in India, France and Switzerland, as well as across the UK and Ireland. He says the opportunities available to those starting out in Northern Ireland have improved significantly in recent years. "We're giving these guys a platform to try out new characters, to try out new moves, to see what works, and get them in front of an audience," he said. "Just watching them get that little bit better every single week is amazing as a coach, but it also leads me to have high hopes for the future of what we can do in Northern Ireland wrestling." Dylan says he would sleep outside if it meant he could wrestle full time Carrickfergus man Dylan Todd, known in the ring as DD Crooks, is among those hoping to turn wrestling into a career. Growing up, he was more interested in drama and skateboarding than traditional sports and despite being a wrestling fan, did not realise it was something he could pursue locally. He says being around wrestlers who have progressed in the industry makes it feel much more achievable. "When you see those guys doing it and you're like, 'well, it wasn't long ago they were probably in my position'," he said. Dylan believes the "immense" talent currently coming through across the island of Ireland could lead to more wrestlers making their mark in the ring. "I'd sleep outside if it meant getting a job wrestling one day. Honestly, it's my dream job," he added. title: Winless Villa and Spurs face telling early showdown
description: Aston Villa and Tottenham are winless in the Premier League - and both in need of inspiration as they prepare to face each other on Saturday.
body: Aston Villa have lost three of their opening four Premier League games More than half a billion spent between them, for just three points and one goal. Tottenham and Aston Villa are in need of Premier League inspiration. It is not a surprise that a summer of change at both clubs has failed to bring immediate results - but they need to ignite their season. They meet at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday as the past two Europa League winners but sitting in the bottom four of the early Premier League table. With 10 new players, and six key sales - including Morgan Rogers and Ollie Watkins - Unai Emery is shaping a new Villa team. Tottenham also added 10 players for more than £300m but goodwill is in short supply after two years of relegation battles. Victory is paramount for both teams. At VIlla, Emery has credit in the bank after turning them from a team floundering in mid-table to Europa League winners - qualifying for Europe every season since his arrival, and getting them back into the Champions League this year. This term there is a different remit, to be successful while integrating 10 new players - having spent more than £250m - following the summer exits. Emery conceded he did not know exactly why Villa lost control during last Saturday's defeat by Nottingham Forest - but knows he was unable to make a significant impact from the touchline with all the new players still fitting in to their new set-up. He can look frantic in his technical area during games, but has an impressive ability to decompress immediately and speak to the players calmly by the time he has returned to the dressing room. Emery remains confident Villa will improve yet is relying on John McGinn and Tyrone Mings, as two of the senior players, to help him and the squad through a difficult patch. It is a reason why both played in Wednesday's Carabao Cup win at Coventry rather than being rested. Captain McGinn has previously described learning Emery's methods as doing "a lot of homework". That may be why Aaron Wan-Bissaka has struggled in his opening three games as he tries to adapt quickly - the same too for other new signings perhaps overthinking their roles. An extended three-week break follows Saturday's match. But the head coach will not get the much-needed time on the training ground with his squad, as many go on international duty. "This break is crazy because it's three weeks," Emery said. "I don't like to be three weeks but we must accept it. "We are not going to have the players we want. [Johan] Manzambi played the first two matches with us and Saturday the third and then he goes with the national team. "Back with us, we must again try to join him with us in our structure and his mind will maybe be confused. "We don't want to use the international break as an excuse. "Saturday is very important as we lack points but we continue in our process trying to work as well as possible." Manzambi, brought in from Freiburg, and £47m winger Ibrahim Mbaye, who has moved from Paris St-Germain. made their debuts last weekend, coming off the bench against Forest, and are set to form part of a new attack. Nicolas Jackson, signed from Chelsea in August, will start on Saturday after coming off the bench at the CBS Arena as Emery gets close to his preferred line-up, with Villa looking to click after notching just one point in their opening four games. This video can not be played Tottenham's wait for league goal continues after Everton draw Only Villa, with 3.39, have a worse xG in the Premier League so far this season than Spurs' 3.45. Alysson's header in the 2-1 defeat by Forest was their first goal in the Premier League this term, with Spurs still searching for theirs. Both are still worse than bottom club Coventry, who are pointless and goalless, but have an xG of 4.21. Villa have had the lowest number of shots in the Premier League with 33, compared to Tottenham's 51, while their six on target is also the worst in the top flight followed by Spurs' 12. Only Hull have had fewer touches in the box (47) than Villa's 62. Yet Villa's defence must still be wary of struggling Spurs despite the hosts' lack of goals. Matty Cash is available after recovering from a muscle problem but fellow defenders Pau Torres and Ian Maatsen are out for a match in which Villa can expect to face pressure. Only Manchester United, Arsenal, Brighton and Liverpool have made more passes in the final third than Tottenham (617), who have the highest successful pass completion rate, at 81.4%. Villa's tally of 32 crosses, the lowest in the league, is half as many as Tottenham have managed. It has been 407 minutes since Spurs last scored in the Premier League. They have failed to score in four successive Premier League matches - the first time that has happened since September 2006. Their stalemate with Everton was their first goalless draw at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in the Premier League after 140 games. But despite both sides' struggle for goals, history does not point to a 0-0 draw. None of the past 22 Premier League meetings between Spurs (15 wins) and Aston Villa (seven) have been drawn. As Villa rebuild, they might hope a match against opponents struggling for wins might be the chance to kick-start their season. But they cannot afford to be lulled into a false sense of security. title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
description: "This is a community that knows tragedy and has had to contend with tragedy in recent years," says rector.
body: Noah Woods' family said he was "the sweetest and most innocent little boy" who will be "missed forever" When three-year-old Noah Woods disappeared, hundreds came together in the hope of bringing him home. It was at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday when he became separated from a relative while at a playground in Brantham, Suffolk. The following day the news came that nobody wanted to hear: a child's body had been recovered from a nearby pond. At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him, coming together in hope then grief. It is not the first time this village of about 2,600 people has been hit by tragedy. Just how does a community come to terms with such a loss? Tributes have been left next to the playground in Brantham where Noah was playing before he disappeared In July 2024, Anita Rose, 57, who lived in Brantham, was taking her dog Bruce for a morning walk when she was attacked. She died three days later. It would be three months before her killer Roy Barclay - a violent offender and one of the county's most wanted criminals - was arrested and charged with her murder. The large police and media presence that descended on Brantham on Tuesday as the search for missing Noah grew, will have brought back painful memories for the village's residents. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public began scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border. Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf, which added complications to the search efforts. Noah's father Rhys Woods, from nearby East Bergholt, Suffolk, praised those who joined the search. "The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives." Reflecting after Noah's death, the Reverend Chris Willis, rector of St Michael's Church, in Brantham, said: "This is a community that knows tragedy and has had to contend with tragedy in recent years. "All I can say, unequivocally, is this is a community that has been amazingly positive. It has dealt with the pain of loss and I have no doubt we'll pull together. "There was a love shown that was my first impression, and I hope and believe we'll see that continue." More than 1,000 people from as far as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help find Noah James Cartlidge, the MP for South Suffolk, was standing with the volunteers when the police delivered the news of his death. "That was pretty hard to watch to be honest because they were in deep grief. And that will remain the case," he said. "I've been many times to Brantham and always get the feeling it is a strong community. "There's history, there's community, and there is strength. And they showed it with the terrible case with Anita Rose. And they will show it now, and they are showing it now, the way they've responded." Mal Bridgeman, the chairman of Brantham Parish Council, said he was not sure the community could ever come to terms with the events of the past week. "I think that Noah will live in the memory of everybody," he said. "As time goes on, the emotions will quieten down. People will come to terms with it but I think people will just come to terms with it in their own time." It was a view echoed by the parish council's clerk, Sarah Keys, who said: "People were really hopeful and they felt empowered and really wanted to help. "So I think finding out that they weren't able to do that anymore was just completely devastating. "Not the outcome we wanted, but it has really restored your faith in community and in people and in, well, Brantham." Supt Tom Pearse delivered updates to volunteers at Brantham Leisure Centre during the search Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief. She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases. "We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture. "There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so. "Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it." Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve. She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more. "In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could." For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said. "The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say. "People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'. "It can mean even more coming from a stranger." Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies. "But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said. Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do. title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
description: The AI model accessed the internet and guessed credentials to three websites, a Google official told the BBC.
body: Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act. Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped". The affected companies have been informed about the breach. It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree. The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations. Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly." Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches. In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services". As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation. Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week. On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development. title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
description: Residents later received the all-clear after explosions were reported in the capital.
body: Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital. It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July. The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate. Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted. The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson. title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
description: The reforms to Parenting Orders could also see parents losing benefits, Jake Richards MP told the Times.
body: Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said. Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe". His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines. Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion. He described the proposed changes as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach. "Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times. "Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well." Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective. When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour." He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can". He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely". Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence. They can also consider an order for 16 and 17 year olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences. However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23. The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed. title: Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it?
description: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy looks at some of the scenarios being imagined and assesses how likely they are.
body: This video can not be played Recent AI (artificial intelligence) safety concerns have been fuelled by stark warnings from AI scientists about the growing risks of the technology going rogue. Some of the most pessimistic predictions warn that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could wipe out all humans in the next 10 years. Many of the apocalyptic messages come from observers of the AI world known as 'AI Doomers' - but the big question many are asking, is how these Doomers think AI could actually bring an end to mankind. Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy looks at some of the scenarios being imagined and assesses how likely they are. Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it? title: The Papers: 'Monstrous words' and 'Russia to ramp up war'
description: The fallout from Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana leads most papers on Saturday.
body: Many of Saturday's papers continue their coverage of the fallout from Earl Spencer's book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC, Earl Spencer said he was telling the truth about the nature of a phone call he had after his sister's death with the then Prince Charles. In excerpts published by the Daily Mail, the earl claimed King Charles III told him "we'll forget her soon enough", but Buckingham Palace said in a statement that fraternal grief could "colour memory". The Mail says Earl Spencer hit back at the King in a "defiant" interview. The Daily Star also leads with Earl Spencer's interview with Laura Kuenssberg. "Monstrous", is the paper's one-word headline in reference to how the earl characterised the King's words. The Sun says the earl has been branded a "hypocrite", reporting that in a 1998 interview he claimed he would "never profit from my sister's life" but now "rakes in [a] fortune" from her death. The Daily Express leads with claims from author Tom Bower that the earl is "undoubtedly" working with his nephew, the Duke of Sussex, to "damage" King Charles. The paper dubs the alleged pairing the "Spencer alliance". The front page of the Times carries a photo of Earl Spencer, captioned "I don't hear denial from the King". It also reports that the Treasury is considering lowering the "mansion tax" threshold to £1.5m ahead of next month's Budget, citing unnamed government sources. The paper says if Chancellor John Healey announces the change, thousands more homes will be hit by the tax. "Russia prepares to ramp up war" is the main headline on the front page of the Daily Telegraph. It says Western intelligence officials believe Russian President Vladimir Putin is "laying the ground for a 'stealth mobilisation' over this weekend, in which thousands of Russians could be drafted". According to the i Paper, the British Army "secretly relaxed security checks", claiming this led to "letting in far-right extremists who backed Russia" over the course of two years. Leading the Guardian is an investigation revealing that "sensitive" police data is being held on a "vulnerable" cloud platform. New Great British Bake Off presenter Nigella Lawson is also on the front page alongside a chocolate cake, as she says "eating is my superpower." The founder of Betfred "attacks high taxes" in Britain in the Financial Times's lead story. Fred Done, who according to the paper is "Britain's biggest taxpayer", says at aged 83 he is "too old" to leave the country for tax purposes as others have done. "My dear friend Ann" is the headline of the Daily Mirror, as Strictly Come Dancing judge Craig Revel Horwood describes the late politician as "an amazing human being, and brave." He tells the paper he spoke to her six days before her death. Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished
description: The BBC’s Caitríona Perry spoke to the late president's niece, as protesters gathered at the venue to condemn demolition threats.
body: This video can not be played The BBC's Caitríona Perry spoke to Kerry Kennedy, the niece of late president John F Kennedy, about demolition threats to the performance centre named after him. A US federal judge ruled the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs to the Kennedy Center, as President Donald Trump warned the Washington DC performing arts venue could be "ripped down". The order comes after Trump was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Protesters also gathered at the venue on Friday to demonstrate against demolition threats. Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished. title: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
description: Mary Timby flew to Ireland on a whim last year and met her boyfriend at a matchmaking festival.
body: This video can not be played "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in Ireland Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch. The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland. So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit. Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps. Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance "It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her. They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting. From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own. She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen". Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says. When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up". A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media." She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker. Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beau That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world. Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand. But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out. Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night. "My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby. So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her. "I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing. "Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.' "It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you." The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festival He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out. "It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer. What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves. When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going. "It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit." They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returne

title: Tata Sons: India's corporate crown braces for upheaval amid boardroom revolt
description: The Tata boardroom battle has intensified over a re-appointment of its chairman and a diktat to go public.
body: Noel Tata (l) and N Chandrasekaran (r) are at the centre of the feud This week, the board of Tata Sons - one of India's oldest conglomerates and owner of iconic British brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea - defied its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, by reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman and backing a public listing of the holding company. Tata Trusts, which owns 66% of Tata Sons called the decision "illegal" under its articles of association and also opposed the listing, setting the stage for a period of prolonged upheaval and possibly a protracted legal drama at Bombay House, the headquarters of the 158-year-old company. For the Tatas, who are no strangers to boardroom battles, a cloud of uncertainty now prevails at multiple levels. The resolution to reappoint Chandrasekharan, while approved by the board, could be defeated at the company's Annual General Meeting as Tata Trusts is likely to vote against it, putting a question mark over his future. The meeting has to take place before 31 December as per reports, after the previous one was adjourned for lack of quorum, but no new date has yet been announced. "The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Board of Tata Sons which reappointed him has no power to take this decision. They can only make a recommendation. Also, their decision flies against the governance code of the company that requires executives to step down from active roles at 65. These are serious lapses," Nitin Potdar, a prominent Mumbai-based corporate lawyer told the BBC. Chandrasekharan, who got a five-year extension, will turn 65 in 2028. Tata Group stocks first soared and then crashed as the tensions mounted, reflecting hope and uncertainty about leadership and business continuity amid several high-stakes but loss-making bets by Chandrasekharan in sectors like semiconductors and airlines. But beyond the leadership tussle, the bigger question to contend with is the group's public listing, "which now looks increasingly inevitable", Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC. Bombay House, the Tata Group head office in Mumbai In 2022, India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), classified Tata Sons as an "upper layer non-banking financial company" because of its systemic importance and investment activities. This created a listing obligation on the group. Tata Sons sought to get out of this classification by repaying their debt and arguing that they do not borrow directly from the public markets. But after sitting on its application for over two years, the RBI rejected the company's bid to get out of the framework earlier this month, pushing the group closer to a stock market debut. In a statement, Tata Trusts reiterated its long-held opposition to going public and said "all available options and not a listing alone" are being explored even though its trustees are no longer unanimous in their position on the matter. Potdar says the regulator has no power to force any company to go public and the issue will almost certainly be legally challenged by Tata Trusts. The RBI meanwhile has pre-emptively, external approached the courts seeking to be heard first in any matter related to the ‌listing. The issue has sharply divided opinion among corporate pundits. Many in the group, including the late Ratan Tata and veteran director NA Soonawala, have long argued strongly for keeping the group private. A publicly held Tata Sons could significantly reduce the control and special rights the Tata Trusts wield over the group. They say the Tatas have a unique operating structure where the majority shareholder is a charity which uses dividends received from commercial arms to fund hospitals, universities and research. A listing, they say, will destroy its character by making it accountable to outside shareholders whose focus would be financial returns. "A new group of shareholders might say, 'Don't declare dividends; we need to reinvest this money in the companies.' What happens then? The first casualty will be the hospitals they run," said Potdar. Opponents of the initial public offering (IPO) also worry that bringing in public investors will weaken the group's internal support function to rescue distressed businesses and expose the company to quarterly performance pressures. Moreover the timing is another crucial factor. "The group currently faces large financial commitments from recently formed subsidiary companies, including Air India, investments in long gestation projects, and losses in newer ventures," Soonawala wrote, external in a piece for Times of India. "The current situation in the case of Air India would be an acid test. All these would need to be disclosed fully in an IPO prospectus. Consolidated financial statements – reflecting subsidiary losses and borrowings – may not present an especially attractive picture to sophisticated investors, pointing to wrong timing for an IPO at the present time." Many, including Potdar, also argue that globally, industrial foundations are being protected as sources of patient capital - money that can be committed for years to fund long-gestation projects and social goals. By forcing the Tatas to list, India is going the other way. Tata Group officially regained control of the national carrier Air India in 2022 But supporters of a listing say it would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to a group that is systemically important to India. "There should be tougher scrutiny of their capital-allocation decisions being so central to the Indian business ecosystem. Everybody wants complete control over their empire and the freedom to take capricious decisions, but that is not a good thing for the organisation," said Kumar. Collectively, listed Tata companies including Tata Motors and TCS have a market capitalisation of more than $260bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders, pension funds, insurers and mut

title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
description: Ineos founder Sir Jim Ratcliffe tells the BBC he thinks the country is "on the slide" and calls for more investment in the North Sea.
body: This video can not be played Sir Jim Ratcliffe says the UK economy is "on the slide" One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide". The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration. He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter. In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years. A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply." Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020. The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos. Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK. "In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment." He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better". Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved. Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030. Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil. "You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down. "If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening." Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security. Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary. The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses." Ineos has invested in the EU's first carbon capture project in Denmark Sir Jim warned that low gas storage levels in Europe posed a risk to the UK in the months ahead. "If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we'll run out of gas and have to switch industry off... our storage is not full," he said. The UK does not typically store a great deal of gas, relying instead on LNG (liquidfied natural gas) and gas imports from Europe. Energy specialist consultancy Cornwall Insight said that current gas storage levels in the EU were at about 69%, when typically they would be at 85% at this time of the year. However, Adam Bell of consultancy Stonehaven, said supplies were unlikely to run short. "We are down compared to where we normally would be but not what I'd regard as catastrophic," he said. "The physical risk of running out of gas is relatively low, especially if Jackdaw gets the go ahead." He said the main source of uncertainty was policy in the US, which supplies LNG to the UK. Sir Jim was speaking in Denmark at the launch of the EU's first carbon capture and storage system (CCS). Ineos has invested in the scheme which is being subsidised by the Danish government and the EU. He said he had hoped to develop CCS in the UK but there had not been enough government support. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said the government had committed £21.7bn for CCS projects over 25 years, however, no projects are yet operational in the UK. At the project in Esbjerg in the south west of Denmark, carbon captured from around the country arrives in huge zeppelin-like tanks before being pumped into a ship called Carbon Destroyer 1. It is then pumped into a depleted oil field nearly 200 miles off shore. Critics say CCS is expensive, money that could be better used to invest in renewables rather than supporting continued fossil fuel use. Sir Jim's critique of the UK is not limited to energy and tax policy. He said the country had at one time been "a fantastic place". "We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars," he said. But he said immigration and welfare spending were both currently too high and that politicians had proved reluctant to tackle either. "Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem. Nobody's tough enough to deal with the benefits problem. But somebody needs to do it," he said. Earlier this year he caused controversy by saying the UK had been "colonised by immigrants". He later offered an apology for "offending some people". You can listen to the full interview here on the Big Boss Interview podcast with Simon Jack. title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
description: Many of the Royal Family's current troubles can be traced back to the aftermath of the then Princess of Wales' death.
body: The legacy of the shocking death of Diana, Princess of Wales, is still the rawest of wounds for the royals, as demonstrated by the no-holds-barred memoir from her brother Earl Spencer. It might be almost 30 years ago, but Buckingham Palace's unusually angry rebuttal to the book's allegations of a callous response to his ex-wife's death from the then Prince Charles shows how much this still matters. That late summer in 1997 was a moment when the Royal Family looked out of touch, lacking in empathy for Diana's loss, and at peril of losing public support, as people laid siege to the palaces with flowers. While the royals dealt with their own private grief, they were also facing a reputational disaster, at risk of becoming the focus of public dismay at the sudden death of the "People's Princess" in a car crash in Paris. An outpouring of public grief saw flowers laid outside palaces and Diana's homes "It was a very febrile mood. Everyone was taken by surprise by the strength of feeling, and the strength to which the Royal Family was unpopular. The palaces were deemed to have treated Diana badly," recalls royal author Valentine Low. Low was inside Westminster Abbey for Diana's funeral and vividly remembers the public response to the electrifying speech made by Earl Spencer. "I heard this noise. I couldn't quite make out what it was, and then I worked out it was the crowd outside the abbey, who'd been listening on the speakers," he says. "That noise appeared to come through the stone walls of the abbey and it was the most extraordinary thing - as people then started to applaud inside the abbey. It was so astounding, in front of Charles and all of the Royal Family." 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview A volatile public mood followed Diana's death, with the late Queen Elizabeth eventually having to respond with a live televised address paying tribute to the princess and acknowledging how difficult it can be to articulate grief. "We have all been trying in our different ways to cope. It is not easy to express a sense of loss, since the initial shock is often succeeded by a mixture of other feelings: disbelief, incomprehension, anger - and concern for those who remain," said the late Queen. A fresh-faced new prime minister, Tony Blair, was said to have been a modernising influence on sending such a direct message - an intervention later depicted in the movie, The Queen, starring Helen Mirren. There was disagreement about whether it was right for the princes to walk behind Diana's coffin So many of the current tensions in the royal world can be traced back to the trauma of those events. The death of a mother at such a young age was inevitably a huge shaping influence on her sons - and it can feel as though those unresolved tensions are still playing out. In the Duke of Sussex's memoir Spare, Diana's absence is a huge presence, his sense of loss unabated. There is still a graphic sense of his distress at walking behind her coffin, with Prince Harry mentioning Earl Spencer's opposition. "Mummy's brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell. 'You can't make these boys walk behind their mother's coffin! It's barbaric'," wrote Harry. Harry's accusation that the interests of the institution of the monarchy had been put above the happiness of individuals has been part of the narrative that saw him stepping down as a working royal and remaining at loggerheads with his brother, Prince William. There was a wave of applause from outside Westminster Abbey when Earl Spencer finished his eulogy The disputes that followed Diana's death, within the family and between in-laws, are still being aired loudly in Earl Spencer's book - Swan Song: Diana, My Sister - and in the global news coverage it has triggered. It opens up old questions about King Charles's character, his treatment of the young princess and his relationship with the now Queen Camilla. On social media, Diana's fans are believing Earl Spencer's version of events, says Prof Pauline Maclaran. She says the royals remain "highly vulnerable" to anything that evokes the story of a "beautiful princess whose life was cut short in such tragic and ambiguous circumstances". Royal commentator Jenny Bond described it as a "fantastically hostile, absolutely rude book... it's a very unpleasant portrayal of a man - but it's his memory of it, and who knows who's right?" Prince William was 15 and Prince Harry just 12 at their mother's funeral At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough." He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death. Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that. The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise". Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death. Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds. Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one. title: Is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
description: The retailer hosted its first-ever London Fashion Week show this week, celebrating 100 years of producing clothing.
body: M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026 "I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. She says it's officially cool to buy your clothes from the high street retailer now. According to Clark and others on social media, Marks and Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too. "For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand". And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive. So how is M&S attracting and retaining a younger generation of shoppers in a highly competitive market? The BBC went to the catwalk show and spoke to experts to find out. Speaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months". For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lie. Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown. The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market. But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops. Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archive The retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis. But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board. "They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi. Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion". M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways. Clark notes that the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate". This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us". "As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them." She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester". During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%. This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025. But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too. It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26. Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh". And that's something Clark has noticed too. "Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity." According to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators. "I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's £500 from the runway.' "And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi. "And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says. Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing. She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers. title: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
description: Dineo Motapane is one of nine recent victims whose deaths have left a nation traumatised over the level of violence against women.
body: This video can not be played 'We are dying': Aunt of murdered woman pleads for action on femicide "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give." "For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?" Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body. The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni. Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death. "How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish. "There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over." Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July. The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. Dineo Motapane's body was "discarded like a piece of rubbish", her aunt said Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one. His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni. The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge. "We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining. "I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her. "No family should have to deal with what we are faced with." Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July. Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women. Itumeleng Kekana's killing has left her young daughter without a mother Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths. Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked. Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis. South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered. The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder. Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events. And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster. Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis. It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit. This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further. Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime. "Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide. "Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman." Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa. It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue. "It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking." Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done. President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls." Activists held a demonstration when South Africa hosted G20 leaders last year Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity. "The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994. "What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed. "This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on -

title: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
description: Increasingly frequent and ferocious attacks on the Ukrainian capital have left many on edge.
body: Daria left her apartment in Kyiv this summer after Russia's attacks on the city intensified For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling. Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world. But this year that has changed. In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital. In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September. A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home. She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut. When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared." At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks. But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether. She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector. A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in July Daria's experience is far from unique. Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives. Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics. It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions. Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says. She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv. Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advance Yet, for many, leaving is not an option. Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina. Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world. From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files. She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target. This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions. "It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns." Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bed Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glass With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside. Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass. Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night. "They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night. "People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies." The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morning An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night. At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires. According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August. As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens. Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted. When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time. title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
description: After a changeable week, drier and warmer conditions will dominate for some next week, but with little rain for those who need it.
body: Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK. Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September. Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland. The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions. The changeable conditions that have dominated the past week will continue into the weekend, with blustery winds coming in off the Atlantic and gales for some western coasts and hills. While Saturday will become a day of sunshine and passing showers for many, in southern parts of England and Wales a weather front draped across the area will mean mostly cloudy conditions and rain or drizzle at times, especially in the south-west. Despite the cloud, it will feel warm and humid due to the south-westerly winds dragging in warm and moist air from the mid-Atlantic. Over the coming days the jet stream will buckle to the north of the UK allowing high pressure to build The much more autumnal look to the weather charts at the moment is down to a particularly brisk and straight jet stream roaring through the skies across the Atlantic. It has meant rain-bearing areas of lower pressure to the north of the UK, high pressure to the south and stronger winds in between, creating the changeable conditions. However, as the jet stream starts to buckle through the second half of the weekend the weather will slowly being to calm down. On Sunday, early rain in the far north and south of the UK should move away to leave most parts dry with sunny spells by the afternoon. Strong winds in north-east Scotland should ease too. While it will feel pleasant in the sunshine, temperatures will be close to the seasonal average of 15-21 Celsius. Into the start of next week, high pressure will build across the UK more widely at first. Other than early rain in Scotland and northern England, most places will see increasing amounts of sunshine breaking through during the day. Temperatures will lift by a degree or so compared to Sunday and humidity levels will creep up too. That more humid air paired with light winds across England and Wales into Tuesday means some will start off rather misty and foggy. Once the sun has broken through though, it will feel like late summer warmth has returned. Temperatures could peak at around 25 or 26 Celsius in south-east England, but reach the low 20s in many other parts of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Eastern Scotland. 2026 has already been a record-breaking year for the number of days above 25C, with last week exceeding the record of 89 days set in 1959. A weather front moving into western Scotland is likely to bring some rain and could be the focus for a developing low pressure system that will bring more widespread rain midweek across the northern half of the UK. Temperatures lift across the UK early in the week As high pressure holds on across the south, many will stay largely dry and warm here through the rest of the week. While many may enjoy the warm weather, it is not good news for declining reservoir and water storage levels. While recent rain has been welcome, it has been well short of what is required to break the drought across most of England and Wales. By Friday morning Leconfield, East Yorkshire had only received 11% of its normal September rainfall, and Durham just 14% - both well below the 50-60% that would be typical by now. Some forecasts do show the potential for rain returning more widely from late week and into next, but others hint at continuing high pressure and potentially even warmer air.
