title: Watch: Voting under way in Russian election tightly controlled by Kremlin
description: Russia's parliamentary elections are under way, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
body: This video can not be played Russia's parliamentary elections are under way, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ruling party United Russia, which is backed by President Vladimir Putin, is expected to be the biggest party in parliament. Critics say the election is neither free nor fair, with all ten parties on the ballot either backing - or not openly challenging - the policies of Putin and the war in Ukraine. The only anti-war party, Yabloko, was removed the ballot in the run-up to polling day – although some candidates remain in some constituencies. The Kremlin will likely to claim the results show public backing for both the president and the war. Voting takes place from 18 to 20 September, with no surprise wins expected. The BBC's Steve Rosenberg looks at how or the elections will or will not affect the political landscape in Russia. Watch: Voting under way in Russian election tightly controlled by Kremlin. title: North Korean anthem played for South Korea at Asian Games
description: Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan.
body: This video can not be played North Korean anthem blunder for South Korea at Asian Games Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan. South Korea, who thrashed Bangladesh 5-0, looked confused as the incorrect national anthem was played. South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that Bangladesh's national anthem followed before South Korea's actual anthem was played. A stadium announcer did apologise for the mistake. "This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared; there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," South Korea coach Min Tae-seok said. "But this is something that simply should never happen." North Korea's national anthem, along with other symbols of the secretive state, are banned in South Korea. The two countries are still technically at war, after the 1950-53 conflict between the two ended without a peace treaty. The build-up to the Asian Games, which officially starts on Saturday, has already seen complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week. Field hockey at the Asian Games started on Friday and runs until 3 October. title: Warren Buffett steps down after six decades at Berkshire - 'Father Time always wins'
description: Since taking control in 1965, Buffett grew a struggling textile mill into a global conglomerate.
body: Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values." Warren Buffett has stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, handing over leadership to his son Howard in the final chapter of a long-planned transition at the US business giant. At 96, the world-famous investor will move into an advisory role as chairman emeritus and remain on the company board to offer his "judgement and perspective", according to a letter to shareholders, external. The decision comes nine months after Buffett passed the chief executive role to Greg Abel, with his son, Howard, who has been a director since 1993, taking over non-executive board duties. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett built one of the most successful investment track records in modern history. He took control of Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 when it was a struggling New England textile mill and turned it into a $1.1 trillion (£822b), global conglomerate. Today, the business owns a wide range of well-known brands including GEICO car insurance, Dairy Queen, and BNSF railway system. It also owns large stakes in companies like Apple and Coca-Cola – a brand close to Buffett's heart, as he famously drinks five cans a day. Buffett has made his mark through "value investing" – a strategy focused on finding companies with solid fundamentals, buying them at fair prices, and holding them for decades. His annual letters to shareholders and festival-like annual meetings turned him into a leading mentor across the financial world. Despite his retirement from the top board post, the change is considered an orderly passing of the baton rather than a sudden shock. "The timing is right to complete the transition," Buffett wrote, noting he had recently celebrated his 96th birthday and the first birthday of one of his great-grandchildren, who is "moving a bit faster" than he is. The company assured investors that day-to-day operations will remain steady. While Greg Abel manages corporate strategy and capital decisions, Howard Buffett's main duty as chairman will be guarding the firm's "culture and values". A former farmer, philanthropist, and sheriff, the younger Buffett brings more than three decades of board experience to the role. Buffett concluded his letter by saying it had been the "privilege of a lifetime" to serve as chairman, but acknowledged that in the end, "Father Time always wins". title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
description: O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless" and said "it won't happen again".
body: O'Leary had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists". He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments. O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders. Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC. O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe". He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate. "British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added. Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime". In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair". "I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors. "I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors." O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again". "I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future." Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments. She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said". She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise. "I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote. In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape." He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training". It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business. In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges. He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories". In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws. title: Men lose appeal for harrassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary
description: Kristofer Deichler, Jatinder Kamra and Sukhraj Singh were given community service and restraining orders for their harassment of Catrin Nye.
body: From left to right: Kristofer Deichler, Jatinder Kamra, and Sukhraj Singh Three men have lost their appeal for harassing BBC journalist Catrin Nye, who presented the podcast series and documentary, A Very British Cult. Kristofer Deichler, 47, Jatinder Kamra, 46 and Sukhraj Singh, were sentenced for harassment after visiting her home where she lived with her partner and children, first in a group in August 2024, and then again as the three of them in September 2024. "We accept she was terrified by the unexpected attendance" at her home, said Judge Pounder at Snaresbrook Crown Court, adding there was "heightened concern" as her children were also home. All three men are members of Lighthouse, which was investigated for the 2023 documentary and podcast fronted by Nye. Three men sentenced for harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary Three men guilty of harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years. They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade. A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC. "While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said. After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered. The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping. "The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder. "What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable. During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours. The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism". "They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained. "That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster." The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said. Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested. The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest. Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return". Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property. It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said. Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard. The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs. Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address". The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC. On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional £1,000. title: Uefa & Concacaf demand Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members
description: Uefa and Concacaf issue a joint statement calling on Fifa to pay $10m from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Uefa and Concacaf have written to Gianni Infantino calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations. It is the latest chapter in the war of words between the governing bodies, in response to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's aborted private equity proposal. Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to an investment company. The idea was scrapped after four days following widespread opposition from national associations. The letter, seen by BBC Sport, was signed by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin and his Concacaf counterpart Victor Montagliani. It outlines that "Fifa is on course to close 2023-26 with reserves of approximately $6bn (£4.5bn)" which is "considerably more than is required" through to the 2030 men's World Cup. It said that Fifa should "make at least $10m available to each of its 211 member associations over the 2027-30 cycle" which should be used "for investment in infrastructure and football development". This "one-off release of reserves" would come at a cost of $2.11bn (£1.57bn), and would be in addition to the regular funding in the cycle. When the controversial plan was revealed in the days following the World Cup final, Infantino told members they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed it. Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m). In the letter, Ceferin and Montagliani said analysis carried out on Fifa's published financial statements and budgets raised doubts that the FFE proposal was "necessary to deliver greater resources". It added that the analysis was "deliberately conservative" and a larger distribution from the reserves should be considered by the Fifa Council once the financial position at year-end is known. An "independent review" of Fifa's finances should be commissioned, it added, with "full access to the underlying figures and assumptions". "Fifa currently holds billions of dollars in accumulated reserves," it read. "These resources belong to football and exist to serve the game and its 211 member associations. "Prudence should not prevent a careful examination of whether a portion could responsibly be released to the extent those reserves exceed Fifa's foreseeable needs. "Releasing part of these reserves would demonstrate that member associations should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits. "Development is an institutional responsibility of Fifa – not a matter of individual discretion." Another letter, also seen by BBC Sport, has been sent to the presidents of the other confederations - Asia, Africa, South America and Oceania - asking them to support the motion. The news comes a day after Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt sent a letter to Infantino and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom demanding that all documents relating to the controversial FFE plan were released. Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. Infantino was told he should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October. Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. title: Man admits to killing woman in Londonderry, court hears
description: Ciaran Edward Murray, 30, of Malvern Terrace in Derry is charged with the murder of a 65-year-old Spanish national in 2024.
body: The body of Montserrat Martorell was discovered in a flat in Harvey Street on 24 August 2024 A man has admitted to killing a woman who was found dead in a ground-floor flat after a blaze at the property more than two years ago, a court has heard. Ciaran Edward Murray, 30, of Malvern Terrace in the Waterside area of Londonderry, is charged with the murder of 65-year-old Spanish national Montserrat Martorell. Her body was discovered in a flat in the Harvey Street area of Derry on 24 August 2024. Appearing via video link before Belfast Crown Court on Friday, when the charge of murder was put to him, the 30-year-old replied: "Not guilty, but guilty to manslaughter." Following this, prosecution lawyer told the court that his instructions were to proceed with the murder case. A defence lawyer said a psychologist was due to examine the accused in late October. They added that the defence had been instructed by the accused "at this first opportunity, to apologise to the family of the deceased for his actions". Prosecution counsel Simon Reid KC said that, in light of the defence seeking a report from a clinical psychologist, he would have a clinical psychologist for the prosecution on standby once the defence report was delivered. Mr Justice Fowler said he would list the case for November for an update on progress with the medical report. title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
description: Princess Diana's brother tells the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg that "we'll forget her soon enough" were "exactly" the words used by the then-Prince of Wales.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died Princess Diana's brother has told the BBC exclusively that he is "telling the truth" about a phone call with King Charles in the days after his sister's death. Earl Spencer claims in a new book the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession. In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss". But in his first interview since, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said." Earl Spencer spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuennsberg from his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that." Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous". In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary." When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth." Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments. The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law. Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, walked behind their mother's coffin alongside Earl Spencer and their father In excerpts of his book published by the Daily Mail, Earl Spencer claims the phone call took place after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young princes to walk in the procession. In his BBC interview, he says the King "went ballistic" and "ranted for a while", accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty. "And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate," Earl Spencer said. "And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'." He said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was "just so stunned", adding: "I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him." Diana is buried at the Spencer family's Althorp estate Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa. A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time." The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood. Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36. Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST. title: Brother didn't match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
description: Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".
body: This video can not be played The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and the police showed "no urgency" to clear his name. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless". Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation. Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health deteriorated after his arrest and questioned why the police were not able to carry out DNA tests that could have proved his innocence. title: Man in court charged with murder over Armadale shooting
description: Billy Watson was pronounced dead after police were called to a property in the West Lothian town on Saturday morning.
body: Billy Watson died in Armadale on Saturday A man has appeared in court charged with murdering another man who was shot dead in West Lothian. Police were called to a property on Harestanes Road in Armadale at about 11:50 on Saturday. Billy Watson, 35, was found injured and died at the scene. Frank McCarthy, 57, appeared at Livingston Sheriff Court on Friday, charged with murder and attempting to defeat the ends of justice. He made no plea and was remanded in custody. A 29-year-old man and 44-year-old man have also been arrested in connection with the incident. Police Scotland said inquiries were ongoing. Police were called to the property on Saturday Detectives previously said they were also investigating whether a nearby car fire in Netherhouses and a fire at a derelict house on Wotherspoon Crescent on Saturday were linked to the incident. Uniformed officers were seen in the Netherhouses area where the car was set ablaze. A cordon was also put in place on Wotherspoon Crescent. The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said nobody was injured in the fires. title: 'Get in' - woman joins police chase by giving officer a lift in Nissan Micra
description: The suspect reverse-rammed a police car and crashed into parked cars while trying to escape.
body: This video can not be played Police officer given lift by driver in Nissan Micra mid-chase A driver came to the aid of a police officer who was chasing a suspect on foot - telling him to "get in" after stopping her Nissan Micra and offering him a lift. The officer had been pursuing Jacob Roberts, 25, who had reverse-rammed a police car twice and crashed into parked cars and a building while trying to escape. Roberts sped away from officers who had smelled cannabis coming from his van, with the chase seeing him drive in an erratic manner, failing to stop at multiple junctions, mounting pavements and putting pedestrians at risk. The driver helped PC Kerswell catch up to Roberts, who was arrested and later jailed for one year and two months for a number of driving offences. While fleeing from police in his white van, Roberts had driven into a dead-end street in Abercwmboi, Rhondda Cynon Taf, where he ditched the car and tried to escape officers on foot. Police bodycam footage captured the moment the officer then runs to a red Nissan Micra driven by an un-named female driver and tells her: "I need a lift." "Get in," the woman replies. As she gave chase the woman is heard asking the officer to direct her, saying: "Where to?" The officer is seen jumping out of the car after spotting the suspect and takes out his taser and arrests him. During a search officers found two cannabis cigarettes on him. Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years. He was sentenced at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on 16 September, where he pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs. Kerswell said: "Roberts was already banned from driving when he committed these offences - he showed complete disregard for all other road users, including pedestrians. "I hope it acts as a deterrent for others who think of driving dangerously. "It's lucky that no one was seriously injured during this pursuit. We hope this sentence will give Roberts time to reflect on his actions." title: Ex-Brookside star who fled after fraud trial arrested in Spain
description: Philip Foster was already serving a jail sentence for conspiracy to defraud, as of last year.
body: Philip Foster played Christian Wright in the Merseyside TV soap A former TV soap actor has been arrested in Spain after skipping bail before his trial for a £13.6 million fraud that conned would-be models. Philip Foster, 51, who played Christian Wright in the Liverpool soap, is wanted and must serve an eight-and-a-half year jail sentence after being convicted of fraud and money laundering last year. He ran an operation involving sham modelling agencies that exploited the dreams of aspiring young models and their parents for more than eight years. The National Crime Agency (NCA) said that after jumping bail, Foster was convicted and sentenced in his absence at Sheffield Crown Court in February 2025. He was arrested by officers on Thursday in Alicante. Extradition proceedings to return him to the UK are now under way, the NCA said. A National Trading Standards (NTS) investigation found that more than 6,000 victims parted with large sums of money on the false promise of securing paid modelling work in the fraud that Foster ran from his base in Marbella. He used a network of associates in England to run a string of sham agencies and photography studios in cities including London, Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, Coventry and Nottingham which was uncovered after a six-year NTS investigation. The victims were duped into thinking that a model agency was interested in them, with emails telling them they had potential after they responded to a local photographic studio and social media advertising campaign. They were told they had to buy their portfolio photographs from the studio in order to join an agency and become an agency model. Some of them used credit deals arranged by the fraudsters or expensive payday loans to make the upfront payment. In return, the victims got poor quality digital photographs that stood no real chance of landing them professional jobs and most did not get paid modelling work. Foster bought high-end watches and cars with his share of the proceeds while many victims told NTS investigators they had been left financially and emotionally devastated, and felt humiliated and betrayed. title: Why an American football game played the Canadian national anthem
description: The field in Buffalo was decked out with the flags of both countries, as tensions simmer and a trade war escalates.
body: This video can not be played Watch: In a border city stadium, American NFL fans sing Canada’s anthem with gusto There are no Canadian teams in the NFL - but there are millions of fans. At the Buffalo Bills game in New York on Thursday night, plenty of Canadians wore the team's trademark red, white and blue while drinking beside their pick-up trucks, which were parked to tailgate - a very American pre-game tradition. The Bills' stadium is only 112 miles (180 km) from Toronto - about a two and a half hour drive for fans - and right across Lake Ontario, which President Donald Trump has sought to rename Lake America. So it was no surprise that many Canadians arrived long before kick-off to soak up the atmosphere and enjoy the sights of the new Highmark Stadium for their team 's home opener against the Detroit Lions. What was unusual was that their national anthem rang out through the stadium. The field was decked out with both the stars and stripes of the US flag and the maple leaf of the Canadian one, and the 1990s Canadian band The Barenaked Ladies belted out Oh Canada! in front of a massive crowd. There was a fireworks display for the team's home opener at their new stadium The Barenaked Ladies belted out Oh Canada! in front of a massive crowd It was an emotional moment for many of the Canadian fans, who said they felt an extremely warm welcome even if their country's mood has recently grown more frosty towards the US. "I've always felt welcome here," said Ben Kerr, from Bradford, Ontario. "I think it's a nice acknowledgement," he added. "I appreciate that the Bills are doing that for Canada." The relationship between the two countries, which began to sour when US President Donald Trump returned to office and made repeated calls to annex Canada, has frayed further with an escalating tit-for-tat tariff showdown. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada, which shares the world's longest undefended border with the US, is "at war" with its southern neighbour over trade. Trump has called Canada "nasty" and "entitled". The Bills' new home, Highmark Stadium, cost $2.2bn to build Both sides are feeling the economic impact, with Canadian industries reeling from tariffs and Canadians boycotting travel and spending in the US. The ongoing tensions made the decision to travel to Buffalo a little more complicated for Kerr. "I try to spend as little money as possible in the US," he told the BBC. "Buy our food in Canada, buy our beer in Canada, bring it across and drink it here. We're not big in supporting the American economy in this trade war." Canadians dream of Europe as Carney floats longshot plan for living and working in EU Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member' Many Americans at the game expressed their own frustrations with the escalating trade war, and the way it has divided the two neighbours. For Drew Grier, an American who lives eight minutes from the stadium, "the anthem playing tonight is a core part of who we are as a border city". At a Buffalo Sabres playoff ice hockey game in April, a microphone died while the Canadian anthem was being sung and the audience's voices filled in. "You sang the Canadian anthem because it needed to happen," Grier said. Canadian Blake Parnham recalled that moment: "I was sobbing watching the game at home because I felt so vindicated, that Buffalo is different." He couldn't make it to Buffalo for the Bills home opener, but he enjoyed it from his elaborately decorated backyard in Keswick, Ontario. Grier said that singing the Canadian anthem tonight is "not that polarising of a thing". "If anyone is polarising it, it's coming from those outside here, because those of us here, we love Canada," he said. But some thought it was a step too far. "The only acceptable reason to sing that anthem would be if they were playing a Canadian team, but they don't play any Canadian teams," posted one fan on social media. "I don't think it's really necessary," said David Waring, who attended Thursday's game. Blake Parnham's Bills-themed backyard in Keswick, Ontario Many Canadians are boycotting the US, so this is where they're travelling instead In the end, it may all come down to simple economics. The Bills' new home, Highmark Stadium, cost $2.2bn to build. While the population of western New York is a little over 1.5 million, the nearby Toronto and Hamilton greater metro areas is home to more than 8 million. Simply put, the team needs Canadian fans. Gavin Kemp, who has run the NFL-Canada office for eight years, told the BBC that Canada's relationship to the NFL was "extremely important". Asked why the Bills chose this year to play the Canadian anthem, Kemp said the team was "leaning into one of their biggest parts of their market". Canada boasts nearly 15 million NFL fans – about one-third of the country's population, and roughly 10-15% of Bills season ticket holders are Canadian, according to the team. "Sports really transcends all of this," Kemp said. "All this politics is kind of secondary to the fact that your team is doing fantastic right now." Carol Breed, a die-hard Lions fan, took her family to the first home game of the season last weekend Even American fans who traditionally cheer for other teams found themselves siding with the Bills. Carol Breed, who backs the Detroit Lions, considered travelling to Highmark Stadium from her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, after she heard they would play the Canadian national anthem. "I love our country's relationship with Canada," the 74-year-old told the BBC, adding that in Michigan the country is viewed more as a "relative". title: Gabriel, 15, in Barcelona amid speculation over future
description: Man Utd youngster JJ Gabriel travels to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature.
body: JJ Gabriel has told Manchester United he wants to leave Manchester United youngster JJ Gabriel has travelled to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature. The 15-year-old has told United he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect. BBC Sport reported on Thursday that Real Madrid have a firm interest in the forward, and Bayern Munich, Paris St-Germain and Barcelona are also known to be keen. It is understood Gabriel left the UK on Thursday and went to France, but is now in Barcelona. If United hold on to the Londoner's registration, it would stop him moving to another English club until the end of the season. But if he obtains an European Union passport through either his father - a former Republic of Ireland international - or mother, who has Greek-Cypriot heritage, he could join a club in he EU when he turns 16 on 6 October. What next for Gabriel and Man Utd? Gabriel has not trained at United since scoring a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut on 10 September. Tournament rules prevent him from playing for a side other than United in this season's competition. Sources close to Gabriel were furious the club did not register him for their Champions League opener with Sabah FK, which Michael Carrick's side won 4-0. Carrick was again asked about Gabriel on Friday at his news conference to preview Sunday's Premier League match against Fulham. "He's a young boy, JJ, and I think it's important we don't play anything out here," he said. "With the exposure and scrutiny and everything, you got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything. "The situation will work itself out, whatever way it's going to work itself out. Making sure he's OK is the important thing." Gabriel scored in his first two Premier League 2 outings for United this season but will not be involved against Brentford at Leigh Sports Village on Friday. title: Harry Potter and the goblet of no booze
description: The proposal to allow alcohol and music at the event sparks concerns among people living nearby.
body: The real-world, non-alcoholic version of Butterbeer is a popular drink at Harry Potter-themed events Organisers of a Harry Potter-themed event have failed to conjure up a licence to sell booze after the plan was turned down amid residents' complaints - and a politician's swipe that "normal men" would not drink the fare on offer. Forestry England wanted people to have mulled wine and Irish cream hot chocolate as they made their way around an illuminations trail at Cannock Chase Forest in Staffordshire, set to run from October. The bid was turned down by Cannock Chase District Council which received more than 75 objections, plus the jibe - during a licensing hearing - from a Reform UK councillor. The applicant had told the hearing that it would ensure there was no adverse impact for neighbours. Permission was also sought to play music along parts of the designated route lined with illuminated features depicting scenes from the Harry Potter franchise. But as the suitability was thrashed out by the council's licensing sub committee and ultimately rejected, member John Parkes questioned the sort of drinks that would be sold, claiming "normal men" would not partake of such beverages. The branded, non-alcoholic drink Butterbeer was unaffected by the ruling. Parkes described Butterbeer as "horrendous". The event is set to run between 1 October and 3 January Jon Payne from Forestry England told members at Wednesday's meeting: "It's very much a family-orientated event. "The amount of alcohol consumption is very small, served from limited outlets in the forest, and not available throughout the site." One resident who objected to the application said people should not be encouraged to "drive to an event, have a drink and then drive home", claiming it could put children in danger. "We don't need Harry Potter, it's already a magical place," she added of the event's location. "We're not trying to be killjoys but the woods can be challenging at night – it's dark and it's dense. "Add alcohol and the risks multiply. Must we tell our children that every event we do should be soaked in alcohol?" The licensing application proposed to sell alcohol and play music between 15:30 and 22:30 while the event was taking place. Another resident raised concerns about those timings, describing the evening as a period when people expected "to enjoy peace and quiet". "Residents are concerned about lights shining into bedrooms and repeated vehicle noise," he added. "They have experienced problems at previous events including noise, parking problems, and anti-social behaviour." Emily Sewell, from event producers Culture Creative Limited, said background music would be used in "limited areas" of the site. She added that, in the company's experience, one in five visitors drank alcohol at these events. The committee's chair Maureen Freeman, Labour, said the panel was "not minded to grant the licence as requested". This news was gathered by the Local Democracy Reporting Service which covers councils and other public service organisations. title: No Norrie as GB bid for Davis Cup Finals spot
description: Cameron Norrie will miss Great Britain's Davis Cup tie with Ecuador this weekend, with qualification for November's eight-team finals on the line.
body: Great Britain have not reached the Davis Cup Finals for the past three years Cameron Norrie will miss Great Britain's Davis Cup tie with Ecuador this weekend, with qualification for November's eight-team finals on the line. British number two Norrie felt pain in his arm during a practice session and will be replaced in Saturday's singles by world number 95 Toby Samuel. "He wasn't able to accelerate on the ball like he wanted to," Davis Cup captain Leon Smith told BBC Sport. "It's nothing major, but there's still a lot of tennis to be played this year and with that in mind, we had to make the difficult decision to replace him." Great Britain have not reached the knockout stage of the competition since 2023, and they will have to do so this time with an inexperienced team. Jack Draper has ended his difficult season early, while Jan Choinski and Jacob Fearnley are both unavailable with injury. It means Samuel will make his Davis Cup debut against Andres Andrade in Saturday's first match, with British number one Arthur Fery following against Alvaro Guillen Meza. Both of Ecuador's singles players are outside the world's top 200, but Fery's only previous appearance for his country was in Poland last September. Asked if he was concerned about the lack of experience, Smith said: "I'm not sure it concerns me, but it is obviously a factor. "Neal [Skupski] is in the team, Cam is staying with the team. I've had 16 years at this so I can hopefully help a little bit. "But you want them to experience this. You have to start somewhere and I have a lot of confidence in Arthur, Toby and our doubles team. "If they can put out the level of tennis we've seen over the course of the summer and before that, they'll give themselves a good opportunity." British number seven Harry Wendelken, who is at a career-high world ranking of 175, was at the Copper Box as a practice partner and has been added to the team in Norrie's absence. World number one Henry Patten will team up with new US Open champion Neal Skupski for Sunday's doubles, which precedes two reverse singles. Davis Cup: Great Britain v Ecuador Coverage from 13:00 BST on 19 September and 12:00 BST on 20 September In July, Fery played on Wimbledon's Centre Court in a men's singles semi-final, but this will be the first time he has played for his country as the British number one. He lost in the first round of the US Open in August but reached the Winston-Salem final in the build-up to the final Grand Slam of the season. "I'm aware of the role I have as the number one player and I am representing my country, so there's always a little more responsibility," Fery told BBC Sport. "But at the same time I've been able to deal with high-pressure situations a lot of times this year and I feel like I've done a great job with them. Tomorrow isn't going to be any different to that. "I think there's no shying away from it - if I want to do great things in tennis and push on, be top 20 or top 10, I have to take this responsibility on. "I'm ready to do that and represent my country. It's something new but something that I feel comes with the player I'm becoming." Great Britain beat Norway 4-0 in the first qualifying round in February and are trying to reach the quarter-finals for the first time since 2023. Ecuador may be the underdogs, but they were in the same role when they beat Australia comprehensively in February. And they have won, famously, on British soil before. Ecuador beat a British team that contained Tim Henman and Greg Rusedski 3-2 on Wimbledon's Court One in July 2000. The seven winners of this weekend's qualifying ties will join three-time defending champions Italy in the final eight stage in Bologna from 24 to 29 November. "We've missed not being at that stage and it's up to us now to take that opportunity," Smith added. "We have a good opportunity. It's never ever straightforward, despite what people might look at in the rankings - just ask Australia what happened in February. "We're on it, we've got a good team, and we'd be thrilled to get to the finals." title: Tenko and Doc Martin actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
description: She was best known for playing the character Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama
body: The actress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Doc Martin, has died aged 84. A statement from her agent John Grant, issued on behalf of her family, confirmed the actress had been living with Alzheimer's for several years. "Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television," the statement read. "She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities." Cole's credits included a role opposite Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack Cole appeared opposite David Jason once again in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours Solihul-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, enjoyed a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film. She was perhaps best known for playing the character Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko. The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp. Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the health of the women, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman. During this same period, Cole also played the moody Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow", opposite Ronnie Barker in Open All Hours. She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God. But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, alongside Maggie Smith and Julie Walters, as one of her proudest moments. Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman. Cole also played Roy Cropper's mother in ITV soap Coronation Street for two years from 2011 Cole (pictured alongside co-star Ann Bell) was perhaps best known for the 1970s series Tenko Cole also played the aunt of Martin Clunes's titular character in the ITV medical drama Doc Martin. Her other notable roles included Keeping Mum, Waiting for God and Cabin Pressure. She also appeared in Coronation Street as Roy Cropper's mother Sylvia Goodwin, which won her another comedy prize, in her 70s, at the 2012 British Sopa Awards. Cole reprised her earlier role opposite David Jason in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours, and also appeared alongside Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack. The actress's stage work in Driving Miss Daisy and King Lear at Bristol Old Vic. Her last major TV role was appearing opposite Greg Davis in his BBC comedy series The Cleaner in 2021. title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
description: The French president says he has tasked the government with protecting critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified. In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat. He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response". A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance. Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line. Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war. "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said. This video can not be played Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission. "In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said. "It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves." German airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved? Hand of Moscow? title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
description: The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected.
body: Thousands of passengers were delayed by the NATS outage An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said. The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data. The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred. The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of its chief executive Martin Rolfe. There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances. In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety. The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours. The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm. Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow. The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place. Martin Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption. "It's our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong," he said. "However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question." Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports. "It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway. This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years. In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers. There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations. Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences." He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed". Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience." Addie Kitson was hit with almost £100 in unexpected costs when her flight back from China was diverted to Stockholm Addie Kitson, 26, had been on holiday in China when her flight home was diverted to Sweden. "I thought I landed fine" she told the BBC, "but then they went: 'Welcome to Stockholm' and I went: 'Ooh, that's not London'". After being told about the issues affecting UK airspace, passengers were kept on the plane for a few hours, and then spent 19 hours inside Stockholm airport. Addie ended up with nearly £100 in unexpected costs after having to buy refreshments, adaptors and to pay for Wi-Fi to work. "I got one £11 food voucher that didn't even cover the cost of a sandwich in Stockholm airport", Addie said. Addie questioned the rules around compensation, saying there had been multiple air traffic outages. "It doesn't seem that extraordinary," she said. title: Teenager jailed for life over ambush murder
description: Sulaiman Tajzai travelled from Leeds to London, where he stabbed his victim with a kitchen knife.
body: Sulaiman Tajzai admitted murder and possessing a knife A teenager who travelled more than 150 miles from Leeds to London to stab a man has been jailed for at least 25 years for his murder. Sulaiman Tajzai, 18, ambushed shop worker Farmanullah Sherzad outside the 26-year-old's home in Westminster on 27 March, stabbing him at least 10 times. Sentencing him at the Old Bailey to a life term, Judge Angela Rafferty KC said he had held a grudge against Sherzad "based on a false suggestion of misconduct" and had been "effectively stalking him down like prey". Describing the attack as "exceptionally violent", she told Tajzai: "It is not said on your behalf, nor could it be, that you had any justifiable or excusable grievance against this man." The court heard that Tajzai, an Afghan asylum seeker, wrongly believed Sherzad belonged to the Taliban, which had kidnapped his father and was suspected of killing him. The court was also told Sherzad had been arrested in Leeds in October over an allegation involving a woman known to Tajzai. He told officers he had been invited to the address and was in a relationship with her, and police later said no further action would be taken. In January, Tajzai travelled to London and carried out reconnaissance near Sherzad's Abbey Orchard Street home and his workplace, the court heard. On 27 March he armed himself with a kitchen knife and took a train south, arriving at King's Cross station in a face mask, distinctive jacket and dark gloves. CCTV tracked him across the capital to Abbey Orchard Street, where he waited for Sherzad to cycle home from work at about 22:00 GMT. Farmanullah Sherzad's family said they were "deeply shocked and angered" by the circumstances of his death Prosecutor Lisa Wilding KC said Tajzai had given his age as 14 when he arrived in the UK in August 2022 and claimed asylum the following year. In mitigation for her client, who admitted murder and possessing a knife, Frida Hussain KC said he had post-traumatic stress disorder after exposure to violence in his village and the deaths of relatives. Sherzad's family described him as "kind, gentle and free-spirited", a keen cricketer who often worked six or seven days a week. In a statement, they said they were "deeply shocked and angered by the circumstances surrounding his death". title: Will England boss Tuchel 'embrace the chaos'?
description: After the World Cup, England boss Thomas Tuchel wanted greater control. Two months on, he is keen to "embrace the chaos" after naming his squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures.
body: This video can not be played Tuchel recalls Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to England squad England manager Thomas Tuchel left the United States in July pining for greater control. At his first squad announcement since the World Cup on Friday, the German spoke of "embracing the chaos". Is it possible to have controlled chaos? It seems Tuchel is ready to find out. England's third-placed finish in the US was the nation's best performance at the World Cup since 1966. But the memories of the team's semi-final loss to Argentina linger. In the aftermath of the heartbreaking defeat, Tuchel pointed to his team's inability to find control having taken the lead via Anthony Gordon's opener as a key factor behind his side's late collapse. Fast-forward two months, however, and the messaging is rather different ahead of the four upcoming Nations League games. "Football is about adapting to situations and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach, if you look at the 6-4 against France [in the World Cup bronze-medal match]," said Tuchel. "But people talk about it like it's one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match, so maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best." Tuchel recalls Alexander-Arnold and Palmer with warning Mixed signals? Or maybe it is just a sign that Tuchel wants his side to become more unpredictable in their search for success. Because that is what the best teams do - mix it up when required. Despite Tuchel's remarks, his latest squad for the fixtures against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia rather contradicts any thoughts of a havoc-rich approach. The return of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer, two of English football's most technically gifted players, screams control. So do the call-ups of Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall, who are both extremely adept in possession of the ball. Of course, there is certainly a balance to be struck. That would be Tuchel's ideal scenario. Rio Ngumoha's first senior call-up will certainly add an air of unpredictability to Tuchel's options. The Liverpool winger, 18, has had an exciting start to the season, catching the eye with his invention and trickery down both flanks for Andoni Iraola's side. That Tuchel revealed Fulham attacker Josh King is also close to earning his first senior call-up provides further indication the England manager wants to reinvigorate his forward line ahead of the forthcoming Nations League campaign and beyond. Yet, we shouldn't expect Tuchel to completely let go of the handbrake just yet. In response to a question as to whether his team can replicate the fast-paced approach of a Premier League team but harnessed with a greater control, Tuchel responded: "That would be the wish, that we become for 10 minutes a little bit more like Spain, here and there. "The more I reflect on it, it's maybe more buying into our strengths and play more minutes like we played the second half against Croatia, and more minutes like we played the first half against France, and buying into these strengths, because I think we get a lot of value out of it, we get a lot of connection to the fans, this is what the Premier League reflects. "We are maybe not the most economical team to play football but this is maybe also a characteristic of the Premier League. The Premier League is not a very economical league, you have to play. "You need to max out every single match otherwise you cannot compete for the title so this is something more beautiful. But this is where we are, where I am in my mindset and I think where the players are, so it's still a bit ambiguous." But while Tuchel may not have total clarity with regards to whether control or chaos is the way forward, he showed no hint of confusion over who he believes his best players are. Tuchel refuted assertions his decision to recall Palmer and Alexander-Arnold was an admission he'd got his World Cup squad wrong. Indeed, Tuchel has hinted he would have picked a vastly similar squad for the upcoming games to the one he selected for the US had all his options been available. "Before we did the nomination in the last month, I thought we had more of a continuation of the World Cup squad but then a lot of members of our World Cup squad - Reece [James], Dan [Burn], Dean [Henderson, [John] Stones, [Jordan] Henderson, Djed Spence - can't be with us due to injuries, so it is not like a full continuation. "These players were crucial for us in building the brotherhood, in building the spirit and taking care of the mentality that took us the long way in the tournament. We will not negotiate on that, we will not give in on that. "So other players will step up, this is basically how I see this camp. "My mindset at the moment is not to change too much within the formations." England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September then travel to the Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October. title: Woman detained indefinitely for stabbing two boys
description: The victims were found with non life-threatening injuries after police raided a flat in Friskney.
body: Officers found two boys with stab injuries when they raided a flat in Friskney A woman who stabbed two 10-year-old boys has been detained indefinitely in a psychiatric hospital. Armed police found the injured boys after forcing their way into a flat in Friskney in November 2022 following a stand-off lasting several hours. Ann Marie McEvoy, 45, of Church Walk, Colchester, was tasered and arrested. In July, she pleaded guilty to two counts of attempted murder. On Friday, she was sentenced to a hospital order under the Mental Health Act at Lincoln Crown Court. The boys were treated in hospital for non life-threatening injuries. McEvoy was seen holding a large knife prior to her arrest, the court heard. Dr Tim Rogers, a consultant forensic psychiatrist, told the latest hearing the offences would not have happened had McEvoy been mentally well. McEvoy suffered from schizoaffective disorder, the expert said, adding it was clear she needed treatment, potentially for the remainder of her life. Judge Simon Hirst said he was satisfied the best way to protect the public was to impose a hospital order. Doctors and the Secretary of State will decide if and when she can be released. Addressing McEvoy, Hirst said: "Your need for treatment is likely to be significantly longer than a prison sentence. "It is necessary to protect the public and it is not possible to say for how long that will be." McEvoy was previously deemed unfit to stand trial and was made the subject of a hospital order in September 2024 after a jury found she was responsible for stabbing the boys. The Crown Prosecution Service chose to resume criminal proceedings against McEvoy in March this year after her condition improved in hospital. She was deemed fit enough to enter her pleas. Mark Knowles, defending, said McEvoy had entered guilty pleas because she not want to subject the boys to the ordeal of a trial. Impact statements from both boys were read out in court. One of them described how he suffered a punctured lung and was rushed to hospital for surgery on his neck. The other boy said he had only just started feeling better. Hirst also made a restraining order which prevents McEvoy contacting the children. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North. title: 'Not a catastrophe' - Carrick dismisses Man Utd job fears
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says there is no point wasting any time worrying if his job is under threat.
body: Michael Carrick has won 14 out of 23 games since taking charge at Manchester United in January 2026 Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to start thinking how long he has left in the job after "two or three" bad results. His side visit Fulham on Sunday after an awful week. After United lost at home to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men after 23 minutes, Brighton became the first side to come from two goals down to win at Old Trafford in 50 years in their Carabao Cup tie. United supporters responded to the midweek setback with boos and by chanting against their team. Carrick said in the aftermath he was "not bothered" by the pressure - a sentiment he reinforced as he spoke to the media before the Fulham trip. "I know the club, I know the role, I know what's expected here in terms of playing to a certain standard and achieving certain things on the pitch," he added. "In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, that's totally not in my thinking. It's ridiculous to think that way in the position I'm in, that's just not on the radar. "It's two or three games. It's two or three games too many because I really hate losing, but that doesn't mean the world caves in. In some minds it does, it can't for us." There has been no sense from senior figures inside United that Carrick's position is under threat. They are more focused on the perceived under performance of so many players given the 12 games out of 17 that were won under the 45-year-old over the second half of last season. By contrast, they have two victories from six games so far, against newly promoted Ipswich - when they had to come from behind - and Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. "It's not a catastrophe or a disaster," said Carrick. "It's not the end of the world." Yet it is the measure of the noise around a club of United's size that is often feels that way. Carrick accepted issues at Old Trafford are frequently amplified, so they look to be bigger than they actually are. Despite this, he loves his job - and the club he served with such distinction as a player, and began his coaching career. "There's great feelings, and there's obviously disappointments, and sometimes the smaller disappointments lead to being a little bit bigger," he added. "It's just part of coping and being at this great football club. "I wouldn't want to be anywhere else, genuinely. "It's the best place for me to be, in part because of the times when it's maybe not going to plan. Sometimes they are best times to work your way through, to find out a few things and come out an awful lot stronger." Externally, the inquests have tended to focus around recruitment - or lack of it, specifically at left-back - United's finances and debt levels, Carrick's relative inexperience and, other than assistant boss Steve Holland, that of his coaches. "It's not a blame game," said Carrick, who revealed Luke Shaw and new signing Carlos Baleba "have a chance" of being fit for the Craven Cottage meeting. "We all search for things to look at and point at, or whatever reason it may be and find a blame. Blame me. No problem. I will take the responsibility. "But it's not about blaming people. It's about us, it's about us finding solutions and being better. That's as a whole football club." title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
description: Chan Mathok Atak has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison after piloting the boat.
body: The dinghy carried 165 migrants across the English Channel on 23 July A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison. Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July. Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat. At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August. At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified". She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence. James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus. The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels. Chan Mathok Atak admitted endangering others during a sea crossing The dinghy, which had 31 children on board with the youngest aged 14, had two outboard engines but one was not working, the court heard. The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the boat was "severely overcrowded", had limited food, drinking water, and medication, and had been at sea for almost 24 hours. The quality of the lifejackets on board was also "completely inadequate" and the fire risk was "considerable" due to how close batteries were to fuel cans, the NCA added. Harrison said just before the boat was intercepted, Atak moved away from the engine into another part of the vessel and took off his jacket. This video can not be played Atak was seen piloting the boat during 90 minutes of aerial footage He said this was an attempt to not to be identified as the helmsman. However, Atak was seen during 90 minutes of aerial footage to be piloting the vessel using its one remaining functioning engine while wearing a black jacket with an "Italia" logo on it, the court heard. Footage also showed one person "constantly pumping" to try to re-inflate the rigid-hulled inflatable boat. Harrison said: "There's no evidence to suggest that the defendant had any training or experience of conducting this type of navigation. "The size of the vessel and the number of people on board presented an obvious danger. The vessel would have been unstable because of it deflating." Harrison said the risks of the crossing "would have been apparent to Atak". In an interview, Atak said he paid €200 euros (£172) to a gang for the crossing but denied he was the helmsman. NCA senior investigating officer John Turner said: "Atak was unimaginably reckless and his actions could have easily resulted in many deaths had this boat not been intercepted. "Not only did he place the lives of 165 migrants in severe peril, this flimsy vessel was entirely unsuitable for crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes." Endangerment at sea was made a new offence this year to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel. Anna Turley, Minister for Border Security and Asylum, described Atak as an "evil criminal". "He joins 16 other pilots sentenced in just three months for endangering lives with flimsy, overcrowded dinghies," she said. "This is a stark reminder of the ruthless acts used by smuggling gangs to exploit desperate people for profit, but today shows there is nowhere for them to hide." The court heard Atak moved away from the engine and took off his jacket to avoid being identified as the helmsman Defending him, barrister Audrey Mogan said there was "not a single shred of evidence" to suggest Atak had "anything to do with the number of people on the vessel, the state of the dinghy, or the fact that there were no life jackets or that the jackets were inadequate, or the lack of safety equipment or flares". "The idea that he had anything to do with the state of the boat and its overcrowding just flies in the face of reason," she added. Mogan described Atak as someone who had "escaped the horrors of South Sudan", where he saw people being shot and having their throats cut, and militia setting fire to a neighbourhood. title: Live forever: Unheard Oasis recordings to be sold
description: The hidden tapes have been in the possession of a former sound engineer's family for 20 years.
body: The recordings were made by a former front-of-house sound engineer in the 1990s Oasis fans are set for a Wonderwall experience when they get the chance to bid for unheard recordings of the Supersonic boys at their peak. The archive includes recordings of 63 live shows, soundchecks and more than 100 hours of rehearsals from the band's rise and rise in the 1990s. The lots, which also include original setlists, tour itineraries, a band-played Epiphone guitar and an Oasis tour parka, will be offered for sale on 3 October in Evesham, Worcestershire. The collection, known as The Desk Tapes, has been in the possession of Owain Richards for 20 years, after his dad, a former front-of-house sound engineer joined the band's crew during their heyday. "Dad labelled everything, recorded everything and backed it all up to cassette, over and over," he said. "I grew up listening to these recordings. Oasis were part of the family as much as they were part of the culture." The previously unheard Oasis recordings will go on sale next month Littleton Auctions is handling sale and say the tapes, recorded directly from the sound desk, form the only master archive of their kind. Also among the items due to go under the hammer is a pair of Adidas Kegler Super Ostrich trainers gifted to Noel Gallagher. Only 100 pairs were produced in 2000 to mark the 100th anniversary of Adidas founder Adi Dassler. The unheard archive includes recordings of 63 live shows Ben Homer, managing director of Littleton Auctions, described it as "one of the most exciting collections" the auction house had brought to market. The sale will take place online and in person with bidders, who are required to register in advance and pay a deposit, hoping they won't be looking back in anger on the day. title: Football club apologises for United 93 shirt advert
description: Oxford United apologises for the image, which features the call sign of one of the planes used in the 9/11 attacks.
body: Oxford United's new clothing range has been withdrawn from sale A football club has apologised after it published images of a new clothing line with "United 93" printed on the back - the call sign of one of the aircraft hijacked on 9/11. The clothing was supposed to make reference to Oxford United's founding year of 1893. However, it said it had been released "without understanding of the historical context and associations". United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all 44 people on board after being hijacked on 11 September 2001. A docudrama film titled United 93 was made about the tragedy and released in 2006. Oxford United was founded in 1893 as an amateur club called Headington and now plays in League One - the third tier of the English football pyramid. In a statement, the club said its Campus Clothing range had been withdrawn and it "sincerely apologised" for the error. "It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence," it said. "We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again." The 9/11 attacks saw 19 Al Qaeda members hijack four commercial passenger planes in the US. Two of them were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, resulting in them both collapsing. Another plane struck the Pentagon, near Washington DC, while the fourth plane - United 93 - crashed in rural Pennsylvania. It was believed to be destined for the US Capitol Building, also in Washington DC. The attacks killed 2,977 people and injured tens of thousands more.
