title: New sighting of missing Lillia, 13
description: Lillia went missing from Bolton last week and has not been seen by her family since.
body: This video can not be played Sighting of missing Bolton girl Lillia, last seen in a McDonalds in Piccadilly in Manchester. Police have received fresh CCTV of a girl who has been missing from home for a week. Lillia, 13, from Bolton, was last seen by her family last Friday, but was seen later that evening in Manchester's Picadilly bus station, and at the Trafford Centre the following day. Officers who have been handing out hundreds of leaflets to try to locate Lillia have now released new footage of her at a McDonald's restaurant in Piccadilly from Sunday at about 20:20 BST. Greater Manchester Police Ch Spt Int Helen Critchley said: "Officers are making every effort to locate Lillia, and our team have been working through hours of CCTV footage and exploring every avenue to try and find her." At a press conference on Thursday, Critchley issued an appeal on behalf of Lillia's mother Jessica, saying: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe. "You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home." Lillia's mother Jessica sat beside police as her statement was read out Lillia was seen boarding a 247 bus from the Trafford Centre on Saturday, heading in the direction of Altrincham, but it was not known where she got off. Critchley said the McDonalds sighting was the last confirmed sighting of her, adding: "Our investigation currently covers the whole of Greater Manchester with officers across the force being asked to support our enquiries. "We are also mindful that Lillia could have travelled outside of the Manchester area and are keeping an open mind regarding this possibility." Police describe Lillia as about 5ft 5in tall with light brown hair and glasses The force wants to hear from anyone who may have relevant CCTV or doorbell footage, or who has had any contact with Lillia since she was reported missing. The teenager is described as slim, about 5ft 5in (1.67m) with light brown hair and glasses, and was last seen wearing a black zip-up hooded top, light blue baggy jeans, and a black Nike backpack. Lillia was reported missing from Bolton on Friday 11 September. Critchley added: "If you have any information that could help us find Lillia, I would urge you to come forward. Her family just want her home. Please report any information, no matter how small." title: Resident Evil: The video game adaptation with a lot to prove
description: The video game adaptation is a hit with critics, but director Zach Cregger says the fan response surprised him.
body: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil follows Bryan - a courier having a very, very bad day at work One of the hottest horror directors on the planet adapting the world's most popular scary video game series? On paper Zach Cregger and Resident Evil are the perfect unholy alliance. The film-maker was widely praised for his original, imaginative work on horror hits Weapons and Barbarian and is a long-time fan of the video game series. But in the lead-up to the film’s release, Cregger’s spent a lot of time defending himself against complaints he’s cashing in on the Resident Evil name. Speaking to BBC Newsbeat, the director says he was "not prepared" for what came his way. The original Resident Evil game was a smash-hit when it came out in 1996 First launched in 1996 on the original Sony PlayStation by Japanese developer Capcom, Resident Evil was a sensation. Rather than casting players as super-powered characters, as was the case with most video games in the 90s, it forced them to survive with limited resources. Thanks to smart reinventions and remakes, the series has managed to stay relevant, selling a total of 213 million copies since its debut. Some of its characters are among the most well-known in video games, and there are whole communities dedicated to discussing the lore of their universe. Cregger's Resident Evil follows the story of Bryan, an original character played by Austin Abrams who worked with the director on Weapons. He's a courier who agrees to deliver a package to a hospital in Raccoon City - a key location from the games. As Bryan makes his way to the drop-off, it becomes apparent he is caught in the middle of some sort of viral outbreak, with the infected becoming monstrous creatures. When the first trailer appeared online, many users swamped comment sections to complain about what they'd seen. Where were the beloved characters? The familiar monsters? Cregger says he had little interest in simply retelling the story of the Resident Evil games, but that didn't seem to calm some fans. "I think I was naive," he says. "I think I was expecting people to be excited to see a Resident Evil movie that felt in the spirit of the games. "What I was trying to do is make a movie that really honoured the experience of playing them." Zach Cregger impressed horror fans with his previous films, Weapons and Barbarian According to most reviews, Cregger has achieved what he set out to do. In its three-star review, NME , externalasked whether it was "the first great horror movie game adaptation". "For a large chunk of the film's runtime, the answer is a resounding yes," wrote reviewer Jordan Bassett, who said Bryan's encounters become repetitive as the film wears on. Doug Jamieson, of The Jam Report, external, awarded four stars and said Cregger "understands adaptation as translation rather than imitation". In an eight out of 10 review, Looper, external critic Alastair Ryder wrote: "Zach Cregger has done the best job I've seen of translating the experience of playing a video game and making it feel cinematic." The verdict from fans remains to be seen, but Resident Evil looks to be on track to have a successful opening weekend at the box office. It follows recent video game adaptations such as the Minecraft and Super Mario Bros films, which were poorly reviewed but hugely popular. Zach Cregger and Austin Abrams reunited after working together on Weapons This isn't the first adaptation of Resident Evil, which was brought to cinema screens in 2002 - the first of six films overseen by writer-director Paul WS Anderson. His wife, Milla Jovovich, starred in each one, and while they have grown a cult following they were never a hit with critics. A 2021 "reboot" heavily based on the games and a 2022 Netflix series also failed to impress. The live-action rights to Resident Evil are owned by German production company Constantin Film - a fact fans have blamed for the perceived low quality of previous adaptations. Reports online suggest the company's agreement with Capcom prevents Constantin from setting its films in the same timeline as the games. Cregger told Newsbeat he'd had no contact with the game developer while working on the film. "Nobody from Capcom ever reached out to me, ever, in any way," he said. Constantin Film declined to comment, but BBC Newsbeat has been told there was co-ordination between the developer and the film's producers behind the scenes. Cregger says it's "probably" impossible to please everyone, but it was never his intention to recreate the game on-screen. "If I had delivered a faithful retelling of one of the stories in the games, I feel like those people would probably be upset with me for that too," he says. "Because I would have messed it up somehow, inevitably. "So all I can do is just tell the story that I think is going to be the very best story. "If somebody's going to have a problem that it doesn't do exactly what they had in their mind of what a Resident Evil movie is, I can't say anything to that." title: British Steel plan lacks credibility, MPs say
description: A committee report says the government has not set out how British Steel will become profitable.
body: British Steel was taken into public ownership in July after years of uncertainty over its future The government has no credible plan for the future of British Steel, MPs have claimed. A report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST) had not set out how British Steel, which runs its main plant in Scunthorpe and has operations in Teeside, would become profitable. MPs warned steel tariffs could drive firms out of business or to move abroad. A spokesperson for DBIST said it welcomed the report and would review the recommendations, adding securing the long-term future of the UK steel sector "was in the national interest". A 26-page report, external, published on Friday, said the government was unable to provide clear estimates of how much the overall nationalisation could cost. It had projected costs to reach £642m by 30 June this year, but the government later said it had only been £555m. In April last year, the government passed an emergency bill to take control of British Steel amid reports the then-owner Jingye was planning to switch off two blast furnaces in Scunthorpe. The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill became law in July, taking the company into public ownership. The government then published its steel strategy in March this year, which included an ambition for 50% of steel used in the UK to be made in Britain. The strategy confirmed electric arc furnaces as the future of British steelmaking, replacing traditional blast furnaces, which resulted in job losses at steelworks including Port Talbot. It also highlighted concerns that British Steel's 4,052 workers face uncertainty and the steel strategy is still vague about when the 50% target would be achieved. The report said: "Without a credible long-term plan, uncertainty and costs for workers, industry and taxpayers will continue to increase." The report also shared concerns the new tariff regime, made in a bid to boost British Steel production and usage, could cause smaller businesses to go bust. From July, Britain lowered the tariff-free quota level for steel importers by 51% in order to stop the UK becoming a "global dumping ground". It also doubled import taxes on steel coming into the UK above certain levels from 25% to 50%. However, firms said that some steels that they need would be affected by the tariffs, but are not able to be bought from the UK. The PAC said: "This risks steel manufacturers having to pay tariffs on types of steel that they cannot avoid importing. "There is a risk that businesses reliant on these products will face higher costs, which could result in smaller firms going out of business or companies moving production overseas." The PAC said the government needed to set up a "formal route" for steel companies to raise concerns about the new tariff regime. The DBIST spokesperson said: "Taxpayer value for money remains a central consideration in our assessment of the future of the site and we are also backing the communities that rely on it through our steel strategy to build a sustainable, competitive and decarbonised steel sector for the years ahead." title: Ronaldo named in Jesus' first Portugal squad
description: Cristiano Ronaldo is named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus for their upcoming Nations League games.
body: Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 233 appearances for Portugal Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football. Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July. But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October. Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit. The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years. The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit. When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head." This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football. Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028. The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024. Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea). Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October. title: Economy minister accuses SoS of 'mischief making' in social media exchange
description: Dr Caoimhe Archibald posted on X about a new one-off electricity bill reduction, which Sir Chris Bryant reposted saying the UK government funded it.
body: Dr Caoimhe Archibald posted on X about a new one-off electricity bill reduction which Sir Chris Bryant reposted, saying the UK government funded it Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald has questioned whether the secretary of state is "mischief making" after a social media exchange around energy payments. The Sinn Féin MLA posted on X, external about a new one-off electricity bill reduction announced on Thursday, which Sir Chris Bryant, reposted, external saying: "I'm really glad that the UK government is funding this." Archibald said she was "bemused and surprised" at his "intervention on social media". A UK government spokesperson said the funding for the Household Electricity Discount Scheme was provided through the prime minister's "commitment to remove VAT and some levies from electricity bills". "As I have set out, the British government initially didn't intend that this support would apply here, we had to make the case for that, we then had to design a scheme," Archibald told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme. She described what Sir Chris said as "a little bit condescending". "Frankly I'm not sure what the secretary of state was up to, mischief making? I don't know. But I think that question would be better posed to him." The minister said she has not been in touch with the secretary of state personally since the online exchange, but said she will continue to focus on finding a way forward in budget negotiations. You may want to read X’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’. Households across Northern Ireland will get the one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month and it will be applied automatically without the need for an application. The schemes are being funded by the UK government. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. In announcing the scheme, Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". She said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". Her department agreed the NI scheme with the government and will deliver it to consumers. A UK government spokesperson added that the scheme will "provide families in Northern Ireland with some breathing room on bills this winter". Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise" Speaking to Talkback on Friday, Archibald said: "People here rightly would expect that if support is being put in place for people in respect of their bills in Britain that it absolutely should be put in place for people here also. "We have made the case, we have delivered the scheme. "It is tax payers from here that are contributing to that and I think if there are going to be interventions in cost of living support then it has to apply here. "Ultimately the British government are the ones with the levers with the ability to make the interventions that we really need to see in terms of cost of living. "Ultimately I'm not sure the tone of the engagement from the secretary of state was particularly helpful," Archibald said. title: Tuchel recalls Alexander-Arnold and Palmer with warning
description: England boss Thomas Tuchel recalls Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer but says players have to "perform".
body: This video can not be played Tuchel recalls Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to England squad England head coach Thomas Tuchel says "the door is always open" after recalling Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer to his first squad since the World Cup - but has warned players they have to "perform". Tuchel controversially left Real Madrid right-back Alexander-Arnold and Chelsea forward Palmer out of his squad for the summer tournament in North America. Both return for four Nations League games during an extended international break after this weekend's club fixtures. Alexander-Arnold, 27, won the most recent of his 34 England caps when he came on as a substitute in a 1-0 win against Andorra in June 2025. He has made five appearances, including three starts, for Real Madrid so far this season, registering one assist. Palmer, 24, last played for England in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Japan in March. He has scored four goals and provided two assists in six games this season. "They had a good start to the season," said Tuchel, who has again omitted Manchester City's Phil Foden. "They never did something wrong. We just chose different players. "So now it is a new competition. Some players, some positions, have more injuries. Some have less injuries. Cole has his starts that he always had but he has his numbers back - he has his assists back, he has decisive goals back - so that is why he is in the squad. "I think he has a point to prove, and the same goes for Trent. He was never off the list. He was never non-selectable for us, and it is his chance to show, come to camp and be the best version of himself." Alexander-Arnold played in midfield in Real's Champions League win over Inter Milan earlier this month, but Tuchel said he had picked the former Liverpool player as a full-back. "He had a good start in two positions for Real Madrid and he comes as a right-back for us," he said. On his trust in Alexander Arnold, Tuchel said: "[He needs to] perform, that's just what it is. It is a competition and I understand the question because he was not with us at the World Cup. We trusted other players. "I still stick with this decision and it is now time to fight for his place. He always said he is up for a fight, he always said he is up to fight for his place - especially for England - so it is on him to prove and he is more than welcome in camp. "We have a long camp and I am sure he will show up." Tuchel said the onus was now on players to impress in the international set-up. "It is one thing to be nominated, like with Cole, and getting your ticket back in the squad but it's another thing to perform for England," he said. "Cole needs to step up when he comes and he needs to show these kind of numbers to get his place, keep his shirt and justify the nomination." England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September, then travel to Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October. Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha, who were both in the Three Lions' pre-World Cup squad, both feature again. Dominic Calvert-Lewin, whose three top-flight goals so far this season have helped Leeds United go third in the Premier League, is also included. Tuchel has also picked Newcastle United left-back Lewis Hall, Everton centre-back Jarrad Branthwaite, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly, who can play at left-back or in midfield, and Brighton keeper Jason Steele. Dean Henderson, Jordan Henderson, Reece James, Djed Spence and John Stones, who were all in the World Cup squad, miss out, with Tuchel saying they were not selected because of injuries. Along with Foden, other notable absentees are Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White, Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton and Manchester United's Harry Maguire. The Three Lions took a 1-0 lead but conceded two late goals, with former England captain Wayne Rooney saying the team "crumbled" and became "too passive", which he said started from "the manager and the decisions he made". Though England missed out on their first men's World Cup final in 60 years, they beat France 6-4 in an thrilling bronze-medal match to finish third. "The more I reflect on it, it's maybe more buying into our strengths and playing more minutes like we played in the second half against Croatia and the first half against France," said Tuchel. "Buying into these strengths because we get a lot of value out of it. We get a lot of connection to the fans. This is what the Premier League reflects. "Football is about adapting to situations, and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach if you look at the 6-4 against France - but people talk about it like it's one of their most nicest experiences ever. title: Michael Sheen's 'constructive' meeting with first minister over toxic dumping claims
description: Michael Sheen said his meeting with the first minister was "early days but that's really encouraging".
body: Michael Sheen said his meeting with the first minister was "early days but that's really encouraging" Hollywood actor Michael Sheen said he had a "constructive" meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth over toxic dumping claims raised in his BBC documentary. Buried with Michael Sheen explores toxic chemical dumping in 14 sites in Wales and England. Sheen initially said an offer to meet the first minister "was not taken up" before the documentary was broadcast in August. On Thursday, the Welsh actor said he met the first minister, speaking about how they could move forward adding it was "early days but that's really encouraging". Speaking on Instagram, external, he said "I've just come from a meeting with the first minister. "Talking about how we can move forward and address all the issues that Buried [the documentary] raised around the toxic dumping, and that was really constructive. "So early days but that's really encouraging." In the UK Parliament last week, Sheen urged MPs to back a national testing programme for historic toxic dumps to make sure sites were safe, after high levels of cancer-causing chemicals - known as PCBs - were found in soil samples and in the blood of people living near sites linked to chemical giant Monsanto. Sheen interviewed farming consultant turned campaigner Douglas Gowan shortly before his death, who had spent decades warning that communities were at risk of toxic chemicals. The actor later teamed up with investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby who had inherited all of the campaigner's documents and research. They set about testing 14 sites in Wales and north west England where it was thought Monsanto had been dumping PCBs, and found elevated levels at all but one. Sheen appeared before the Welsh Affairs Committee alongside investigative journalists Lucy Taylor and Dan Ashby, who co-presented the BBC series, Buried with Michael Sheen Susan Smith, who worked at Monsanto in Wrexham, said her happy memories of working there have been replaced with fears following the documentary. Susan and her husband Geraint's home, which they have lived in for 53 years, is separated from the decommissioned Ruabon chemical works by a thin tree line. Geraint was diagnosed with prostate cancer 13 years ago before more recently developing skin cancer, while Susan developed breast cancer when she was 38. While they admit they are not certain that Monsanto was responsible, the documentary has made them question the possible impact of the factory on their family's health. Susan worked as a secretary for four years when she was 19, then returned once for temporary cover and another time to overhaul a failing system. "Most of my time was spent in the telex office next to the warehouse. We used to send delivery notes, instructions, requests on little pieces of ticker tape through a machine to other Monsanto offices," she said. "We had a small glass hatch that the instructions would be passed through and it was never closed because people were passing things through so often. As a result dust and powders and all sorts would blow through and coat the desks, the paper, even our sandwiches." Susan said she wasn't given a "safety briefing, protective clothing or anything" and office staff never knew they were at risk. Susan had her blood tested by the documentary team and while the PCB levels in her blood were not deemed high, the fact there is no safe level of PCB and the lack of accountability from Eastman – the US company which now owns what was once Monsanto – has left her with unanswered questions. The couple have joined the Monsanto Contamination Action Group – which was set up for people in Wrexham who live in communities affected by historic industrial waste dumping. Eastman was approached for comment. title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
description: Police reportedly fired into the air on Friday morning as they struggled to contain crowds jostling to secure a place at the tented site.
body: Migrants in Ceuta push Spanish Civil Guard members as they are transferred to a camp Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa. Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air. Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people. Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave. The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe. During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control. More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue. The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined. More than 3,000 migrants being transferred on Friday, according to Spanish media The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis. Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants. Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker". "The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said. The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened. Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died". Pedro Sánchez denies knowing about the migrant rush in advance The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez. The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco. The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds. Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities. title: Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
description: Authorities linked the deaths to disease, but this has been disputed by intelligence reports and relatives of the accused.
body: Relatives of those who died protested in Minna, capital of Niger state Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said. Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report shared with the AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in Niger state. "We believe they suffocated because there was no ventilation," the father of one of those detained told the BBC. Abdullahi Dalhatu said his son had survived because he was near a small window. "His friend slumped and fainted, and many others also collapsed." His son described how detainees began collapsing in the heat of the overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, his father said. He said the detainees repeatedly knocked on the door for help but nobody opened it. The BBC has not independently verified his account. After news of the deaths spread, angry miners and relatives started attacking public institutions and public transport buses, using stones and sticks before they were dispersed by police who fired tear gas, according to local residents. State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday. An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January. The protesters targeted public transport buses Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining. Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC, a paramilitary agency responsible for protecting critical infrastructure and tackling crimes including illegal mining. It also assists police with internal security operations. The NSCDC told the BBC that illegal mining was widespread in Niger state, where artisanal miners often operate in open fields. Its spokesperson, Babawale Afolabi, said more than 50 people were arrested during an operation earlier this week. They had not been charged because profiling and documentation were still under way before the deaths, he said. "Illegal mining in Niger is serious," Afolabi said. The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal. But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests. "The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement. Dalhatu told the BBC that security officers had been pursuing suspected illegal miners in the community for several days before making arrests. He said relatives went to the NSCDC office seeking their release but were repeatedly told to return later. "Unfortunately, the following day we got the news that our children had died," he added. The NSCDC mining marshals unit has been cracking down on illegal mining recently One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives took him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination. Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards. Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened. Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement. The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in the state capital, Minna, for examination. It is not clear yet whether any of the suspects had been charged. Nigeria's constitution requires anyone detained on suspicion of a criminal offence to be brought before a court within a "reasonable time" - generally within a day where a court is available within 40km (25 miles), or two days in other cases, unless a longer period is considered reasonable. The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts. Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found. title: AI not a threat to films, say Shaun the Sheep creators
description: The Bristol-based institution have released the third feature film in the Shaun the Sheep franchise.
body: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is now out in UK cinemas Shaun the Sheep creators say AI will not replace the craft of storytelling as the franchise's latest film arrives in UK cinemas. Directed by Steve Cox and Matthew Walker, Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom has a Halloween flavour as Shaun has to turn into a mad scientist to save the day. Speaking ahead of its launch, producer Richard Beek said despite the rise of AI and CGI within the film industry, stop-motion movies are still being made and winning BAFTAs. "Maybe somewhere down the line there's a tool we use which uses AI but I don't think it would ever replace the storytelling and creation of those stories," he said. Despite the film having no dialogue, it has a star-studded voice cast, including Dani Dyer, Justin Fletcher, Nina Sosanya, Paul Whitehouse and Roman Kemp. It will also feature a brand-new remix of Shaun the Sheep's iconic theme tune, Life's A Treat, by British hip-hop duo Rizzle Kicks. PC banned for 'derogatory' WhatsApp comments School in 'outstanding' inclusion rating first Under-fire ambulance service improves in ratings Aardman celebrated its 50th birthday this year, after it was founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976. The Bristol company went on to create Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, and become the world's most successful stop-motion film. Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest stars. Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions - which is part of his global appeal. Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice, when the first TV series launched and the first feature film was made in 2015. Shaun the Sheep is popular in Japan, where he has his own theme park Students at Aardman's Academy are also being taught to embrace imperfection in the painstaking art of stop-motion, where every blink, smile and movement is created by hand. Art director Kitty Clay said a lot of the models are still being used 20 years after they were made. She said a lot of the props have "a personal touch" too, from her mum's ironing board to her granny's lampshade in the living room. Co-director Matthew Walker said: "It's been really exciting to explore a Shaun story in a new genre. "We did sci-fi with Farmageddon and now we're in Halloween horror but without the scares - it's more comedy," he said. The Shaun the Sheep franchise enters the horror genre for the first time Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is showing in UK cinemas this week and next. The film will then be available to watch later on Sky Cinema and NOW TV. title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
description: It is the first time the juror, who refused to side with the others and acquit Clancy, has spoken publicly about his decision.
body: The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating. Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated. Warning: This article contains distressing details The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window. To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition. The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder. Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings. "I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented." 'Emotional rollercoaster' - Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ends in a mistrial? Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind. "We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said. The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster". She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity." Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side". But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial. The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday. In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began. He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them". During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis. Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong. A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children. However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association. Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility. The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial. He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy. He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset." The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts. title: Brewdog's unpaid workers to receive nothing after takeover deal
description: Administrators say about £489,000 was owed for staff wages and holiday pay and £2.4m was owed to HMRC for unpaid VAT.
body: Aberdeenshire-based Brewdog had more than £500m of debts when it was sold Former Brewdog staff and several creditors of the collapsed Scottish beer giant are not expected to receive anything from the administration process. A report from administrators AlixPartners said there were "insufficient funds" for payouts to those owed money by Brewdog's retail arm. The Aberdeenshire-based brewer had more than £500m of debts when it was sold in March to US drinks firm Tilray in a £33m rescue deal. Administrators said about £489,000 was owed for staff wages and accrued holiday pay. A further £2.4m was owed to HMRC for unpaid VAT. From a £1bn dream to a brutal collapse: How Brewdog hit the rocks BrewDog's takeover saw 38 bars close across the UK and £20m in unpaid bills left to hundreds of UK businesses. Unpaid businesses ranged from coffee shops, bakeries and laundry services, to lawyers, councils and holiday parks. Creditors included West Ham United FC, Lord's Cricket Ground and Manchester University. AlixPartners said there were now "insufficient funds" for preferential creditors to be repaid. This is due to lower than expected funds raised through sales of Brewdog assets and increased costs during the administration period. Martin Dickie and James Watt founded Brewdog in 2007 The administrators cited unforeseen costs around the security of closed Brewdog pubs after a number of "unauthorised occupiers" gained access. AlixPartners said it worked with landlords and lawyers to remove them. The report highlights small amounts of money raised through asset sales. These include: A 7.8 acre field in Potterton, Aberdeenshire, which sold to a local farmer for £41,300 Nine Brewdog vehicles of "old age and varying roadworthiness" that made only £6,250 from just one sale. The rest were abandoned. A settlement involving drinks equipment sold to Marylebone Cricket Club, which owns Lords, which generated £62,000. Are you a Brewdog creditor or worker affected by this? What impact has it had? Parent company BrewDog PLC is still expected to pay its preferential creditor, HMRC, in full for £3.66m tax owed - mainly VAT and excise duty. Brewdog's biggest debt was to financial services group HSBC, which was owed more than £61m across various banking arms. It has recovered tens of millions of pounds, but still faces an estimated shortfall of £16.8m. The report noted that this could be reduced through asset sales in the United States. Private equity backer TSG, which took a 22% stake in the brewer in 2017, is set to lose £27.6m. Brewdog also owes around £190m to unsecured creditors. They are expected to receive less than a penny in the pound of what they are owed. Brewdog's collapse brought the immediate closure of 38 UK pubs In March 440 staff were made redundant and 736 employees transferred to Tilray, after the US firm bought Brewdog's brand and UK operation. Eleven bars were retained as part of the sale while 38 other pubs closed immediately. Former staff can claim for unpaid wages through the UK government's Insolvency Service. AlixPartners said workers had been given information on this support. Brewdog's collapse also rendered the shares of about 200,000 crowdfunding investors worthless. Earlier this year, Alixpartners confirmed that investors in the Equity for Punks scheme would get no return on their shares. Investors typically spent about £500 on shares - although others invested much larger sums - in return for a stake in the company, discounts and perks. The administrators stated these shares now had "no value". Brewdog, which was founded in 2007 by friends James Watt and Martin Dickie, had four breweries and about 100 pubs across the world at its peak. Watt said he was "heartbroken" after the collapse and apologised to staff and investors. Brewdog's owner Tilray has been approached for comment. title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
description: It is the first time MI5 has confirmed the BBC's revelation that it gave evidence based on lies in court while defending the violent informant.
body: The case centres around a BBC investigation over how an MI5 agent used his role to abuse his girlfriend The security service has accepted it gave evidence based on lies to three courts and that senior MI5 officers were repeatedly dishonest. It is the first time MI5 has accepted that lies were told to the courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy whose abuse was uncovered by the BBC. The lies were revealed by the BBC in February 2025, which the security service then vehemently denied. Timothy Otty KC, representing MI5, announced the position during a High Court hearing in London on Friday. A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence. In particular, the judges will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented. Otty announced that "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant. MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him. But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020. How I exposed MI5's lie about its violent abusive agent MI5 court evidence based on lies, report says The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told. He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case. Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again. He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum. Otty argued against contempt of court proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform. He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal. Lawyers for both officers argued against contempt proceedings. Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the report was "sufficient" - but that, should further action be deemed necessary, it would be better handled by the police and Crown Prosecution Service. In written submissions, he said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret. But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings. Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty. He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the "threshold" for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation. The court will hear legal submissions later on Friday from barristers for the BBC. X physically and sexually abused Beth, attacking her with a machete The case centres around the foreign neo-Nazi misogynist - an MI5 informant known as Agent X who used his security service role as a tool of abuse. He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while under police investigation. The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block its investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court. Arguing for secrecy in all three courts, the security service told judges that it had always stuck to its core secrecy policy and never told anyone whether X was an agent, including me. The courts were told this in a sworn statement from a senior officer, a deputy director called Witness A. The courts accepted MI5's arguments. This meant Beth and everyone else was banned from ever officially being told X was an agent and denied access to the key evidence. She was left at a serious disadvantage and may have lost the case. Officer 2 had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. Following the court decision in late 2024, I challenged MI5 and said they had lied to the courts. MI5 aggressively maintained its position that its NCND policy had been maintained until I produced evidence proving it was untrue, including a recording of one of the calls with Officer 2. Because of the BBC's revelations, two official inquiries took place which absolved MI5 and its officers of deliberate wrongdoing, claiming the false evidence was down to mistakes and poor memories. But, in July 2025, a panel of senior High Court judges ruled that the investigations carried out by MI5 suffered from "serious procedural deficiencies" and that "we cannot rely on their conclusions". Sir John's investigation was ordered by the prime minister in September 2025 after MI5's explanations about what happened were rejected as deficient and unreliable. Watch our pick of stand

title: At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque
description: A vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque building during Friday prayers, a senior police official says.
body: The blast occurred at a mosque building near police headquarters At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar. A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way. In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion." Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack", according to Reuters news agency. There has been no immediate claim of responsibility. Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast. Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police. Islamabad says militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem. title: Ex-Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir
description: Lord Watson praises his new employers but says there are "legitimate questions" about big tech firms that "require answers".
body: Former cabinet minister and Labour Party deputy leader Lord Tom Watson has become a senior vice president at US tech firm Palantir. Announcing his appointment on X, Lord Watson said Palantir was "the most interesting company on the planet, doing work of real consequence". He said the company had "challenges" and that while some criticism was "propaganda" there were "legitimate questions about large technology companies and sovereign control". Green MP Sian Berry said: "This is yet another example of the corrosive revolving door between politics and big business lobbying that has no place in public life." She added: "Palantir, with its work for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) in the US and the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), has no business at all in our NHS and public services. "Tom Watson has been employed to lobby his friends in the Labour government." Palantir builds software aimed at allowing organisations to make better use of their data and holds a large number of UK government contracts including with the NHS, the Ministry of Defence and 11 police forces. The company has attracted controversy, with some MPs calling for more scrutiny of its use of data within NHS contracts. Palantir is currently involved in a legal battle with the Mayor of London's office, over its decision to block the Metropolitan Police from agreeing a contract with the company. The Mayor's Office said it was not satisfied the deal adequately ensured value for money but also raised concern about the firm's values. Palantir has argued that its software has improved NHS databases in a number of areas such as waiting lists and hospital supplies, while its work with police forces has helped tackle corruption and identify women at risk of domestic violence. Louis Mosley, head of UK and Europe at Palantir Technologies, welcomed the appointment of Lord Watson saying he brought a "deep understanding of how AI is changing the ways the state can help people in Britain, where more than one in six Palantirians are based". Lord Watson was a Labour MP for more than 20 years and became a senior figure in the party, serving as a minister as well as a key behind-the-scenes operator, who reportedly orchestrated efforts to remove Tony Blair as prime minister. In 2015, he was strongly criticised for publicising unsubstantiated claims of sex abuse by the Conservative politician Leon Brittan. Brittan died before learning that the police had dropped their investigation and that he had no case to answer. At the time, Lord Watson said he was "sorry for the distress Leon Brittan's family experienced" but that he felt he had a "duty" to report claims. After leaving the House of Commons he was given a peerage and took up a position as the chair of UK Music. In a statement, he said Palantir was "helping Britain and its allies defend themselves, helping police protect our citizens and helping NHS staff get patients treated and home sooner". "We have challenges. Some criticism is propaganda. Some raises legitimate questions about large technology companies and sovereign control. Both require answers. "Part of my role will be to correct false information while working with our engineers to ensure privacy, security and respect for sovereignty are at the heart of everything we do." title: British rapper Sway dies aged 44
description: Sway, whose hits included Still Speedin' and Level Up, was living in Ghana at the time of his death.
body: The award-winning British-Ghanaian rap artist Sway DaSafo has died at the age of 44. He was the first unsigned rapper to win a Mobo Award in 2006, and scored a top 10 hit in 2012 with the single Level Up. The news was first shared online by the Mobo organisation, and confirmed to the BBC by the musician's friend Kash Ahmad, who said he died at his home in Ghana. No cause of death has been announced. Sway was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in 2010 and went into remission later that year. Sway was born Derek Andrew Safo in London, albeit accidentally, while his mother was on a stop-over between Amsterdam and her native Ghana. After a brief period in her homeland, he was raised in north London and honed his craft on pirate radio. He credited the BBC's radio station 1Xtra with providing him with his first break in 2002. Emerging during the first wave of grime, alongside artists such as Dizzee Rascal and Lethal Bizzle, he stood apart for his witty, literate style. "I'm a positive person. The positivity comes out in my music," he told the Guardian as his career took off. "I don't go round holding guns to people's heads so I won't rap about holding guns to people's heads." Despite widespread interest from the music industry, he remained independent - releasing music on his own label, and selling mixtapes at markets and independent record shops. He made headlines in September 2005 when he was named best hip-hop act at the Mobo awards - defeating US heavyweights such as 50 Cent and the Game. In his early years, the musician often kept his identity hidden The following year, he released his debut album This Is My Demo, accompanied by the top 40 single, Little Derek, which celebrated how he had "ended up in HMV instead of HMP". Although the album stalled at number 78 in the charts, it earned him a nomination for the Mercury Prize, alongside acts like Arctic Monkeys and Muse. In 2006, he supported The Streets on a UK tour and appeared alongside frontman Mike Skinner on the Mitchell Brothers' single Harvey Nicks. But in 2010, DaSafo was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma. "It felt like I had been dropped in the middle of the sea with no lifejacket," he later recalled. "I didn't have time to think about how I was going to get to the other side, I just had to deal with it." After receiving chemotherapy and radiotherapy, he went into remission, releasing his biggest hits Still Speedin' (which sampled Black Box's Ride On Time) and Level Up (featuring a verse from Kano) in 2012. He enjoyed further critical and commercial success with albums including Deliverance, and Verses from the Vault; and collaborated with artists like Mark Ronson, Ed Sheeran, Akon and Childish Gambino. Through his record label Dcypha, he also signed and developed artists including Tiggs Da Author and KSI. All three appeared on the 2013 single No Sleep, and KSI went on to become a hugely successful YouTuber, with a sideline in music. DaSafo also dabbled with an acting career, appearing in two episodes of the crime drama Top Boy and the 2012 film The Grind. At the time of his death, he was working on new music. His final Instagram post, shared last week, external, celebrated his 44th birthday. He is survived by two sons, Jalil and Ammar-Joseph, and twin daughters, Queen-Inaya and Queen-Imara. At the time of his death, he was raising them as a single parent in Ghana, his friend Kash Ahmad told BBC News. "It was an honour and a pleasure to have known and worked with him, and my thoughts and prayers are with his family," he added. Other tributes came from the Mitchell Brothers, who wrote: "We were privileged to have worked with you", and praised Sway's "true penmanship level and delivery". The musician was nominated for the Mercury Prize for his debut album, This Is My Demo "This hit me like a ton of bricks," said rapper and record label executive Kardinal Offishall. "Rest in eternal peace and God cover your babies. Til we meet again my friend." So Solid Crew's Megaman simply posted "RIP"; while The Mobo Awards said they were "proud to have him as part of our history," adding: "Our love goes out to his family, loved ones and fans." Rapper Baby Blue posted on Instagram: "In my heart I worried this day was coming but I wasn't prepared for the reality of losing Sway. "He was my confidante and he guided me through so much of my life musically and personally... I will miss you forever my friend. I am lost." Breaking the news to her listeners on BBC Radio 1Xtra, broadcaster Remi Burgz said it was a "sad day for British music" and called Sway a "UK Rap pioneer". "One of north London's finest," she said, "he was mine and many others first experience of UK rap [and] hip-hop in mainstream media". "He was a literal example of paving the way and showing that UK rap can take up space in music. "Rest in perfect peace to Sway." title: Mother expected to plead guilty over child deaths
description: Yasmeen Ali is expected to plead guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.
body: Fares, Joury and Mohammed were found dead at their home in Sea Mills A mother is expected to plead guilty to killing her three young children, a court has heard. Seven-year-old Fares Bash, three-year-old Joury Bash and nine-month-old Mohammed Bash died at their home in Sea Mills, Bristol, on 18 February 2024. Yasmeen Ali, 44, is expected to plead guilty to their manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, and the infanticide of her nine-month-old son. An inquest previously heard that the three children died of knife wounds, with injuries to their chests and necks. Fares Bash also showed possible signs of asphyxia. PC banned for 'derogatory' WhatsApp comments School in 'outstanding' inclusion rating first Under-fire ambulance service improves in ratings Ali, of no fixed address, is currently charged with three counts of murder and was due to face trial next month at Bristol Crown Court. Anna Vigars KC, prosecuting, told the court earlier that two psychiatrists had prepared reports which had made the reduced pleas available. "As the court will be aware we have received two psychiatric reports," she said. "Both of them, perhaps unsurprisingly in the circumstances of this case, indicating that the partial defence of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility is available to Ms Ali. "The third count, as far as infanticide is concerned, that's simply because of the youngest child's age at the time of his death. "The defence of diminished responsibility applies to all three deaths. "Having been able to spend some time with the children's father, Mr Alfil Bash, and to explain the position to him, I am in the position to indicate to the court that were those pleas to be forthcoming they are pleas that would be accepted by the Crown." Andrew Langdon KC, defending, told the court he was due to speak with the defendant in the coming weeks but expected the guilty pleas to be formally entered at the next hearing. "We are grateful for that indication, and our position is that we anticipate that guilty pleas to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility in relation to all three of the children will be entered," he said. "There isn't going to be a trial is our confident prediction." Mr Justice Linden scheduled the next hearing for 23 October, when the case is expected to conclude. Ali, who was not required to appear at the hearing, is being held in a secure psychiatric hospital. Following the incident, Avon and Somerset Police referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over prior contact but the watchdog said no investigation was required. title: We have a duty to 'progress' Good Friday Agreement, taoiseach tells PM
description: The pair were expected to discuss a further strengthening of ties including boosting trade, security and working with the European Union.
body: Burnham said it "feels very fitting" to welcome Martin as the first international visitor to Number 10 North Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin has told Prime Minister Andy Burnham their governments have a duty to "mind and progress" the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Burnham said the relationship between the UK and Ireland matters "on every single level" as they met at Number 10 North for talks on Friday. The pair were expected to discuss a further strengthening of ties including boosting trade, security and working with the European Union. The prime minister said they were "working together" to uphold the principles of the peace deal for Northern Ireland. Speaking ahead of their talks, Burnham said it "feels very fitting" to welcome Martin as the first international visitor to Number 10 North in Manchester. "The relationship between the UK and Ireland matters so much on every single level," he said. Burnham added that as "co-custodians of the Good Friday Agreement, we are working together to uphold its principles as we approach the 30th anniversary". The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a political deal designed to bring an end to 30 years of violent conflict in Northern Ireland, known as the Troubles. The taoiseach expressed his sympathies with Burnham following the recent death of his father. Martin said he appreciated the meeting going ahead, telling the prime minister: "I think your sense of duty shines through." The taoiseach said "in a global world marked by uncertainty" it was "important that two close neighbours continue the very strong engagement". He added: "We are co-guarantors of the Good Friday Agreement. We have very significant obligations to mind it and to progress it and so forth." Martin said he was also looking forward to discussing "even stronger and closer relationships between the European Union and the United Kingdom, which will be of benefit to the European Union and to Ireland". title: Canada captain loses sleep 'four to five nights a week' over England's World Cup win
description: Canada captain Sophie de Goede says she still loses sleep over their World Cup final loss to England last year.
body: De Goede's Canada side were beaten 33-13 by England in the 2025 World Cup final It is nearly a year since Canada lost the Women's Rugby World Cup final to England - but time has not been a healer for everyone. "Four to five nights a week I can't fall asleep because I'm still thinking about the final," says Canada captain Sophie de Goede, who is preparing to take on the world champions this Saturday at Sandy Park in Exeter. So, is this match revenge for the side ranked third in the world? Canada head coach Kevin Rouet is keen to play this down: "Revenge is a good brand but they [England] won the final of the World Cup - that was the most important game to win, the next important games will be in the World Cup 2029." After Canada, England play New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, before two more tests against Canada in Toronto and Ottawa. In recent history, England's women have never faced such tough successive opposition. Red Roses head coach John Mitchell says the games are an "audition" for the 2029 World Cup. "You look at the geography that we're going to cover, we're not always going to be in our training base. We're going to be going to different facilities. It's a challenge," he said. "It's going to be really cool to see how they handle pressure as well. I think the Red Roses are very good around pressure because I think it reveals how much they care". England Women v Canada Women Saturday, 19 September at 15:00 BST There continues to be misconceptions around the status of the Canadian women: they are professional athletes but contracts, as with most other nations, do not yet compare to England's women. The Canadian programme involves a clever strategy of using England's domestic PWR league to develop its players. There are 25 Canadians in PWR and the current Canada coaching staff includes Kevin Rouet and Alex Austerberry, who both coach Saracens Women, and Nathan Smith from Loughborough Lightning. "It's not like we're coming in to spy," joked De Goede. "We just don't have the quality league [in Canada]." Canada are not the only country to do this - PWR is littered with top internationals from across the globe. Mitchell has told BBC Sport that he and Charlie Hayter, head of women's performance at England Rugby, have lobbied to increase PWR game time for English Qualified Players (EQP) from next season. Mitchell has frequently pushed his theory that players who can reach 1,000 PWR playing minutes a season "gives them a higher probability" of playing for the Red Roses. "I haven't enjoyed seeing young English players between 21 and 23 not getting enough minutes," he said. "I think that number [1,000] is very meaningful." The RFU confirmed to BBC Sport the current requirements around 13 EQP players on average across matchday squads will remain. However, the lure of signing foreign talent will be dampened by the removal of club injury credit, which helps cover the cost of replacing an injured player. From the 2027-28 season, only players who sustain an injury while on international duty for one of England's representative teams will be eligible. Besides this, if any EQP player is captured by another union, they will only be able to hold their EQP status until the end of that season. title: Oasis will not headline Glastonbury 2027, organiser Emily Eavis confirms
description: The rock band will not be stopping at Worthy Farm despite being on tour at that time next summer.
body: Oasis last played Glastonbury in 2004 (singer Liam Gallagher pictured) Oasis may be back on tour next summer but they will not be playing Glastonbury Festival, according to co-organiser Emily Eavis. The band announced a series of 2027 gigs across the UK, Ireland, Europe and the US last week, leaving a potentially Glastonbury-shaped hole in their calendar. Oasis are due to play concerts at Manchester City's Etihad Stadium on the Friday and Saturday of Glastonbury, but don't currently have their own gig scheduled on the Sunday. This led some fans to conclude the Gallaghers may have been planning to rock up at Worthy Farm's Pyramid Stage to close the event. But Eavis has put those rumours to bed in a direct response to one Glastonbury-goer on social media. "Please say you've got Oasis," commented one follower on Instagram. Eavis replied: "Sorry Jimmy, not this time!" This tallies with what frontman Liam Gallagher posted on X last month, in response to one fan-site noting they were bookmakers' favourites to headline the festival. "It's not happening," he wrote. "So all you croc wearing flag waving [people] can calm [...] down." The band will play gigs in Manchester in June 2027, around the same time as the Worthy Farm event Like Glastonbury, Oasis took 2026 off. The band's 38-date tour marks the next phase of their comeback following their acclaimed 2025 live reunion, which made an estimated £300 million. "Come see. It will not be televised," they announced ahead of the last tour. It was, however, ultimately documented in their own concert film titled Don't Look Back in Anger, released earlier this month. The UK's biggest festival, Glastonbury - which is broadcast on the BBC - offers worldwide exposure for artists, but Eavis has been open in the past about paying headliners far less than they'd get elsewhere. Also, the Gallagher brothers, now both in their 50s, did not play three nights in a row throughout their comeback tour - making the prospect of Glastonbury seem even less likely. Oasis made their Glastonbury debut in 1994 as cool young things on the NME Stage, now called the Woodsies Stage, before the release of their debut album Definitely Maybe. They returned to headline the Pyramid Stage the following year, with Take That-turned-solo star Robbie Williams joining them on stage, and again in 2004. Both Gallaghers performed at Worthy Farm as solo acts during their years apart but it seems they will not return there together, in 2027 at least. Glastonbury tickets will go on sale on 1 October, though the lineup is not expected to be revealed until the spring. Taylor Swift has not played at Glastonbury Last year's Glastonbury Festival saw headline performances from The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with Rod Stewart in the so-called legend slot. Oasis had been among the favourites to headline next year, alongside the likes of the perennially rumoured Taylor Swift and Madonna, as well as Harry Styles, Sam Fender, Ed Sheeran, Sabrina Carpenter and Fred Again. Previous headliners Radiohead, Pulp and Florence and the Machine have also been mentioned in some quarters along with Rihanna, Lady Gaga, Chappell Roan and Eminem. Bookies have also provided odds for possible headline sets from Charli XCX, Raye, Bad Bunny, Adele, Miley Cyrus, Kendrick Lamar, Justin Bieber, Bruce Springsteen and Little Simz. Last month, Eavis confirmed they had booked their headliners for next summer but scotched rumours that Madonna will be among them. Speaking to Katie Razzall on BBC Radio 4's PM programme, Eavis said: "No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that." She added: "But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well." Swift was announced as a headliner for Glastonbury's 50th anniversary in 2020. But that year's festival was cancelled entirely due to the Covid-19 pandemic. So, like Madonna, she is yet to make her Worthy Farm debut. When asked about the possibility of a performance from Swift at last, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more. We'll put her down as a definitely maybe then, for now. title: Council staff refused anonymity for Sara Sharif inquest
description: A coroner rejects an application for three workers after the media, including the BBC, opposed it.
body: Sara Sharif died after a campaign of abuse A coroner has rejected a request for anonymity made on behalf of three council workers who are expected to give evidence at the inquest into the death of Sara Sharif. The 10-year-old was found dead in a bunk bed at her family home in Woking, Surrey, in August 2023. Her father and stepmother – Urfan Sharif and Beinash Batool – were jailed for life in December 2024 after being found guilty of her murder. At a pre-inquest review hearing last week, Surrey County Council applied to prevent the identities of the workers being reported by the press during the full hearing, but that application was resisted by media organisations, including the BBC. Concerns were raised about Sara's care within a week of her birth in 2013, and her parents were known to social services as early as 2010, it has been reported. Surrey County Council workers tried to visit the family home the day before she was murdered but visited the wrong address, a review also found. It also found that services in Surrey failed to identify that Sara was at risk of abuse and did not question unexplained bruising. This included a failure to properly investigate why she started wearing a hijab - that covered the bruising - for "fear of causing offence". Urfan Sharif and Beinash Batool (pictured) were sentenced to life imprisonment Alethea Redfern, representing the council, said anonymity would protect the employees from "harm to their health and private and family lives". She added there would be a "risk that the employees could no longer work if their identities were revealed", which would be a "loss of valuable resource" to the authority. Senior coroner Richard Travers said: "I am not satisfied, on the basis of the evidence provided, that granting anonymity is justified by reference to common law principles of fairness." He said that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights on respecting private and family life is balanced against Article 10 on the freedom of expression for the media, which Travers added was an "important principle of open justice". The BBC, Times Media Limited, and Guardian News & Media Limited opposed the anonymity application. The coroner previously ordered Surrey County Council to disclose 24,606 pages of documents about Sara's case. This video can not be played Sara Sharif loved to sing and play the guitar and dreamed of being on The X-Factor Urfan Sharif was jailed for a minimum term of 40 years, while Batool has to serve at least 33 years in custody. Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, 31, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and jailed for 16 years. Sara died after a campaign of abuse, and a post-mortem examination found she had suffered dozens of injuries. Surrey County Council has previously said it was "deeply sorry" after the review into Sara's case. The full inquest is expected in October 2027.
