title: Early Bowie music available to stream for first time
description: Previously unheard material from the start of the artist's career has been released for the first time.
body: Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read. What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name. From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream. "They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist. For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums. He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons. Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles. "It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao. In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time. But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats. In 1965 Bowie made an appearance on the BBC show 'Gad Zooks Its All happening' but caused controversy with his long hair. It was within Talmy's collection that Palao came across the valuable 12-inch acetate. That material and the five other previously unheard tunes, as well as demos and remastered songs, form part of a new, posthumous album called The Shel Talmy Recordings. A limited edition vinyl will be sold at Record Store Day and HMV outlets. In 2022, David Bowie's estate sold the publishing rights to decades of the singer's work to Warner Music Group. For this new material, Palao, along with Talmy Enterprises Incorporated, licensed the album to Warner, and it will be released by the company's subsidiary, Parlophone. Royalties will be paid to Bowie's estate by Warner. "I think it's wonderful that people can get to hear the early Davie Jones music," said Dana Gillespie, an early collaborator of Bowie's. She met him after a performance at the Marquee Club in London when Bowie was 17. "They're songs that don't really sound like David but it's him trying to find his voice. He was experimenting." Gillespie became close friends with Bowie, eventually working with him on his "Ziggy Stardust" album. Talmy worked with both artists and Bowie's song "Andy Warhol", on his fourth studio album, was originally written for Gillespie. "He was very driven," remembered Gillespie, who is still touring and making music at the age of 77. "Some time in the sixties, he asked me to come and visit his parents. We were in his little house in Bromley, and when his parents left the room he turned to me and said: 'Whatever it takes, I want to get out of here.' And he did," she said. It is a decade since Palao found the recordings. Since then, it has been a long process to bring them to market. The result is an album that he says is "absolutely pure rock 'n' roll". "If you're looking for clues as to what he was to become, there's maybe less of that," said Palao, "but objectively speaking, I feel it's important stuff." Gillespie is excited by one song in particular. "There was a famous café called the Gioconda in Denmark Street where I often used to go with David," she said, recalling the centre of musical life in London in the 1960s. "One day when I was sitting there, David rushed in and took me by the hand. He said: 'You have to hear this'. "He ran with me around the corner and squeezed us into a small listening booth. I had one speaker and he had the other, and he played me 'I Pity The Fool'." A remastered version of the song can be heard in the new album. For music historians, fans of Bowie, and those who were there, the new album is another chance to reconnect with an enduring cultural icon. "David always wanted to be a big star," said Gillespie. "I'm so happy that his early stuff hasn't been forgotten." title: Why we bought our first home with a 100% mortgage - despite the risks
description: The share of UK mortgages with smaller deposits is the highest it's been since 2008. The BBC spoke to borrowers about how they manage the risks.
body: The couple are aware of the risks that come with their no-deposit mortgage Until last year, Conroy, 32, and his partner Amber, 28, saw little prospect of owning their own home. They were renting in central Manchester where they work and could not afford to save up for a deposit. Then they came across a relatively niche, and some experts say riskier, type of mortgage that offered a solution. The Track Record mortgage from Skipton Building Society covers 100% of the value of a property, with the borrower paying nothing upfront. Borrowers must meet strict eligibility checks and pay a higher interest rate - in Conroy and Amber's case 5.33% fixed for five years - but they were happy to do this. And in August they bought a four-bed home for £242,000 in Swinton on the edge of Manchester. "I don't think it's dawned on us it's really ours," says Conroy, a video editor. According to the Bank of England, the share of UK mortgages with deposits worth less than 10% of the property's value is currently the highest it has been since 2008, external when such loans were widely available. The average deposit for first-time buyers is currently around 20%. It comes as lenders such as Lloyds, Santander, Skipton and Yorkshire Building Society have launched a raft of new mortgage deals over the last few years covering upwards of 95% of the value of a property, and in some cases as much as 100%. They say they want to help first-time buyers get on the housing ladder as property prices continue to rise and while saving for a deposit remains a struggle. But these loans tend to charge higher rates, aren't available for all types of property or borrower, and come with risks customers should be aware of. Conroy and Amber thought they would be renting for the foreseeable future Conroy and Amber, a solicitor, have a 25-year loan with monthly repayments of £1,500 - roughly what they were paying in rent. He says they feel comfortable with the higher cost because they "earn quite well" and expect their salaries to rise. But he is aware there is a greater risk of falling into negative equity with a no- or low-deposit mortgage. That is when the value of a property falls below the value of the loan still owed on it - leaving the borrower with potentially painful costs if they suddenly have to sell. Conroy says they plan to overpay their mortgage for the first five years to build up more equity in their home. "There is always the element of a gamble with the property market," he says. "But I have researched the area we moved to and don't think house prices are going to drop." Twenty-seven-year-old Bronya and her partner George, 29, also used a low-deposit mortgage to buy their four-bedroom house in Rhuddlan, North Wales in August. Lloyds lent them £258,000 - roughly 98% of the property's value - over a 33-year term and they only had to put down £5,000 as a deposit. The couple pay an interest rate of 5.89%, fixed for five years, equating to monthly repayments of £1,400 - about the same as what they paid to rent a one-bed flat before. Bronya and George bought their first home this year with a roughly 2% deposit Bronya, a civil servant, says they could have put down a bigger deposit but wanted to use their savings for a renovation project costing upwards of £20,000. They are aware of the risks of negative equity but believe the refurbishment will boost the value of their home. "We also plan to stay here our whole lives," George adds, explaining that they are prepared to ride out any dips in the property market. The couple are renovating their home Widespread uptake of low-deposit mortgages by borrowers who could not afford them was seen as a major factor in the 2008 global financial crisis. But today's deals have much stronger affordability checks and do not pose the same risks, says David Hollingworth, associate director at brokers L&C Mortgages. Borrowers of Skipton's zero-deposit mortgage, for example, have to prove they have kept up with their rent for at least 12 consecutive months and credit payments for the last six months. And Lloyds won't issue one of its £5,000 deposit mortgages for new-build properties and shared ownership homes. Hollingworth says lenders are recognising that some people have "good affordability but may be struggling to save for a deposit while paying a rent and dealing with cost of living pressures". Following a recent rule change, he adds, lenders are also offering more "flex" on how much someone can borrow as long as it's within their means. Nevertheless, he urges borrowers to use common sense. "Think carefully - what do monthly payments look like? Are you aware that interest rates could go up?" Are you buying your first home? How have you managed it? title: The virtual worlds where robots are trained
description: Training systems that allow robots to negotiate the real world are getting more sophisticated.
body: This video can not be played Freddo the robot in action at Vsim Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottled offered by a staff member. Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement. But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills. I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace. But there's a long way to go. "It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says. Vsim founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo. Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it. In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools. As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs. "The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says. Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before. "Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu. The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around. "It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains. And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home. "Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says. Robot training systems use virtual environments where tasks are practised Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers. It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots. That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model, external, called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around. But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world. "Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia. But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not. "When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour. "We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says. Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations. Rika Antonova has spent more than a decade working in robotics Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge. Her research is focused on, external developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour. Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code. "It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says. She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising. "If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says. But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained. "There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says. It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on. title: Watch: Can humpback whales experience grief?
description: Rare footage captured by researchers off Australia's Gold Coast suggests humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die.
body: This video can not be played Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found. The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull explains everything you need to know about the sighting off Australia's Gold Coast, and why it's so rare. Watch: Can humpback whales experience grief? title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into 'Made in Europe' industry scheme
description: The chancellor wants the Made in Europe programme to deepen ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers".
body: John Healey is meeting EU finance ministers on Friday The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition. John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday. But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC. Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme. That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join. The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries. There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains. Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK. Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places. "To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses – wherever they are based across the UK – get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow." Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing. "The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said. It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister. Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November. Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending. He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea. Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending. Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review. title: Rapist police officer was first arrested and released 17 years ago
description: Police officer Campbell Petrie was convicted of raping two women at the High Court in Glasgow.
body: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges against two women A former police sergeant convicted of rape was first arrested 17 years ago following a complaint from one of his victims. Campbell Petrie, 50, is facing a lengthy jail sentence after being found guilty of sex offences and violence against two women between 2006 and 2022. Police Scotland told BBC News that one of the women, who he met through his job, made a complaint of threatening behaviour against Petrie in 2009. He was arrested and held in a police station for five hours, but no further action was taken because of a lack of evidence. Petrie remained a serving officer until another woman made an allegation of rape against him in October 2023, prompting an investigation by specialist sexual crime officers. He was arrested, charged and suspended in December 2023, and retired from the force two years later. Petrie denied the allegations but was convicted of nine charges after a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years The case has appalled workers at Rape Crisis Scotland, which supports survivors of sexual violence. The organisation's external affairs manager, Nicola Love, said: "It does stick in the throat that someone like that is allowed to leave the force on their own terms, instead of as a result of what they've done. "We know perpetrators come from all walks of life, and that does include the police force, but it provokes an intense reaction because these people have a duty to protect us. "There's an expectation that they keep us safe, and this flies in the face of that." Petrie was found guilty of indecently assaulting one of the women while she was asleep and on various occasions between 2006 and 2009. He was convicted of raping the second woman on multiple occasions between 2011 and 2014. A trial found he assaulted both women to the danger of their lives by grabbing their throats and restricting their breathing. Petrie remained a serving officer with Police Scotland until October 2023 Petrie's conviction means that three serving or former Police Scotland officers have been exposed as rapists this year. In July, Cameron Ross was jailed for ten years for raping two women and subjecting a third to a campaign of abuse. Three weeks later, a BBC Disclosure investigation revealed that Alan Greer - a police officer who took his own life in May - was a violent rapist who had attacked and attempted to murder women over at least 14 years. Further BBC Scotland inquiries established that Greer had passed vetting checks to join Strathclyde Police in 2009, despite having two reports of criminal behaviour against women on his record. At least 15 potential victims of Greer have been identified so far and the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) has been brought in to carry out an independent investigation. Under its terms of reference, published this week, the NPCC will try to identify whether his crimes could have been discovered any earlier. PC Alan Greer was exposed as a violent rapist who attacked a number of women over a 15-year period The Petrie case has raised fresh questions over background checks on police in Scotland. In 2023, all UK forces carried out a "historic data wash" following the crimes of Met officers Wayne Couzens, who abducted and murdered Sarah Everard, and serial rapist David Carrick. Officers and staff were checked against the national police data base to identify whether they had a criminal past which had been missed. Police Scotland's deputy chief constable Bex Smith told BBC Scotland: "In 2009 Campbell Petrie was arrested and questioned in connection with a complaint of threatening behaviour, however, the case did not proceed due to insufficient evidence. "The independent historic data wash, carried out by UK policing between March and July 2023, interrogated the Police National Database and did not identify any unknown information on Petrie. "The checks carried out by Police Scotland went further than UK forces and included robust interrogation of both the vulnerable person's database and intelligence system." UK police forces carried out a "historic data wash" following the crimes David Carrick and Wayne Couzens In total, 23,822 Police Scotland officers, staff and volunteers were checked during that process. Concerns were raised about just eight individuals, with a civilian member of staff facing a criminal investigation. In the wake of Petrie's conviction and the Greer case, the Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland (HMICS) said they were "deeply concerned" about vetting at the force. The chief inspector of constabulary, Craig Naylor, said: "HMICS have previously scrutinised Police Scotland's arrangements for vetting, misconduct and the management of officers subject to allegations of wrongdoing, and have made a number of recommendations for improvement. "We have recently raised concern with both Police Scotland and the Scottish Police Authority about a lack of progress in relation to the vetting of officers within Police Scotland, including the effectiveness of a historic data wash exercise and the associated assurance around these issues." Justice secretary Neil Gray said Petrie's crimes were "extremely disturbing" Strengthening vetting procedures is a key aim of the Police (Ethics, Conduct and Scrutiny) (Scotland) Act passed by the Scottish Parliament in January 2025. The intention is that all officers will now undergo a career-long, structured regime of on-going vetting. Scotland's justice secretary Neil Gray described Petrie's case as "extremely disturbing" and his abuse of his position of trust as "abhorrent." He said: "Police officers are rightly expected to uphold the highest standards of integrity, which is why we have strengthened vetting through legislation and Police Scotland have been clear there is an ongoing programme of work to re-vet all officers." title: 'Just the beginning' - Samba, 17, steals Man City show
description: Floyd Samba's scintillating debut stole the show at Etihad Stadium but also took the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester.
body: Floyd Samba's brother Tyrone is also a Manchester City player Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester. Website articles, social media posts and column inches have been filled this week with the news that highly rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United. But that particular saga will be overshadowed in Friday's football cuttings by 17-year-old Samba's stunning bow on the professional stage, scoring twice in Manchester City's 5-0 Carabao Cup third-round thrashing of Norwich City. Samba was prolific in City's under-18 side last season and those impressive performances led to him being promoted to the first-team set-up by new manager Enzo Maresca this summer. The show of faith is already being repaid. "I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team," Samba told BBC Radio 5 Live. "To get a debut like that is mind-blowing. "I couldn't believe it myself - but that is just the beginning, I have got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut. "I spoke to all of them [first-team players], they have all been brilliant with me - before the game, giving me advice like 'play your game, be you' - those words have given me confidence and helped me score those two goals today." Samba with debut double as Man City thrash Norwich The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term. Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May. On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity. With City struggling for openings, Samba broke the deadlock by flicking home a header - he celebrated by blowing a kiss in the direction of family and friends in the stands, before curling in a delightful second later in the game. Samba was afforded a generous ovation towards the end of the game when being deservedly named man of the match. "[I'm] satisfied not just for the goals but for the performance too," said manager Maresca. "I asked him in the last three, four days - when I decided to play him as nine - he said he never played there. He is not a nine for sure, but he was good. "He is young, full of energy, strong, can finish, can set [players up]. He made some good decisions in the first half. I am happy but they are young and we have to go slowly, slowly. "Hopefully we can give him more chances." Christopher Samba (left) played for Blackburn in the Premier League between 2007-12 The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League. Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa. The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut. As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back. "Coming from under-21s to first-team training, that is a big jump," added Samba. "The sessions are more tiring, you have to run more - they demand more of you and you have to cope with it." Former Norwich striker Chris Sutton added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Absolutely brilliant moment for Floyd. His dad was in the stadium and will be extremely proud. It's the journey, he has been nurtured at Man City, got his moment and what a night for him. "He has given Enzo Maresca a bit of food for thought moving forward. Of course, he is not going to play ahead of Erling Haaland but it is a great evening for him and good for his development. "Maresca can think he can trust him a little bit more." title: Councils to share £5m in 'emergency food aid' as living costs rise
description: The money from the Welsh government will amount to around £200,000 to every council.
body: Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams says families are facing a "tough winter" with inflation rising Welsh councils will receive £4.8 million to provide "emergency food aid" and other support for people struggling due to cost of living pressures. The cash from the Welsh government will be split between the 22 local authorities, with those in rural areas getting a premium due to "the added challenges" of delivering support to more sparsely populated regions. Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams said rising fuel and energy costs meant many families faced another "tough winter" and she was "targeting support where it's needed most". Reform UK Wales said it welcomed the support, but said the government could do more to help people in need. The ongoing US-Iran war and pressures on oil supply in Saudi Arabia have caused fuel prices to spike in recent days. With inflation increasing and energy bills going up next month, many people could feel more of a squeeze on their household budgets. Local authorities will be able to give the emergency money to community organisations like food banks, lunch clubs and advice providers. Gareth Banks volunteers at Down to Zero, which grows organic vegetables for the local community Down To Zero, a project which has received funding previously, grows vegetables on allotments near Llantrisant in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and provides free vegetable boxes to low income families as well as lower cost subscriptions to other households within the county. Gareth Banks has volunteered with the organisation for two years and "absolutely loves it". "We can offer really good value, organically grown, fruit and vegetables to local people who might not always be able to afford that kind of thing," he said. Angharad Rogers says families with incomes are "still not able to pay for food" The project is run by Cynon Taf, a social housing provider. Angharad Rogers, Cynon Taf's director of housing and communities, said food poverty was a growing problem for tenants. "We've seen quite a shift lately in the people... who are most in need and accessing food banks," she said. "Families with incomes coming into the household are still not able pay for food and things like that, so we're seeing a lot families coming to us and asking for help." Contact advicelink Cymru, external for free, impartial advice on debt and benefits Contact your local council to see if you are eligible for emergency help from the Discretionary Assistance Fund, external If you are on a prepayment meter and cannot afford fuel you can contact the Fuel Bank Foundation, external for help If you are on a low income, you may be able to get your council tax reduced via the council tax reduction scheme, external. Joy says fuel prices are "extraordinarily high" UK inflation hit its highest level in five months in the year to August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year. In Ystradowen, Vale of Glamorgan, drivers filling up their cars said they feared prices would increase further. Ron Jones, from Cowbridge, said he was driving less but higher prices were "to be expected, given the world as it is". Joy Thomas said prices were "extraordinarily high" and she had searched for the cheapest petrol station she could find. Lewis Wall, 28, from Ystradowen, said prices were "ridiculous". "But what can we do about it? You can't control the price and everyone needs fuel." Sioned Williams said the government would "do all we can to support families who are going to be finding it tough this winter". "But we need to see wider measures and many of those leavers reside in Westminster," she added. Williams called on the UK government to bring in a system of cheaper energy prices for low income households, known as social tariffs. "Social tariffs on energy is one of the main things I think that could really make a difference to people," she said. The UK government said: "We have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, on top of the £150 we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills." Reform said support to help ease the pressures of the cost of living "should be welcomed if delivered in the right way". But it also said the Plaid Cymru government "could be doing more" if it did not "waste money" on projects like "spending taxpayer cash on planting trees in Uganda", referencing the long-running climate resilience program funded by it. title: Champion Van Gerwen loses in first round to Gurney
description: Defending champion Michael van Gerwen falls to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney in the opening round of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
body: Michael Van Gerwen was hoping to win a record-extending seventh title Defending champion Michael van Gerwen fell to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney in the opening round of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. Northern Ireland's Gurney raced into a 3-0 lead before the Dutch top seed reeled off five consecutive legs to put himself on the brink of victory. However, Gurney, who was drafted in as a late replacement when Lourence Ilagan withdrew from the 32-man field, responded by taking the ninth leg. And when Van Gerwen missed six match darts, he was able to level the match at 5-5 and win the decider with the throw. Gurney will now take on England's Ross Smith in the last 16 on Saturday after he advanced past Kevin Doets 6-3. World number one Luke Littler will get under way on Friday against former UK Open champion Danny Noppert, having recently whitewashed the Dutchman 6-0 on his way to winning the Czech Darts Open. World number two Luke Humphries also emerged victorious in another England versus Netherlands encounter, progressing 6-4 against Jermaine Wattimena. Dutch number one Gian van Veen gained a measure of revenge for the home fans with a 6-2 triumph over Chris Dobey. Dirk van Duijvenbode fought back from 4-1 down to defeat Sweden's Viktor Tingstrom 6-4, while Ryan Searle threw four 180s as he dispatched former world champion Rob Cross 6-2. Searle goes on to play Josh Rock, who won the last three legs to edge out Stephen Bunting 6-5. Karel Sedlacek marked his debut at the tournament with a 6-4 win over New Zealander Ben Robb and will take on Van Veen next. title: Andy Burnham to meet Irish Taoiseach for first time
description: Martin will be the first international leader to visit Number 10 North, the government said ahead of the talks.
body: Micheál Martin will be in the first international leader to visit Number 10 North The Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin will hold their first official meeting in Manchester on Friday. Martin will be the first international leader to visit Number 10 North, the government said ahead of the talks. The men are expected to discuss further strengthening of the UK/Ireland relationship including boosting trade, security and working with the EU. Burnham said he was "delighted" to be hosting the taoiseach and said it was an "historic and proud day for Manchester". "No10 North is all about creating opportunities for working people, and our partnership with Ireland as we improve the lives of people in both of our countries is a key part of that," he said. "There is so much we can achieve together: from our shared commitment to the Good Friday Agreement, to trade, to working with Europe and supporting Ukraine. We are the closest of friends, and I look forward to further strengthening that friendship." Following their meeting, the leaders will visit a local Irish community centre to meet with representatives from the Irish community in Greater Manchester. The visit comes days after US President Donald Trump made remarks supporting a "unified Ireland". On his visit to Northern Ireland last month, Burnham said a border poll was "off the table", but later said he stood by the Good Friday Agreement. It is also expected that the two leaders will discuss reform of the Stormont institutions as well as progress on replacing the controversial Troubles legacy act during their meeting. Andy Burnham said he stood by the Good Friday Agreement In a statement, Martin said they will discuss the "UK-Ireland 2030 programme of strategic cooperation" as well as "a range of matters relating to Northern Ireland". The statement said these matters include legacy and the Good Friday Agreement. He added: "Our discussions will also cover EU and international issues, including Ireland's current Presidency of the Council of the EU and the next EU-UK Summit, and the situation in Ukraine, Gaza and the Middle East more broadly.'' Last week, the taoiseach said there should be "greater clarity" about what would lead to a border poll being called. Martin said that in his view it's "not satisfactory" that the decision to call a referendum is left simply as a "judgement call" for the Northern Ireland secretary. During his first visit to Northern Ireland last month, Burnham said a border poll was "off the table" and that votes on Brexit and Scottish independence showed the "risks that come from those situations take a long time to heal". Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant later said he and the prime minister "stand full square" behind all of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, including its provisions for a border poll. "I welcome his [Burnham's] comments in terms of accepting... and he clarified very clear that he accepts the principle of consent, he said that within the Good Friday Agreement a referendum is allowed for," Martin told BBC Radio Ulster's Borderland podcast last week. "Obviously the circumstances around that, as to the triggering of that was deliberately left somewhat ambiguous at the time. "I think there needs to be discussion on that, no question, as part of a wider discussion between all of us, because we are all co-guarantors of the agreement and in addition to that I welcome what he said on legacy as he did commit to legacy and I agree with him on the need for reform of the institutions." The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a political deal designed to bring an end to 30 years of violent conflict in Northern Ireland, known as the Troubles. It was signed on 10 April 1998 and approved by public votes in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. It set up a new government for Northern Ireland, representing both nationalists and unionists. The agreement says that Northern Ireland is part of the UK and this can change only through a referendum. The secretary of state must hold a border poll if it appears likely that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish unification. There is no detail in the agreement on how the secretary of state should judge whether there is majority support - but they can decide to hold a border poll at any time, provided that there has not been another in the last seven years. There is also debate as to what form a border poll should take, for example whether the poll should be held on the general principle of unification or after specific proposals have been set out for how a united Ireland would be governed. title: Learner drivers turn to YouTube and TikTok to cut costs - but instructors warn of risks
description: One learner says social media clips saved her money, but there was also misinformation online.
body: Megan is one of many people who used social media to help her learn to drive Learner drivers say they are turning to online tutorials to help with the cost of obtaining a driving licence. Driving lessons in the UK are now about £35 to £50, according to the RAC, with the average learner needing 45 hours of lessons and a further 22 hours of practice. Megan Kielthy, who passed her driving test in August, said social media videos "definitely" saved her money, but she also had seen AI-generated images and misinformation that she had warned could confuse learners. The Driving Instructors Association (DIA) said while digital education could be "excellent" it should go "hand in hand" with practical lessons, and that road safety was a matter of "life and death". This video can not be played BBC journalist Lola Mayor explains why some learner drivers are turning to social media Megan, 18, opted for a trainee instructor to save money but said learning to drive had still cost her more than £1,000. She earns £10 an hour babysitting, which she said had gone towards her £30 lessons alongside help from her parents. "I don't think that I would have been able to do it without the financial support from my parents," she said. "I found that having access to YouTube allowed me to cut costs. "I would learn all the content with my instructor but then I was able to revisit content and then if there was something in a YouTube video that I didn't know, that I didn't fully understand, I was able to go back to my instructor and ask him." She added: "I had part of high school online because of Covid so I already knew how to use recorded content for learning so it felt very natural for me." Megan warned that not all of the content she had seen online had been helpful. "I stumbled across an AI image of a roundabout showing which lane to be in for the exit and it just made no sense. I showed it to my driving instructor and he agreed it was ridiculous. "If people solely relied on online content it could lead to people going on their test unprepared or misinformed of what they're going to experience on their test and driving after." Betsi says young people are already facing financial barriers and learning to drive is a big commitment The total cost of learning to drive is about £2,460, according to the DIA, a rise of more than £570 since 2020, external. Learners also need to pay for a theory test at £23, a practical test at £65 and temporary driving insurance in personal cars which can cost £40-£50 a month. Betsi Seward, 18, is currently learning to drive alongside studying at college and working part-time. "I am lucky I have a part-time job and can afford to fund it myself but if I didn't, it would be so difficult," she said. "Over the last couple of months my whole TikTok and Instagram is just people learning to drive. It's like my algorithm knows, it's quite scary," she said. "I find them helpful. I was practicing how to do an emergency stop and I was watching videos on how to do that and it really helped to see like where to put my foot on the clutch and stuff like that." But Betsi said not all the content she had seen was helpful. "When you post people making mistakes, that is what is going to get the attention and interaction," she said. She said there were also "random accounts of people using AI to generate mock tests like the routes... and it's obviously not real. "But then if you're just learning to drive and you haven't had a few lessons, you wouldn't know that and it's quite scary actually, because if you take that information into the car with you and it's wrong, then it's quite dangerous actually and quite scary." Savannah passed her test earlier this year Savannah Jones, 20, from Cardiff, who works in childcare, passed her driving test in June. Her dad paid for her lessons, which totalled about £2,000. "I'm very grateful. He was very chuffed when I passed first time," she said. "I was watching a few YouTube videos. I saw a lot of TikToks. It was very much most of my algorithm was learning to drive, tips and tricks. "I think it could help someone cut the cost but not for me personally. I would watch to understand it a bit more and apply that when learning." John Reynolds says students are looking for more affordable ways to learn to drive John Reynolds has been a driving instructor for 13 years and started making his own social media videos last year. These include clips showing test routes, common mistakes and videos of manoeuvres. "I started making short videos for learner drivers to actually learn something outside of driving lessons and to learn things which they need to know for the driving test," he said. "I also do long videos on YouTube so people who can't afford driving lessons have got the opportunity to find out the correct way to do things for the test. "So by doing these extra lessons online, it can help bring down those costs." He said while his videos could be a useful tool, they did not mean learners should opt out of formal lessons. "I know straight away [if] they have been watching another video," he said. "I found that there was a lot of things on there where instructors would say 'this is how you do it, this is how you shouldn't do it' and being very specific to the car they're actually teaching. "So what I try to do with mine is make it more universal so it doesn't matter what car you're driving." He warned that people should use online material responsibly. "It needs to be used responsibly and it's looking for those snippets of information to actually improve your driving. You need the practical skills to make those actual decisions. "When you then try that road, it's a totally different scenario." Carly Brookfield from the DIA said she understood gaining new skills online but said there were risks. title: Sinn Féin calls on Taoiseach to meet residents over Drumcree dispute
description: The route the Order hopes to take includes the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.
body: The Orange Order Drumcree march is turned away from going down the Garvaghy Road every year Sinn Féin MLA John O'Dowd has asked the Taoiseach Micheál Martin to visit the Garvaghy Road and speak to residents about the Drumcree dispute. O'Dowd said he was concerned there had been no visible engagement from the Irish Government on the issue. The earliest date for a decision by the Parades Commission on the planned Drumcree march by Portadown Orange Order is 23 September – four days before the scheduled parade. The route the Order hopes to take - including the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road - has been published on Parades Commission website, external. The taoiseach's office has been contacted for a response. On Thursday Portadown Orange District said on social media that the Parades Commission have appointed a surprise mediation facilitator. Portadown District said it had confirmed their readiness to commence the mediation process as a matter of urgency without any preconditions. The Parades Commission has been contacted for comment. On Thursday evening Garvaghy Road residents met to discuss the Orange Order's application to parade down the road. Speaking after the meeting, O'Dowd said "the reality is there is no requirement for an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road". "There is no support for an Orange Order march through this community on a return parade," he said. O'Dowd called Westminster, and particularly the Irish government, to "listen to this community". "There is a responsibility on the Irish government to stand up for the rights of these citizens." The Sinn Féin MLA added that many in the unionist community are "aghast" at the Orange Order's proposal. Breandán Mac Cionnaith said the people of the Garvaghy Road have been scarred by events of the past Breandán Mac Cionnaith, a spokesperson for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, said they had rejected the Parades Commission mediator on the basis they were not neutral. "The organisation appointed had actually been employed to do mediation work on behalf of the Orange Order," he said. Mac Cionnaith added that signatures are being collected from households from around the area in support of preventing the parade. He said the signatures will be provided to the Parades Commission as evidence that the "vast majority of people" want the march re-routed. "The commission, and those above them in government, must take good notice of this." title: England crush Sri Lanka to seal T20 series win
description: England comfortably chase a below-par target of 146 to thrash Sri Lanka by six wickets and seal the three-match T20 series with a game to spare.
body: Sri Lanka scored just 12 runs from the final four overs of their innings Sri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32 England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25 England won by six wickets; lead series 2-0 England's impressive T20 form continued as they thrashed Sri Lanka by six wickets in Cardiff to seal the series with a match to spare. Tom Banton's unbeaten 52 ensured England made light work of chasing a below-par 146, reaching the target in just 12.1 overs. Jos Buttler and Aneurin Donald raced to an opening stand of 51 in 4.3 overs before they both fell in the space of four balls for 30 and 21 respectively, but England's middle order followed suit in their aggression. Captain Harry Brook needed to score 49 to break Tilak Varma's record of 336 T20 international runs without being dismissed, and he looked on course, whacking three sixes in his 23 off just eight balls, before he was brilliantly caught by a diving Eshan Malinga. Banton then took on the charge, clubbing four sixes in his 24-ball knock as England remain unbeaten in the shortest format this summer. Brendon McCullum's side have now won 22 of their past 25 completed T20s since the start of last summer - a win percentage of 88%, with India (73%) the next best among full-member nations. England's fluency juxtaposed Sri Lanka's innings as the tourist batters struggled again, limping to 145-9 after being bowled out for just 135 in the opener on Tuesday. There will be added frustration from this innings, though, as their openers started so brightly by reaching 55-0 from the first five overs. But Liam Dawson took two wickets in the final over of the powerplay to halt their momentum and the middle order failed to recover, losing 9-90 thereafter and adding just 12 from a dire final four overs. Dawson finished with 3-32 and Jamie Overton 2-23, while Sonny Baker impressed again with his pace and control in a miserly spell of 1-15, including a wicket maiden in the 19th over. The series concludes at Old Trafford on Saturday and is followed by three one-day internationals. Though it is proving to be a mismatched series so far, England are building a well-balanced line-up under Brook's leadership and have barely broken sweat in notching a 2-0 lead. Sri Lanka's explosive start, led by Pathum Nissanka, who top-scored with 37, was the only time England have been on the back foot, but it was the ever-reliable Dawson who dragged it back, having become a mainstay in Brook's T20 line-up. The two soft dismissals highlighted Sri Lanka's woes - Lahiru Udara was caught at mid-on and Kamil Mishara chipped one straight back to the slow left-arm spinner. What followed was a series of soft dismissals, most caught trying to find the boundary, as Overton and Baker hammered away at a good length before Archer, who had started expensively, claimed two wickets at the death to revive his own figures. Sri Lanka managed just two sixes in their innings compared to England's 10, with it being only the seventh time their top five have all hit at least one in T20 internationals. Newcomer Donald started the carnage, ramping Dushmantha Chameera's first ball over the ropes, before Buttler joined the party and Brook then launched three of his own into the stands. England's intent was clear from the fact Donald's strike-rate of 161.54 was the lowest of the top five. Spinner Wanindu Hasaranga took most of the damage as he conceded 42 off just three overs, with a couple disappearing out of the ground. Banton, one of few batters to miss out in England's 254-4 on Tuesday, made the most of his opportunity to produce a fine finish by sweeping and striking firmly down the ground. England have set themselves up nicely to finish unbeaten in T20s this summer after thrashing India 4-0 earlier in the year. title: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York as war passes half-year mark
description: The BBC understands Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are among the delegates allowed to enter the US.
body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian (L) shakes hands with the UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres at last year's assembly The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month. The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products. The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries. "Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year." Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars. The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday. Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron. Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran. Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA. The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row. title: Archbishop of Canterbury withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
description: The award was handed out last week, on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
body: Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, left, is pictured accepting his award from Dame Sarah Mullally The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden. Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007. Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context". In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance". His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him. He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie. But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people. Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden. In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy. But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s. They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too. Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands. But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs". The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities". title: White House withdraws Trump's ICE nominee as Republican senator objects
description: One senator from Trump's party blocked the bid as he demands information about the fatal killings of US citizens by immigration enforcement.
body: The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump's nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after a Republican senator joined Democrats in opposing his confirmation. Richard Schroyer was serving as a senior aide to the secretary of Homeland Security when Trump picked him to lead the immigration enforcement agency in June. The White House withdrew his nomination on Thursday in a short memo, which did not explain the decision. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Republican Sen Rand Paul had stalled the nomination as he pressed for more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis in January. Schroyer had worked with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol for 29 years, and also served in the US Marines. He is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department oversees ICE and other immigration and border agencies. His selection by Trump was seen as a surprise given his lack of experience overseeing such a large law enforcement agency. The position is one of many that needs to be confirmed by the US Senate. Schroyer's nomination did not manage to make it to a full Senate vote and had stalled in the Senate's Homeland Security committee. ICE has not been led by Senate-confirmed leader since 2017 and instead has had a host of temporary chiefs. It is currently led by David Venturella, a former private prison executive, after Todd Lyon announced his departure from the top job in April. The withdrawal on Thursday marks a defeat for Trump and Mullin, as the White House continues Trump's campaign pledge to lead the largest deportation effort in US history. Paul, who serves as chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings. National protests took place earlier this year following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Both US citizens, the two were protesting when they were fatally shot in separate confrontations with ICE agents in January. title: Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
description: People the BBC spoke to are excited by the prospect of working and studying in the EU, a suggestion Carney made this week.
body: This video can not be played Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with Europe Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc. "I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto. Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy. "We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said. Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture". But before Canadians start packing their bags, "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement. Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread. Miriam Levin-Gold is excited about potentially greater opportunities for young Canadians to be able to explore the EU Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits. "It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said. Canadian social media has lit up with the topic. One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France. "Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter. The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US. Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool. "I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower. But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation. "I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said. David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US. "It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe." For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music. "I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added. "However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals." These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city. Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons. Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations. Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021. A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America. However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce. A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards. "It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday. Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations. Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble. "I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil. Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems." But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil. "I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid." title: Royal row intensifies after fresh claims in Diana's brother book
description: Diana’s brother has published fresh claims about King Charles saying he was "giddily elated" in a phone call after the death of the Princess of Wales.
body: This video can not be played Fresh claims have emerged in the upcoming book from Diana's brother, Earl Spencer, as he described the then-Prince Charles "giddily elated" in a phone call after the death of the Princess of Wales. In an extract published on Thursday in the Daily Mail, Spencer claimed Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" during the call. "I suspect the Prince's first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not," he wrote. This comes after Earl Spencer claimed the then-Prince Charles said, referring to Diana, "we'll forget her soon enough" days after she died. To this statement, Buckingham Palace put out a strong rebuttal saying: "His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week. BBC News has not seen the book in full. Royal row intensifies after fresh claims in Diana's brother book. title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
description: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.
body: Queensland's Fitzroy River, home to saltwater crocodiles, has been approved as an Olympics rowing venue for 2032 The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention. Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton. "We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC. But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes. While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans. And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern. "Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition. Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue. "Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said. "I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on." The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane. But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language. "Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting. "It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right." Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks. But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing. Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion". The Fitzroy River passes through the Queensland city of Rockhampton Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability. On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games. "Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said. There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide. The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered." In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics. The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle. But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors. The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week. Queensland premier David Crisafulli said "interstate and overseas elites" had pushed against the Rockhampton venue So what about the crocodiles? They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment. The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times. "The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says. "Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free." Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile". Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
description: An 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by England's former national cancer director.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform adult social care in England Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England. An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care. In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century". In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report, external. She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on." The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long". She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives." The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year. McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise". Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England. In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment. Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target for dementia patients was achievable. He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding. "All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said. The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey. In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target". Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care. She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now." Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer. About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040. Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease. Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make". In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England. Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.
