title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
description: Rhys Woods pays tribute to his three-year-old son and offers "deepest gratitude" to local people.
body: Noah Woods was playing at a playground with a relative before he went missing The father of Noah Woods has said the three-year-old "will be loved forever" and no words can describe the pain of the family's loss. Noah disappeared from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday after becoming separated from a relative. At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond. Earlier, police said his body had been formally identified. "Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much," said father Rhys Woods. "This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him. That's what we kept telling ourselves the whole time." Tributes are being placed next to the playground in Brantham where Noah was playing before he disappeared People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border. Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation. "You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound." He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it". "The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives." He finished the post by addressing his son. "It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us." Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner. Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches". "It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond. "I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time." title: Zelensky appoints new chief prosecutor after predecessor's corruption scandal
description: Former chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko after searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has appointed a new acting prosecutor general, after the predecessor resigned over an anti-corruption investigation. Anton Kovalskyi, 42, was appointed on Thursday to replace Ruslan Kravchenko, who stood down last week after searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials related to illegal call centres in the country. Officials said they identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office, a claim he rejected. The investigation into Kravchenko's office is the latest corruption scandal impacting Kyiv during the war against Russia. Accusations have been levelled at several members of Zelensky's inner circle. According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets". The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu. Kravchenko released a statement denying any involvement and dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated". He resigned a day later before leaving Ukraine. He also alleged documents were stolen during the search of his office with the aim of covering up criminal investigations against anti-corruption officials themselves. Separately, he accused Nabu chief Semen Kryvonos of forging documents in a case nearly 20 years ago. Both Nabu and Sap denied Kravchenko's claims, while Kryvonos dismissed them as "nonsense" and criticised "fierce" attempts to disrupt corruption probes. The two anti-corruption agencies claimed it was the latest in an "unprecedented" campaign aimed at disrupting high-profile investigations they were conducting. Nabu's Kryvonos also claimed that anti-corruption detectives, their offices and vehicles were under surveillance, without giving specific accusations. He added: "It all looks like an attempt to obstruct the work of Nabu and Sap by gaining access to sensitive information regarding planned investigations." Nabu and Sap are currently investigating a number of top Ukrainian officials including Zelensky's former chief of staff Andriy Yermak, former ministers and other influential people. Yermak's lawyer has described the allegations against the former official as "baseless". In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Zelensky later reinstated their freedom but questions have remained over his commitment to anti-corruption reform. title: Tower block arsonist jailed for setting woman alight
description: Reece Brivitt is jailed after dousing the woman in petrol and vodka before setting her alight.
body: Reece Brivitt set fire to the woman "in a cruel attack" which left her with "life-changing injuries", police said A man who set a woman on fire inside a flat, after dousing her in petrol and vodka, has been jailed for 11 years and nine months. Reece Brivitt, 33, set the victim alight inside a tower block flat on Milton Grove, Stafford, on 22 October. The victim suffered serious burns to her chest and legs, leaving her with life-changing injuries, the court heard. Brivitt admitted charges of arson with intent to endanger life as well as wounding with intent and was sentenced at Stafford Crown Court on Wednesday. Brivitt was also served with an indefinite restraining order against the victim. Det Con Jessica Scott, of Staffordshire Police, said the arsonist had "subjected his victim to a cruel attack, which has left her with life-changing injuries". "The incident not only threatened the life of the victim, but of all those who were in the flats at the time," she added. The swift actions of firefighters meant the fire was extinguished quickly, preventing further injuries, she explained. Delivery group manager Mark Walchester, from Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Crews worked quickly to minimise the risk posed to those in the flat block during this incident and to ensure the fire was extinguished as quickly as possible. "Fires in flat blocks and houses of multiple occupancy have the potential to devastate lives." title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
description: The comments were made at a summit in Scotland with participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
body: King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands. He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society. Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic. It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check. "Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives. He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways". "The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group. The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI. Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending. Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta. It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn. Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough. The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind". He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone". "Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added. Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development. He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution". The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added. But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them. "The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates. Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry. The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact. In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face. After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity. He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity. In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance. The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe. Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control. Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves. Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight. Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax". title: GTA 6 soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate
description: Fred Again, PinkPantheress and Travis Scott provide new music for the blockbuster - but not all fans are happy.
body: Music is a key feature of Grand Theft Auto games The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc. Developer Rockstar Games announced a 34-track compilation, set to release on CD and vinyl on the same day as the highly anticipated video game. The company says it will include original music from a "genre-defying roster of the most exciting artists in the world" including rapper Travis Scott, country singer Morgan Wallen and UK singer PinkPantheress. But some fans have pointed out the "irony" of putting out a physical edition of the album following its controversial decision for a digital-only release of the game. The first six tracks, published at the time of the announcement, also include rapper Yung Lean, British DJ Fred Again and Rolling Stone Keith Richards. GTA games feature multiple radio stations, usually themed around a particular musical genre, which players can switch between while driving. In the past the game's soundtracks have largely been made up of licensed music from established artists, although original songs have also featured. Rockstar has said the upcoming game will feature a "dynamic score" and "evolution of in-game radio". In-game radio provides the soundtrack to GTA games Being included in a Grand Theft Auto game can bring a new generation of fans to an artist's music. Spotify streams of Tom Petty's Love is a Long Road, the track used in GTA 6's first trailer, increased by 36,979% after the clip was published. Hot Together, by the Pointer Sisters, also saw a huge jump when it soundtracked the game's second trailer. And a collection of tracks used in the recent Extended Look attracted new listeners in the week after it premiered on Netflix. According to music and gaming publication MusicEXP, external, pop duo Captain & Tennille's 1980 track But I Think It's a Dream saw the biggest spike, jumping from 70 Spotify streams in one week to 80,744. Cliff Richard's Devil Woman was streamed more than one million times, while Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls jumped from 49K to 187K additional weekly streams. It also noted increases in activity on music detection app Shazam around tracks featured in the 26-minute broadcast. Some artists have refused to let Rockstar use their music in GTA games. Martyn Ware, from synth pop band Heaven 17, called the developer out on social media, accusing them of offering a "pitiful" deal to use 1983 hit Temptation. Grand Theft Audio? The tricky business of music and gaming What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview GTA 6 is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment releases of all time when it comes out on 19 November. The previous game in the series, GTA 5, broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since. Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" reportedly topped the streamer's charts, despite a string of leaks in the lead-up to its release. The company is currently involved in an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union. It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here. title: FA chair demands Infantino release World Cup sell-off documents
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup.
body: Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016 Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup in a letter sent by Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt. Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup. Infantino should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October. The letter, also sent to Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, makes accusations of failures in governance and a breakdown in culture within the world football governing body. Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company. The proposal was scrapped following widespread opposition from national associations. Hewitt's letter adds that there should be an independent review of how FFE was conceived, by whom, and how the private investment was put to tender. Last month, Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at three US courts over the FFE plan, demanded the release of all documents. Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation. Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. The Football Association was troubled by the Balogun situation from the outset, and had requested the release of the documents relating to his overturned ban during the World Cup. Forward Balogun, 25, was allowed to play against Belgium in the last 16 when he would have expected to be serving a one-match suspension. The striker had been shown a straight red card for a foul on defender Tarik Muharemovic in the 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last 32. Fifa then said the automatic one-match ban would be suspended for a year. No reasoning behind the move was provided, beyond citing a rule which allows punishments to be suspended. The FA, which had sent a letter of support for Infantino's re-election before the Balogun incident, had deep concerns about political intervention. US President Donald Trump later confirmed he called Infantino asking for Balogun's ban to be reviewed. Then the FFE proposal, revealed through the media just days after the World Cup final, fractured the game. Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation last month. Many national associations, including those of England, Wales and Scotland, have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino's re-election. But Infantino still holds a great deal of support around the globe, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania reiterating their backing. After FFE was cancelled, Infantino called a meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Morocco. But as yet there has been no contact with the Fifa Council to explain the controversial plan. That is set to change next month when Infantino must face Hewitt and the other 35 Fifa Council members. title: 'Trailblazing' moment as modular bridge takes shape
description: The "first-of-its-kind" bridge is being pieced together as work continues to improve a key city artery.
body: The bridge is a "first-of-its-kind" due to its modular construction process The pieces of a "first-of-its-kind" modular bridge are being connected up as work continues to improve a key city artery. The new bridge is part of a redesign of the A11/A47 Thickthorn junction, near Norwich, with the sections built elsewhere and transported to the site. This includes six 100-tonne beams measuring 38 metres long, which were built in Ireland and transferred across the Irish Sea to Liverpool, then across the country via road to Norfolk. National Highways senior project manager Syed Abbas described the build as a "trailblazing" moment for his team, but drivers would face road closures during its installation. "This is a first-of-its-kind, I'm proud to say, for all of the strategic National Highways network," he added. Syed Abbas, senior project manager for National Highways, called the bridge installation a "trailblazing" moment The sections of the bridge, connecting Cantley Lane South with Norwich Road in Hethersett, are being connected up with the help of engineering firm Skansa. A specialist crane, capable of lifting up to 750 tonnes, will begin to move the beams into place on top of the abutments on Friday and road closures will be required from 20:00 BST through to 06:00 on Monday. Parts of the bridge have been built in Ireland before being transported to Norfolk The modular bridge, from start to finish, will be built in four months The A11 is a key route in and out of Norwich New underpasses will be built as part of the project Dan Hutchings, project director for Skansa, said: "The construction of the bridge, from start to finish, is about four months, which is significantly quicker than a traditional build on site." Ongoing maintenance costs are also reduced as it does not have bearings, he said. Human remains found under former shopping centre Hopes new £9.9m unit will cut A&E waiting times First look at homes plan for former mustard factory Work continues on other aspects of the £200m project, which will also include a new footbridge across the A11, widened slip roads, new link roads, underpasses and more. Abbas said the scheme was on track to be finished on target by Spring 2028, with the eventual aim of reducing congestion and removing 12,000 vehicles from the Thickthorn roundabout every day. title: Barclays workers ask for more money to return to the office
description: Unite union, which represents 36,000 Barclays staff, calls for a one-off payment to offset increased travel and childcare costs.
body: Thousands of Barclays staff are demanding concessions from the bank, including a one-off payment, after it said it wants employees to work from the office more often. Staff who have been expected to work in the office for two days per week should be in the office for at least three days a week from next month, according to the company. Unite, which represents about 36,000 Barclays staff, is calling for the bank to reverse its decision. The union is also pressing for exemptions to offset increased travel and childcare costs. Barclays said many employees already work in the office for three or more days, depending on business need. The bank sent a memo to staff in July outlining its expectations, which include that senior leaders work at least four days per week in the office. As first reported in the Financial Times, external, the bank is facing a growing backlash against the proposed rules change. Unite national officer Rick Coyle said thousands of employees have signed an open letter calling for Barclays to reverse the decision, and the number of signatories "continues to rise". He added that Barclays is "trying to fix a problem that doesn't exist" in making its working-from-home rules less flexible. The open letter, external says workers are delivering "strong financial results and improved customer services" with its current working from home policy. It adds that thousands of workers have made suggestions, which the union has condensed into a series of demands. an exemption for commutes longer than 40 minutes or 35 miles exemptions during Christmas, summer, and school holidays a maximum one day in the office for carers flexibility for wrap-around childcare, and childcare vouchers and onsite creches to be explored a one-off payment to offset costs Barclays said in a statement that it recognised "the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations". "Our minimum time in office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business," a spokesperson said. The bank declined to say how many staff would be affected by the rules change. However, the BBC understands that there are different rules depending on teams, with, for example, investment bankers in the office for five days per week. The coronavirus pandemic forced many businesses to allow working from home, depending on the nature of the business. Since then, many organisations have been clawing workers back into the office, despite evidence that hybrid working may be the best fit. Amazon, Boots and JP Morgan are some of the organisations that brought in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day after the pandemic. This week, Ewan Venters, the executive chair of fashion brand Paul Smith, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that working from home "just doesn't work" for young people and urged the government to stay out of decisions over where employees work. In June, digital bank Revolut said it was shifting away from its "remote-first" policy for new recruits in 2027, but for other employees that policy wouldn't change. Have you been asked to work in the office more regularly? Tell us about your experience. Working from home 'not proper work' - ex-Asda boss Amazon says workers must be in the office. The UK government disagrees. Who is right? title: Crocodile attack suspect has bail extended
description: The 30-year-old arrested on suspicion of attempted murder must return bail in three months' time.
body: The young boy from Cambridgeshire was visiting the zoo (picture from 2025) with family A man who was arrested after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure is still on bail. The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June, when he ended up in the enclosure and was attacked by at least one of the reptiles. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested at the time on suspicion of attempted murder and was bailed until 18 September after being assessed as not "fit for interview". A police spokesperson confirmed the individual, who was not known to the child, had been rebailed until 17 December. The BBC understands the arrested man has learning disabilities and was on a trip with carers. The parents of the boy said their child received injuries to his arms, neck, head, face and suffered broken bones and underwent seven surgeries. In the latest update on a fundraising page set up by the family, his parents said he had returned home and faced lengthy rehabilitation. The Care Quality Commission launched an investigation in July into the care that the man - later arrested - had been receiving. Norfolk County Council – which did not provide any care for the man – has also launched an inquiry under the Care Act 2014. Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. title: Tributes paid to 'deeply caring' dad killed in Swiss Alps plane crash
description: Owain Davies’ family said they had “suffered an unimaginable loss”, describing him as “driven and determined”.
body: Owain Davies was one of the two Britons killed in the plane crash A prominent Welsh businessman has been named as one of three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps. Owain Davies, 55, from west Wales, was managing director of engineering firm Amcanu, based in Burry Port, Carmarthenshire. His son Aron Davies said the family had "suffered an unimaginable loss", describing his father as "driven, determined and someone who simply didn't accept that a problem was too big to solve". Davies was killed when the Cirrus SR22T crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday. Formal identification of the other two victims is under way, including another Briton who is yet to be named. Police released a picture from the crash scene, where witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke Authorities said the plane took off from Sion airport in the Rhône Valley and, for unknown reasons, crashed into a mountain slope about 10 minutes later. Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters. Amcanu announced his death with "profound sadness", describing Davies as "strong-willed, spirited, determined and deeply caring". The statement also said family was "at the centre of Owain's life". "He was devoted to his wife Michelle, immensely proud of his children Aron and Ffion, and adored being a grandfather to Oakley and Albie, " it said. His son Aron described him as "a real character", and said he was "immensely proud of everything he achieved". "He was my mentor throughout my life, personally and in business, and I know many people at Amcanu will feel that they have lost a mentor too," he said. The firm was founded by his father, Spencer Davies OBE, in Burry Port in 1975, and he took over the leadership of the business in 2000. Amcanu noted Davies was "a proud Welshman and Welsh speaker" and had been a trustee of Wales Air Ambulance Charity since 2017. The charity's chair of trustees Dr Kyle Jacques said Davies had made a "significant contribution to the Wales Air Ambulance and the vital service we provide". "Owain was a valued colleague and friend, whose loyalty and generosity of spirit meant so much to us. He will be greatly missed," he added. Earlier in his life, Davies served for nearly 25 years as a helmsman with Burry Port Lifeboat, the firm said. The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation and the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched an inquiry. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland". It said officials were in contact with the local authorities. "Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it said. title: Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen
description: BBC Verify tracks down the location of a Houthi video showing the wreckage of an F-15 they claim to have shot down.
body: This video can not be played BBC Verify has confirmed the footage was filmed in western Yemen. Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen. The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday. Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia. Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib. The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces. This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait. In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number. The fate of of the crew is not known. The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile. BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment. Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran. "They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said. Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains. "An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added. BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib. Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site. The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors. A similar Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 Strike Eagle formed part of an escort for US President Donald Trump during a visit to Saudi Arabia last year The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia. This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters. The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan. Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting. The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours. title: Rayner to rule on landmark green belt appeal
description: Campaigners say their Albrighton appeal could shape future green belt decisions.
body: The appeal centres on land off Patshull Road near Albrighton The fate of a controversial plan for 800 homes on green belt land near a Shropshire village will be decided by Housing Secretary Angela Rayner in a case campaigners say could test Labour's planning reforms. A 12-day appeal is underway into whether Boningale Homes should be allowed to build the estate south of Albrighton after Shropshire Council rejected the application. Instead of being determined by the planning inspector overseeing the appeal, the government told the council on Wednesday that Rayner would make the final decision. A letter sent on her behalf said the appeal raised "important or novel issues" and involved "significant development in the green belt". The case centres on land off Patshull Road, which Boningale Homes argues should be considered "grey belt" rather than green belt. Under planning reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's Labour government, some lower-quality or underused green belt sites could be released for development to help boost housebuilding. The government is aiming to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, although ministers have acknowledged the target will be difficult to achieve. Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Rayner said there was only a "slim chance" of meeting it by 2029. Campaigners say the appeal could become a key test of green belt planning policy Campaigners opposed to the development said they had long argued the appeal was of national importance because of what it could mean for future green belt decisions elsewhere in England. The Albrighton Development Action Group (ADAG) described it as "the biggest test case of its type to date". "If we are successful, then we will give confidence to hundreds of places across the country that their vital open spaces and productive farmland can be protected for their children now and for the generations to come," a spokesperson said. The group said it remained confident that both the planning inspector and Rayner would dismiss the appeal. It argued the site remained "productive farmland and core green belt" and should continue to be protected from development. Conservative MP Mark Pritchard has criticised the government's decision to determine the appeal The area's Conservative MP, Mark Pritchard, criticised the government's intervention, describing it as "chillingly egregious". "It is in many ways ideologically driven, which is possibly one of the most worrying things of all," he said. "Who knows, she might pleasantly surprise me, but I'm afraid her track record [for building homes] is not boding well for Shropshire." Boningale Homes declined to comment while the appeal hearing is ongoing. title: Reform accuses departing councillors of 'betrayal'
description: Durham councillors Lyndsey Fox, Nicole Brown and Paul Sexton quit Reform to sit as independents.
body: Lyndsey Fox, Paul Sexton and Nicole Brown are now listed as independent councillors Three councillors who have resigned from Reform UK have "conned " voters and "betrayed" those who helped get them elected, the party has said. Lyndsey Fox, Nicole Brown and Paul Sexton have had their party affiliation changed to independent on the Durham County Council website, external, although none has given precise reasons for their shift. It leaves Reform with a small majority, with 51 councillors, on an authority the party emphatically won control of when grabbing 65 seats at last year's election. Council leader Andrew Husband told the BBC the three former members "have let their residents down" but he offered no explanation for their departures. Fox, who represents Bishop Auckland, confirmed her departure from Reform to Cathy Newman on Sky News, external on Tuesday. The councillor said she had reported a "very serious safeguarding issue" to the party on 14 July but "had heard nothing" since. Neither she nor Reform has given details on what the safeguarding issue was. She made further allegations about a "group chat going wild" and said she had been "thinking about resigning for quite a long time". Reform's majority on Durham County Council has now slipped to four Sexton, who was elected as an independent in Chester-le-Street before switching to Reform, confirmed he had resigned from the party but declined to say why. The BBC has also made attempts to contact councillors Brown, who represents Aycliffe South, and Fox but they have yet to respond. The BBC asked Durham Reform a series of questions including what the safeguarding claims were, what reasons the three had given for resigning and what was being done to address the issue of councillors leaving the party. In response, Husband said: "These people have let their residents down. "They have conned them using Reform colours and betrayed the many members who spent their time and money to help get them elected." title: Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections
description: New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.
body: Jurgen Klopp was Liverpool manager from 2015 to 2024 New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of securing an absolute majority in the regional parliament. The anti-immigration party also expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Speaking at a news conference to announce his first squad, Klopp stressed he is not a political "expert" but added: "We had an election where some people may have thought it was OK, while others were saying, 'my God, what is happening here?' "From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us. "I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country." No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, when the ruling Nazi party carried out the Holocaust. "I do not want to entrust national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, who prefers the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he fears can be misunderstood. The former Liverpool boss added: "I can be proud to be German while also being open-minded and diverse, and kind and friendly." Klopp also said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can "foster a sense of community, so that people can truly feel the power of sport". Klopp named 16 uncapped players in a 44-man squad for four upcoming Nations League matches over the space of two weeks. A group of 24 players will be available against the Netherlands in Amsterdam on 24 September and at home to Greece in Augsburg three days later. Most of those players will then return to their clubs while the other 20 players will join the group before Germany face Serbia in Munich on 1 October and Greece in Thessaloniki on 4 October. The first group includes Premier League trio Kai Havertz (Arsenal), Kevin Schade (Brentford) and Anton Stach (Leeds), while Jamal Musiala is selected after twice collapsing during pre-season games for Bayern Munich. Brentford's Vitaly Janelt has received his first call-up as part of the second group, which also includes Florian Wirtz (Liverpool) and Malick Thiaw (Newcastle). Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and defender Antonio Rudiger retired from international duty after Germany's second-round exit against Paraguay at this summer's World Cup. That led to the departure of coach Julian Nagelsmann and the subsequent appointment of Klopp, who had been working as global head of soccer for Red Bull. title: Baby was garroted and hidden under floor - coroner
description: The boy was found beneath floorboards in a 1910 paper with twine around his neck, an inquest hears.
body: Baby Auckland was buried in April, some 116 years after his presumed birth and death A baby found beneath floorboards and wrapped in a 1910 newspaper was probably garroted shortly after birth, a coroner has said. The skeleton of the full-term boy was discovered during the renovation of a building on Bishop Auckland's Fore Bondgate in July 2024. A piece of twine wrapped around his neck raised suspicions for detectives, County Durham and Darlington Coroner Crispin Oliver heard. After concluding it was most likely a homicide, Oliver said it was a "very sad and singular case". The boy, named Baby Auckland by authorities, has been buried in Bishop Auckland Town Cemetery. His date of death was listed as 29 July 2024, the day he was discovered. The inquest in Crook heard the building's owner, Peter Moody, was pulling up floorboards in the second floor living room when he saw an object wrapped in old brown paper. He picked it up believing it to be a ball, but then "took a look and thought this is a baby," he said in a statement. He could see a skull, bones and "the little feet", Moody said, adding he also noticed a piece of "garden twine" wrapped around the baby's neck. Baby Auckland's skeleton was found beneath a floorboard Durham Police immediately launched an investigation, the inquest heard. Det Ch Insp Mel Sutherland said forensic anthropologist Dr Micol Zuppello worked for several days to "painstakingly extract the body", with all but the tip of a toe and some small eye socket bones recovered. Zuppello concluded the child was a full-term baby of between 38 and 40 weeks development and had been placed face down. Sutherland said his aim was to identify the baby, what happened to him and when he was placed under the floorboards. "We had quite a lot to look at with not much to go on," he said. Acid testing of the child's teeth, a technique developed by the universities of Durham and Bristol, coupled with DNA analysis concluded the child was most likely male, the inquest heard. Baby Auckland was wrapped in a 1910 newspaper and had brown twine knotted around his neck Radio carbon dating found the boy dated from any time between 1655 and the start of the nuclear era 300 years later, the coroner heard. Forensic pathologist Dr Louise Mulcahy said due to the limited remains, it was impossible to test if the child had any natural diseases or if he had been poisoned. The skeleton showed no signs of traumatic injury, she said, and the cause of death was deemed to be "unascertained". It was also not possible to determine if the child had been alive or was stillborn, the inquest heard. Mulcahy could not say if the 3ft (1m)-long piece of twine, which had been wrapped three times round the child's neck, knotted and then looped round again, would have been tied tightly or loosely. Baby Auckland was buried in Bishop Auckland Town Cemetery in April Sutherland said investigations continued to try and determine when the baby was placed beneath the floorboards. He said the building was built in about 1890 and the child was wrapped in an edition of The Umpire from Sunday 19 June 1910. The detective said the "most likely scenario" was the baby came from about the date of the paper. Investigators also looked to see if they could find living or deceased relatives through official DNA databases but none came up, the inquest heard. Two sisters came forward to say they believed they might have been related to a servant working at the building at the time, but they were found not to be a DNA match to the boy, the inquest heard. The baby's skeleton was found in Bishop Auckland in 2024 Sutherland said they also considered using genetic genealogy, databases of people who had voluntarily given DNA to trace relatives and family histories, but that was not usually allowed in the UK. "It was assessed we wouldn't get to the identification of Baby Auckland even if we used that technique," Sutherland told the coroner, adding: "We would still be some generations off." Officers also looked into getting a knot expert to examine the twine, but the nearest was in the Netherlands and the cost would be too expensive and the findings unlikely to be of much use, he said. Sutherland told the coroner he was not aware of any religious practices or midwifery techniques from the time which would have involved the tying of string around a child's neck. The detective said the twine was only around the boy's neck and appeared to have been deliberately placed there. "I would ask why you would do that to a child who is already deceased?" he added. Baby Auckland was found in a building on Fore Bondgate Oliver said it was unusual in the 21st Century to find it so difficult to answer all the coroner's key questions, namely who the deceased was, when and where they died and how they came by their death. "This a very sad and singular case," he said, adding the police had "left no stone unturned". The coroner said the "critical piece of evidence" was the twine and it "seemed unlikely" it would have been tied to a baby who was either stillborn or died of natural cases. He said the "most likely explanation" was a "person in a position to care for him while he was most vulnerable... took the decision to end his life by means of strangulation using twine as a garrote". "This was a homicide," the coroner said, with the baby never officially recorded as existing and "disposed of by means of concealment". He also said it most likely happened in or around 1910. "Clearly this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant," Oliver said, but he added it was "heart-warming" to see how people had "stepped up to do the right thing" after he was found. title: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies".
body: This video can not be played Carney: Canada welcomes EU ambition for it to become 'associate member' Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member", calling for closer cooperation on defence, critical minerals and energy security. Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture". His comments came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada's associate membership, a status that does not currently exist. US President Donald Trump earlier called the idea "laughable" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act". This video can not be played Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with Europe Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month. "Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade". "Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said. "Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited." He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc. "I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs. "This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others." Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility." Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president." "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added. Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework". What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member' Speaking at the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said she wanted Canada to become the EU's first associate member, with closer cooperation in areas such as manufacturing, technology, defence, energy critical minerals and economic security. It is unclear exactly what that relationship would look like because the "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement. Any new arrangement would require the agreement of all 27 EU member states, with some governments having previously expressed reservations about creating a new form of membership. The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement, and cooperate in areas including trade, defence and research. In his address, Carney said Canada and Europe could strengthen their "strategic autonomy" through "deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals". He said Canada could supply liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to support European energy security, while benefiting from Europe's expertise in clean-energy technologies. He also proposed pooling technological resources and deepening "people to people ties", including allowing young people to "work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic" through Canada joining the EU's Erasmus+ programme. Carney described the proposed relationship as "a unique, positive approach that we will define together". He added that there would be a debate and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the proposals, but emphasised the two sides were still at the "start of a road". A Canada-EU summit is due to take place in Montreal at the end of October, where Carney said they would "drill down the details". title: RNLI station out-of-service after anti-migrant protests
description: The RNLI says it hopes to have the lifeboat station operational again as soon as possible.
body: The RNLI said it hoped to have the lifeboat station operational again as soon as possible Portsmouth's lifeboat station remains temporarily out of service following anti-migrant protests. Protesters blocked roads in the city on 6 September after about 120 people arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area following a Channel small boat crossing. The RNLI helped bring them ashore. The RNLI also said it helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant demonstrators who went into the sea. Following the protest, the charity's chief executive said staff had faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse. The lifeboat station was taken out of service on 10 September, meanwhile, abuse aimed at volunteers also forced the lifeboat museum in Poole to shut for several days. The RNLI said: "Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets. "We hope to have the lifeboat station back on service as soon as possible." After abuse was directed at its crews tasked to assist the incident, its chief executive issued a statement. Peter Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel. "Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse. "The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe." He added: "Stand by them, not against them and their families. I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work." The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill. The protests led the RNLI to also review its security procedures. As part of this, volunteers were told to consider not wearing RNLI-branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity. title: 'I can get more time': Breast cancer patient finds out she can get life extending drug
description: Patients in England with an incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS.
body: This video can not be played Patients in England with a specific type of incurable breast cancer can now access a life-extending drug on the NHS. Enhertu can give patients almost seven extra months to live on average. Women in Scotland have had access to the drug on the NHS since 2023, and it is available in 26 other European countries. Doctors in England are now able to prescribe it, with Wales expected to follow shortly but the guidance doesn't automatically apply to Northern Ireland. Kate Wills, 51, has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. When she hears it will be available on the NHS, she immediately starts crying. "I really can't believe it. I'm so relieved, I'm overjoyed," she says. "It's so hard keeping hope when you have stage four cancer. This gives me enormous hope." title: Family of 'Putney pusher' suspect blame police pressure for his death
description: The family of Nicholas Brandram said there was no forensic evidence linking him to the incident.
body: Nicholas Brandram was under police investigation over the 2017 incident The family of Nicholas Brandram have insisted he was not the so-called "Putney pusher" and have blamed the Metropolitan Police for his death. The 44-year-old was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017. Brandram's family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation" and there was no forensic evidence linking the banker to the incident. The Met has been asked for comment. In a statement, the family said there was "no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage". "In fact, the evidence proved the opposite." Brandram was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Met confirmed he had been released under investigation. The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The force said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious". title: Ninth woman's body found as South African police investigate string of deaths
description: South Africa police have cautioned against assuming that all the killings are linked but many women are afraid.
body: The latest body was found wrapped in a sheet on the side of the road in Dawn Park Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg. The latest victim was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Dawn Park on Thursday morning, police said. Her identity has not yet been released. The discovery follows the deaths of eight other women whose bodies have been found since July across Ekurhuleni, a major urban area of Johannesburg. Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible. Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings, which he said were "causing fear and uncertainty in our communities". Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo, who disappeared last week after leaving her home for an afternoon run. Her body was found three days later behind a hotel in Kempton Park. Two other victims have since been identified as Itumeleng Kekana, who had been missing since July, and 38-year-old Dineo Evelyn Motapane, whose body was discovered by the roadside in KwaThema on Tuesday. The first of the nine bodies was discovered in Kempton Park on 15 July. A suspect was arrested two days later in connection with that case and remains in custody, but police have not linked that suspect to the other deaths. Further bodies were discovered in August and September, including in Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Clayville and KwaThema. The latest body is of a woman believed to be in her 30s and appeared to have bruises and stab wounds, local media reported. The discovery has sparked fear in the area, particularly among women who say they no longer feel safe. "We are scared to come out of our houses. We are scared to go to the shops. We are no longer free in a country where we are supposed to be safe as women," local resident Bongeka Sebela told the BBC. Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team of detectives, intelligence officers, forensic experts and other specialists to investigate the deaths and establish whether there are links between the cases. They are also pursuing a person of interest, although they have not disclosed which case or cases that person may be connected to. "Let's not get emotional, the gloves are off," said Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday, adding that the authorities had the capacity to deal with the killings. In a statement on Thursday, South African police said the recent rise in serious and violent crimes against women remained a "matter of grave concern", urging women in the country to remain vigilant about their personal safety. They advised women to avoid walking alone or using isolated routes, remain alert to strangers and suspicious vehicles, and share their location or travel plans with someone they trust. They also advised against walking with earphones or earbuds at high volume, warning this could reduce awareness of their surroundings. "Practising personal safety measures can save lives." Authorities have offered a 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) reward for information that could lead to arrests and have appealed to families with missing relatives to help identify the remaining victims. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concern about high levels of violence against women in South Africa. Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has cautioned against speculation, saying investigators were dealing with what appeared, at this stage, to be "quite distinct, separate events". South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women. Last November, the country classified violence against women a national disaster following an online campaign that culminated in countrywide protests. title: Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
description: Left-wing opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson look set to form the next government.
body: Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election. He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people. Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament. Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election. His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority. The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend. In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments. Andersson has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government. But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes. After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days. Sweden's centre-left opposition, led by the Social Democrats' Magdalena Andersson, has defeated the right-wing governing bloc The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals. The SD had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm. But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022. A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week. On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day. title: Eleanor Donaldson to appeal trial of the facts verdict
description: The Northern Ireland Courts Service confirmed that an application for leave to appeal had been lodged to the Court of Appeal.
body: Eleanor Donaldson, pictured in 2024 Eleanor Donaldson has applied to appeal the verdict from her trial of the facts, which found she had done the acts in relation to all five charges she faced. Four of those charges were of aiding and abetting the offending committed by her husband Jeffrey Donaldson. The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children. The Northern Ireland Courts Service confirmed on Thursday that an application for leave to appeal had been lodged to the Court of Appeal by Eleanor Donaldson's legal team. She faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds. It ran alongside her husband's trial at Newry Crown Court in May and June. She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge. The judge from her trial is due to decide on this in October. Jeffrey Donaldson's solicitor has said he is also to appeal against his convictions. title: RTÉ boycotts Eurovision for second year in a row
description: In a statement, RTÉ said it feels Ireland's participation "cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza".
body: In a statement, RTÉ said it feels Ireland's participation "cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza" Irish broadcaster RTÉ will not broadcast or participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. It is the second year in a row that the broadcaster has not participated in the competition. In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the 2026 contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part. In a statement they said: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk." Last year Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands and Slovenia boycotted the Eurovision Song Contest, after it was decided Israel could compete. RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory". Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden. Noam Bettan represented Israel in the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest, finishing in second place The 2027 contest will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the Grand Final being held at the Arena Burgas on 15 May. The semi-finals will take place on 11 and 13 May. Bulgaria earned the right to host the contest after DARA won Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with Bangaranga, the country's first victory in the competition. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS has also said it will not participate in Eurovision 2027. It said the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict. Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. title: Aztec document goes on display in Mexico after 186 years abroad
description: France's national library is lending the manuscript recounting the history of the Aztecs to Mexico.
body: Codex Azcatitlán tells the story of the Aztecs, including their battle to defend Tenochtitlán from the Spanish conquistadors A centuries-old document telling the story of the Aztec civilisation and its fall after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors in pictograms is going on display in Mexico for the first time in 186 years. The manuscript, known as Codex Azcatitlán, has been held in France's Bibliothèque Nationale since 1898, but had already spent decades outside of Mexico before that. It is thought to have been drawn in the 16th Century - a few years after the arrival of the conquistadors in what is now Mexico - and is widely considered one of the most valuable and insightful tellings of the history of the Aztecs. France has lent Codex Azcatitlán to Mexico to mark 200 years of Franco-Mexican relations. The arrival of Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés in what is now Mexico is among the scenes depicted in the Codex Azcatitlán In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there. The pictograms in the Codex Boturini narrate the story of the migration of the Aztecs, also known as Mexica, from their ancestral homeland to the shores of Lake Texcoco, where they built Tenochtitlán. The temporary exchange of the two codices was agreed by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and her French counterpart, Emmanuel Macron, during a visit by the latter to Mexico last year. Mexico has long lobbied for the return of historical artefacts taken from the country in past centuries. According to Mexico's ministry of foreign relations, last year more than 2,000 objects were successfully repatriated. The Codex Azcatitlán will be exhibited at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City from Thursday. title: Six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury retires
description: Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury retires from professional tennis.
body: Salisbury won the doubles titles at the Australian Open and US Open Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury has retired from professional tennis. Salisbury chose this month's US Open as his final event and reached the semi-finals with his long-time partner Rajeev Ram, who had also decided to retire. The venue was fitting, as in 2023 Salisbury and Ram became the first pair in history to win three consecutive US Open men's doubles titles. Salisbury is Britain's most successful men's doubles player of the Open Era. He also won the 2020 Australian Open with Ram, and two mixed doubles titles with Desirae Krawczyk. The 34-year-old says he has been thinking about his future for a while, and is now "very happy with the decision". "Tennis has been my life for as long as I can remember and I have been incredibly fortunate to have had all the opportunities, experiences and success that I have," he posted on Instagram. "To be able to travel the world and call playing tennis my job has been a dream come true and I never believed I could have lived the life and had the career that I have. "I gave it my all and know I can be proud and look back with no regrets." Salisbury took a three month break at the start of this year, having told BBC Sport about the anxiety which had been affecting him on tour. While he did not think it affected his tennis very much, he said it left him with a "feeling of dread" which made life on the road far less enjoyable. Salisbury finishes his career with 17 tour level titles, including the season ending ATP Finals of 2022 and 2023. title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised
description: The Merlin pass, to be also in use at Legoland and Thorpe Park, is to be launched at Alton Towers.
body: The new virtual queuing pass has been welcomed by disability charities, and will be first introduced at Alton Towers A new virtual queuing system for visitors with accessibility needs to be introduced first at Alton Towers has been praised by charities. The upgraded ride access pass (Rap), to be in use later at other Merlin-run parks like Thorpe Park and Legoland Windsor Resort, enables queuing for rides via an app rather than in physical lines. The news follows a backlash in February when proposed changes led to visitors with conditions such as ADHD and autism being told they would not be able to use a physical Rap. There will be no change to the eligibility criteria for the pass, available to those who have problems queuing for long periods because of a physical, emotional or learning need, Merlin says. Staffordshire-based Alton Towers will start accepting the revamped pass at the end of the year, with Merlin's other theme parks taking it on next year. During the row earlier in the year, families of children with additional needs told the BBC the restrictions would mean their children could not visit because of waiting in long queues, or sensory overload felt in crowded environments. Under the plan, visitors to places like Alton Towers, Chessington World of Adventures and Legoland Windsor over half-term who had "difficulty with crowds" would no longer have qualified. Merlin backtracked on the proposal days later following an online petition against it signed by more than 25,000, saying they had listened to the feedback and would pause the changes while considering other options. The changes would apply at parks including Chessington World of Adventures, Thorpe Park and Alton Towers However, disability experts, charities and partners such as Disability Rights UK, Scope, ADHD UK, and the National Autistic Society have welcomed the new virtual system, which they helped to shape. Lisa Myers, of the National Autistic Society, said she was pleased Merlin had consulted with autistic people and their families and that the Rap eligibility criteria would not change. "This is an example of an adaptation that can make a real difference to autistic people, enabling them to access facilities and venues," she said. "We have worked with Merlin for many years so we know how committed the team is to ensuring their facilities are welcoming and inclusive for autistic visitors." John McLachlan, interim chief executive of disability charity Scope, said the new system represented "a positive step in removing unnecessary barriers, to improve the experience of disabled visitors". Currently Merlin-run parks operate a reverse queue system for Rap holders, meaning they must pre-book a slot in advance to skip the queue for a ride, then wait before they can go on another. Under the new system, pass holders will wait for the same amount of time as those in physical queues and be notified on the app when they are near the front, meaning they can pass the time where they are most comfortable. Pass holders will then be helped to join a separate queue using a dedicated entrance. Merlin's chief operating officer, Rob Smith, said the firm had "listened carefully" to feedback from Rap users, charities and partners and believed the new system would "significantly improve visits". "It's clear the current experience does not always provide the flexibility and comfort some guests need," he said. "This new virtual queuing approach has been designed in response to that feedback." He added the firm wanted every guest to enjoy "memorable days out" and would continue to work closely with Rap users and advocacy group as the new system was rolled out.
