title: Shop closures among concerns in ancient capital
description: Declining trade, parking and the cost of living at among concerns in Arbory, Castletown and Malew.
body: Patsy Lockerby said a drop in footfall for businesses in Castletown had led to several closures The increasing number of empty shops, parking provision, and the rising cost of living have been raised as issues facing voters in Arbory, Castletown and Malew. Although stretching out to include the two parishes, at the heart of the southern constituency is the ancient capital of the Isle of Man. Boasting Georgian and Victorian architecture and overlooked by the Medieval fortress Castle Rushen, concerns have been raised over a severe decline in the number shops in Castletown's centre. Tearoom owner Patsy Lockerby said the drop in footfall had left small shops and businesses "suffering". She said: "I'm the only shop open in Malew Street, so that sort of speaks volumes, doesn't it?" "It's affected the town - people don't bother now, they bypass Castletown. You can't rely on the tourists and coaches coming because there's nothing for them." She called for action from the government to help independent businesses in the short term to get up and running in the town centre. "They need to come up with something that they can afford that would be beneficial to people who want to start a new business," she said. Repeated closures of parking in Market Square by the commissioners in previous years was cited by her as a significant reason for shop closures due to dwindling footfall in recent years. Barry James said more strategic thought needed to into sorting the town's parking issues Fellow business owner Barry James agreed that parking in general was one of the biggest issues affecting footfall in the town. "We've had parking problems – we've got an ageing population as well, a lot of retired people, and accessibility is not good," he said, adding it was an issue that also affected the coach passengers visiting. "You can't make a car park that's not there, you can't expect people to walk too far either, but there are professionals who spend their time planning and they understand how communities work," he said. "Rather than small, whimsical changes, you'd think there would be an overall plan for a town and that has to start to with accessibility." A need for steps to address the declining number of shops was echoed by local resident Maggie Richards who said: "You see people arrive by coach and they're bussed in and they're saying 'where's the shops?' "When I first came down here it was thriving, you had different shops and it was lovely, but it's just gone downhill." She added that rents could be playing a part in the decline and it would "have to come from the government to begin with to help more" for shops to return. Scott Findlay said wages not keeping pace with inflation was a concern For Scott Findlay, who runs his own window cleaning firm, the rising cost of living was an increasing issue. "Everything just seems to have gone up, whereas the inflation in the wages doesn't seem to have gone up the same to capture it. "It just becomes a bit harder once things get more expensive, and then if you have a bigger family it just becomes even more expensive because there's more of it." Maureen Sloan said, as a pensioner on a fixed income, her outgoings on the basics including utilities and rent meant she was left with very little else to spend each month. She also lamented the lack of a choice of Manx produce on the shelves of multinational supermarkets. Maureen Sloan said the rising cost of living meant her much of her pension went on utilities and rent The cost of living was also on Lisa Corkill's mind. She described it as "absolutely shocking". The government's stance on taxing some benefits was something she said presented a problem. "Pensioners certainly shouldn't get taxed, they've worked all their lives and they get taxed on their pension," she said, adding: "I work hard, my partner works hard, and then they tax you on child benefit." When it comes to casting a vote, she said she felt there was "no point" because "absolutely nothing will change". Julie Essex and Loraine Sansbury said the need for a replacement high school for the area was an issue for many people But for first time voter in an Isle of Man election, Julie Essex, the Manx system has proven a refreshing change. "I've lived in a Labour town, so our vote never made a difference because the Labour MP had such a big majority - but here our vote will make a difference," she said. "And we've never had two votes before, so we really have to think about who we want to vote for." She and fellow charity shop volunteer Loraine Sansbury both agreed one of the issues of concern to many parents was the ongoing need for a replacement secondary school for the area as the existing Castle Rushen High School was now "very old". title: Metal detectorist finds 3,000-year-old gold bracelet 'worth up to £20k'
description: Having only ever found a silver coin while metal detecting, Idris Thomas was shocked to strike gold.
body: The bracelet was found in a field in Llanuwchllyn and is believed to be about 3,000-years-old Having only ever found a silver coin while metal detecting, Idris Thomas was shocked to strike gold - a late Bronze Age gold bracelet which has been declared treasure. Believed to be about 3,000 years old, the bracelet was found to be 92.8% gold by experts from Museum Wales. Brett Hammond, CEO of Timeline Auctions, estimated its value at between £15,000 and £20,000. An official value has not yet been given. Thomas was scanning on farmland belonging to Geraint Edwards, in Llanuwchllyn, Gwynedd, for about 20 minutes when his detector alerted him. "I thought it was another bit of tin foil to begin with, and I just saw a flash of gold and dug a little bit around it," he said. Geraint Edwards and Idris Thomas are very excited to find out more about the find At a hearing in Caernarfon to establish whether it was treasure, north west Wales deputy coroner Sarah Riley described the finding as "absolutely stunning". Experts said at the hearing the bracelet would have once belonged to a man or woman of high status within their farming community. Edwards previously said he always believed his land had a "quite unique feeling to it". "There's no stamp or anything on it, but I suppose they hadn't started stamping gold at that time." He said he was interested to find out where the gold originated from. The bracelet was being sent away to be analysed and recorded. "Some people never have the chance to find such a thing on their own land," he said, saying it was "a great feeling" and that he had become "quite attached" to the bracelet. Idris Thomas said he was inspired by TV to start metal detecting two years ago Thomas described it as a "once in a lifetime" find. "I'm absolutely shocked, over the moon and it's hard to describe the feeling," he added. Thomas had been scanning with a metal detector for two years, having seen people doing in on television. "I'm sure some people have been at it for 10 years and haven't found anything like this," he said. British Museum and Museum Wales have been contacted for comment. Storiel Museum and Art Gallery have expressed an interest in acquiring the treasure find, following its independent valuation by the Treasure Valuation Committee. title: Traumatised Smith says he was 'thrown to wolves' over 'sandpapergate'
description: Australia batter Steve Smith says he is still traumatised by the aftermath of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 and still gets flashbacks.
body: Steve Smith was confronted by media before leaving South Africa in 2018 Australia batter Steve Smith says he is still traumatised by the aftermath of the 'sandpapergate' ball-tampering scandal in 2018 and still gets flashbacks. The Aussies are set to play their first Test series in South Africa since Smith and two team-mates were sent home before the fourth and final Test of that tour. Cameron Bancroft was caught tampering with the ball by rubbing it with sandpaper during South Africa's second innings of the third Test between the two sides. Following the end of that day's play, Bancroft admitted he attempted to alter the condition of the ball, with Australia captain Smith later admitting to having knowledge of it. Smith was stripped of the captaincy and banned for a year by Cricket Australia, and broke down in tears as he apologised during a news conference at Sydney airport. "I'm not a big fan of cameras, I get anxious around cameras," he said in an interview with News Corp,, external published on Thursday. "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that, in a way." Vice-captain David Warner was also banned for a year while Bancroft was banned for nine months. Australia's then prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said the affair "bitterly disappointed the whole nation" and there was intense media attention on Smith as he left South Africa and on his return to Australia. Smith added: "The 24-48 hours after being told by James Sutherland (then Cricket Australia chief executive) that I was getting banned for a year, going through the airport in Johannesburg getting absolutely mobbed, and then flying back and doing that press conference... I still have little flashbacks here and there of it. "I felt like I was kind of thrown to the wolves through [Johannesburg] airport. I didn't have any support there at all." This video can not be played Steve Smith breaks down as he apologises for his part in 'sandpapergate' The 37-year-old returned to the Australia team in 2019 and re-established himself as one of the best batters in world cricket. After a two-year leadership ban, he was named Australia's Test vice-captain before the 2021-22 Ashes series and has stood in as captain when Pat Cummins has been unavailable. "It was certainly a difficult period, particularly the initial few days after," Smith said. "The mental state I was in was not great. "That's somewhere I'd like not to get to again, but I certainly learned from that and have been able to move forward with my life. "I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened," he added. "I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank." Smith has returned to South Africa for a one-day series in 2020 and has played in front of hostile crowds during multiple Ashes tours to England. "It's something I'm kind of used to," Smith said. "I've copped a lot at times away from home, at different venues across my career, and it's something that I take in my own stride. "I use it as motivation to try and go out and do well, and try and take a positive from it." Australia's three-Test series in South Africa begins in Durban on 9 October. title: Call for £375k elected mayor referendum rejected
description: Politicians vote against a motion to have a residents' poll on abolishing the post of mayor.
body: Tom Wootton was elected as mayor in 2023 An attempt to force a referendum on whether an elected mayor should be abolished has failed. Councillors in Bedford rejected a Labour motion to let residents decide the future of the role. They were told a referendum would cost £375,000 to organise. Opponents of the elected mayor system said the poll could still happen if enough residents signed a petition. Bedford has had an elected mayor since 2002, when residents voted in favour of the move in a referendum. The leader of the Labour group, Abu Sultan, told a meeting of the full council on Wednesday that, after more than 20 years, it was time to give the people a chance to vote again. Sultan added that the motion was "not about settling a political score with any particular person". Carl Meader (Labour, Kempston South) said abolishing the role would save money and the referendum would give people under 40 their first chance to vote on the issue. Others said it was difficult to remove a serving mayor and noted the current incumbent had remained in post, despite a vote of no confidence in his leadership. The vote against the motion had a majority of eight Opponents questioned whether spending £375,000 on a referendum was a valid use of the council's money. The current mayor, Tom Wootton (Conservative, Wyboston), told the meeting he had not seen "Bedford residents marching through the streets demanding a referendum". Christine McHugh (Liberal Democrat, Goldington) said she had originally campaigned against having an elected mayor but "found, to my surprise, that the public seemed to like the system as there was a clearly identifiable, responsible individual, and the buck stopped there". Henry Vann (Liberal Democrat) said the vote was not even close Labour has 12 seats on the council, while the Conservatives have 14 and the Liberal Democrats have 13. The Green Party has four. When it came to the vote, 16 councillors voted for a referendum while 24 opposed it. The Liberal Democrat leader, Henry Vann, said: "The vote in the end wasn't even close at 24 to 16. "So, frankly, we now need to all, as councillors of all parties, actually get down to the job of protecting services and sorting out the financial crisis at Borough Hall." Labour's Zara Layne said it was a shame residents would not have a say Zara Layne (Labour, Harpur) said: "I think it was a shame that residents aren't going to get a chance to have their voice heard on a matter that we believe as a Labour group is really important." If a referendum had been successful and the post of mayor had been abolished, it is likely that the council would have adopted a strong leader model. The full council would have elected a leader who would then select a cabinet. One advantage of that system would be the ability of the full council to remove a leader, something that councils cannot do with an elected mayor. But opponents argue that a strong leader system puts too much power in the hands of one person who residents had no say in appointing. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? title: River home to 500 crocodiles chosen as Olympic rowing venue
description: A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles is given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.
body: Saltwater crocodiles are the largest reptiles on the planet A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles has been given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games. The course on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has passed an independent technical assessment into its suitability. The assessment did not consider the crocodiles but instead looked at "how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the Games". The report was commissioned by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), which noted, external that the Fitzroy River Flatwater Facility "is already a training and competition venue for flatwater sports, supporting school state championships, local regattas, and national team training camps". World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide, formerly International Canoe Federation, both endorsed the course. "Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing," World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said., external Paddle Worldwide President Thomas Konietzko said: "The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes." Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris played down the issue of crocodiles last year. "There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing... it's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here," he said at the time. Speaking on Thursday about the venue having now been given the go-ahead, he said: "The endorsement provides additional certainty as we move into the next phase of venue planning and Games delivery, ensuring all future design and operational work continues to focus solely on Rockhampton." Saltwater crocodiles - known locally as Salties - live in both freshwater and saltwater and can grow to be in excess of six metres long. title: Conservatives urge Burnham to rule out tax rises at Budget
description: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith says UK taxes are forcing young people to "seek their fortune" elsewhere.
body: The Conservatives are urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham to rule out tax rises at next month's Budget. Speaking to the BBC ahead of his first major speech as shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith said young people were "seeking their fortune" elsewhere due to high taxes in the UK. He did not confirm reports the Conservatives could pledge to scrap inheritance tax, saying he would "love" to cut the tax but it would have to be "subject to an ability to set out properly how we would fund that". Labour said: "We won't take any lectures from the Tories on the economy – not least when it was only last week that Griffith was praising the 'lots of good things' in Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget." Chancellor John Healey is due to set out his Budget on 28 October against a backdrop of rising inflation and global energy prices. On Thursday, trade unions will meet the chancellor to push for their proposals, with the Unite union urging the government to reverse the freezing of tax thresholds. Burnham has warned that the Budget would be "challenging" due to the war in the Middle East but insisted he was prepared to take "difficult decisions" on the economy. Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises Griffith - who was appointed as shadow chancellor last month - told the BBC, Labour had raised taxes at its last two Budgets and that the "pips are well and truly squeaking". In addition to ruling out tax rises, he said the government should "pause job-destroying red tape" adding: "Whatever its intentions it is causing a real chill in the vacancy market." The Conservatives pointed to figures from the Federation of Small Businesses estimating that tax compliance costs small businesses £25bn a year and the average small business spends 44 hours a year on tax admin. The party has appointed Lord Mackinlay of Richborough and Robert Colvile, the outgoing director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, to produce a report on reducing regulations for small businesses. Griffith said governments have to "balance the books" and that the Conservatives would change the welfare system, "prune" back the amount spent on foreign aid and cut "some of the central cost of Whitehall" in order to save money. Over the weekend, the Mail on Sunday reported, external that the Conservatives could promise to abolish inheritance tax if they win the next election, with the policy potentially being announced at the party's annual conference in October. Asked if he would be taking such a move, Griffith said there was "work to be done" adding: "We've got to fully find the money." "I'm going to be responsible and only want to make promises I can keep," he said. He added that he had recently been on a fact-finding trip to Sweden, which scrapped inheritance taxes in 2005. Reform UK has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax, but speaking at the party's conference, Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said it would not be a priority. "It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he told a Reform conference fringe event. Asked if getting rid of inheritance tax would amount to a tax cut for the wealthy, Griffith argued that it would boost growth and that the wealthiest people were often able to "arrange their affairs" to avoid the tax. title: Helen Jenner likely to take over as Reform Wales leader, sources tell BBC
description: A source says the party's Welsh deputy leader is the favourite to take over from Dan Thomas, who quit after an arrest.
body: Helen Jenner is Reform's deputy Welsh leader Reform is likely to appoint Helen Jenner to take over from Dan Thomas as the party's Welsh leader, sources have told BBC Wales. A source said she is the favourite to replace Thomas, who quit following an arrest on suspicion of assault, and that "very senior" Reform figures had backed her. Jenner, an MS for Bangor Conwy Môn, is the party's deputy leader in Wales. The party's Senedd group is meeting on Thursday morning to decide if it needs to hold a vote or can appoint someone to the role. Thomas stood down after he was arrested and bailed by police at the weekend on suspicion of assault and controlling coercive behaviour. He says he has done nothing wrong. He has not been suspended and continues to represent Reform in the Senedd as MS for Casnewydd Islwyn. Jenner is yet to speak publicly about her intentions. The party's health spokesperson James Evans claimed on Wednesday he had majority support in the group but decided not to stand after speaking to his family. If there is more than one candidate it is expected there will be a secret ballot of Reform MSs - but no vote of the membership. title: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
description: Flooding has caused widespread disruption across Valencia and Catalonia in north-east Spain.
body: The downpour caused flooding across Valencia and Catalonia North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region. Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline. Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said. The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations". Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents. Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman. Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass. In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport. Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET. "Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X. Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption. In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted. A football match between Levante and Athletic Bilbao was postponed after the pitch became waterlogged and water leaked into the player's tunnel The downpour comes as Spain emerges from its hottest summer on record and an exceptionally warm start to September. Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn. The Mediterranean Sea absorbs heat during summer, increasing evaporation and contributing to heavier rainfall when storms develop. The flooding comes less than two years after devastating flooding in Valencia killed more than 230 people. title: How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
description: No player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals than Donyell Malen since his Roma debut in January - BBC Sport examines his transformation.
body: Donyell Malen has been in prolific form for Roma, scoring more goals than any other player in Europe's top five leagues since his debut for the club on 18 January Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa. Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January. The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards. Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period. He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18). No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal. The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater. In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches. His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome. On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form. The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts. While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence. At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage. The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans. "He has been incredible since January," said Laurens. "He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball." Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy. Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22. His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour. Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike. But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19). Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role. For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic. Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs. For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year. title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
description: Under the plans, only children over 15 would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
body: The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-16s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety. Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms. Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account. The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove their platforms were safe by design, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat". She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world". Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts. Von der Leyen has previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored". The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address to the EU Parliament on Wednesday. Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain. title: 'Everybody was as one': Reverend reflects on search effort for Noah Woods
description: The Reverend Chris Willis says the public reaction has been a "thread of positivity" in the sadness.
body: Noah Woods was playing at a playground with a relative before he went missing The love shown by a community who rallied to search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods was a "thread of positivity" amongst the tragedy, a reverend has said. Noah disappeared from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday after becoming separated from a relative. At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond. Reverend Chris Willis said: "Everybody was as one... what we saw throughout was a real coming together of people and a willingness to work together which, in spite of the deep sadness, was a thread of real positivity seeing how people cared." Reverend Chris Willis said he hoped the positivity and love seen during the search would continue About 100 bunches of flowers have been left at the playground where he was last seen and more than £15,000 has been donated to a fundraiser to support his family. Willis, parish rector of St Michael's Church in Brantham, said he had "never seen anything like" the outpouring of support. "I was moved, overwhelmed and staggered actually that people were coming from far and wide," he said. "It was hundreds, even into the thousands, coming together with one deep, common concern to find a little boy, who longed to find a happy ending for him and his family. "Sadly, very sadly that wasn't to be." People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help find Noah, who was from East Bergholt. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Essex border. Willis said it was "devastating" when news came that a body had been found. "It was a moment of, in one sense, the news that you don't want to hear and obviously, as time went on, it was the news we feared the most," he said. "Then immediately, while we all feel that deeply, we've got to then be thinking of Noah's family for whom it is incomprehensible." People have been leaving flowers, toys and messages at the playground where Noah was last seen Willis said Brantham would pull together, as it had after a previous tragedy. In 2024 Anita Rose was murdered while walking her dog on a footpath in the village. "This is a community that knows tragedy and has had to contend with tragedy in recent years," he said. "All I can say, unequivocally, is this is a community that has been amazingly positive. [It] has dealt with the pain of loss and I have no doubt we'll pull together. "There was a love shown, that was my first impression, and I hope and believe we'll see that continue." Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. title: Real Madrid keen on Man Utd forward Gabriel, 15
description: Real Madrid have a strong interest in signing 15-year-old Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel.
body: JJ Gabriel has told Manchester United he wants to leave Real Madrid are among the clubs trying to sign Manchester United academy player JJ Gabriel. Earlier this week, the 15-year-old sent United formal notice he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect, but the club can challenge the request. It is understood a number of major teams across Europe, including Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Bayern Munich, have a firm interest in the forward, but multiple sources have described Real's efforts to sign him as strong. The Spanish side want to recruit the teenager immediately and position him in Real Madrid Castilla - the club's recognised reserve team. Unlike in England, Castilla play in senior football and are in the regionalised third league of the Spanish system. Last season, they were coached by Alvaro Arbeloa, who then took over the senior Real side following Xabi Alonso's dismissal and has since moved to Fulham. Thiago Pitarch, who was 18 at the start of last season, played for Castilla in a Premier League International Cup encounter against Southampton in October, and made 16 senior appearances across the campaign. Sources close to Gabriel, who turns 16 on 6 October, feel let down by United, arguing promises around the pathway to the first team have not been kept. The club say it was anticipated Gabriel would become their youngest senior player by playing in Wednesday night's EFL Cup tie with Brighton. Given they lost 3-2 after leading 2-0, it is debatable whether that would have actually happened. United have not given up hope of keeping Gabriel, though they are unsure precisely why he wants to leave. It is understood the player is not currently training with the club. What next for Gabriel and Man Utd? What are the Premier League rules for academy players? Speaking after the Brighton game, head coach Michael Carrick, who gave the youngster his senior debut during the pre-season match with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm said everyone needed to be mindful of Gabriel's age. "I just think we've got to be really careful of the whole situation," he said. "He's a young boy. He's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation." Sources close to Gabriel have dismissed concerns over the player's age and physicality and feel the likes of Max Dowman, who made his debut for Arsenal at the age of 15 last season, show a willingness to trust youth in a way they do not see at United. Chelsea are also believed to have a major interest in the teenager. Any imminent move away from Old Trafford for Gabriel is complicated because of rules regarding the registration of young players. United say Gabriel's registration runs to the end of the season. It would be easier for him to leave United then, when he will be 16. However, as Gabriel has an EU passport, it is possible he will be allowed to join a club within European Union borders on his 16th birthday. This video can not be played What next for JJ Gabriel? title: Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds
description: The body of veteran broadcaster Owen Ndlovu was found hours after armed men kidnapped him near Johannesburg.
body: Owen Ndlovu was a familiar face to South African sports audiences after years as an SABC presenter Tributes are pouring in for a veteran South African sports broadcaster who was found dead on Wednesday hours after being abducted when his vehicle was hijacked in a township near Johannesburg. Owen Ndlovu, a former presenter with the country's public broadcaster, the SABC, was seized on Tuesday while collecting his wife from a church in Katlehong, police said. His body, which witnesses said had gunshot wounds, was discovered by residents the following morning. Police have launched a manhunt for three suspects and are investigating the circumstances surrounding his killing, which has once again drawn attention to South Africa's high levels of violent crime. South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg South Africa's deadly love affair with guns Provincial police spokesperson Col Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said Ndlovu had gone to pick up his wife from a religious service when the attackers struck. "As she approached their vehicle, three unknown men, one reportedly armed with a firearm, suddenly approached them, pushed her aside and forced her husband into the back seat," she said. "The suspects then drove off with the victim." The vehicle, a Ford Raptor pick-up truck - commonly known as a bakkie in South Africa - was later recovered abandoned in Walkerville, an area south of Johannesburg, police said. Ndlovu's body was found by local residents beside a road in Thokoza, which neighbours Katlehong. They said he appeared to have suffered gunshot wounds. A bag of his was found a few metres away. Police said they were investigating a case of murder but a post-mortem examination would establish the cause of death. "At this stage, the family is awaiting further information from the relevant authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Owen's death," said family spokesperson Eugene Mthethwa. The family described the loss as "devastating" and thanked residents, police and members of the public who had helped search for him after news of his abduction emerged. Ndlovu was a familiar figure to South African sports fans after years working as a presenter and producer at the SABC. He was also involved in radio coverage of the country's Premier Soccer League and later became an advocate for musicians' rights and royalty payments. The 54-year-old was also associated with Artists United and the SABC Summer Song of the Year initiative. Lelo Mzaca, a fellow journalist, remembered him as a man who lived a "colourful, energetic life" and brought enthusiasm and flair to sports broadcasting. "South Africa has lost a unique and spirited individual whose light shone brightly while it lasted," Mzaca added in a tribute on the Mail & Guardian news site. The provincial government urged communities to help police with the investigation, saying tackling crime remained a priority. The killing has again drawn attention to violent crime in South Africa, where armed robberies and vehicle hijackings remain a major concern. The latest national police figures, covering April to June 2026, recorded more than 5,000 murders and close to 4,000 carjackings. When releasing the figures last month, acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said serious crimes continued to create fear in communities and that some were carried out by "organised, heavily armed criminal groups that operate with planning and sophistication". title: Why dealing with defeat is key for Lampard at Coventry
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains why Coventry boss Frank Lampard needs to manage himself as well as his players after their poor start to the season.
body: Managing a newly promoted team in the Premier League is very demanding, as Frank Lampard is finding out at Coventry. It's the highest level, not just for the technical ability of the players that your team faces but also the sheer physicality that these players possess, and it feels like the gap to the Championship is getting greater every season. From my experience in the same situation, you have to be really smart in the way you approach each game and recognise the importance of preparation for each specific opponent, because your team has to be organised in possession, and definitely out of possession. Teams in the Premier League counter-attack with greater efficiency so being solid behind your own attacking play is absolutely vital. But the real advice I would give to managers in Frank's shoes is to manage yourself, and your own time, as well as your players. By that I mean you have to try to stay fresh and positive, because invariably you are going to go on bad runs of defeats like Coventry are on, which can drag your mood down. Lampard's Coventry side have lost all four of their Premier League games so far. They only lost seven of their 46 games in the Championship last season I can tell you now that, whoever you are playing, if you get beaten - and especially beaten heavily like Coventry were by Brighton on Sunday - then it resonates with you. It's the same for every manager. For Frank, whether it is losing at home to Hull or Brighton, or against Arsenal and Manchester City, then it will hurt. But it is how he deals with those defeats that will decide what happens next. Being the leader of a group of young men, you cannot look washed out and empty on a Monday morning after a heavy loss. Yes, inside you will be hurting and your pride will be taking a bashing but everyone at the club will be waiting for your reaction, and will act accordingly. Walking into the training ground in a dark mood and with your head around your backside just does not work, irrespective of what you are feeling inside. I've been in that situation many times myself as a manager and what you have to do is puff your chest out and find a way of getting everyone back on track and working even harder with a set focus on the next game. That's what all good leaders do. It is draining at times, but that is why managing your time and prioritising the issues that you can resolve is so important. When I took Stoke up to the Premier League in 2008, I was learning on my feet. We did not make a great start and I had to roll my sleeves up and get on with what I'd got in my squad, and really focus on getting results. But away from that I was always forward thinking and I was quick at recognising what was needed to improve our chances of staying up. When the window opened again in January, we were already in discussions with Tottenham for Matty Etherington, to supply us with crosses and chances from the wing. We needed more goals too, so I took James Beattie from Sheffield United. They were a Championship side but that didn't matter because he had a record of scoring goals in the top flight. We have heard so much about recruiting the right players in the right positions, and it is true today as it was in my day. Both lads played a significant role in keeping us up. Coventry haven't scored a goal yet, and people might look in from the outside and feel the forward areas are an issue for them because the usual thinking is that the centre-forward has to lead the scoring charts, or a wide player or the number 10. But the emphasis is on everyone to chip in and I would also reinforce one of the points I made in this column last season, about the importance of defending properly too. On average, clean sheets earn you more points than scoring a goal, which is something I always stressed to my players. Nailing down the importance of both ends of the pitch is the narrative, whatever kind of run of results you are on, because games are won and lost there. Coventry are the only Premier League team yet to pick up a point this season. Tottenham are the only other top-flight side yet to score a league goal Coventry have made a poor start but what has happened in their first four games does not have to become the story of their whole season. With Stoke, we got a win in our first home game - against Aston Villa - but that was our only victory in our first seven league matches after getting promoted. The thing I remember most from that time is that Hull had come up with us and, after seven games, they had won at Newcastle, Arsenal and Tottenham and were in the top five in the table, while we were third or fourth from bottom. I went out for dinner with my chairman, Peter Coates, and he said how Hull had made a wonderful start. I replied by telling him I bet you now that we finish above Hull... and we did. The reason I thought that was because of the mindset of the team, and the fans. I was confident my players were not going to go weak at the knees, and the togetherness we needed was already there in the squad, while the support was just off the scales, which helped us enormously at home. Every defeat was taken on the chin, and accepted, but the lads were always ready to go, again and again. It is a very unusual situation, to go from being in the Championship and winning regularly week after week, to dealing with defeat after defeat. Steve told me to get ready for going on runs where we would not win for five or six games on the bounce, but then if we could win two or three games in the same period after that, we would fly up the table. title: USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest
description: United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.
body: Savannah DeMelo collapsed during a league match between Racing Louisville and Seattle Reign United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year. Midfielder DeMelo, who has seven senior caps for the USA, has filed a lawsuit against University of Louisville Health (UofL Health) for negligence. The 28-year-old, who plays for Racing Louisville, collapsed in the first half of a National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) match on 14 September 2025. According to documents, external seen by BBC Sport, the case was filed on Tuesday morning with Jefferson Circuit Court in Kentucky, where her club is based - a year and a day after her on-field collapse. DeMelo's filing claims UofL Health and two doctors, Dr Sarabjeet Suri and Dr Jennifer Daily, "failed to act as a reasonably prudent and competent medical practice, and such negligence was a substantial factor in causing DeMelo to suffer severe physical injuries, including, but not limited to, her cardiac arrest". Dr Daily, according to her online UofL biography, external, is Racing Louisville's chief medical officer. The lawsuit states DeMelo was under the care of Dr Daily from January 2024 to July 2026. It states that in March 2025, Dr Daily referred DeMelo to Dr Suri for "evaluation and treatment" after she had been complaining of chest pain, dizziness and shortness of air; Dr Suri obtained a history, performed a physical examination and ordered diagnostic tests. Nearly six months later, DeMelo suffered the cardiac arrest. "She was subsequently diagnosed and treated for ventricular tachycardia [an abnormal heart rhythm]," the suit states. DeMelo, who has spent her entire professional career with Racing Louisville, has not played since her collapse. In a post to her Instagram page, external on Tuesday, De Melo - who was picked in the USA squad for the 2023 Women's World Cup and started their first two games - marked the anniversary of the incident. "A year ago today, while playing soccer, I collapsed due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia, that caused me to go into cardiac arrest," she wrote. "I respect and appreciate the privacy everyone has met me with while going through everything I have this year. I'll never be able to fully put into words how emotionally hard this year has been. There has been a lot of uncertainty and emotions intertwined with it all." title: 'The choir was a great lifter when the fields fell silent'
description: Dairy farmer Mervyn Kelso struggled with the sadness of the empty fields when he lost his entire herd to bovine TB.
body: Mervyn Kelso lost his whole herd to bovine TB When bovine TB led to the loss of his entire herd, dairy farmer Mervyn Kelso struggled with the sadness of the empty fields and the silence of the milking yard. It was a traumatic time for a man who had farmed his whole life, and it was hard watching his neighbours tend to their cows. His sister suggested he should join the Farmers' Choir and that turned out to be a "great lifter". Fast forward four years, and Mervyn has sang for the King, met musical royalty and his choir is up for a national award. Mervyn's first batch of cows were lost in November 2021. At the same time, a friend who had been around the County Antrim farm for three generations died. Then another 120 cows had to be removed, followed by 40 more two months later. "The department decided to buy the herd out," said Mervyn. "So by March 2022 we had no stock, no milking stock or adult stock." Mervyn and his wife Ruth, who live near Portglenone, relied on their faith for "the strength to carry on". Mervyn would sing in church and so when the Farmers' Choir restarted in nearby Ballymena that autumn, he decided to give it a go. He said it had been rewarding and different - a relief to the tough challenges of day-to-day farming. "Farming is one very lonely job, even more lonely than it was a generation ago, because labour is so difficult to get," he said. "And it's a very dangerous job, especially for a man who's working on his own. "It has the effect of depressing you, and that's why being involved in such a thing as a choir or any social event outside farming is good for anyone." Mervyn's wife Ruth is also a member of the Farmers' Choir Ruth says the choir came at the right time. "It was a hard time for both of us and the choir was definitely a great lifter," she said. "Mervyn was so enthusiastic and enjoyed it so much. "It was just great to have something to lift us because you weren't busy on the farm - well, you did some extra odd jobs, but it wasn't like the usual level of busyness." She said she has made "some lovely friends" and they get to see each other at choir rehearsals, concerts and céilís. "Sometimes you see a different side of a choir member when you're not just sitting beside them singing, and that's really good, socially," she added. Barkley Thompson said the choir was an antidote to farmers' stresses Barkley Thompson is the musical director of the choir. He grew up on a dairy farm and remembers his father talking about people at harvest time, helping each other out then sharing "a bit of craic and banter". He said the choir helped fill a social gap that has emerged in rural life as farming has become more automated. "Social isolation and loneliness - the sad thing is in rural communities, people don't always like to talk about that and acknowledge that," he said. "And that's why the choir is important to so many people. "It's not just about the singing. It's about the friendship." Nine of the friends, including Mervyn and Ruth, found themselves singing in the choir as part of the King's Coronation concert. They met the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, and Mervyn also met one of his heroes - Welsh bass-baritone Bryn Terfel, whose father was a sheep farmer. "We were running around with these Farmers' Choir vests, and he spotted us and he stopped and talked to us," he said. "And he thought we were worth chatting to because we were farmers." Barkley saw membership of the choir grew after the coronation appearance. "It's work that I see as very, very important in rural communities. "I'm a teacher - teaching can be stressful and farmers have their stresses on the farm, and you can see it on their faces. "They go into their practice, they just leave - and I leave myself - feeling so much happier and upbeat." The choir is the only one from Northern Ireland and, Barkley said, the only rural one, to be nominated for the Making Music UK volunteer group of the year award. Mervyn and his sons started rebuilding the herd in 2022 Mervyn has now largely handed the reins of the farm over to one of his two sons, offering assistance when required. They began rebuilding the herd in the summer of 2022, with the first heifers arriving from Denmark a few months later. "We had started off from zero, built right up to what we see here today, " he said. "So there's been tremendous work put in by, well, myself, but my son mainly, my two sons." He now has more time to sing. "You always come out of that singing feeling far, far better than you went into it," he said. "And that's the key to living, isn't it?" title: The Deadlifting Grandma: 'I'm a world champion'
description: Martine Barons, 65, has three world titles under her belt after only starting weightlifting in 2024.
body: Martine Barons who began lifting weights during lockdown is now a three-time world champion A 65-year-old grandmother has become a three-time world champion powerlifter after only starting the sport two and a half years ago. Martine Barons, from Stratford-upon-Avon, said she began lifting weights during lockdown after listening to a seminar that said women going through menopause should run less and lift more. Her colleague at the University of Warwick, who is also a personal trainer, then showed Barons how to deadlift, and spotted her potential. Barons is now nicknamed The Deadlifting Grandma. On Monday, she won at the AWPC World Powerlifting Championships in the 65 to 85 age group, becoming a three-time world champion, after starting out entering competitions just for fun. Barons said she has seen a "huge change" in her physique and capabilities "I have seen such a huge change in my own physique and my capabilities – I am sure that my body is at least 20 years younger," she told BBC CWR. "When they invited me to the British and European Championships, I thought, 'Well I have been invited it would be rude not to go', but who thought it would lead to this? I didn't," she said. Barons said her journey, down to hard work and dedication over the past couple of years, has been "so exciting". "I have learnt so much, I have met people all around the world, and it has been delightful," she said. For women who want to get fit and improve their strength, Baron said there were lots of options, one route is to join a gym and develop a tailored programme with a coach. Alternatively, Baron said those who prefer more privacy could "start really gently at home with some resistance bands and a programme". She added her powerlifting has led to having more capability on a day-to-day basis, along with now being able to touch her toes first thing in the morning. "If I need to move furniture at home, I can do that, I can toss my grandchildren in the air, I can play games with them," she said. "My posture is better and I just feel more capable and more confident in everyday life". title: India faces 100% tariff threat over Russian oil after US House vote
description: Trump’s tariff threat puts India’s Russian oil strategy- and its access to the US market - in a new bind.
body: A worker checks a sample of oil in Russia - India and China are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil For four years, India, one of the world's biggest oil importers, has turned Russia's war-driven disruption of global oil markets to its advantage. Russian crude, displaced from western markets after the invasion of Ukraine, has flowed instead to Indian refineries, often at attractive discounts. The arrangement has lowered the cost of one of India's biggest imports and given its refiners an abundant source of crude. Now that bargain is becoming a source of geopolitical risk. The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation giving President Donald Trump broad powers to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will now go to Trump to be signed into law. India and China are among those most exposed because both are major buyers of Russian oil. China accounted for half of Russia's crude exports, followed by India at 37%, Turkey at 5% and the EU at 5% between December 2022 and August 2026, according to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). Donald Trump and Narendra Modi at the White House in February 2025 Russia supplied 30.3% of India's crude imports in fiscal 2026, worth $40.8bn out of a total crude import bill of $134.7bn, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a Delhi-based think tank. In July, Russian crude accounted for more than half of India's imports. Other suppliers lagged far behind: the UAE accounted for 10.8% of India's July imports, Saudi Arabia 9.6%, Venezuela 6.3%, Brazil 5.5%, Oman 5.3% and the US 2.9%. Russia alone supplied more crude than all six combined. "The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices," says Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs GTRI. To be true, the economics of Russian oil have shifted. The crude no longer carries the steep discounts that made it particularly attractive to Indian refiners in the early years of the war, while competition for Russian barrels has intensified and shipping, insurance and sanctions risks have risen. "China and India, you better buy your oil and gas somewhere else," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal told reporters , externalafter the passage of the bill. These countries would normally have 180 days to cut Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington, but the president can shorten the deadline. India said in a statement that it was "monitoring further developments on this matter" and that it remained "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" for its people. "This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it added. India can find alternatives to Russian crude, but replacing it at scale would come at a price. S&P Global says alternative supplies, external can mean higher crude, freight and insurance costs, while longer shipping routes add to the burden. "The issue is not simply whether Russian barrels can be redirected to other buyers, but whether enough alternative crude is available to replace them without tightening the global market further," says Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at maritime intelligence firm Kpler. But the tariff would hit India elsewhere, too. The US is threatening tariffs on Indian exports to America, not a tax on Russian crude entering India. The impact would be felt through Indian exporters, the rupee, refinery margins and the trade balance. "This new bill could have major problematic impacts for India, and at the worst possible time, amid sensitive final-stage trade talks and shaky broader relations," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. "India has built some insulation to fend off the shocks of US tariffs through new trade deals with key markets in the EU and elsewhere, and through bolstering an already strong trade partnership with China. But [up to]100% tariffs from a critical export destination is real bad news, no matter how you slice it and even with successful hedging tactics." Indian refineries supplied some 70% of Russia's oil product imports in August The scale of that exposure is considerable. The US imported about $104bn of goods from India in 2025, while two-way US-India trade in goods and services was roughly $240bn, according to the US Trade Representative. India's exports to the US include electronics, pharmaceuticals, machinery, jewellery, chemicals, textiles and petroleum products. In 2025, electrical and electronic equipment alone accounted for about $25.8bn of Indian exports to America, pharmaceuticals about $9.7bn and machinery about $7.2bn. The new threat comes after an earlier round of Trump tariffs on Indian goods, which peaked at 50% in 2025 before being reduced. That creates an uncomfortable calculation for Delhi: how much should India pay for Russian crude before the savings are outweighed by the risk to its exports to the US? There is no simple answer. It will depend on the Russian discount, global crude prices, freight and insurance costs, the tariff Trump ultimately imposes, and whether Washington offers exemptions or reaches a broader settlement with Delhi. The picture gets more complicated once the crude is refined. India is not merely a buyer: its refineries turn Russian crude into fuels that can then be exported. title: 'My mother apologised': A survivor's journey after genital mutilation
description: Sara Kahsai was 29 when she found out she had FGM as a baby.
body: Sara Kahsai wants all survivors of FGM to seek help and not suffer alone Sara Kahsai grew up in Sudan but moved to Birmingham, England, in 2022 after a marrying a bus driver from the city. But as she settled into married life and her new home, she was coming to terms with a life-changing discovery. Sara realised she was a victim-survivor of Female Genital Mutiliation (FGM), a procedure she had endured as a young girl. She was floored by the revelation and, not least, the excruciating pain she was now beginning to fully understand. "The shock was massive," she said. "It made it difficult with my physical relationship with my husband - but he was very kind and very patient with me." Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation Sara turned to the one person she knew must have orchestrated it - her mother - and asked her why. "I was a baby. It was the culture to do it for everybody," she said her mother, still living in Africa, told her. "When I spoke to my mum she was really upset and she apologised to me." FGM involves the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons, and is practiced in some parts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia. It also happens within some migrant communities in the UK, where it is illegal and treated as child abuse. It is also against the law to take a girl abroad for FGM. Reasons include social acceptance, religion, misconceptions about hygiene and preserving a girl or woman's virginity. The Home Office website cites World Health Organisation figures showing three million girls undergo some form, external of the procedure every year in Africa alone. The mum received help for her FGM after she found out she was pregnant When Sara fell pregnant, she finally told health professionals she had endured FGM as a child. She was immediately referred to the specialist FGM Clinic, run by midwives at Birmingham Women's Hospital. Midwife Renata Hanif deals with around 200 cases each year and says her job is to ensure the wellbeing of women and safeguard unborn children. "Some types of female circumcision can affect the vaginal delivery," she said. They offer deinfibulation - a procedure that can be carried out during pregnancy that to separate fused tissue and enable safer births. What is FGM, where does it happen and why? Victim-survivors of FGM can also experience difficulty with urinating and menstruating, the midwife said. Women are more prone to infections and sepsis, and can suffer from severe and ongoing pain, as well having to deal with psychological trauma, anxiety and depression. Many patients find it hard to talk to her about what's happened to them, Hanif said. "It is very difficult, very emotional. It's very difficult for the woman to actually come forward and to come to the clinic, attend the clinic, and have a conversation with me as well," she said. "I explain to them that I'm here to help and I try to explain to them what happened to them when they were a child." She said most women leave the clinic with a better understanding of how they have been affected and how they can take back control of their bodies. "We talk about every part, what that part is there for and what's been removed and what cause for concern and what effect this will have for the rest of her life," Hanif said. Counselling is also offered as well as information on how partners and husbands can support them. Midwife Renata Hanif runs the FGM centre at Birmingham Women's Hospital In 2015, children's charity Barnardo's set up the National FGM Centre to help better protect women and girls. It works to prevent FGM, raise awareness of it and support those affected. The centre said schools are legally required to teach pupils about FGM and the law surrounding it as part of relationships and sex education. But how it is delivered can vary between schools. It's also not mandatory for it to be taught in primary schools and they want to see that change. "For us, a huge part of tackling FGM is prevention," Roma Ullah, from the centre, said. "Yes, a conviction, a prosecution, can provide justice, accountability and send strong messages into communities, but by then the harm has already happened." Sara says that if she knew help was out there, she would have sought help sooner In April, the government held its first dedicated FGM Summit in a decade, to discuss ways to better protect women and girls. Among improvements on the way are new guidelines to help identify girls at risk of being taken abroad for FGM. Sara wants to urge other women in a similar position to take immediate action. "I have a message to all ladies who've had FGM," she said. "When they come to the UK it is different. There's help here - go to their GP, seek help, ask for help. "If I knew I could seek help I would not have waited until I was expecting... because I did suffer a lot before." If you have been affected by the contents of the article, support is available through the BBC Action Line website. title: Review of legal framework launched in wake of Eleanor Donaldson trial
description: The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and end by the end of February 2027.
body: Lady Eleanor Donaldson arriving at Newry Crown Court for a hearing in 2025 Stormont's justice and health ministers have launched a joint review of the legal framework on trials of the facts in the wake of the Donaldson trial, BBC News NI understands. That's according to a letter from the Department of Justice's assembly liaison officer. Eleanor Donaldson, wife of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds. The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and conclude by the end of February 2027. The letter to Stormont's justice committee said the move came in the wake of "public concern and interest" on trials of the facts, and that work would now take place on the terms of reference of the review. Both the Department of Justice and the Department of Health have been contacted for comment. A trial of the facts is an option that is open to prosecutors if a court determines that a person is unfit to stand trial and criminal proceedings cannot go ahead. It takes the place of a criminal trial and is used to determine whether an accused committed the acts alleged. It cannot result in a conviction, but if the court is not satisfied that the accused committed the acts alleged, then he/she will be acquitted. The procedure is allowed for in legislation by Article 49A of the Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986. The mechanism is not used often but one high-profile example was in the trial of former IRA leader Ivor Bell in 2019. In some ways, it is similar to a normal criminal trial - the prosecution puts its evidence against the defendant before a judge and jury in a courtroom. However, perhaps the key difference, is that the accused does not play a part in proceedings, and does not even need to be in court. That was the case with Eleanor Donaldson, who was not present on any day of the four-week trial in which evidence was heard against her and her husband. However, in a trial of the facts the accused will be represented by a legal team and their lawyers can question the witnesses, challenge the evidence and make legal submissions on their behalf. Ian Turkington KC represented Eleanor Donaldson during her trial of the facts, cross-examining witnesses and issuing closing remarks on behalf of his client towards the end of the trial. Then there is the major differences in what the outcome can be in a trial of the facts. Instead of being asked to return a verdict of guilty or not guilty, the jury are asked to decide whether or not the accused committed the offence with which they were charged. The focus is on what they are alleged to have physically done - not their state of mind at the time. In a normal criminal trial, a jury would be invited to decide whether or not a defendant had the mental faculties required to be guilty of the offence as well. The standard of proof remains the same - a jury must be sure beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused committed the acts alleged. The accused cannot be convicted but they can be acquitted if the jury decide they didn't commit the acts alleged. title: Inside the 'scariest house on Rightmove'
description: The station house in Bleasby, dating back to the 1840s, has been dubbed the "scariest" on Rightmove.
body: It is believed the "creepy doll" left standing in the corner of a bedroom had captured people's imaginations An old station house that is up for auction in Nottinghamshire has had unexpected attention after being dubbed the "scariest house on Rightmove". The property in Bleasby dates back to the 1840s, when the railway station opened, and would have been home to the station masters who were responsible for opening and closing the station barriers. Although steeped in local history, the eerie character of the house in its listing images is what seems to have gathered interest. Area manager at Auction House Notts & Derby, Jonathan Way, said he believed it was a "creepy doll" left standing in the corner of a bedroom that had captured people's imaginations. The house had been empty for some time and a number of break-ins eventually led to the downstairs windows being boarded up, which had not helped the atmosphere, Way said. He added the house had been left untouched before the images were taken for the listing. Speaking about his first visit, alongside his colleagues, Way said: "It was a little bit unsettling. "It was all boarded up downstairs, there wasn't any natural light downstairs. The lights weren't working either so we had to use phone lights to move around. "Upstairs wasn't too bad but the doll and the pram were a little bit creepy. "I definitely wasn't expecting that when I walked up the stairs." Part of the old station house in Bleasby can be seen in this old image The property caught the attention of the content creator behind the Housing Horrors TikTok account, where a video was posted dubbing the old station house the "scariest house on Rightmove". The social media account regularly shares videos of property listings, often highlighting some of the strangest looking houses on the market across the country. But the post had not put people off, Way said. The area manager said the property had still proven to be very popular. He said: "You get the odd quirky [property] but I've not really done one like that before. "It's a really old station house. "It's still got the original brickwork and the design in side obviously hasn't been touched for a number of years." The property is due to go under the hammer on 28 September.
