title: What next for Gabriel and Man Utd?
description: On the night JJ Gabriel was supposed to become Manchester United's youngest player in history, the scramble is on to persuade him not to quit.
body: JJ Gabriel in action for Manchester United in Premier League 2 this month Before what was intended to be a historic night at Old Trafford, Manchester United are still digesting the reality that JJ Gabriel wants to leave. The club have been left reeling at the sudden downturn in relations. Only a week ago Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut at Leigh that seemed to be the prelude to becoming United's youngest player in history by making his debut against Brighton in the Carabao Cup third round on Wednesday. Now United are scrambling. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are involved in talks they hope will result in their 15-year-old reversing his plan and choosing to stay. It feels like a forlorn task. A belief that promises have been broken and a certainty over Gabriel's current abilities and eventual destiny mean trust is low. Real Madrid, Barcelona and Paris St-Germain are among the European heavyweight clubs monitoring the situation. Gabriel's potential is well known. All England's leading clubs have seen it first hand given he was named Under-18 Premier League player of the year last season, even though he was only 14 when the campaign began. He scored 23 goals in the Premier League Under-18 competition and three in the FA Youth Cup. He was the star man in a United side that reached the Premier League Under-18 cup final and the FA Youth Cup final. He was the Premier League Under-18 Player of the Year and United's Under-18 Player of the Year. The achievements and accolades were in recognition of a player who has balance, pace, close control and a powerful shot. This season he has shown a willingness to get stuck in to try and win the ball back. "The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how the forward was described by one United source recently. United Under-21s coach Adam Lawrence made a salient point in the aftermath of that Uefa Youth League victory over Sabah FK. "The first thing in my job is not to ruin him," said Lawrence. "When you have a talented player like JJ, you obviously don't want to stifle their freedom and their creativity." Talent like that grabs attention and is not confined to these shores. Real, Barcelona and PSG focus on elite youth players. That is what is happening here. This is where is gets tricky. United's initial response to the publicity around Gabriel's future was to say privately that they would try to persuade him his future was best served staying where he is. They also advised that Gabriel's registration with them runs until the end of the season. That may well buy them time when it comes to potential moves to Premier League rivals. But what about European giants? Gabriel has a European Union passport. His mother is of Greek-Cypriot heritage and his father won two caps for the Republic of Ireland. In 2016 the Court of Arbitration for Sport rejected an appeal by Argentine club Velez Sarsfield - who tried to block one of their 16-year-old players moving to Manchester City - on the basis he was a dual Argentine-Italian national and, as an EU national, should be allowed to transfer to a club within the European Union even though he was coming in from an external country. West Brom received no compensation when a 16-year-old Louie Barry left for Barcelona in 2019 as Fifa ruled that West Brom failed to formally offer him a scholarship. West Brom had claimed 130,000 euros (£111,000) in training compensation. Barry left Barca for Aston Villa for just under £1m six months later. The worst-case scenario for United is Gabriel walks away when he turns 16 on 6 October and they end up with no compensation for a player whose market value, even at this tender age and with so much promise unfulfilled, can be measured in millions. Gabriel made his senior United debut against Atletico Madrid last month Gabriel is not the first young player to find himself at odds with his club over their future direction. Jadon Sancho was 17 when he stopped training at City to force through a £10m move to Borussia Dortmund in the belief that he would play more often in Germany than under Pep Guardiola. Morgan Rogers was Barry's team-mate in the West Brom side that reached the FA Youth Cup semi-final in 2019. Within three months he had left for City, a move completed on his 17th birthday. Sources feel that, in meetings with the United hierarchy that led to Gabriel committing his short-term future to the club last summer, promises were made over his career path that have not been kept. He did start to appear in senior training sessions, initially under Ruben Amorim and then Michael Carrick, but speculation around a senior debut last season, which could only be in the FA Cup, was doused by Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher, who had by now taken the senior team manager's role on an interim basis following Amorim's dismissal. Fletcher felt it was too early for Gabriel. It had been anticipated that Gabriel would feature during United's pre-season programme. His absence from the trip to Helsinki for a meeting with Wrexham on 18 July was put down to the date he returned for pre-season training. He was part of every squad after that, but played only once, for eight minutes against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm. Did that lack of action sow the seeds of discontent? Gabriel travelled to Trondheim for a meeting with Rosenborg on 24 July. Carrick used 11 substitutes that day. Gabriel was one of two United players who did not come on. Five of those who did have left, either permanently or on loan. It was noted that 18-year-old Tynan Thompson was given a 45-minute senior debut against Leeds United at Croke Park - another game Gabriel travelled to but was not involved in - three weeks after his arrival from Tottenham. Nevertheless, it was felt Gabriel was likely to become United's youngest player this autumn - probably in the EFL Cup. While the third-round draw delivered an Old Trafford rema

title: Man, 57, arrested over death in suspected shooting in Armadale
description: Police Scotland said William Watson, 35, was pronounced dead at the scene of the incident on Saturday.
body: William Watson, known as Billy, died in the targeted attack in Armadale A 57-year-old man has been arrested over a man's death in a suspected shooting at a house in West Lothian. William Watson, known as Billy, died at the scene of the incident on Harestanes Road, Armadale, at about 11:50 on Saturday. Police Scotland described the 35-year-old's death as a "targeted attack" and said its inquiries were ongoing. A postmortem examination is due to take place, and the death is currently being treated as suspicious. Police outside the house on Harestanes Road on Monday Officers had also been investigating whether a car fire on Saturday in nearby Netherhouses and a fire at a derelict house on Wotherspoon Crescent were linked to the incident. Det Supt Michelle Findlay, from Police Scotland's Major Investigations Team, said her thoughts remained with Watson's family and friends. She added: "Specialist officers are supporting them as we continue to try to get answers about what happened. "We've been carrying out extensive inquiries, including door-to-door in the area, CCTV review and forensic analysis." Police Scotland urged anyone with information about the death to contact officers, external. A dedicated online portal, external has also been set up. Supt Jocelyn Thomas said: "We understand the local community is concerned by what has happened, however we believe this was a targeted attack. "I want to reassure everyone, these incidents are rare. "An increased police presence will remain in the area as we continue our inquiries and anyone with concerns can speak to these officers." title: Wildlife trust wants marina silt disposed offshore
description: Brighton Marina wants to restart dredging next year but still needs a site to dispose of the silt.
body: The marina said there were limited options available for disposal sites A wildlife trust has called for a new offshore disposal site to be found for sediment dredged from Brighton Marina, saying it remains concerned about plans being explored off Newhaven. Brighton Marina has been looking for a long-term disposal site since Sussex Wildlife Trust successfully challenged a licence in 2025 for disposal of sediment at Rottingdean. The marina has said dredging is needed to maintain safe access and there are limited options available for disposal sites. Sussex Wildlife Trust said Newhaven was a "protected area" that sat adjacent to the Beachy Head West Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ). Campaigners previously claimed the silt was a "black, thick, slimy, petrochemically smelling sludge", but Premier Marinas, which owns Brighton Marina, said dredged silt was regularly sampled to confirm it was not harmful. Protesters opposed the use of Rottingdean in a demo by the marina in January 2025 John Cervenka, Premier Marinas chief operating officer, said: "Maintaining safe navigational access to Brighton Marina is not optional. It is a legal requirement and fundamental to the operation of the marina." He said the marina was a major centre of economic activity. According to the marina, about 150 businesses depend on the site, creating jobs for about 1,200 people, with more than eight million visits each year. Premier Marinas said Newhaven had been identified as a potential alternative by Sussex Wildlife Trust. However, the trust said in a statement on social media, external: "We have not promoted or endorsed Newhaven over any other option." Campaigners said last year that local rock pools filled with sludge after dredging The trust said: "Newhaven sits adjacent to Beachy Head West MCZ, and we remain concerned about potential impacts on this protected area. "Our preferred option is a new offshore disposal site, well away from the MCZ." The trust said that Newhaven was already used for dredge disposal by Newhaven Port, and there was currently no available data on the impacts of additional disposal there. Until it saw further evidence, it did not have a view on whether Newhaven was suitable, it added. "We will respond to any future licence application based on the ecological evidence it contains," it said. Brighton Marina hopes to submit a marine licence application to the Marine Management Organisation in November. If approved, maintenance dredging could restart next spring. title: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on sister Diana stolen in the Netherlands
description: The theft of Earl Spencer's memoir about his late sister comes one week ahead of the book's release.
body: Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands. The BBC understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse. Dutch police said they were aware of the incident and have been approached for comment. Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be released in the UK and globally on Tuesday, and tells the story of Princess Diana's life from the Earl's perspective. A source said the truck driver was taking a mandatory break in a car park and was sleeping in his cab at the time the books were stolen. They added Dutch police are investigating. They did not say where the theft took place. The Daily Mail, who first reported the theft, external and is serialising the book, said the theft took place earlier this week in the Dutch countryside. The book's publisher Penguin Michael Joseph - a division of Penguin Random House - and Dutch publisher Overamstel, who have rights to the book in the Netherlands, were approached for comment by the BBC. Earl Spencer said he wanted "to tell the truth about Diana" from his perspective Princess Diana, who died aged 36 following a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year. Her sons Prince William and Prince Harry were aged 15 and 12 respectively at the time of her death. Last month announcing the book's publication, Earl Spencer explained ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death he had been inundated with interview requests and he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than "having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others". "The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother's perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral," he added, referring to the eulogy he delivered in Westminster Abbey in September 1997. "I want to speak on Diana's behalf and do so in an openly positive way." In his eulogy, Earl Spencer described Princess Diana as the "very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty", adding: "All over the world she was a symbol of selfless humanity... a standard bearer for the rights of the truly downtrodden." He also used the speech to criticise the media, calling her the "most hunted person of the modern age" and pledged to protect Prince William and Prince Harry and prevent them suffering a similar fate. In 2023, copies of Prince Harry's memoir Spare were accidentally put on sale in Spain days ahead of the official global release. title: Author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
description: Her husband says the playwright and cultural and political commentator died after a brief illness.
body: Greer's work often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said. In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice". He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her." Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together." BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart." Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting. A true life force". He added: "I will never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin on Question Time. I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship." London Mayor Sadiq Khan said her voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation. "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously." Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan. Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a powerful panellist on programmes like Newsnight Review and Question Time. She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009). Once named by the Observer, external as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions. Greer was made an OBE for services to the arts in 2010 Speaking to the Guardian, external in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world." She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'." Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University. Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes. Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published. Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts. In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature. title: US accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukrainian allies overseas
description: The FBI says five men "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".
body: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe. In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine". "It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts". It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location. Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence. Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said. Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB). The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network". Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants. The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident". The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world". One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US. Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (£743) and $1,500. Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident. The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims". The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia. It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine". His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history". Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence. It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind. Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw. Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons." In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall. Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously." The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025. A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation. The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine". title: Reform defector says party in Wales 'falling apart' and she backs independence
description: Sarah Cooper-Lesadd also revealed she voted Remain in the 2016 Brexit referendum.
body: Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was elected as a Member of the Senedd for Reform in May A member of the Senedd who quit Reform to join Plaid Cymru says she would back Welsh independence if a vote were held and has revealed she voted Remain in the 2016 Brexit referendum. Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, one of 34 Reform MSs elected in May's Senedd election, defected to Plaid on Tuesday. She told the BBC's Walescast that her former party was "completely chaotic" and was "falling apart at the seams". Her defection - which came on the same day Dan Thomas stepped down as Reform's Welsh leader - means Plaid has 44 members in Cardiff Bay, and Reform as the largest opposition party has 33 seats. Senedd member Sarah Cooper-Lesadd quits Reform to join Plaid Cymru Reform members will not get vote on new Welsh leader Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault Thomas quit on Tuesday after he was arrested over the weekend on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. He was bailed pending further enquiries, and denies doing anything wrong. Cooper-Lesadd said on Wednesday she had approached Plaid Cymru after a "period of deliberation". "It's been a journey for me since coming to the Senedd, it's come after a period of thinking about it, so it has been a while," she said. She described speeches by Reform Caerdydd Penarth MS Joe Martin in June, including one making allegations about Sudanese asylum seekers, as "flashpoints" for her. In the speech he implied asylum seekers from the country posed a safety risk. Martin's words, Cooper-Lesadd said, "just completely did not chime with the type of person that I am and the values that I have". "There were other several things. The party's completely chaotic, it's falling apart at the seams, it really, really is." Cooper-Lesadd, a former Conservative, was elected as a Reform MS for the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency in May's election. Her swap to Plaid Cymru means she has been in three political parties since 2024. She said she felt uncomfortable with some of the language used by Reform members. During the interview, Cooper-Lesadd was also asked about her view on independence, and further powers for the Welsh government, two things that Plaid Cymru has campaigned on. "I support the ability of people to choose their own future, and that is self-determination and Plaid have said, that it will happen when the time is right. "I would vote yes, because, I have seen increasingly the fact that Wales is short-changed in so many different ways, but we aren't there yet. "The nation is on a political journey, and I'm on a political journey as well, and it's about bringing people with us." The new Plaid MS was also asked about the idea of the UK returning to the European Union. "I've never, ever spoken about Brexit, and I'll be honest I voted remain in the referendum and it's been quite difficult for me not to be able to talk about it, and it has damaged our trading relationships. So yes, I absolutely do support that. "In the public discourse over the last 10 years, we haven't been able to have that debate about the European Union. Even parties such as the Labour Party have struggled to talk about it, because they just get shut down." "When I came into Reform, I did think that there was a certain element of being a broad church, and that's what I believed. "It has become extremely narrow, whereas Plaid has a set of values that is values-based, and that's what I believe in." The Senedd, in common with the other parliaments in the UK, has no requirement for members to face a by-election if they leave the party they represented when they were elected. "What I would say is that my work with my constituents doesn't end today, I'll continue fighting for them, continue standing up for them. "I appreciate [Reform's point of view], but I'm going to keep on fighting for people in my area and working extremely hard." Reform MS Llŷr Powell told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday that the party had "made a lot of effort to try to communicate" with Cooper-Lesadd prior to her decision to leave Reform. He questioned whether Cooper-Lesadd "fully understood the core values of the party that she was standing for" and the reasons given for her defection. Responding to her defection on Tuesday, a Reform Wales spokesperson said the party had planned to expel her "as soon as we discovered" she was "in favour of Welsh independence and the break-up of the United Kingdom". They added: "Her separatist sympathies are not welcome in our party. Our policy on maintaining the Union is clear. "Plaid are welcome to her, she is now in her third party in two years." title: Endangered water voles introduced to reserve
description: Efforts are being made to reintroduce the locally-extinct species back to the River Wey in Surrey.
body: Water voles have been functionally extinct since the early 2000s, Surrey Wildlife Trust said Surrey Wildlife Trust has introduced 30 nationally-endangered water voles to a nature reserve near Elstead. The release on the River Wey comes following a "successful" release on the upper river. The water voles are being introduced downstream on 10 sites between Frensham and Elstead, the wildlife trust said. James Herd, director of reserves management at the trust, said: "As we work towards the restoration of natural ecosystems and landscapes county wide, I hope this release is one of many reintroductions of native species that we'll see in the years ahead." Water voles have been functionally extinct in Surrey since the early 2000s, but co-ordinated reintroduction and habitat improvement efforts by nature restoration groups are working to help the endearing species thrive again. The efforts to bring back water voles are funded by the Environment Agency's Environment Improvement Fund The trust said in a statement that it hoped that over the coming months, the aquatic rodents will "adapt easily to life on the 16-hectare reserve at Thundry Meadows and establish widely across the top of the Wey catchment". Their return would also benefit other species which depend on healthy wetland habitats including herons and birds of prey, they added. David Elliott, National Trust lead ranger for the South Downs West said: "Nature wins when we work together." "It's so encouraging to see the water voles returning after all this time, they have been locally extinct for decades. "The return of this enchanting species adds a missing piece to this jigsaw." The release is part of a wider effort led by the National Trust, River Wey Trust and South East Rivers Trust to reintroduce the locally extinct species back to the River Wey. title: Top judge explains decision to free murderer who absconded
description: Gary Anderson, who is serving 15 years for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018, remains on the run on Wednesday.
body: Gary Anderson, who is serving a 15-year sentence for the murder of Karol Kelly, remains on the run Northern Ireland's top judge has explained a court's decision to grant convicted killer Gary Anderson temporary release to attend his father's funeral, despite opposition from prison authorities. Anderson, 29, who is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018, failed to return to Maghaberry prison on Monday. The prison service had refused to grant Anderson compassionate temporary release (CTR) to attend the funeral, but that was overturned by a court on Sunday. The Office of the Lady Chief Justice (LCJ) said the court had held that the governor's decision not to grant CTR was "not substantiated by the evidence provided to the court". Karol Kelly died after being stabbed in the Grafton Street area of Derry in 2018 "This was an individual judicial decision, and it is not appropriate for this office to make any further comment," the Office of LCJ said. Anderson's brother Sean, who is serving 17 years for the murder of Karol Kelly, also challenged the decision not to release him from Magilligan Prison to attend the funeral, but that was upheld. "The application was brought on the grounds that the decisions breached the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) rights of the applicants," the Office of the LCJ said. "The court found that the decision by the governor in respect of Sean Anderson was carried out lawfully and refused the application for leave to challenge the decision." Anderson was released from Maghaberry Prison on Monday to attend his father's funeral, but absconded from his court-approved chaperone. It is unclear who that chaperone is or what powers, if any, were given to that person. The funeral took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry on Monday morning followed by cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, that afternoon. It is unclear if Anderson had been granted permission to cross the border to attend the cremation. Justice Minister Naomi Long said it was not about apportioning blame and that lessons had to be learned from the episode Speaking on Wednesday on BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme Justice Minister Naomi Long said she believed the prison service had reached "the right conclusion" in relation to Anderson's release. "They have the experience of doing these assessments on an ongoing basis. They felt it wasn't safe on this occasion for him to be released," Long said. "But he has rights. He was able to exercise those rights in the court and a judge with that information reached a different conclusion." That, the minster said, is "part of the process" and "entirely legitimate". Long said the majority of prisoners on short term release return to custody as required. "This is an unusual situation that we find ourselves in but it is a deeply concerning one," she said. "It is not about apportioning blame, it is about trying to find out how we ensure this doesn't happen again but also how we get this person back into custody." The minister, who urged Anderson to hand himself over to police, said he is "a threat to the public and he is potentially also at risk." However, the DUP MLA Trevor Clarke, who sits on the policing board, said the whole process needed looked at. "I think there's clear evidence that there was an issue in this case and that's now been borne out because this person hasn't come back," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. "All of the things that the courts have involved themselves in this one, I think, has been wrong. "A chaperone as opposed to a proper prison guard, this is an individual who cannot even handcuff the person while they're chaperoned, so all of the safeguards that could have been put in place weren't put in place." On Wednesday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that Anderson was last seen in the Eastway area of Creggan in Derry. They also confirmed that they were liaising with An Garda Síochána (Irish police). title: Colonel cleared over handling of soldier abuse case
description: Jaysley Beck, 19, took her own life at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire after she was sexually assaulted.
body: Maj James Hook (L) and Col Samantha Shepherd (C) were accused of conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline A senior Army officer has been cleared of failing to properly deal with abuse allegations made by a teenage soldier who took her own life. Col Samantha Shepherd has been on trial at Military Court Centre at Catterick Garrison in North Yorkshire, in connection with the handling of concerns raised by Gunner Jaysley Beck, from Cumbria. The 19-year-old took her own life at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire in 2021 after former Battery Sgt Michael Webber "pinned her down" and sexually assaulted her. A board - which consisted of an Air Commodore, a Royal Navy captain and an Army colonel - returned a not guilty verdict for Shepherd, on the directions of a judge. Gunner Beck had filed a complaint about the sexual assault Assistant Judge Advocate General Edward Legard had told the board: "The Crown has concluded that there is insufficient evidence upon which you can safely convict Colonel Shepherd of the charge she faces." Shepherd has been in court alongside Maj James Hook, whose trial continues. The two senior officers were accused of "conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline". Gunner Beck was found dead in her barracks at Larkhill Camp on 15 December 2021 On Tuesday, the military court heard claims the 19-year-old had been "let down" when she told Shepherd and Hook "enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted" five months before she took her own life. The board was told a chain of command failed to properly deal with the case. Hook and Shepherd were charged by the Service Prosecution Authority over their handling of the case earlier this year. Shops v shoplifters - who is winning the battle? Is bankrupt competitions boss behind new scheme? Plans for massive solar farm enter next stage In October, Webber was jailed for six months for sexual assault. The attack happened at a Royal Artillery adventure training exercise on Thorney Island, in Chichester Harbour, in July 2021. At the time, Minister for Veterans and People, Louise Sandher-Jones MP described Jaysley's death as a "tragedy". She said: "Let me be clear, there is no place for criminal or unacceptable behaviours within the military." Assistant chief of general staff Maj Gen Jon Swift said the Army was "sorry we didn't listen to Jaysley when she first reported her assault". He added: "We are determined to make sure the same mistakes don't happen again." title: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of Ed Sheeran's career
description: Sheeran tries to stay away from politics and controversy, but that stance has come in for criticism.
body: This video can not be played Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit? Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments. Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts. Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners. He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk. He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians. But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump. "People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig." When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity. This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career. By now, you probably know the story. Macklemore was picked as opening act on Sheeran's US tour, and on the first night made a speech saying "Free Palestine" and showing images of the destruction in Gaza. The following night, he referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects. He faced condemnation, with the organisation StopAntisemitism accusing Macklemore of "ambushing" the audience. Stadium owners, apparently led by the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft, put pressure on Sheeran and his promoters to drop him from the tour. After a week of backroom discussions, they got their way. On Tuesday, Sheeran issued a statement saying the decision was made by the promoters, not by him. He said he had tried to build bridges between the parties, to no avail. And he said he was "not complicit", arguing that his decision to remain out of the Middle East debate in public wasn't proof he "didn't care". "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," he wrote. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated." He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds." All support acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour quit after Macklemore dropped Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'Free Palestine' speech The statement landed with a thud. If Sheeran is so concerned about children, critics said, how come he hasn't mentioned the thousands of children killed in Gaza? Others pointed out that his abstention from politics was not absolute. He wore a "justice for Grenfell" T-shirt at Wembley Stadium in 2018 after the Grenfell Tower fire, played the Concert For Ukraine in 2022, and recorded a protest song about the Ukraine war with U2 earlier this year. Questions were also raised about his relationship with Kraft. Sheeran sang at the businessman's wedding in 2022, and in a subsequent interview called him "super sweet". Music journalist Jeffrey Ingold said Sheeran's apparent acceptance of the decision to drop Macklemore seemed like "cowardice". "He is one of the biggest musicians in the world," Ingold told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has power and he has leverage. And he has essentially washed his hands and said, this is not my responsibility. "He had options, right? He could have said to the promoters and the owners of the venues, including Robert Kraft, 'You know what, we're not going to do the shows there. If you're not going to let us all perform, we're not going to do it'. He could have found alternate venues." Hours after Sheeran's statement landed, his tour went into crisis. All three support acts for the remaining shows - Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham - pulled out, voicing support for Macklemore. Beoga - who back Sheeran to play songs like Galway Girl and Nancy Mulligan - also quit. Many of them said Macklemore's axing, at the hands of a group of billionaire venue owners, represented a chilling effect on free speech. Others from music and beyond have spoken out. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining why she was critical of the rapper's comments. Suddenly, against his will, Sheeran has become the centre of a political storm over one of the world's most divisive issues. Ed Sheeran performing with Macklemore at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in 2014 Could Sheeran have handled it better when the controversy blew up? Absolutely. In his statement, he said he wanted to continue the tour, to avoid letting down fans and the crew who rely on his concerts to make a living. If he had threatened to pull the plug on the shows, he could have framed it as a protest for free speech - although that would still inevitably have been interpreted as an endorsement of Macklemore's statements.

title: Philippines' Duterte seen in person at International Criminal Court for first time
description: He is due to be tried for crimes against humanity over thousands of deaths linked to his war on drugs.
body: Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since March 2025 Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity. He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily. The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt on Wednesday, which marked the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago. He did not speak but waved at family members in the public gallery when proceedings ended. Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and then skipped multiple hearings. The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial . The first trial date is scheduled for 30 November. The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy. The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, until 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC. Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes recently told the court his client was suffering from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise. Judges are deliberating whether Duterte is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three specialists. That assessment has not been made public but according to AFP, defence lawyers say it shows Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and was found to be unable to recall Donald Trump's name. Relatives of those killed in Duterte's brutal anti-drugs campaign watched the proceedings over a livestream in Manila. Llore Pasco, who lost two sons, told Reuters: "We're happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight." Randy Delos Santos, who lost his teenage nephew in 2017, told AFP he was happy to see Duterte in court, adding: "We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings." Relatives of those who lost loved ones during Duterte's war on drugs cheered as the former president appeared in court. In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election. Duterte's family is currently caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos. The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025. Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term. But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office. She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated. title: Seated exercises help physical and mental health
description: Laugh, Move & Groove, nominated for the Make a Difference Awards, holds sessions around Jersey.
body: Many Laugh, Move & Groove classes are fully booked People attending free seated exercises classes and laughing yoga said it has helped improve their physical and mental wellbeing. Laugh, Move & Groove takes its sessions around community centres and care homes in Jersey to help keep people moving. The not-for-profit group also works with charities as well to support people of different physical abilities to stay active. It has been shortlisted for the BBC Radio Jersey Make a Difference Awards for its work. Linda Crawford said the classes have made a difference to people like herself Linda Crawford started coming to the classes in St Ouen's Parish Hall nine months ago. She said: "I want to keep as fit as I possibly can... I thought it was sitting down so it wouldn't be very strenuous, but it is very strenuous. "Because my body feels it's moved a lot, my mind feels calm as well. "It's made an enormous difference for people on all kinds of levels, with all kinds of perhaps physical restrictions on how they can move." Jackie Turner from the group says the classes help build social connections too More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Jackie Turner is one of the volunteers who helps lead the sessions. She said: "It's just a fun environment and you can see that people enjoy it because it's a different way of exercising. "It's also about the friendships and the social aspects as well because as you get older, sometimes the social aspects of your life fall away a little bit." The winners of the BBC Radio Jersey Make a Difference Awards are due to be announced on 14 September. Follow BBC Jersey on X, external and Facebook, external. title: Nandy pledges crackdown on 'doxxing' after RNLI volunteers see personal details online
description: The Culture Secretary condemned how RNLI volunteers and others have had their addresses published online.
body: The Culture Secretary has said tougher action is needed on 'doxxing' Lisa Nandy has vowed to strengthen the law on "doxxing" after lifeboat volunteers involved in migrant crossing rescues had their personal details published online. The culture secretary said she would "tighten up the law" to make doxxing, which involves leaking people's home addresses, a criminal offence. Currently, she said this kind of behaviour is only illegal if it is done with clear intent to cause fear, harm and distress. Nandy convened a meeting with social media firms on Tuesday afternoon to discuss such abuse, but she called social media company X a "disgrace" for failing to turn up. Last week, the chief executive of the RNLI - the Royal National Lifeboat Institute - condemned online and physical abuse volunteers for the charity had received over English Channel migrant crossings. That followed protests after 120 people landed on Portsmouth's shores from France with the RNLI's assistance. Nandy told BBC Breakfast she was "appalled" that the likes of RNLI volunteers, police officers, social workers and journalists were "being doxxed online" - having their names, photos and addresses published. In her meeting with social media companies, she said she found "wildly varying standards" from them on doxxing material. TikTok told her it would automatically remove such posts while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it would not, she said. "And frankly, X didn't even bother to turn up yesterday which shows real contempt for people's safety and security and their obligations to society," she added. She said the government "will not hesitate to take action" to make clear that "where people's addresses are being published online, that is an offence and action has to be taken swiftly". A source close to Meta said it removes content that shares, offers or solicits personally identifiable information that could lead to physical harm. It is undersood the Crown Prosecution Service can currently treat doxxing under offences such as malicious communications if a victim is threatened or harassed. BBC Verify found viral social media posts about those involved in migrant crossing operations, some of which wrongly identified RNLI crew members and called for their families to be tracked down. The RNLI has said only 109 of its 9,058 lifeboat launches last year were for people "in distress in the Channel" - 1.2% of its total rescue work. The charity's chief executive added around 95% of small boats were intercepted by the UK Border Force. Nandy has also taken aim at "incredibly slow" progress with enforcement of the Online Safety Act, the government's flagship law to tackle online abuse, as she called for regulator Ofcom to move faster. Describing the "major challenges" with enforcing the Act, she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme two penalties had so far been issued to companies but no fines had yet been paid. title: Pokémon fans queue for 30th anniversary release
description: Avid collectors of the Japanese trading card game call it "the biggest day in a decade".
body: This video can not be played Fans of Pokémon queued for hours outside toy shops for an eagerly-anticipated new release. The brand has brought out a special anniversary edition of its trading card game, which has been played for 30 years. The BBC spoke to avid collectors in Norfolk waiting outside Roys Toys in Wroxham and Kerrison's Toys in Norwich, and there were at least 150 people queuing outside Smyths in Costessey. One fan, Charlie, who had queued since midnight, said he was "really excited" about the new release, and found the game was a great way to bond with his son. title: Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
description: Hashim Thaci has been jailed for crimes including torture and murder during Kosovo's independence war with Serbia.
body: The former president of Kosovo, Hashim Thaci, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes. A hearing at The Hague on Wednesday sentenced the 58-year-old for crimes during Kosovo's independence war against Serbia in the 1990s, in which more than 10,000 people died. He was convicted after a three-year trial of crimes including murder, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment. A number of other allegations against him were not proven. Thaci was a co-founder and commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a group that fought for independence. He is regarded as a hero in Kosovo. He was accused of killing nearly 100 people and of committing other atrocities including enforced disappearances. Thaci was facing trial alongside three former commanders of the KLA who faced similar charges. Supporters of Thaci have gathered to hear the judgment The Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) was set up in the early 1990s as a militant group of ethnic Albanians, in what was then a province of Serbia, and during the war is alleged to have carried out attacks on the region's ethnic Serb minority. Thaci became Kosovo's first prime minister when it declared independence in 2008. He later became president but resigned in 2020 to face the charges in The Hague. Thousands of people gathered in Kosovo to watch the verdict on large screens as they were handed down. In the capital, Pristina, photographs and videos showed people in tears as they learned of the verdict. Kosovo ex-leader pleads not guilty to war crimes What was the Kosovo Liberation Army? title: Lucy Letby: Families' solicitor blames hospital bosses for police delay
description: The Thirlwall Inquiry found repeated failures by hospital leaders to act on concerns.
body: Tamlin Bolton represents seven of the families affected by Lucy Letby's crimes. A solicitor representing seven of the families affected by Lucy Letby's crimes has said responsibility for the delay in contacting the police "lies squarely" with hospital executives. On Tuesday, the Thirlwall Inquiry report revealed bosses at the Countess of Chester Hospital repeatedly failed in their duty of candour to parents, investigators and regulators. Tamlin Bolton said each of the 1,100 pages of Lady Justice Thirlwall's findings contained "another opportunity where action could have been taken". In a statement, former hospital executives named in the report said they were reviewing its findings and recommendations, but could not comment further while investigations remained under way. Lucy Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice. The offences took place between 2015 and 2016, but concerns raised by consultants were not reported to police until May 2017. Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others "The overriding conclusion is that responsibility for the delay in contacting the police lies squarely with the executives," said Bolton, from Irwin Mitchell. Bolton said two senior consultants had raised "legitimate concerns", but that they had gone unanswered. "They were bullied, threatened and marginalised. So the families knew there was an issue at this trust. There was a cultural divide caused by the approach taken by the executives." The report concluded chief executive Tony Chambers was "dictatorial" in his approach to consultants and that presentations by executives to the hospital board were an "exercise in spin". Bolton said the report had made for "difficult reading" but added that she hoped it would "bring change". Chambers issued a joint statement with other senior leaders named in the report, saying: "Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time. "Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital." While Bolton said she hoped the inquiry would prove to be a "pivot point", publication of the report came amid continuing efforts by some campaigners and medical experts to challenge Letby's convictions. Bolton criticised Letby's barrister, Mark McDonald, after he described the inquiry as having been based on a "false premise" of Letby's guilt. "The purpose of the inquiry was to bring in recommendations that would ensure children aren't harmed, so to call it redundant so outwardly seems quite an unusual stance to take", she said. Bolton added that protests outside Liverpool Town Hall during the publication of the report had also been "very difficult" for her clients to see. "The families place great reassurance in the fact that most of this evidence has been tested at several different levels by people who are experienced to test this evidence. "[The protest] is an entirely inappropriate response to a public inquiry designed to look at patient safety." title: Husband who drugged and raped wife for 20 years no longer part of trial
description: Twelve other men are still due to stand trial accused of serious sexual offences against the same woman.
body: The trial is being held at Minshull Street Crown Court in Manchester A man who drugged and raped his wife for more than 20 years without her knowledge will no longer be involved in a trial involving other defendants, a jury has heard. The husband, aged in his 60s and from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, has admitted a total of 60 offences against the woman including rape, assault by penetration, administering a substance with intent and sharing indecent images without her consent. Twelve other men are still due to go on trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court accused of serious sexual offences - including rape - against the same woman. The nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, have been asked to return to court on 5 October. The court has heard the husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, has admitted abusing his wife since 2004. He had already pleaded guilty to 15 offences against her going back to 2022, but admitted to a further 45 counts on Monday. His wife, who was comforted by other members of her family, watched from the public gallery as he answered "guilty" to dozens of charges. From left: Graham Brougham, Alan Keelan, Sean Peers, Jonathan Kirk and Jordan Wallace, along with seven others, will still be tried The other defendants in the case are alleged to have sexually abused her since September 2018. A 14th man has also pleaded guilty to sexual offences against the woman. On Wednesday morning the court heard that when the jurors were sworn in on 4 September they were given a questionnaire which included a short summary of the prosecution case. Trial judge Maurice Greene told them: "You were told, amongst other things, that the prosecution case concerns allegations of sexual offences by a number of men on a female. "You were told 14 men had been identified and one was [her husband]. "No doubt you will be wondering why you have not been back since. "Some of you may have seen or heard on the news on Monday that a man from Stockport had pleaded guilty to drugging and raping his wife, and had admitted multiple offences including rape, attempted rape, sexual assault and administering a substance with intent. "Now his identity is prohibited in the public domain to protect [his wife's] identity. Logical and obvious you may think. "Of course the man who pleaded guilty was [the husband], so he will no longer be a defendant in this case. As a result of these pleas there is work to be done by parties in this case." The other accused men are: Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire Richard Townsend, 37, from Rochdale Karl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, Somerset Daniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, Kent David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, Derbyshire Judge Greene told the jury he expected the prosecution to open the case on 5 October and that the trial should be completed by 18 December. title: Burnham thanks well-wishers following his father's death
description: All opposition leaders sent condolences to Burnham as he cancelled engagements earlier this week.
body: This video can not be played Andy Burnham: Dad would want me to be back out there Prime Minister Andy Burnham has thanked party leaders for their support following the death of his father, Roy, on Monday. All opposition leaders sent condolences to him as he cancelled engagements earlier this week. Burnham had previously spoken about the fact his dad did not know he had become prime minister, due to his advanced Alzheimer's. Posting on social media, he thanked, external "everyone who has shared a kind message about my dad, particularly the leaders of the other parties". Burnham added: "My family and I have been helped though this difficult time by people's warmth and compassion. It means a great deal to us and we wanted to say thank you." Speaking to journalists on his first day back at work on Wednesday, Burnham thanked all those who had sent "so many lovely messages" to him and his family. "It's hard and it will be hard for a little while but better to get back to the job," he said. "I also want to thank the leaders of the other parties, all of whom sent a message, and it shows there is decency in British politics still and that's lovely to see, so thank you from us all, the whole family. "But my dad would want me to be back out there bringing some of the changes that he always pushed me to make." He has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire. In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England. title: Parents of Southport attack victim 'devastated' by data breach
description: The Ministry of Justice says an urgent investigation has been launched after court files were accessed.
body: The attack happened in the Merseyside town in July 2024 The parents of a child injured in the Southport attack have said they are "devastated" after court files were accessed without authorisation. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said an urgent investigation had been launched after court files detailing victims, their families and survivors of the attack on the dance class in July 2024 were accessed without authorisation. It comes after it emerged earlier this year that the North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) was looking into whether staff inappropriately accessed the records of victims. The parents of one of the injured children said: "Our family has once again been devastated by two data breaches that involve our daughter, NWAS and now the MoJ." The parents, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, continued: "This culture of snooping across agencies and services must end and that will only happen if those individuals are held to account and not protected by the very confidentiality laws they flouted to access our daughter's information. "We expect each of these despicable individuals to lose their jobs, and full transparency from NWAS and the MoJ about what happened to the information they stole. "Two years on, our focus should be on our daughter's continuing recovery, not having to manage further failures by the state that have put our daughter at risk once again." From left to right: Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, were killed in the attack The family said their worst fear was the information could be used for profit. "We are exhausted by apologies. We are exhausted by offers to meet with government ministers and CEOs; all of which amount to nothing. "It is not acceptable any more to continue to heap more risk and stress on to our family and the other families affected." Nicola Ryan-Donnelly, partner at Fletchers Solicitors, which represents 22 of the 23 surviving children, called for the government to launch an independent investigation to address the "grim, voyeuristic culture" that prompted the data breach. She said: "Week after week we are learning of a new data breach against victims who have endured the worst atrocities this country has ever seen. "It is disgraceful that these public bodies have known of these breaches for months and only choose to disclose them as the media pressure mounts and their internal investigations are all but over. "These families have suffered enough trauma, they need transparency and accountability now." It is understood court staff accessed the files without approval and the data breach was discovered during a review of digital systems. The information accessed for a limited number of people included sensitive and personal data, which is considered likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. There is no evidence any personal data has been shared with third parties, but the incident has been referred to data watchdog, the Information Commissioner's Office. An MoJ spokesperson said: "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families. "We apologise to those affected – unauthorised access to court files is completely unacceptable. "This is now being investigated urgently, and the Prime Minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this. "All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action." The Prisons and Probation Service and the Courts and Tribunals Service are investigating, and anyone impacted is being notified directly. Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine; Bebe King, six; and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, were killed in the attack at the Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport on 29 July 2024. title: Legendary Nigerian actor Olu Jacobs dies aged 84
description: Olu Jacobs was one of Nigeria's most recognised actors, whose career spanned several decades.
body: His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns. Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84. His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns. Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought". Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day. He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country. "We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement. Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films. He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility. His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours. In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry. Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria. In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health. Were Christians the target of the Palm Sunday attack in Nigeria? title: Maresca criticises focus on controversial Manchester derby winner
description: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says it is "quite poor" that the controversy surrounding Erling Haaland's winner has overshadowed his side's win at Manchester United.
body: Enzo Maresca was part of Pep Guardiola's coaching staff at Manchester City before returning as manager Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca says it is "quite poor" that the controversy surrounding Erling Haaland's winner has overshadowed his side's performance at Manchester United on Sunday. Haaland's goal on the hour mark, which was awarded after the virtual assistant referee ruled in City's favour, secured a 1-0 Premier League victory despite the visitors playing the majority of the derby at Old Trafford with 10 men following Phil Foden's red card. The VAR decision was subsequently ruled to be incorrect by the referees' body and the aftermath of City's fourth successive league win has been dominated by the fall out from the incident. "Talking about one episode or one moment after that game when we played for 70- 75 minutes with 10 players, I think it's quite poor," Maresca said, speaking before Thursday's Carabao Cup third-round tie against Norwich City. "I think the performance was unbelievable, and I'm pleased with the performance." Haaland's goal was initially disallowed on the field for offside but the VAR review found the striker was just onside, and the goal was awarded. However, it soon became apparent that the officials had made an error in failing to identify an offside offence by Enzo Fernandez, diving at the ball in a central position and interfering with opponents. "There is knowledge that there was a mistake and that's all. Sometimes it goes for you, sometimes against you. It's football," the Italian said. This video can not be played Haaland scores controversial winner as Man City win derby despite Foden red Maresca, who succeeded Pep Guardiola in the summer, said previous VAR decisions have gone against City, including in a 2-1 defeat by United in January 2023. "Three years ago when I was here [as Guardiola's assistant], it happened the exact same against United," he said. "The goal was not a regular goal and no one apologised. We are still waiting for the apology for that." Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief Howard Webb has admitted the VAR did not consider whether Fernandez was offside before Haaland turned home the winner. "I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are," said Webb, speaking on 'Match Officials Mic'd Up'. "None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation." This video can not be played Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes in the 23rd minute and United hit the post either side of half-time before the Norwegian's controversial goal on Sunday. "The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland," said Webb. "He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal. "He doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score." City host Norwich on Thursday (19:30 BST) before returning to league action against Sunderland on Sunday, 20 September (14:00). title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says
description: The two countries accounted for 52% of killings of environmental activists in 2025, according to Global Witness.
body: Juan López was one of the environmentalists killed in Latin America recent years. The anti-mining activist was shot in Honduras in 2024. Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external. Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26. Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012. Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states. Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years. Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says. Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed. Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining. Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed. While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory. Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024. As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found. Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders. The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported. title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
description: Canada is seeking closer ties with EU after a breakdown in relations with the US and its president Donald Trump.
body: Mark Carney (left) walks alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (centre) and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (right) The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member". Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade. Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength". She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system". Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday. Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours. Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics. "And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy." She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation. Von der Leyen said it was time to bring the EU's relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible" Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems. In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark. But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years. Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status. Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership. In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying. Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada. Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia. "For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality." Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society. Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU. A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined. Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.
