title: Mbappe, Vini and Konate cover up Real's message of support for Ceuta
description: Vini Jnr, Mbappe and Konate cover up Ceuta message of support ahead of Real Madrid's match against Elche.
body: Real Madrid have won six out of seven matches in all competitions this season Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta. Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar. Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city. While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan. Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities. This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause. The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco. At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor. Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants. The representatives of the players have been asked for comment. The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time. Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game. The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign. Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended. title: White-tailed eagle chicks fledge for fourth year
description: The Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation reintroduction project began in 2019.
body: The reintroduction project began in 2019 and has since released 56 white-tailed eagles White-tailed eagle chicks have successfully fledged from wild nests in England for the fourth consecutive year. Two out of five pairs of eagles released by a reintroduction project successfully bred and raised young with one chick fledging from a nest in Dorset and two more in Sussex. The project, run by Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation, aims to return the species to England. Nine birds have been born in the wild since it began in 2019. "This year's breeding success is another important milestone in the return of this lost species to England; it shows what can be achieved by very skilled wildlife managers," Roy Dennis OBE from the foundation said. The foundation has called the breeding attempts "remarkable", adding that one of the male adult birds has only one leg after losing it five years ago. Human persecution had caused the bird's extinction, with the last pair breeding in southern England in 1780. "Restoring a species takes many years and requires the support of a wide range of communities and organisations, in particular landowners and farmers," Dennis added. Steve Egerton-Read, white-tailed eagle project officer for Forestry England, said: "We are delighted that these three chicks made it through and will be closely watching their progress as they begin to explore the landscape." To date, 56 young white-tailed eagles have been released including, for the first time this year, additional releases of six birds at Exmoor National Park, in partnership with Exmoor National Park Authority. title: Ranking the greatest all-time fantasy football icons
description: There's nothing quite like the satisfaction of unearthing an absolute Fantasy Premier League bargain - so who are the most iconic picks ever?
body: Scanning the newspaper, inky fingers and fuzzled minds, scrambling for the calculator and jotting down the codes for Julian Dicks and Juninho. These lads will carry the team until you remember to pick up the house phone and cash in a transfer a few months down the line. Before templates and triple captains there was a world of fantasy football that existed by writing out your XI and ringing in the names. Parents used it as a summer-holiday maths lesson. Yet whether in print or online, there's nothing quite like the satisfaction of unearthing an absolute bargain. That free-kick taking defender, the undervalued forward, out-of-position goal-getter or cheap keeper posting clean sheets. Since it began for the 2002-03 season, Fantasy Premier League has evolved into a huge database boasting millions of players across the globe, with substitutions and wildcards and the maths done for you. But who, over the past quarter of a century of the competition's official game, are the biggest icons of all time? With the help of our resident FPL expert Thomas Woods and some extensive research by the Fantasy Football Scout, that's what I'm digging into this week. Based on stats and a touch of sentiment - Michu, we see you - I've ranked my top 10 below. We'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments, too. Firstly, let's look at what makes a player iconic. Is it purely posting massive numbers? Thierry Henry's total from the inaugural season, for example, still ranks seventh overall. Indeed the Arsenal man was top scorer in three of the first four campaigns, but also the most expensive. Frank Lampard, arriving late in the box, topped the charts three times with his goals from midfield for Chelsea, while the twinkle-toed Cristiano Ronaldo did it twice at Manchester United. The pair rank fourth and fifth for best individual seasons, respectively. It's tempting to say we should discount such "obvious" picks for this debate, but then there's Mo Salah. The Liverpool asset might have eaten up a decent chunk of your budget, but packed guaranteed points for those premium pounds. As the Fantasy Football Scout explains, since the game began, 52 players have reached 200 points in a season at least once. Salah has done it eight times. And the Egyptian is the only player to ever top 300 points. In fact, he's done it twice. So Mo probably deserves a go. But we're really searching for those who have offered the most value over the years - cheap picks who seriously delivered. Some went on to become Premier League stars, others became cult heroes, one-season wonders or bargain buys who got virtual tongues wagging. 10. Harry Kane, Tottenham, 2014-15, starting price £5m England captain and record goalscorer, three-time Premier League Golden Boot winner. Harry Kane was hardly a secret at Tottenham, right? After a series of loans and having not yet established himself at White Hart Lane, the young Spurs striker began the 2014-15 campaign as a likely £5m back-up to Emmanuel Adebayor and Roberto Soldado. Kane didn't find the net until November in the Premier League, a 90th-minute winner after coming off the bench at Aston Villa, but it was the first of 21 goals in the competition that season as the homegrown striker established himself in Mauricio Pochettino's side. As the Fantasy Football Scout notes, an eight-match run from gameweek 18 to 25 saw Kane notch 77 points with nine goals, four assists and 16 bonus points. For those who gambled on him early, Kane proved a bargain. He rose from £5m to a peak £6.4m, racking up 191 points and ranking 11th on the all-time value list, despite playing fewer minutes than all those above him. Kane started at £5m but registered 191 points in 2014-15 9. Charlie Adam, Blackpool, 2010-11, £5m. The great budget enabler. Blackpool's Charlie Adam took penalties, free-kicks, corners and would probably have had goalkicks too if they let him. He'd had a good season in the Championship, scoring 16 times, but no one really gave the Seasiders any hope on their Premier League debut and thus there was little expectation on the Scottish midfielder from FPL bosses. Despite Ian Holloway's outfit eventually succumbing to the drop, Adam delivered a points tally that was only bettered by Manchester United's Nani that season - on the back of 12 goals, his 192 stood as the highest score by a promoted player at the time. Charlie Adam scored in Blackpool's defeat at Old Trafford on the final day of the season 8. Michel Vorm, Swansea, 2011-12, £4m Michel Vorm conceded four goals on his Premier League debut. That stacks up for a £4m keeper, you might think. Yet the Dutchman made 11 saves that day at Manchester City, more than anyone else would manage in a single game that season. Vorm swept Swansea City's end-of-term awards but also became a FPL legend in the process. He made saves but also kept clean sheets, 14 of them in total, and earned the second-most points for a goalkeeper behind City's Joe Hart, who started the game £3m more expensive. The Dutchman peaked in price at £5.3m and was the fourth-most owned player in the game at one point. Both virtually and in real life, it would be his standout season. Michel Vorm saves Clint Dempsey's penalty on his way to earning 158 points in the 2011-12 season 7. Stuart Dallas, Leeds, 2020-21, £4.5m Under Marcelo Bielsa, Stuart Dallas was a FPL dream. Racking up defensive clean sheets while operating further forward than his listed position suggested, cheap as you like, and even doing it against league heavyweights Manchester City, where he scored twice for 17 points. "The Northern Ireland international's versatility played into the hands of FPL managers because, even though he was a classified as a defender, he played all over the place for Leeds in 2000-21 - more often than not as an attacking midfielder," explains Woods. title: Watch: Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?
description: Sheeran's backing band and all of his support acts pulled out of his US tour, so what happens now?
body: This video can not be played Ed Sheeran's backing band and all of his support acts have pulled out of the artist's US tour. It began when rapper Macklemore was dropped from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made by his tour promoter, not him. title: Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says
description: South Korea's delegation slams the wooden containers housing its athletes at the Asian Games in Nagoya city.
body: These container houses are expected to house around 2,000 athletes at the Asian Games in Japan Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday. Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been". "Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable." The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected. The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too. Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games. Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them. Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations". They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said. As well as the container huts, thousands of athletes will be staying on board this Italian cruiseliner Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors. Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels. Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games. But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included. Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes. "There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements." But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation". "The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read. Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb". Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October. title: What is happening to UK prices?
description: UK inflation rose in August, pushed up by higher petrol and diesel prices.
body: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target. The rise was in line with what economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months. Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%. The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026, while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed. The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation. The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), external, and the latest figure is published every month. The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%. Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises. But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy. For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals. Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment. Although CPI inflation of 3.1% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That was the highest rate for 40 years. While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly. The higher figure for August was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 23% compared to August last year. Food price inflation remained at 1.3%. But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran. Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine. Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026. But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario. When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July. As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the increase in household energy bills from 1 July when the new Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher. The new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that VAT on household electricity bills will be scrapped, but that will not take effect until October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation. Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs. Core CPI was 2.6% in the 12 months to August 2026, unchanged from the 12 months to July. Why are UK fuel prices rising again? What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023. In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario. At its June meeting, just after a tentative agreement to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, the Bank held interest rates, but oil prices have since risen. The Bank held rates again in July and is expected to do the same in September, but it has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates. Will UK interest rates go up? The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment. The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to July. Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.5%. The ONS said this had been relatively stable in recent months, after a year of slowing growth. After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.6% between May and July. The 20-somethings juggling three jobs to make ends meet What needs to change to get more people working? The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation. The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.3% in August, according to EU data, external - up from 2.9% in July. The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%. US inflation was in 3.4% in August, the same as in July, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs. The Federal Reserve is set to make its latest announcement on interest rates later on Wednesday. President Donald Trump has made it clear he expects new Fed chair Kevin Warsh to cut rates more aggressively than his predecessor Jerome Powell. However, the central bank is widely expected to

title: Baby born during Harry Potter screening has 'Cineworld' on birth certificate
description: Elsie Lamb was born in the Cineworld at Broughton, Flintshire, about 40 minutes into the film.
body: Elsie Lamb was born at a Cineworld in north Wales A woman gave birth in a cinema after going into labour in the middle of a movie, with the newborn's birth certificate officially recording the unusual place of birth. Molly Connah, 32, had been overdue by a day when she took her nine-year-old son Alfie to see Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. Baby Elsie Lamb was born in the Cineworld at Broughton, Flintshire, with staff assisting and paramedics arriving moments later. Molly said the whole family had been in "complete utter shock" at the 7lb (3.2kg) arrival. Molly went to the cinema the day after her due date Molly said that when she went to register the newborn, she was asked where the baby was born. "We had to say Cineworld in Broughton, and it does say on her birth certificate, Cineworld Broughton," she said. Molly went to the cinema with her parents and Alfie on 28 August, the day after her due date, having attended a midwife appointment for a sweep earlier that afternoon. But about 40 to 45 minutes into the film, the labour pains began. Molly said: "I can remember the scene I was watching when I walked out. It was when Hagrid and Harry are buying his stuff to go to Hogwarts. "I thought, 'something doesn't feel right'. It was getting more and more intense, and I didn't want anything to go wrong. "At that point I think my body just went into shock and it was pure adrenalin." Cineworld manager Michelle McClean and team leader Leah Prytherch were among those who helped as staff called 999 and gathered towels and sheets. Molly said: "The staff at Cineworld and Starbucks were absolutely amazing. "They shielded me with towels and sheets so no-one could see. They were absolutely amazing." Describing the moment she gave birth, she said: "I said to my mum, 'I feel like I need to push,' and she said, 'you can't'. "I said, 'I can't, I need to. I've got to'. Two pushes and my daughter was out." Molly gave birth to Elsie Lamb at 16:57 BST. There were no medical professionals present at the moment Elsie arrived, with Molly's mum picking her granddaughter up and placing her on Molly's chest. A rapid response paramedic arrived moments later. Molly's partner Scott arrived seconds after his daughter had been born, having tried to call Molly three times while she was giving birth. Molly was taken to Wrexham Maelor Hospital in one ambulance while Scott accompanied Elsie in another. Molly said both she and Elsie are doing well, with the newborn described as a "really contented baby". The family have since returned to Cineworld to thank the staff who helped them, taking chocolates, gifts and a card. They were also given four cinema passes after missing the end of the Harry Potter film and hope to return to finish their unusual family outing. title: F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco
description: Formula 1 increases the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 World Championship.
body: Monaco will hold a sprint event for the first time in 2027 Formula 1 has increased the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 World Championship. Sprint events, which feature a shorter race on Saturday and an extra qualifying session on Friday, will be held for the first time in Bahrain, Australia, Japan, Monaco, and Abu Dhabi. The other sprints will be in Canada, Britain, Italy, Brazil, and Qatar, it was revealed as the calendar was formally announced. The maximum number of sprints previously in a season has been six. The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, followed by Saudi Arabia a week later, but both events will remain in doubt while the war in the Middle East continues. Bahrain is the default season-opening race, but Australia has hosted the first grand prix for the past two years because of the timing of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan. The 2026 season is due to end with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and while F1 is planning to complete the calendar as scheduled, it is working on contingency plans if those races cannot be held as a result of the continuing conflict between the US/Israel and Iran. The same applies for the start of next season as F1 considers its options for an alternative opening schedule if racing in the Middle East looks impossible by the end of this year. On Sunday, a summit involving some of the nations involved in or affected by the conflict released a statement urging "maximum restraint" in the war. The British Grand Prix will be on 2-4 July, and the 2027 season re-introduces races in Portugal and Turkey, returning for the first time since being used as placeholder events during the pandemic. Sprint events usually come at a higher price for race organisers but they are in demand because they increase the chance of selling more tickets, with competitive action on each of the three days of the meeting rather than only Saturday and Sunday. Silverstone believe holding a sprint this year was a large part of the reason for the British Grand Prix’s highest ever attendance - 64,000 more fans attended over the course of the four days compared with the year before, which was not a sprint. The inclusion of a sprint event in Monaco will inevitably raise eyebrows, given it is almost impossible to overtake around the historic street circuit. However, F1 is selling it on the fact that it means there will be two qualifying sessions at Monaco - qualifying around the demanding track is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. Two separate qualifying sessions could also provide two different grid orders, increasing variability. The flip side of a sprint in Monaco is that, because of the lack of overtaking opportunities, the finishing order of the sprint will be pretty much locked in once the cars have completed the first lap, barring accidents. F1 president and chief executive officer Stefano Domenicali said: "We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Turkey to the championship and to expand sprint racing to 10 events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special." Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of F1's governing body the FIA, said: "The 2027 FIA F1 World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport. "With 24 grands prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Turkey, and the opportunity for an expanded sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards." Pre-season testing is also scheduled to be held in Bahrain on 24-27 February. title: Council tax bills in Wandsworth could almost double
description: The council says it will have to raise council tax by that much unless the government rethinks cuts.
body: A Band D property in Wandsworth could see a council tax rise of £958 next year Wandsworth Council could raise council tax by £958 for a Band D property, an increase of 94%, under proposals described as "outrageous". The Conservative-led London borough said the rise was needed unless the government reconsidered cuts to its funding. Under changes, announced earlier this year, the council said it stood to lose £84m a year in funding by the end of the next three years. Plans to increase the council tax were heard at an extraordinary council meeting on Tuesday but a final decision will not be made until early next year. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the changes were needed to reform the "outdated" council funding system. Wandsworth has a long history of setting low council tax. While an increasing number of London boroughs have seen council tax on a Band D property rise above the £2,000 mark, in Wandsworth, council tax on an average Band D property is currently £1,020.35. Of that figure £509.84 is the part that the council sets and £510.51 of that is the Greater London Authority (GLA) precept set by the mayor of London. Wandsworth Council, along with Westminster City Council, Richmond Council and the Royal Borough of Kensington & Chelsea, is currently consulting on plans to use a piece of legislation called the Sustainable Communities Act to try to challenge the government proposals that would see its central government funding reduced. Changes to the funding formula for councils under the Fair Funding Review 2.0, external will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. After deciding to reduce their share of central government funding, the government gave five London boroughs - Kensington & Chelsea, Westminster, Wandsworth, Hammersmith & Fulham and the City of London - and Windsor and Maidenhead Council in Berkshire the power to raise council tax above the usual 5% cap for two years. At Tuesday's meeting, Conservative deputy leader and cabinet member for finance, Peter Graham, said he was reluctantly considering raising council tax and blamed the government. Graham said: "This administration recognises the financial pressures that many households already experience and the extent to which they are already taxed by other means. "Higher council tax will not be easy or welcome. We do not regard it as fair and will continue to challenge the government by every possible means. "Residents can help us with that challenge by responding to the consultation that was launched in the last week or so." The leader of the opposition, Labour councillor Simon Hogg, said: "Wandsworth Conservatives have decided to double your council tax. "It's outrageous, it is stunning. People who don't know how to run the council panicking and making you pay the price. "This increase is unfair, it's unnecessary and we oppose it." A MHCLG spokesperson said: "We have consulted extensively on reforming the outdated council funding system to ensure money goes where it is most needed, following on from a long-standing consensus... We're also protecting councils through transitional arrangements so no area faces a cliff edge." A final decision on how much local people will pay in council tax will not be made by the council leadership until February next year. title: Alcohol consumption scorecard to help track intake
description: The Health Improvement Commission says it is to help people get a clearer picture of their intake.
body: The Health Improvement Commission for Guernsey and Alderney said residents would receive the scorecard through their letterbox An alcohol consumption campaign with scorecards to monitor units, is aimed at helping islanders make informed decisions about their health. The Rethink Your Drink scheme, set up by the Health Improvement Commission for Guernsey and Alderney, encourages residents to fill in scorecards noting their weekly alcohol intake and compare the results to the recommended guidelines. The charity said islanders will receive a scorecard through their letterbox. Andrea Nightingale, substance use lead at the Health Improvement Commission, said the scorecard was "a simple, interactive and engaging way to help people understand their intake". More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey The charity said the 2023 Wellbeing Survey found that 35.2% of adults aged 16 and over who drink alcohol reported consuming more than 14 units a week. The UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk drinking guidelines, external recommend men and women drink no more than 14 units per week, spread over three or more days, with at least two alcohol-free days each week. The commission added alcohol units can be difficult to estimate, so the scorecard provides "a tried and tested tool" to help people calculate their weekly units and compare their results to the guidelines. Nightingale said: "The scorecard is about helping people get a clearer picture of where they are today and giving them the confidence to think about where they would like to be tomorrow. "Small changes really can add up to a big difference, and for many people, simply knowing their number could help them consider whether any changes might benefit their health and wellbeing." title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
description: The US president has pushed the issue to the forefront of American politics - even at the risk of losing supporters.
body: This video can not be played Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI? According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax. It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term. Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology. The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party. OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will. Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies. "We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate." Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI. "Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing." This video can not be played Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in? According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies." A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order. It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs. Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development. But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead? Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years. According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026. The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI. Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion. Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind. "We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins." The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control. Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative. Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president. "I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear." Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this admi

title: Village votes to leave UK over asylum housing plan in symbolic referendum
description: Piddington residents vote over proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers nearby.
body: Villagers voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic referendum Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base. Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester. The 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall, the community hub of Piddington. The referendum was organised by the local parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, there were 26 no votes, and one ballot paper was spoiled. Delivering the result, Susannah Parden, vice chair of the parish council, said: "We are Piddington the village that roars." Following the result, council chair Tim McNally said: "This is an example of democracy in operation. "We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world." Responding to the village saying it had "roared", Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told BBC Breakfast: "I think they have – we have heard it, we are listening. "I do really understand that when changes are made that affect your community it can be very distressing. "We inherited an enormous asylum backlog, we are processing claims much more quickly, we are removing people who don't have the right to be here," she said. "Small boat crossings fell this summer for the first time in many years because of the action we have taken. "While we get a grip on the asylum chaos that we inherited we do need to make sure that we live up to our obligations and house people coming to this country seeking safety." A "Principality of Piddington" sign has been placed on the village boundary Joe Marshall, a Piddington parish councillor, said the village could elect leaders for its new "principality" and even create ID cards. Asked how far it could take its independence campaign, Marshall said it depends on how much the government was willing to listen. He added its main aim was to encourage other communities unhappy with local decisions "to push for similar things". He cited the Principality of Sealand as inspiration - a former military platform in the sea off East Anglia declared an independent territory in 1967. Tim Beader, Oxfordshire County Council leader, said the campaigners had done an incredible job at highlighting their concerns about the proposed asylum centre. "It's partially about the proposal itself, and partially about how the government has gone about this without engaging with the local community or looking at the feasibility of this site," he said. "It's the wrong site for the local communities, for the asylum seekers themselves, and for the taxpayer." The Home Office announced the plans in June as part of wider proposals to move migrants out of hotels. Known as "Site A", MoD Bicester is located between the villages of Piddington and Upper and Lower Arncott. In 2005 it was the target of similar plans for an asylum seekers accommodation centre, external, which were abandoned by the then-Labour government. This year's announcement sparked widespread criticism, including from the district council and human rights groups, with many residents expressing shock. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned. Piddington falls within the constituency of Lib Dem MP for Bicester, Calum Miller. He previously said the plans had been "veiled in secrecy" and that the process did not guarantee public participation "beyond a narrow list of statutory bodies". title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
description: The Houthis deny targeting the Islamic holy city after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen accuses them of a "disgraceful act".
body: The Houthis denied they had targeted Mecca, where Islam's most sacred shrine is located Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act". The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression". But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies". "There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said. Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province. There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour". On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city. Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities. The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces. Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal. The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week. The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. title: Fernandez signs new London City contract
description: London City Lionesses defender Jana Fernandez signs a new contract, keeping her at the club until 2029.
body: Jana Fernandez joined London City in August 2025 from Barcelona London City Lionesses defender Jana Fernandez has signed a new contract, keeping her at the club until 2029. The 24-year-old has become a key player for Eder Maestre’s side since joining from Barcelona a year ago. She played in every Women’s Super League match for London City last season as they finished sixth in their debut campaign in the top flight. Her performances at right-back earned her the fans’ votes for club player of the season. "I'm absolutely delighted to sign a new contract here at London City," said Fernandez. "When I arrived in England one year ago I joined this club with dreams for the future. "Potential, excitement and progress are three words I associate with the club and I'm pleased to commit my future. I feel at home and settled here. "We are building something special together, as players, staff and fans, and I can't wait to play my part." Before her move to England, Fernandez spent her career at Barcelona, graduating from their academy and becoming a five-time league champion. She also won the Champions League and Copa de la Reina three times. Fernandez was part of the Spain team that finished runners-up to England at Euro 2025. She has been joined at London City by former Barcelona team-mates Alexia Putellas - the two-time Ballon d'Or winner - and Mapi Leon. Under US billionaire owner Michele Kang, London City hope to break into the WSL's traditional top three and qualify for the Champions League. Having attracted big names in the summer, it was crucial London City retained their other talent, and they have been able to do that with Fernandez and England winger Freya Godfrey committing their futures in recent months. title: Trio bag ultra-marathon's first women-only UK podium
description: At the Hardwick Estate in Derbyshire, competitors ran a 4.16-mile course every hour.
body: Three women came in first, second and third place in the mixed-sex event Three women scooped the top spots in an ultra-marathon race in Derbyshire, which organisers said made it a first for the event in this country. The Rasselbock Backyard Ultra, in which competitors run a 4.16-mile course every hour, on the hour, until only one person is left standing, was held at the Hardwick Estate on Saturday. There were 141 competitors, and 21% of them were women and 79% men, and race organisers said this was the first occasion an all-female podium was recorded in the UK for a backyard ultra. Matt Dillon, from Hardwick Hall, said: "Given our history and connection with Bess of Hardwick, it feels fitting that female runners made their mark on the event here." Are women better than men at endurance running? The runner who went viral and sparked a campaign for change for women 'I wasn't sporty but I've won a 268-mile race' The Hardwick Estate, now owned by the National Trust, was once home to Bess of Hardwick, who was described as a "bold businesswoman, house builder, mother and wife," and widely regarded as the second most powerful woman of the Tudor age. Speaking about Saturday's event, Dillon added: "It promised to be an exciting event and for it to have achieved records, made it an even more memorable weekend. "This was an extraordinary event organised by Rasselbock and we were very pleased to have been part of it." Runners navigated a course at Hardwick Hall through a farm and shared the path with sheep and cattle The event organisers said Becky Atkinson, from west Wales, won the competition and despite it being her first Rasselbock Backyard Ultra race, she completed 40 hours of continuous running, reaching a total distance of 166.4 miles. Second and third place went to Hayley Wilson, from Worksop in Nottinghamshire, and Hollie Jones, from Easby in Yorkshire. Eric Keeler, the event organiser, said: "We went through thousands of results worldwide and an all-female winning line-up has only happened once before - in Iceland. "Becky's 40-hour debut, and a female top three, was an exciting result for the event." He said the Hardwick event was uniquely challenging. "It features the smallest start line across the series in this country due to single-track trails and estate gates," he added. "Runners navigate a course through a farm and share the path with sheep and cattle, which is always a fun experience, especially at night!" More than 700 Rasselbock Backyard Ultra events take place globally each year, with 55 held across the UK. This video can not be played Watch: Are women better suited to endurance exercise than men? The event comes after recent BBC Sport article examined whether women are better at endurance running than men. It said there was on average a 10% to 12% performance gap between males and females in running distances up to the marathon. This is because men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine. However, as distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow. The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study, external of more than 10 years of amateur ultra-race conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners. Prof Andy Jones, in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, said there were three potential physiological explanations as to why women could perform better over long distances or durations. Fat metabolism. Women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer Muscles. Women have more oxygen-efficient fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities Fatigue resistance. title: At least 12 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
description: Dozens of people are missing beneath the rubble of the building in Gaza City, where 10 families had reportedly been living.
body: Locals said 10 families had been living in the building despite warnings that it was unsafe At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams. Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together. Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe. Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery. On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources. The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed. Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. title: Woods seen on range for first time since car crash
description: Tiger Woods says he "can hit pretty much anything" after returning to the range for the first time since a car crash six months ago.
body: Tiger Woods has not competed at a major since missing the cut at The Open in July 2024 Tiger Woods says he "can hit pretty much anything" after returning to the range for the first time since a car crash six months ago. The 15-time major champion was seen hitting balls at Liberty National in New Jersey in a video shared on his Instagram, external before the Nexus Cup, a charity event he is hosting to raise funds for his TGR Foundation. Woods, 50, also held a clinic where he was asked by the master of ceremonies about his game and replied: "I can hit pretty much anything." It comes six months after the golfer rolled his Land Rover in Florida and had to crawl out of the passenger door of the car. He refused a urine test. Earlier this month, Woods accepted a five-year suspension of his driving licence and a $1,000 (£742) fine, as part of a plea agreement with prosecutors in Martin County, Florida, after not contesting a reckless driving charge. This video can not be played Watch bodycam footage of Tiger Woods' arrest It remains unclear whether Woods is preparing for a comeback. He has not played competitively since 2024 after rupturing an Achilles tendon in March 2025 and having back surgery last October. After March's road accident - his second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence - Woods said he was "stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health". It was the latest in a string of incidents that have littered Woods' recent years. His marriage ended - as did lucrative sponsorship deals - after he struck a fire hydrant, a tree and several hedges outside his home in a 2009 incident, sparking accusations of extra-marital affairs. In 2017, he was sentenced to a year's probation after pleading guilty to reckless driving. That came after police officers found Woods slumped at the wheel of his car near his home. In 2021, Woods survived a serious accident which left him with extensive injuries and he played only a limited schedule since then. title: Rescued moon bears arrive at Suffolk forever home
description: The bears, rescued from a bile farm, are beginning their new lives in a wildlife park
body: The rescued moon bears have arrived in Suffolk from South Korea Five moon bears that spent decades living in cages in South Korea have arrived at their new home in Suffolk. Jimmy's Farm & Wildlife Park near Ipswich and its charity, Space for the Wild, transported the animals 5,500 miles (8,850km) to their new forever home at the park. The bears, which arrived on Thursday, had been kept at one of South Korea's last bear bile farms – sites which have now been banned in the country. Jimmy Doherty, founder of the wildlife park, said the bears would now live a "profoundly better life". Jimmy Doherty said it was "heartbreaking to see" what the bears had been through "I will never forget meeting the bears for the first time," he said. "It was truly hell on earth. You cannot unsee these things. "It made us all the more determined and focused on our mission - to get these bears safe, protected and living a profoundly better life. "The work, dedication and public support of so many have made this a reality. I couldn't be more grateful to all involved." The moon bears were rescued from bile farms in South Korea The rescued bears - Bara, Rumi, Saebit, Yonggi and Huimang - are enjoying a new reserve at the park created specifically for them. It includes space for them to climb, swim and rest among trees and grass. The park launched a campaign to fund the rescue and has raised more than £90,000 out of a target of £200,000. South Korea banned the breeding and possession of the bears last year, along with the extraction of bile from their gallbladders. The bile was used in medicines while the bears themselves were often kept in poor conditions. Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. title: 'He's an idiot, but he's our idiot' - Saints fans on Pollock contract stand-off
description: How has a drawn-out and public contract negotiation affected the relationship between Henry Pollock and Northampton Saints fans?
body: Henry Pollock's exurberant on-pitch persona has pulled in a raft of young fans Henry Pollock is determined not to blink first in his contractual face-off. Despite a deal with Northampton being close, amid reports of an agreement of about £400,000 a year,, external the back row stressed on Monday that his renewal was not signed. He is, he says, still open to offers. Asked if he was looking forward to the end of the saga, stoked by Pollock's advisor Eddie Hearn, Saints director of rugby Phil Dowson joked that "it would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago". The haggling has certainly played out more publicly than most negotiations. Has it taken some of the sheen off a player who was key to Saints winning the Prem title last season and whose public profile has brought new supporters and attention, not just to his club but to his sport in general? Lis Saunders is the chair of the Northampton Saints Supporters Group. "I have known Henry coming up through the academy and he is absolutely delightful," she told BBC Sport. "The perception of his arrogance is wrong. He is just a young bouncy man, living his best life. "Some people are getting a bit fed up with the whole theatre around [the contract stand-off], though. "I am laissez-faire about it. If he stays it will be brilliant, but you can't keep someone who wants to go. "The whole theatre around it is what will grind people's gears. You are starting to see that on some of the fan forums – people saying, 'Either sign or don't. Just don't mess around - we don't need this drama.'" Saunders points out that, while Pollock can pull a crowd, Saints invariably fill Franklin's Gardens anyway. The turnstiles will carry on clicking at the same rate regardless of his presence. It would be an emotional wrench rather than a financial loss if he moves elsewhere. "As the players themselves say, he's an idiot, but he's our idiot," said Saunders. "We've watched him grow up and he's very much ours. It would be really sad if he didn't stay - perhaps understandable, but really sad." Charles McGillivray is one of the hosts of Beneath the Lift Tower,, external a Northampton Saints podcast run by fans and named after the landmark that looms over Franklin's Gardens. He says the stand-off has split fans, even if Pollock, who was superb at the end of last season, still has the support of the majority. "There are probably two ends of the spectrum," he said. "You've got some fans who are just reading headlines, may not be as engaged as others and don't really understand the mechanics of how rugby clubs in England work, with the salary cap and things like that. "But most Saints fans are fairly grounded. They understand that Eddie Hearn coming to Henry Pollock's career is going to be brilliant for the sport and together they're going to make lots of noise. "And they also understand that the money being quoted [Hearn says Pollock is worth £1m a season] isn't really feasible to be earned by someone in England. "We think he's a grounded - if ambitious - lad and therefore Northampton is the best place for him to be. "There isn't a club in England at the moment developing talent at the rate of knots or to the level that Northampton is. And maybe only Bath are having the continued success that Northampton are having." McGillivray's co-host Simon Stacey, who has been following the club for 40 years, points out that Northampton fans have seen first hand the risks that players run for their rewards. In 2018 Saints centre Rob Horne went in for a hard but routine tackle and incurred nerve damage that cost him the use of his right arm. "I don't hold any grudges against Henry," said Stacey. "It doesn't annoy me. I get that they do need to get what they can because it's a short career and they have to look after themselves." Fin Smith (right) is believed to occupy Northampton's 'marquee' slot for salary cap regulations at the moment With a club's spending on salaries capped at £6.4m - with another £1.4m available in various credits and compensations - a bumper pay deal for one player at a Prem club reduces the money available for others. Last autumn scrum-half Alex Mitchell said he and others had prioritised the togetherness, external and quality of Saints' squad over "mega money" elsewhere when opting to re-sign. While Northampton did not pay up to the salary cap in the most recent report on Prem club finances, which covers the 2024-25 season, a raft of renewals is likely to take them closer to the limit in the coming years. However, if Pollock's stance is causing ructions in the squad, they are hiding it well. Fly-half Fin Smith momentarily joined Hearn in lobbying for Pollock to be granted a £1m annual salary this month, telling reporters that "he's worth it" before joking that Pollock had sent him out to do a bit of PR on his behalf. Dowson dropped a request into the squad's group chat, asking if the squad could borrow the private jet Hearn had laid on for Pollock to visit him on the French Rivera. As Pollock gave an interview on Monday, soberly stressing that the forthcoming season could be his last at the club, his straight face briefly broke as Mitchell smirked at him from across the room. Pollock poses with Barry Hearn, father of Eddie, and UFC fighter Ian Machado Garry Hearn has said he found Pollock's current earnings at Northampton, thought to be about £150,000 a year, to be unbelievable. And not in a good way. Certainly, Pollock, one of the faces of the sport, is due a significant pay raise. The league's latest salary cap report is revealing. His current salary is below that of the 2024-25 league average of £191,000. Of the players in his current age bracket (20-22) that season, 27% were paid more than he is now. title: Watch: BBC crew catch thieves in act while filming shoplifting report
description: BBC crew catch thieves in act while filming shoplifting report.
body: This video can not be played A BBC team who came to a Greggs to talk to staff and customers about shoplifting were confronted by thieves openly stealing in front of them. Two men with rucksacks did not bother to hide their faces as they ransacked the fridge for more, swearing angrily at a female worker who tried to stop them, at the outlet in Bearwood, near Birmingham. Workers told the BBC the brazen 55-second raid was all in a day's work, with offenders targeting the outlet multiple times every day. Greggs says it takes the industry-wide problem of shoplifting "extremely seriously", has enhanced security measures across its outlets and works closely with police. title: US limits visas for South African officials over alleged anti-white discrimination
description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says South Africa has not addressed US concerns over racial inequality.
body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says South Africa has not addressed US concerns over racial inequality The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries. The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers. South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim. "The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid ​out concerns," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the restrictions on Tuesday. He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa." Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions. Ramaphosa struggles to mend fences with Trump Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution." But the South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land. It said claims of a white genocide had been widely discredited and lacked reliable evidence. South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that more white people have fallen victim to violent crime than other racial groups. Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances. The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court. Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights. The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures. Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population. In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States". He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities. "The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added. He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law." The South African government is yet to respond to the US restrictions. The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations. It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter." South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House last May with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers. But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited. Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa. The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests. title: Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher
description: Summer holidays and disruption to global oil supplies by the Middle East conflict stoked price growth.
body: UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the year to August after petrol, diesel and airfares stoked price growth. Inflation accelerated from 2.9% in the 12 months to July, according to the Office for National Statistics. Petrol and diesel prices increased further as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. The cost of flying also jumped during the key month for summer getaways. Inflation has moved further away from the Bank of England's 2% target. The bank uses interest rates to control inflation. The rate currently stands at 3.75% and the Bank of England is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to change it. title: Runaway horse captured by police on motorbikes
description: The unharmed horse escaped from its owner before the start of a parade in New Mexico
body: This video can not be played A runaway horse was chased by police on motorbikes in Santa Fe, New Mexico, when it escaped before a parade on 13 September. The unharmed horse was eventually cornered by police, before being lassoed. Police officers followed and cornered the horse on motorbikes, before it was wrangled by a lasso-carrying cowboy. The horse was given a drink of water before being walked back to the start of the Desfile de la Gente parade, Santa Fe Police Department said in a post on Facebook. title: NZ apologises to children forced to live in bush for years with fugitive dad
description: A public inquiry has found that agencies "missed key opportunities" to recover the children sooner.
body: Tom Phillips was not completely cut off from the outside world, the inquiry found New Zealand has apologised to the three children of Tom Phillips who vanished with their father for years until he died in a police shootout after an inquiry found authorities failed to protect them. "There were missed opportunities... and we're sorry about the impact that it's had on those children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said on Wednesday. Agencies involved had "underplayed, minimised or overlooked" how the significant periods of isolation harmed the children, the inquiry found. When Phillips took his kids, then aged five, seven and eight, into the bush in December 2021, it wasn't the first time he had disappeared with them. Yet they would not be found for almost four years. Police did not initially launch a search and rescue operation because of a "misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children's welfare", according to the inquiry's findings published on Tuesday. Former High Court justice Simon Moore, who authored the report, was the sole member of the inquiry. The report also criticised various agencies involved for "often minimising" concerns raised by the children's mother, which include concerns around firearm safety, "as being part of a parenting dispute". Phillips died in a shootout with police on 7 September 2025 in the small town of Piopio in New Zealand's North Island. The three children have been under the care of authorities since. Police later released photographs of what they believe to be one of many squalid campsites where Phillips hid with his children, showing a stash of firearms, ammunition and cans of beer surrounded by dense vegetation. Phillips' case has gripped New Zealand since the day he disappeared. It has also prompted public outrage as to how a fugitive father, who had three children with him, could have evaded authorities for so long. Among the "missed opportunities" the inquiry identified were a handful of reported sightings of Phillips and his children during their years of disappearance, which agencies could have more promptly followed up on. Through interviews with Phillips' family members, among others, the inquiry found that he was not completely cut off from the outside world. For instance, he visited his mother without the children in February 2022, during which she handed him NZ$1,000 ($575; £426) in cash and food. He also managed to move through the community during an hours-long shopping trip in August 2023 where he visited various businesses in the Waikato region. He spent nearly NZ$6,000 in a single day on a haul of goods which include food, children's clothing, gardening supplies, fishing gear, knives and lighters, among other things, the inquiry found. The inquiry also said the agencies involved – the police, the national child protection agency Oranga Tamariki, the defence force and the ministry of education – could have communicated and coordinated more with each other to better protect the children's welfare. On Wednesday, Luxon also apologised to the children's mother, acknowledging that they were "let down through this process that spent four years in the bush". Apart from the prime minister, other government representatives have also apologised and accepted the inquiry's findings. "To the Phillips children directly, this report has found that our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you. For that we are deeply sorry," Social Development Minister Louise Upton said on Tuesday. Upton acknowledged how the children spent four years "in squalid conditions which deprived them of... a happy and healthy childhood". Deputy Police Commissioner Jill Rogers acknowledged the police's failings but said the investigators involved in the case had "put [in] their hearts and souls". "Did it take too long? Did we miss opportunities? Yes, we did. You know, you can't unsee the images of where those children were living in those campsites... It's heart-breaking," Rogers told Breakfast, a talk show produced by local news service 1News. She went on to say: "We have to be better in this. But at the end of the day, our responsibility was to recover the children, and that is what we did."
