title: Why are Man Utd better without the ball?
description: Under Michael Carrick, Manchester United average 1.5 points per game when they have more than 50% of the ball. When they have less than 50%, this number is 2.6.
body: This video can not be played Why Man Utd are less likely to win when they have more of the ball... Under Michael Carrick, Manchester United average only 1.5 points per game when they have more than 50% of the ball. When they have less than 50%, this number shoots up to 2.6. And if you drop possession further, to 45% or below, United have won 10 games out of the past 10 since Carrick took the job. It is a staggering correlation but it brings the Englishman to the same crossroads that former United manager Ole Gunnar Solskjaer found himself at. How do you bridge the game from a seemingly elite counter-attacking side to one capable of beating teams that give you the ball? The answer has long eluded United. Going down to 10 men on the way to a 1-0 derby defeat is far from ideal, but at full-time Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca offered a different perspective. "We had a plan for 11 versus 11, but after the red card the game completely changed, but also for them. "They love transitions and space in behind, but the game became more difficult. "We just dropped, [offering] no space in behind and no more transitions, which is why the game was also more difficult for them." This was an astute analysis of United's most recent game as well as their team this year. As divisive as the phrase "United DNA" is, it undoubtedly remains a key part of the conversation about United both externally and internally. This is because certain coaches have leaned into the club's roots, while others have tried but failed to move away from those ideas. "We want to win; we want to be excited - that's why we love this club. I'm fully aware that we need to do it in a certain way," said Carrick when asked what style of football he wanted his United side to play. Here he echoed the sentiment of United's most successful manager, Sir Alex Ferguson, who in 2017 said: "You have a duty to entertain. We have to always remember there's a public to be entertained." With excitement seemingly non-negotiable for Ferguson, it is obvious why fans and players of that era resonate with a United that create spectacles. Dynamic, direct and open games are sought after to remain connected to a United they recognise. Solsjkaer's side embodied United's DNA before Ruben Amorim looked to play a more choreographed and risk-averse style of play. Carrick went back in the opposite direction. Having established the context, we can take a closer look at how this has manifested on the pitch. With the messaging around Carrick's style of play being one of proactivity, excitement and directness, it is no surprise that United look better with space to attack – something that happens more often for a team with less of the ball. The strengths of the squad are suited to this approach, with goalkeeper Senne Lammens a good long kicker of the ball. In defenders Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez, United have punchy progressive passers from deep too. In attack, Marcus Rashford is a willing runner in behind, often moving into a striker position despite starting on the wing. The same can be said for Bryan Mbeumo. Bruno Fernandes, central to all of this, is a strong passer when attacking in transition, finding runners ahead of him – a role in which he broke the Premier League assist record last term. Bruno Fernandes recorded 21 Premier League assists last season, in large part because of how Michael Carrick platformed him Carrick has also provided certain players a level of freedom to make their own decisions on the pitch. "Giving Bruno the platform to go and perform [has helped him]," Carrick said in April. "We're trying to create a structure to try to bring out the best of everyone, but I like seeing Bruno in attacking positions with a bit of freedom." Although players may enjoy this responsibility, how the team play can be swayed by individual players' natural tendencies. With more risk-taking, direct passers in the side, when United are asked to disorganise stubborn defences their long-standing habits can mean losing the ball more often. When dominating the ball, breaking down a team requires strong one-against-one wingers. Defending teams often clog the centre of the pitch, as City did in the derby, forcing the attacking side to the flank. City's Jeremy Doku, Arsenal's Bukayo Saka, Bayern Munich's Michael Olise and Paris St-Germain's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia have been key in helping those sides win often – while keeping the ball. This season United have used a 4-2-4 shape in possession. The full-backs have pushed up and taken turns with the wingers to hold wide or narrow positions. This, however, often results in Luke Shaw, Patrick Dorgu, Diogo Dalot and Mbeumo – not the strongest one-v-one dribblers - isolated on the wing. Amorim used a system without wingers and the squad built as a result – with the exception of Rashford and Amad Diallo – appear underprepared to create chances from out wide. With wide play an area of concern, play is often funnelled back infield. Carrick has primarily used Fernandes and Matheus Cunha as a floating front two, both with licence to drop deep or pull wider. Both players are more suited to facing the opposition's goal, rather than playing with their back to goal in small spaces, which makes it hard for United to capitalise through the middle. City's Rayan Cherki and Arsenal's Kai Havertz are players suited to this role, albeit in different ways. Fernandes and Cunha's quality means they can still be effective in these positions, often forming triangles with the full-back and wingers, helping United get into the final third. But as they both vacate the striker position, United end up lacking bodies in the box when they play crosses in. In this example against Ipswich, highlighted are Bruno Fernandes and Cunha, United's front two. Both have dropped deep and moved towards the ball. title: Brass band trumpets 14th win as Britain's best
description: Foden's Band, known as one of the world's best brass bands, adds another title to its collection.
body: Foden's Band will be celebrating its 125th anniversary in 2027 A 124-year-old brass band known for being one of the best in the world has won its 14th British title. Foden's Band came out on top at the 172nd British Open Brass Band Championship, held at the Symphony Hall in Birmingham on Saturday. It was the latest accolade won by the group, from Sandbach, Cheshire, which has often been at the top of the world rankings since it formed in 1902. "We're over the moon; the band played fantastic," said Mark Wilkinson, the manager and principal cornet player. The win added another trophy to Foden's collection, which includes 16 National Championships of Great Britain titles and seven Brass in Concert victories. Conductor Russell Gray said the band's success took a lot of practice, and it did not "happen by itself". The brass band has won numerous championships over the years "The dedication these musicians put into the craft is phenomenal," he told BBC Radio Stoke. "I'm always in awe that they actually hold down day jobs as well and then come into the band room in the evening to play so magnificently." Despite all the pressure and hard work that goes into playing "at the highest level", Gray said it was important to remember that it was still a "hobby". But he added: "You choose to do a hobby; you don't choose to do it badly, do you? You don't go fishing to not catch a fish." Foden's victory at the British Open, which featured 19 bands, meant it would be invited to represent England at the European Championships in 2028. Wilkinson, who also won best cornet player at Saturday's contest, said he still got "extremely nervous", not least because of the band's legacy. "We're the custodians," he added, "so we want to do a fantastic job just like the players before us so we can pass on this legacy to the next generation." title: Shoplifters carrying shopping lists, says M&S manager
description: The Marks and Spencer area manager for Shropshire says shoplifting is a "really large issue".
body: Elisa Lewis said there was no such thing as a ”typical“ shoplifter Shoplifters walk into branches of Marks & Spencer with a list in an attempt to get away with hauls worth thousands of pounds, a regional manager says. Elisa Lewis, who is responsible for M&S shops in Shropshire, said shoplifting was a "really large issue" and could be "a daily, possibly even hourly, occurrence". "In my experience it can be anybody," she said. "It can be a bored housewife who's just nicking a jacket for a bit of fun, and the people who we do catch are sometimes those we least expect." Some shoplifters were people experiencing alcohol or drug dependence who said they were "just doing it to survive". As a physically smaller woman, she said she found tackling some of them "intimidating", but had become more hardened to it through experience. Figures collected by the BBC show a slight fall in the number of shoplifting offences across England and Wales in the past financial year and that was mirrored in the West Mercia police force area. Marks and Spencer has a policy of issuing lifetime bans to shoplifters, which Lewis said could be a big deterrent and a big shock, especially to younger offenders. But she said sometimes it turned out to be a genuine accident and they took people to their in-house detention room to try to understand their motivations before acting. Cath Harmer, from Shrewsbury Business Improvement District, says it is important shops continue to report shoplifting In some cases it is no accident though, and she said: "They've come in with a special order, and they go around stealing to order, and that can go into thousands of pounds depending on what people are asking for." She said the run up to Christmas was always a peak time for shoplifting, with people wanting presents and money. She also said the quieter times of the day tended to be the peak hours. "Usually you find in your first hour of trade is where you get people who are reliant on money, drugs, etc," she said. "They will head for your meat, your alcohol, your suits, because that's what they'll get the most money for." PC Joseph Bradley says he has spent 16 years trying to foster relationships with traders in Shrewsbury Lewis said she had seen the level of shoplifting increase and decrease in line with the cost of living, but added: "When there is a presence in the town, they are deterred." Insp Ingrid Tozer, the West Mercia Police officer responsible for Shrewsbury town centre, said an increased police presence there was making a difference. Since October there have been six police officers and a sergeant based in the town, and she said incidents of shoplifting had fallen. "The feedback has been fantastic," she said, and the force believed it had issued criminal behaviour orders to the most prolific offenders. But engaging traders has been a challenge. PC Joseph Bradley, one of the police officers based in Shrewsbury, said: "We spent quite a bit of time trying to encourage the shops to report thefts into us. "We went through a period when we weren't necessarily getting a lot of reports in." He has worked in the town for 16 years and said he had spent a lot of time building up relationships with traders to make that happen. That was backed up by Cath Harmer from Shrewsbury BID - a group that represents businesses in the town. She is the Safer Shrewsbury coordinator, responsible for the Shrewsbury Rangers, external - a security team which patrols the streets, assisting shopkeepers and the police. Harmer said: "There is a tendency for retailers to absorb that theft rather than reporting it," and added she wanted to make sure they continued reporting crime. title: Three dead after LA news helicopter crashes while covering deadly bus collision
description: The NBCLA news helicopter was flying near the scene of a fatal bus crash.
body: This video can not be played Smoke and flames rise from Los Angeles fatal helicopter crash site Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said. NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash. The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC. The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said it was not yet known how many people were onboard, and no victim names had been released. Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD said. During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed. "We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said. Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed. "That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said. Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash. Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported. LAPD's Central Division posted on X that it extended "thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles". Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight". "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she added. California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family". "Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight." The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident. title: Traffic, tourism and economy among election concerns
description: Residents and business owners in Onchan discuss key concerns ahead of the House of Keys election.
body: Sally Hellwich has lived in Onchan for 30 years and runs a family business Residents and business owners in Onchan have said traffic, tourism and the cost of living are among their key concerns ahead of the 2026 House of Keys election. The constituency has the second largest population on the Isle of Man after Douglas, and sits along the east coast. Sally Hellwich, who runs a family travel business, has lived in Onchan for 30 years. She said she had 'lived, worked, and breathed Onchan" and was "sad" no candidates had considered tourism as a priority. She said: "I truly believe that tourism underpins the Isle of Man. And if we don't have tourists, we're not generating income for the economy." As a mother, she added that housing was another big concern for younger generations. She said: "There's not enough access to housing," adding: "Trying to get on the housing ladder now is just ridiculous." Onchan is the second largest populated constituency on the island For Onchan mum Lara, speeding traffic through the town is a big worry, especially with children walking to school on their own. A rollout of more 20mph zones around the island, including near schools and residential areas, began under the previous administration. The all-island scheme started in Port Erin in 2025 after Tynwald unanimously voted in 2020 to support speed reductions in urban areas. Expanding further north, the locations were opposed by residents concerned about congestion. Many children walk along the village's main road to get to school Lara also welcomed the introduction of more 20mph zones and said she could not understand why "there was so much resistance to it." She added that in cities like Belfast there are commonly "speed bumps on the road around schools, but they don't have any of that" on the island. Meanwhile, for Onchan business owners Dinko Matevski and Liliya Slavova, the cost of living was their biggest worry. Dinko Matevski and Liliya Slavova have run a cafe in Onchan for three years Originally from Bulgaria, they have lived on the island for more than 14 years and have run a cafe in the town's Village Walk area for the last three. Matevski said rising stock prices were "crazy", adding that "every day our suppliers are coming with new prices and we're trying to survive". Slavova said: "We want to have staff, but we cannot afford it." In the past three years she noticed a change in customer habits too, with people cutting back their orders. The Isle of Man House of Keys election takes place on 24 September, with polling stations around the island open from 08:00 to 20:00 BST. title: Our shop doors are locked during opening hours after theft
description: Businesses reveal the impact of shoplifting with recorded offences still above pre-pandemic levels.
body: Shop owner Paige Mengers says shop theft has become very organised A shop owner has described how she locks her door during opening hours and customers have to ring the bell to get in after her store was targeted by thieves last year. Paige Mengers, who runs a designer boutique in Surrey, has been speaking about the impact of shoplifting, with recorded offences remaining above pre-pandemic levels. Home Office figures show there were 42,674 shoplifting offences across Kent, Surrey and Sussex in 2025/26 compared with 28,048 cases in 2019/20. The government said overall offences in England and Wales fell 4% last year, with more suspects being charged. Mengers, who has stores in Cobham and south-west London, said she boosted security after a raid in January 2025 involving men with wire cutters. "One barricaded the door, the other came in and cut the wires on the bags and stole quite a lot of them," she said. "It was absolutely awful, I lost two very good members of staff who were terrified after that. "We were really shaken and for about six months I had security on the doors for our staff." The borough commander for Elmbridge Chris Thoday told BBC South East the tactics used by these groups were "pretty sophisticated". "They're very organised, they know exactly what they are doing," he said. "Quite often they will recce the shops beforehand, then go in afterwards, steal the items they want to take, to make sure they're in and out as quickly as possible." Insp Thoday said a number of stores had since trialled the use of lone worker alarms for staff working alone at night in a number of shops in Cobham. Businesses are sharing their experiences of shop theft as a BBC investigation reveals 270 people were connected to more than 28,000 offences across England. Official data shows 23 per cent of investigations across England and Wales led to a charge or summons in the 12 months up to April this year. It's not just high street stores being targeted, rural areas are also affected. Bosses at a family-run farm shop in Wingham, near Canterbury in Kent, said they had suffered thousands of pounds of losses in a year. Andrew Gibson has used social media to appeal for help in catching shoplifters "We're getting small gangs come in or individuals to steal high value goods, either meat products, meat joints or alcohol," said Andrew Gibson, director at Gibson's Farm Shop. "They seem to be more organised, out here you have to drive here, you can't be an opportunist thief." Gibson recently turned to social media to shame offenders online. "We've had the situation where thieves have gone back into a police station with the money for the goods to pay back to us," he said. In Canterbury, Kent Police have set up a dedicated retail crime team. "People are going in, stealing to order, filling up trolleys and just running out of the stores," said James, a plain clothed police officer speaking to BBC South East during an operation to catch thieves. He said crime groups would sometimes scope out stores and film items they wanted stolen, before sending shoplifters in. "We notice people coming in checking out where the CCTV cameras are," he said. "Sometimes a shoplifter will use trolleys, they'll load up what they want to take and then they'll hover by the entrance or exit and when the opportunity comes they just take the whole trolley load of goods. "We've also noticed people with prams loading up the bottom or the top, wandering around pretending they are getting something out for the young child in the pram and then load up the pram and take items out of the store." Paul Stoner, district commander for police in the city, said the team was set up as a response to a rise in crime over an 18-month period. "It's a set few individuals who commit a disproportionate amount of that crime," he said. "Our officers have a really good knowledge of the local offenders, we are able to identify them very quickly through the CCTV images," he said. "What we also have is the ability to put those images through facial recognition, if the suspect is on a database, we're able to identify them." Police also share information with the local City Watch scheme and details about known suspects can be relayed on a radio system to shops. It's run by the Canterbury Business Improvement District (Bid) and links up retailers with the police and the city council's CCTV control centre. Lisa Carlson, chief executive of Canterbury Bid, said they had a street team which trained businesses, helping them gather and submit evidence. "We have 137 radios in circulation, if there is an incident unfolding it can be reported in real time and hopefully we can avoid any crime happening," she said. Nick Strickland from the Brighton and Hove Business Crime Reduction Partnership is patrolling the streets with police In Sussex, the Brighton and Hove Business Crime Reduction Partnership (BCRP) also provides services to fight crime and anti-social behaviour. They are working with other BCRPs around Sussex to identify repeat offenders, according to manager Lisa Perretta. "When someone becomes quite well-known in one area, it will be flagged to our area, so we are forewarned and can identify them a lot earlier before they commit multiple crimes," she said. Perretta said they had also got a lot better at educating businesses to report crime. Recorded shoplifting offences across the South East peaked in 2024/25. Only Kent saw an increase in cases over the last 12 months with reductions in Surrey and Sussex. Olivia Carroll, temporary chief inspector at Sussex Police, said there was a "large number of reports" of retail crime in the county - including "organised criminality" by groups. "Clearly we deal with repeat prolific offenders and our focus is on that as a priority," she said. title: Got lost on Mount Fuji off-season? You'll have to pay for your rescue
description: The fee will be imposed on those who get lost on Japan's most famous mountain during the off-peak seasons.
body: Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say. The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers. A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference. Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans. "We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday. Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded. Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas. They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee. Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year. Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations. However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe. title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies
description: The idea is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives and holding water companies to account.
body: Mayors and other local political leaders could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the government. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plan is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives, and holding water companies to account. The idea was a key recommendation of Sir John Cunliffe's Independent Water Commission published in June last year. Improving the water industry has been a focus for Burnham since he took to power, as water customers in England and Wales continue to face steep bill hikes. But there has been little detail of what that could look like, short of full nationalisation - until now. Some ideas in the Cunliffe report were adopted by Sir Keir Starmer's government, however the recommendation for regional bodies was not. While no final decision has been made, and the timings for any announcement have not been finalised, officials in the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs are understood to be keen on the idea. The regional bodies would be given powers to oversee elements of water companies' spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges. The Cunliffe review said: "This would represent a significant change, and ensure that local voices, customers and experts have stronger authority over companies' boards' decisions on investment priorities." As well as a mayor, or local government figure, the regional bodies could consist of an independent chair, experts, and representatives to cover affected sectors like transport and agriculture. A Whitehall source said it was just one among a number of ideas being explored to bring greater public control of water companies. A government spokesperson said: "Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We're bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment." It comes as the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the industry watchdog rose by a record 84% in a year, driven by customer concern and confusion over rising bills. The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history and showed "just how dissatisfied" many people were. In recent years there has been growing public concern about sewage spills and rising bills, as well as decades of under-investment in the sector, with climate change and population growth straining it further. Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84% During his first address to the House of Commons in September, Burnham said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised, before pointing to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest". Burnham has already committed to giving mayors greater control over public services such as social housing, welfare and education. He aims to achieve this by allowing mayors more power over budgets, in a 10-year plan to transform the economy. The prime minister said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders. Burnham's visions come amid a backdrop of rising water prices for customers in England and Wales. The Consumer Council for Water has said the year-on-year increase was the highest in its 20-year history. The issue of England's water industry was also debated in Westminster on Monday after more than 200,000 people signed a petition calling for a national referendum on whether the water industry should be returned to public ownership. While the MPs who took part in the debate did not agree with the need for a referendum, there was broad consensus that the current model was "broken", and needed to be fixed. title: Magazine returned to US library after 132 years overdue
description: Concord Public Library said it would have incurred a $12,055 overdue fine, had there not been a temporary fine freeze in place.
body: A 19th century magazine borrowed from a library in New Hampshire 132 years ago has finally been returned. Concord Public Library said the overdue September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine was returned last week after the library announced a freeze on fines. The magazine was 48,220 days overdue and would have incurred a $12,055 (£8,950) fine. The patron who returned the magazine, John, said it had been "hanging around" his house for decades, but he had no idea how it ended up in his home. He decided to return the magazine after reading about the library's fine freeze in the local newspaper. "We've witnessed many happy faces since announcing our fine freeze," Concord Public Library wrote on Facebook. , external "Of course, we expected long overdue books to be returned, but certainly not something from the late 19th century!" Concord Public Library declared a year-long amnesty on overdue fines from 1 September 2026, with plans to evaluate the effects of a "fine-free library". "Understandably, it won't be placed back in circulation, but perhaps it deserves a spot in the Concord Room," the post on social media said, referring to a section of the library dedicated to local history. "Thankfully, he won't have to pay the $12,055 fine for being 48,220 days overdue." title: Is bankrupt competitions boss behind new scheme?
description: The man behind a competions company which went bust owing thousands is back with a new venture.
body: Ex-Level Up Giveaways director Anton Hall, pictured in this composite image, has been running new pay-to-enter competitions When Ami Shuttleworth and her fiance Chris Smith were told they had won £10,000 in a pay-to-enter competition, they immediately knew how they would spend their prize. "We were over the moon, our wedding was going to be paid off," recalls the 34-year-old mother-of-one from Middlesbrough. Mel Higgins, 33, also had big plans for the £5,000 she was told she had won. "I was going to pay off my credit card and whatever was left I was going to put into my business," says the driving consultant from Chippenham. "I cried my eyes out because I thought, 'this is going to change my life'." Yet, like many others who were successful playing with Level Up Giveaways, neither of them received a penny of their winnings. The firm, based in Sowerby Bridge in West Yorkshire, was wound up at the High Court in August 2025 over unpaid debts, with its sole director, Anton Hall, also made bankrupt in November 2025 as part of separate proceedings. The BBC understands the company owed tens of thousands in unpaid prizes to its customers before it stopped trading. Admin assistant Ami says she "saw red" when she found out 37-year-old Hall is now involved in a new prize draws venture. "Like a lot of people I'm just angry," she adds. For Mel, "it just feels wrong". Running a business, either directly or indirectly, would breach the terms of Hall's bankruptcy order and constitute a criminal offence. Hall, who according to court documents is now living in York, told the BBC: "I haven't set up or owned a limited company, and I'm not a director of, or managing, a limited company. "The competitions I hosted have been run personally through the Raffall platform." Raffall is an independent website which allows people to host their own competitions. Sometimes referred to as prize draws or pay-to-enter competitions, these enterprises work by selling a set number of entries to a draw, often for a cash prize. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport has described prize draws and competitions as a "significant and growing market". Mel Higgins did not receive the £5,000 she won with Level Up Giveaways Government legislation on bankruptcy restrictions states: "You need the permission of the court to act as a company director. "This includes directly or indirectly, taking part in, or having a concern in the promotion, formation or management of a limited company." There are no restrictions on a person who is bankrupt working as an employee of a company. In a YouTube video released in August, Hall said he would be an employee of the new venture, which would be run by someone else. However, he appears to have played a leading role in promoting and running the enterprise, which is also in his name. In a series of social media posts since announcing the new venture, he suggested he was personally managing draws and openly discussed sales numbers, profit and loss figures and guiding the future direction of the venture. Raffall founder and CEO Stelios Kounou confirmed the account @antonlevelup was registered to Hall personally and said payments had been made only to an account held in the name of Anton Hall. The account had been set up prior to Hall being declared bankrupt, Kounnou added. Kounou said Raffall had been contacted by the Insolvency Service, which manages Hall's bankruptcy, regarding the account. A spokesperson for the Insolvency Service said they did not comment on individual cases. Hall's social media posts hint at him running the competitions Discussing his new venture last month, Hall said the feedback had been "good", adding: "A few people negative, understandably, I get it - potentially the winners from Level Up Giveaways who didn't get paid unfortunately. "We have agreed that if [the new venture] takes off - it's a big if - and it starts making a decent amount of profit we are going to look at trying to pay out people who didn't get paid from Level Up Giveaways. "That is the ultimate goal." Hall's bankruptcy restrictions, which last 12 months, will expire on 7 November. They include having to tell the trustee of his bankruptcy about any additional income on top of what has already been declared. This money could be used to pay back creditors over a period of three years. Hall said he had "not made any net profit" from running the draws. The BBC asked him how he was able to make promises about the payment of potential future profits of the new enterprise, given he was an employee. He said the video was recorded "before I became aware of the bankruptcy proceedings and related restrictions". "At that time, I was discussing working with someone else on a proposed business, but once I became aware of the situation, that proposed arrangement did not proceed." After he was contacted by the BBC, Hall suggested he would no longer be running competitions in a social media post. "The raffle thing isn't worth putting my family through the drama," he wrote. Hall's latest venture has also lost money, according to his social media posts Ami and Chris had previously won £10,000 with Level Up Giveaways in 2023 during seemingly better times for the company. But the following year, when they thought they had once again been successful, the firm's problems appeared to mount, with numerous winners left in the dark. In a YouTube video published in January 2025, Hall said he has been struggling to sell enough tickets for his draws to cover costs, leaving him unable to pay out. Ami recalls making "phone call after phone call" chasing her winnings. "It did cause a lot of stress in the lead up to the wedding," she remembers. "It didn't take the shine off our wedding, but it's always going to be in the back of my mind how it could have changed it." Mel says her experience has been "hugely upsetting". title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
description: As the world debates an AI slowdown, Sam Altman and several other tech leaders say they have incentives to self-police their AI advancements.
body: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has been a leader of the recent AI boom. The heads of artificial intelligence (AI) firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has said in response to growing concerns about AI's threat to humans. "We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products. Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes. Huang's stance on AI safety contrasts with those in the industry who have recently expressed fears that the technology could wipe out humanity. A post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic went viral last week after it claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked. Other AI executives and experts responded saying they agreed. Then, over the weekend, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry. The post was applauded by OpenAI chief exuecutive Sam Altman, co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok. However, some industry figures have said the fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry. Addressing the potential dangers of AI at a salesforce conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Huang referred to current advances as "a new industrial revolution" but insisted that AI companies should be left to essentially regulate themselves. "Safety is paramount. However, safety is an engineering problem," Huang said. He added that if at any time a leader of an AI company lacks confidence in their product they should choose to not release it. "That's a very obvious thing to do," Huang said. "Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel the institution is not in control, take a pause." The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea. Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks". Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external. "The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said. "If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added. AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety. Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development. He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact. "We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said. OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind. "With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote. title: Prolific shoplifters behind more than 28,000 offences, BBC finds
description: Just 270 people were linked to 28,415 shoplifting offences across England, a BBC analysis has found.
body: Prolific shoplifters need to "know that they are going to be punished", the policing minister has said At the height of his offending, Jeff Ashman estimates he walked out of shops with goods worth £400 to £500 on a daily basis. "It's mind-boggling," he said, describing how much he had stolen from stores in Hastings to fuel his addiction to heroin and crack cocaine. "I know the misery and grief and despair that I have caused these people for a long period of time." Shoplifting is now firmly in the past for Ashman, but prolific shoplifters like him continue to plague communities across England. We asked police about the 10 suspects their forces had most often linked to shoplifting offences between 2020-21 and 2025-26. It revealed 28,415 recorded offences had been linked to just 270 suspects by the 27 forces who shared data with us. It is an average of 105 offences per person - and those are just the occasions where a theft was formally reported to police and officers identified a suspect. The suspects identified include one in Sussex who had been linked to 247 shoplifting offences, the equivalent of a reported crime every 10 days. Policing minister Sarah Jones said shoplifting was a "pernicious crime that for too long has gone unpunished". She said: "They need to know that they are going to be punished for what they have done." Official data shows police forces across England and Wales, excluding the British Transport Police, recorded 502,011 shoplifting offences in 2025-26 alone. More than half of those investigations were closed with no suspect identified. The government says it is exploring other avenues of tackling prolific shoplifting, in addition to prison sentences and drug treatment, such as technology or court orders preventing them from visiting certain shops or areas. Back in Hastings, Ashman was brought face-to-face with a man he once considered his "public enemy number one". John Bownas leads a team that supports shops in the seaside town, including working together to reduce crime. "You and this town and shoplifting," Bownas said to him, "it's a bit of a history." John Bownas (left) told Jeff he had "often succeeded" in staying one step ahead of them, but "we got you in the end" Bownas continues to see the impact of shoplifing on local businesses and those who work for them. "It's a frustration that the system is letting so many people down," he said. "What that ends up with is young members of staff who are just paid minimum wage to put a few things on the shelf faced with quite often really quite violent characters. "There are threats of needles and threats of knives and that's not what a young shopworker should be faced with day in day out." The Home Office has made assault on a retail worker in England and Wales a specfic criminal offence through the Crime and Policing Act 2026. Those found guilty can be sent to prison for up to six months and face an unlimited fine. One shop manager in Canterbury said it was "really upsetting" to witness her staff be attacked by shoplifters. Laurissa Woolgar said: "My colleagues have been wrestled with as they've tried to get items off [them]. We've been sworn at, there's a lot of verbal abuse." While tougher laws may make some think twice, the ability to catch and prosecute violent shoplifters will also matter. Around one in five shoplifting offences in 2025-26 led to a charge or summons, with 285,667 reported crimes remaining open or being closed without any action. Some retailers told the BBC they had had to identify suspects themselves to ensure an arrest. That was the case when shoplifters made off with gold jewellery worth £1,000 from Dion Smith's workshop last year. He has run the business in Leeds for 16 years and said shoplifting has "got out of control" in the past five to 10 years. His wife took pictures of shoplifters selling off their stolen merchandise in a second-hand goods store, but police could not identify them until the business-owners shared the images on social media. "We had so many comments and people messaging us telling us they knew who they were and where they lived," Smith said. After the shoplifters were identified on social media, Dion Smith said the police had helped recover the stolen goods and made arrests Smith added: "There has to be consequences; we've got to come up with something to deter them because at the moment they're being given a green light to do whatever they want; they are running amok." Emmeline Taylor, professor of criminology at City St George's University in London, said shoplifting was also being driven by organised crime. "Post-pandemic, we have seen what's been described as a shoplifting epidemic on the streets of the UK," she said. "What we are seeing is organised criminals stealing very specific items, clearing entire shelves and selling that on to other markets, maybe online, maybe at car boot sales," she explained. "But we also have prolific local offenders, these individuals maybe drug affected, they already know where they're going to sell the goods on." Professor Emmeline Taylor said shoplifting remains relatively high despite a slight year-on-year drop in 2025-26 Specialist police unit Opal set up an organised retail crime team two years ago, which often spans multiple force areas. Jim Taylor, a former detective chief superintendent who previously led the unit, says this allows them to link organised crime gangs to offending across the country. "There are individuals exploiting the lack of coordination between stores, between police forces and making vast sums of money," he said. One such case spanned across 30 different forces and the unit has uncovered crime groups responsible for "millions of pounds of theft". The National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) emphasised a strategy launched last year has brought "real results" by uniting policing, retailers and the government. Assistant Chief Constable Alex Goss

title: The Papers: 'Complete failure to protect babies' and 'Sterling mess'
description: The landmark public inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders is the focus of several of today's papers.
body: The landmark inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders leads several of today's papers. After finding there was a "complete failure to protect babies" under Letby's care, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, has called for cot cameras or monitors to be used on neonatal units in hospitals, the Daily Express reports. Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. The "damning" Letby hospital report is also the focus of the Daily Mirror's front page, with Health Secretary Yvette Cooper weighing in on the "reprehensible" treatment of parents who lost their babies. According to the paper, the inquiry found there was a "complete failure" to protect newborns at the Countess of Chester Hospital and parents were kept in the dark for years over the concerns. The Guardian headlines on the reaction from UK ministers promising "sweeping changes to the NHS" after the "devastating" review into the Letby murders. "Cot cams" will be installed on all neonatal units, the UK health secretary has said, following the Letby "inquiry bombshell", as reported by the Independent. Hospital managers have apologised for the significant delays in alerting police about Letby, the paper reports. The Times spotlights the families of the "babies murdered and attacked by Lucy Letby" who have "accused hospital managers of prioritising the nurse 'over a unit full of vulnerable children'" following the inquiry findings. Elsewhere is a picture of British actress Daisy Edgar-Jones posing at the premiere of her upcoming role in the remake of Sense and Sensibility in London on Tuesday night. "Motorway madness" reads the Daily Star for their reporting of former England footballer Raheem Sterling, who has pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide after crashing his Lamborghini in May. A picture of Sterling on the day of the crash is splashed on the front. The Sun also reports on the story following the court case at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, describing it as a "Sterling mess". Chancellor John Healey is facing a "fresh test" ahead of the Budget next month, according to the Financial Times, as the state pension is set to rise above the tax-free income threshold for the first time. Teenagerss in the UK are being offered "money, guns and training" by Russia to make explosives and poisons, according to an exclusive in the i Paper. The paper describes it as a troubling escalation of a so-called "grey war". The Daily Telegraph also features a picture of Daisy Edgar-Jones described as "dashing Miss Daisy", during the premiere for her new film adaption of a Jane Austen classic. Elsewhere the paper reveals mayors will be given powers to control and oversee water companies under plans by Andy Burnham. Copies of a "bombshell new book" by Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's younger brother, have been stolen from a lorry, the Daily Mail reports. The memoir, Swan Song, details revelations about the "crisis that engulfed the Royal Family after her death", the paper says. And the Metro headlines on Reform' UK's "dehumanising" video game called Small Boat Scramble, in which players can send back migrant dinghies to France. The party's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf says it "lets people have a bit of fun with a very serious issue". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. title: Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers
description: The government's climate advisers say Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved under current climate policies.
body: Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved without changes to current climate policies, the government's advisers have said. The Climate Change Committee (CCC) , externalsaid expansion can still go ahead but only if the aviation industry funds cleaner fuels and pays for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air. Making the industry pay could push up the cost of flying with a return trip to Alicante costing around £150 more by 2050, and a return to New York up £400 in today's prices, it said. Once built, the expanded airport would produce more carbon dioxide than any other single sector of the economy by 2050. Heathrow said expansion and climate goals were "not a choice" and it would deliver both. "Our advice today is clear - Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK's Net Zero target," said Nigel Topping, the CCC chair. "Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today." The CCC report cannot block a new runway but it wants the government to pass legislation pushing responsibility for the long-term clean-up of aviation onto the industry. The government would "carefully consider" the advice alongside other responses to its consultation according to the Department for Transport (DfT). The government has an ongoing consultation which aims to judge any expansion against four tests - economy, climate, air quality and noise. It does not approve a runway - that will come in a Commons vote expected later this year. The £33bn project would raise Heathrow's capacity to 150 million passengers a year - up from 85 million. A DfT spokesperson said any expansion would need to align with the country's climate targets, but added it "could deliver around £40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs". The CCC has said carbon-removal machines must be deployed to cut more than a third of the emissions by 2050. But almost none of that technology currently exists at scale, and the committee says credible plans exist for just 1% of these engineered removals needed by the late 2030s. The committee argued making the industry rather than the government bear the costs of clean up was the fairest way of cutting carbon. It believes the extra investment needed would likely be passed on to passengers but would be modest if spread over time. Phased across 25 years, the cost of a flight to Alicante would rise by a few pounds a year - "less than a cup of coffee each way", Topping said. Heathrow expansion an 'outdated' risk, mayor says What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport? However, the airline industry rejected the committee's approach. Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said carriers backed the government's target of net zero by 2050 but added that the transition "has to be affordable". He warned that the CCC plan would put holidays "out of reach for millions" and turn the clock back to "a time when flying was the preserve of the rich". Alderslade said the answer was airspace reform and scaling up sustainable fuels - such as those made from waste oil and plant matter. On carbon removals, he added this was more challenging to deploy, and the aviation sector "cannot and should not shoulder the burden of scaling up this industry alone", and needed government support. Protestors against the planned Heathrow expansion demonstrate outside Parliament in early September Some researchers believe the committee's advice does not act as a barrier to Heathrow's expansion and will fail to achieve the reduction in planet-warming gases required. Dr Lois Pennington of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research told the BBC that because cleaner fuel and carbon removal were unlikely to arrive at the scale needed, the only reliable way to stay within the UK's carbon limits was to stop the expansion of flying - or even to reduce it. "We need to make sure that we are not flying more than we are now," she said. Although the government has said it would consider the CCC's advice, ministers have left little doubt it intends to proceed with the expansion. Last week in response to opposition questions, Chancellor John Healey said of the expansion: "After years of delay, years of indecision, years of often vexatious challenge, we have given the go-ahead to this project quite simply because the economic case stacks up and will help bring growth." A formal vote in the House of Commons will still be needed to approve the planning framework for Heathrow's expansion, and that is expected later this year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham opposed a third runway before entering Downing Street, arguing it would divert investment away from the north and "trap it in London and the South East". The Mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan, has also raised concerns about its climate and noise impact. The plan is also strongly opposed by many residents and councils under the flight path, with around 750 homes facing demolition to make way for the new runway amid long-standing concerns over noise and air pollution. title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
description: Supporters of the scheme say the bank would enable governments to get cheaper loans to spend on defence projects.
body: A British soldier taking part in a Nato exercise in Finland The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank, aimed at raising more money for defence spending. Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea. Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending. Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity." Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister. He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine. He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions. "Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine – but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine." It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea. The DSRB is a multilateral bank aimed at providing cheaper loans to fund defence projects and has backing from Albania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine. Membership of the bank for the UK and other G7 countries would come with an upfront investment cost of around £870m spread over three years. Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review. The government has so far avoided committing to raising defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, only repeating the longer term goal of 3.5% by 2035. As defence secretary, Healey privately pushed for the UK to join the DSRB as a means of raising money. He resigned in June, accusing the Treasury of being unwilling to provide the resources needed to defend the country. In his resignation letter, he said there were "credible ways" to fund extra defence spending, including "working multinationally". A government spokesperson said: "We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity. "We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary." title: Do you feel guilty when calling in sick at work? This might be why...
description: As many as half of people report working when sick. The reasons for this are complex, experts say.
body: You wake up feeling unwell but there's a big day at work ahead. What do you do? If the answer is to go in (or log on), you're not alone. Research suggests, external anywhere between a third to a half of people in the UK work even when sick - something experts call presenteeism. And your approach to sickness says a lot about you as an individual and where you work. "The younger generation get the snowflake tag thrown at them, but it's not true," says University of Manchester psychologist Prof Sir Cary Cooper, who is one of the world's leading experts on workplace wellbeing. Data from the Office for National Statistics, external supports this view. Workers aged 16 to 24 took an average of 2.4 days off sick last year, compared to 6.2 days for those aged 50 to 64. Sir Cary, who has advised the UK government on employment policies in this area, says there are several reasons for this. Younger workers are more likely to work in roles where there is little security, such as zero-hours contracts. They are also less likely to suffer from long-term health conditions and joint problems that are major contributors to sickness absence. This video can not be played When was your last sick day? But Sir Cary adds: "I think younger generations do have higher expectations about how employers should treat them and consider their wellbeing. "Older generations have perhaps been more willing to put up with things, but that doesn't necessarily make that approach healthy. "When it comes to taking time off, younger workers seem more willing to view mental wellbeing as part of their overall health rather than something that should simply be pushed through." There are a variety of factors that influence someone's approach to sickness absence. For some, work is closely tied to identity. Occupational psychologists call this work centrality - and research links this to greater engagement, commitment and willingness to go the extra mile. If work is central to who you are, being absent can feel like temporarily losing part of yourself. "These people feel a strong desire to keep showing up," says Dr Audrey Tang, a psychologist who writes about workplace wellbeing. She says those working in caring professions such as medicine, nursing and teaching have a particular tendency towards this. "They often report they would rather have a physical accident to have a reason not to show up than just take the day off." Others fear being seen as weak or lazy. Younger workers are particularly susceptible to this, says Tang. "They're more likely to be early in their profession and they don't want to leave a negative impression." Workplace culture and behaviour can have a significant influence on people's willingness to take time off sick, says psychologist Dr Tara Quinn-Cirillo. When teams are stretched and there is little or no cover, employees know their absence will increase the workload for colleagues. "The role of guilt and shame is significant in a toxic organisation that prioritises productivity over health and wellbeing," says Quinn-Cirillo. "There is a 'carry-on' culture in some workplaces that encourages people to keep going when they should be resting." Such cultures reward presenteeism. Employees feel valued for turning up regardless of how they are feeling and staff quickly absorb the message if managers praise people for working through illness. Workplace culture can have a significant influence on people's willingness to take sick days "In a healthy work environment, people should be able to have open and honest conversations about wellbeing and sick days," says Quinn-Cirillo. Trust also matters. If absence is routinely questioned or viewed negatively, workers can become reluctant to take legitimate time off for fear of being judged. That, says Quinn-Cirillo, is a "huge red flag". Deciding whether you are too sick to work is not always straightforward. For physical illness, Tang says there are some well-established rules of thumb. "If you're vomiting and have diarrhoea or have a fever, you should stay at home for 48 hours and 24 hours respectively after the symptoms have passed. In those situations, you're unlikely to be able to work effectively anyway." Beyond that, the decision becomes more nuanced, according to Tang. "Where there is more of a grey area is with coughs and colds. Since Covid, workplace etiquette has changed - generally it's considered polite to work from home." But she says an absolute must is that mental health should be treated no differently than physical health. "If you're sick and unable to work, you're sick and unable to work." Quinn-Cirillo adds: "Ultimately it's about capacity to do a job, whether it be physical or mental health." A further warning sign is when work starts affecting basic self-care, she says. "Is your ability to look after yourself changing? Are you able to decompress from work? Is your sleep OK?" If the answer is no, it may be a sign that rest is exactly what is needed.
