title: Home Alone and Schitt's Creek stars pay tribute to late Catherine O'Hara
description: Tributes were also paid to Dolly Parton, James Van Der Beek and Tim Curry.
body: Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to". Referring to the plot of the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her." Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner. Heroes and Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, who died last month, was also remembered alongside other stars including Rocky Horror Show's Tim Curry and Dawson's Creek actor James Van Der Beek. Emmy winner O'Hara, who died in January this year aged 71, was known for playing Culkin's frantic mother in the 1990s film franchise, as well as the eccentric Moira Rose - mum to Murphy and Levy's Alexis and Dan - in Schitt's Creek. "You remember her as the forgetful mother, right?" said Culkin. "There are all kinds of words I could use to describe Catherine. She was encouraging. She was warm. She was funny, but the word that I think of is mom... She was, she was my mom. She was our mom. "So she may have forgotten me twice. But we will always remember her." Murphy noted how, since her death, many people had quoted O'Hara's most memorable lines from her show back at her. "These are only very few of the interactions I've been lucky enough to have that remind me how profoundly Catherine has impacted the world, and it's because she brought us joy," Murphy said. Levy added: "Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness." The emotional moment, which featured a big image of a smiling O'Hara as the backdrop, appeared to bring actors Martin Short and Steve Martin, sitting in the audience, to tears. Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear. Reiner was killed along with his wife last year. A tearful Jamie Lee Curtis paid tribute to the director, writer and performer, who made films such as When Harry Met Sally, This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, Misery and A Few Good Men, calling him a "cherished legend" and "our beloved meathead". The 48-year gap between Reiner's two most recent Emmy wins set a new record, beating his Dad, Carl Reiner. Curtis began her speech by first acknowledging the passing of Cheers co-creator James Burrows, who was also a good friend of Reiner's. There were also warm words for Farrah Fawcett, who died in 2009. Celebrating 50 years, Charlie's Angels stars Kate Jackson, Cheryl Ladd and Jaclyn Smith, handed out the Emmy for best drama and paid tribute to their fellow Angel. Jackson said Fawcett "was the shiniest angel of all, and she was loved by millions of people all over the world. And she still is today. And they'll never forget her and neither will we. And I'm sure you won't either." Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreana paid tribute to the co-stars they have lost recently, including Nicholas Brendon, Anthony Head and Michelle Trachtenberg. Geller said: "David and I would like to acknowledge that it has been a tough two years for our beloved cast and crew, and we feel very lucky to have known and worked with such amazing people." Elsewhere on the night, Remarkably Smart Creatures actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month. Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire. "She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy herself in 2021. "God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on earth who will love you for ever and ever." title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
description: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.
body: Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea. The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide". Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships. It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser." Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added. The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable". Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept." In a statement following the incident, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin accused Denmark of "recklessness" and "provocative actions". Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships". He said he had complained about a similar incident last year, adding that the latest event showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side". Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew. Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday. The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months. President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace." Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally. Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory". It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions". Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
description: A vehicle hit four people before colliding with two cars on White Rose Way in Doncaster, police say.
body: Police say they have arrested a 30-year-old man in connection with the incident Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster. South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway. The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries. The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail. The crash happened in White Rose Way, between Carriage Drive and Middle Bank Roundabout A police spokesperson said they were still "working to identify and inform" the families of those killed in the collision. Anyone who witnessed the crash, which took place between Carriage Drive and Middle Bank Roundabout, or who has dashcam footage is asked to contact South Yorkshire Police. title: Mother sentenced for killing son and attempting to murder daughter
description: The woman was convicted and jailed in 2023 but in 2025 senior judges ruled those convictions were unsafe.
body: Tributes were left outside the property in 2021 A woman, whose convictions for the murder of her baby son and attempted murder of his toddler sister were quashed, has been sentenced to 10 years for infanticide and attempted murder. The woman stabbed both children in July 2021 and they were taken to the Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children. The girl was successfully treated but the baby boy was pronounced dead. The woman was convicted and jailed in 2023 for murdering her eight-week-old son and attempting to murder his toddler sister. In December 2025, senior judges in the Court of Appeal ruled those convictions were unsafe. In March of this year, the court ordered a retrial. In August, the woman, whose identity is protected by an anonymity order, pleaded guilty to infanticide and attempted murder. Infanticide is legally defined as the unlawful killing of a child aged under 12 months, by its biological mother, when at the time the "balance of the mother's mind was disturbed". On Tuesday, Mr Justice Fowler referred to expert medical reports detailing that at the time of the stabbings the woman was experiencing postnatal depression. The court also heard that her relationship with the father of her children was "characterised by domestic abuse, sexual abuse and coercive control". She feared that her partner or people associated with him might kill her. The judge said diary entries by her suggest she was "overwhelmed by feelings of rejection, abandonment and emotional despair". Several medical reports said she felt in her circumstances that she had no alternative but to end her life and that of her children. A statement relating to the woman's surviving daughter detailed the "catastrophic impact" on her explaining that it would be lifelong. The court heard the incident happened at a crucial time in the child's development and she experienced "abandonment, rejection and loss". The young girl is now in foster care and was described as happy and settled but it was reported that she remains hyper vigilant and sensitive to changes in her environment. The woman was sentenced at Laganside Court in Belfast on Tuesday Following indirect contact with her mother the court heard that the child experiences "significant difficulties" and can wake at night and say "she is scared of the dark and mummy". The judge referenced the woman's admissions to police in the immediate aftermath of the incident. She indicated to them that she was suffering from depression, when asked if she had mental health issues she told police: "Considering what I have done, I probably do". When asked if she was depressed, she responded: "Depression? 100% I cry too much." The judge said he was "satisfied that she was suffering from mild to moderate depression. Probably more to the moderate range". He agreed that her judgement was impacted. He noted she had expressed remorse, was a victim of modern-day slavery, and said the offending was an isolated incident but also said it represented a serious breach of trust and that the level of harm done was high. She was sentenced to 10 years, half on licence. Due to time served she is set to be released to start her five-year-period on licence. Conditions imposed include that she is not to have any contact with anyone under 18 years of age and must attend any necessary medical appointments. title: London misses out to Nairobi in World Athletics bid
description: London has lost to Nairobi in its bid to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029, while the 2031 event will be held in Munich.
body: The London Stadium hosted the World Athletics Championships in 2017 London has missed out to Nairobi in the bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships. The decision, which means an African city will host the event for the first time, was confirmed at a World Athletics council meeting in Budapest. World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said Nairobi had presented "a compelling and emotional bid". "We were fortunate to have four outstanding bids for 2029 and 2031, and this was not an easy decision for the council," said Coe. "With this decision today, we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide with the hosting of our World Athletics Championships in Asia, Africa and Europe over its next three editions. "Nairobi presented a compelling and emotional bid, and taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. "It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment." The London Stadium, home of Championship club West Ham United, was the proposed host venue for the UK bid. The stadium was also used for the 2012 Olympic Games and the yearly London Diamond League, and also when the city last hosted the Worlds in 2017. The UK's bid was led by Athletic Ventures, which consisted of UK Athletics, London Marathon Events and the Great Run Company. Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels. "We would like to thank the Government, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Mayor of London and UK Sport for their fantastic support for our bid. Our thanks also to the London Stadium, West Ham United and our many stakeholders for their commitment and hard work to put the bid together. "Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029." Rome was the other city to miss out, as World Athletics also confirmed that Munich would host the 2031 event for the first time. Nairobi, the capital city of Kenya, submitted a bid for the 2025 championships but missed out to Tokyo. The city's Kasarani Stadium is being renovated before the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) in 2027, which strengthened its case as a host venue. Kenya finished second in the medal table at the 2025 edition, winning seven gold medals and 11 in total. This is a painful snub for London, so why did it fail? Those behind the bid had secured £45m in public money, and were confident of replicating the commercial success of the 2017 event. However, there had been uncertainty over whether West Ham would grant permission for the London Stadium to be used. That was finally confirmed last month, but only shortly before the bid had to be formally submitted. Another issue may have been the fact that nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's 23,000-seater Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships last month, with some fans blaming the cost of tickets. Lord Coe has refused to be drawn on whether either were factors in the decision, preferring instead to focus on Kenya's rich tradition in distance running, and the fact Nairobi will make history by hosting Africa's first world championships. However, the spate of doping scandals in Kenyan athletics in recent years will also lead to some scrutiny over whether it is an appropriate host. Britain is still hosting the Grand Depart of the men's and women's Tour de France cycling races in 2027, and then the men's Euros in 2028, and is bidding for the 2035 Women's World Cup. But at a time when government is also interested in a possible Olympic bid for 2040, today's decision is undoubtedly a blow. World indoor 400m champion and British record holder Amber Anning was in the stands as a fan for the 2017 championships, and although she expressed her disappointment to miss out on the experience of a home event as an athlete, added that Nairobi was a chance for something "really special". "There was a lot of disappointment, honestly," Anning told BBC Sport. "That was our dream. In 2017, I saw that we have the best crowds, the best atmosphere. So I would say it is a bit unfortunate that we weren't able to get the bid. "But seeing how Botswana was for the World Relays this year, I think it will be really special to have it in Africa for the first time. It's going to leave a legacy, so while it was not the result we wanted, it's still a chance for another country and another generation to inspire. It's an honour." Greg Rutherford, who memorably won Olympic gold in the long jump as part of Super Saturday at the London 2012 Games, echoed Anning's sentiments. Rutherford said it was a "bitter pill to swallow" for London to miss out but praised the strength of Nairobi's bid and highlighted the need for change. "We've seen over the years how well we can put on these incredible championships - 2017 was massive, record amounts of people through the doors, bums on seats watching some amazing performances," Rutherford told BBC Sport. "We also saw that in 2012 but at the same time, we are seeing something that is going to change the lay of the land. "Of course there is real disappointment but equally, it's going to be incredible to finally see this event in Africa. "I think what may have harmed it [London's bid] is that we had hosted one so recently, and Nairobi's bid was a very strong one. They are looking to invest into Africa so there is more chance for their nations to have the opportunity like this going forward and I do think we need to see change at times." title: McBurnie & seven uncapped names in Scotland squad
description: Hull City forward Oli McBurnie is called up to the Scotland squad for the first time in five years while seven uncapped make new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli's first selection.
body: Oli McBurnie could win his 17th Scotland cap Oli McBurnie has been called up to the Scotland squad for the first time in five years, with new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli saying the Hull City forward fits his "style of play". Uncapped Luis Binks, Colby Donovan, Jon McCracken, Josh McPake and Stephen Welsh also makes Pocognoli's first selection. As expected, Stoke defender Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure receive their first senior call-ups. Scott Bain, Kieron Bowie, Josh Doig, Lennon Miller and James Wilson are recalled but Che Adams misses out. Napoli midfielder Billy Gilmour, 25, returns after missing the World Cup injured. McBurnie, 30, first featured for his country in 2018 and won the last of his 16 caps in 2021. He has never scored for Scotland but did net one of the penalties in the shootout that sealed a place at the delayed Euro 2020 finals. "It's a new opportunity for some players, a really new beginning for the other ones," said Pocognoli. "I have to start a new journey, start a new book. The most important is regarding the style of play that I want to produce on the pitch. We need to adapt quick. "To be honest, I can extend this list because I have to make some choices. There are a lot of names who can be also in that squad for that camp. Players who are not there is because for the style of play, it can be from injury or playing time. "There's many players that I would like to call up. The door is never closed." Binks, 25, has previously played age grade football for England and Scotland and Pocognoli said in reference to the Brondby player: "The timing was right with him." Right-back Donovan, 20, has come to prominence filling in for injured Canada right-back Alistair Johnston in Celtic's side this season. Like McBurnie, he has been capped at under-19 and under-21 level. Pocognoli said Donovan had "played some good games" and had dealt with "expectation". Graham was part of Scotland's pre-World Cup training camp in May after a breakthrough campaign with Dundee, winning the Scottish Premiership club's players' player and young player of the year awards. The 22-year-old was an unused substitute in the country's send-off friendly win against Curacao, which was also Steve Clarke's last game in the dugout at Hampden Park. The defender, who has three caps at under-21 level, has started strongly for The Potters in the Championship, who are unbeaten in their past four games, with Graham an ever-present. This video can not be played Bain 'ticks every box' for Scotland start - Falkirk boss McGlynn Four-time capped Falkirk goalkeeper Bain, 34, and Bradford City keeper Jon McCracken, 26, were in squads named by Pocognoli's predecessor Clarke. Bain and McCracken join Angus Gunn and Liam Kelly in the goalkeeping pool. And Pocognoli commented: "I will not talk about my number one and number two today. "We have a strong generation in the past. Now we need just to rebirth this but we have good quality. We have experienced goalkeepers and we have some young talents." Pocognoli's compatriot, Heart of Midlothian head coach Wouter Vrancken, was "confident" there would be a few players from the Tynecastle club included and winger McPake, 25, and 19-year-old attacking club-mate James Wilson, who has two caps, are recognised for their early-season performances. However, Hearts winger Calvin Miller misses out. This video can not be played Watch best of Josh McPake's scintillating Edinburgh derby display Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh, 26, may win his first cap while Sassuolo forward Bowie, 23, and left-back Doig, 24, as well as Udinese midfielder Miller, 20, make the cut. Former Rangers academy product Ure was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - that took Sirius to the top of the table in Sweden and it resulted in a £5.5m summer transfer to La Liga with Sevilla. Ure, 22, has yet to find the target in Spain, but given his eligibility for Ukraine, the new head coach appears tempted to tie him down as soon as possible. "Players who are there are performing well," said Pocognoli. "Robbie is now challenging to adjust to La Liga level." The inclusion of Bowie, McBurnie, Ure and Wilson come as reports indicate Torino's Adams is injured while Rangers forward Lawrence Shankland is out for up to four months with a hamstring injury. Time for Pocognoli to pick - who could be named in new-look Scotland squad? Stoke best place for me to take step up - Graham Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack? Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay, 29, is unavailable, having recently had minor heart surgery. Of the 28 named in this squad, 14 were part of this summer's World Cup. Gunn and Kelly, defenders Jack Hendry, Aaron Hickey, Scott McKenna, Nathan Patterson, Andy Robertson and Kieran Tierney, midfielders Ryan Christie, Lewis Ferguson, John McGinn and Kenny McLean and forwards Findlay Curtis and Ben Gannon-Doak are all retained. Goalkeeper Craig Gordon has retired while Grant Hanley has recently returned to fitness at Hibernian while Rangers defender John Souttar has not played this season amid reports linking him with Aris Thessaloniki. Defenders Dominic Hyam and Anthony Ralston, midfielder Tyler Fletcher and forwards Lyndon Dykes, George Hirst and Ross Stewart miss out. When asked about the possibility of calling up Scotland-qualified Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes, 28, and Everton midfielder Hayden Hackney, 24, Pocognoli said he was "aware of everything and about the feeling of everybody" and said "it's about timing." "I don't want to convince players," he explained. "They need to be open to representing in the natural way, the country. We'll see in the future." title: US drinks giant completes purchase of viral Au Vodka brand for £300m
description: International spirits brand Sazerac has completed its purchase of Au Vodka for a reported £300m
body: Au Vodka founders Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn will reportedly make £100m each from the sale of the business to Sazerac US drinks giant Sazerac said it has "big plans" for Au Vodka after completing a takeover reported to value the Welsh business at about £300m. The Swansea-based vodka brand, known for its gold packaging and viral social media campaigns, was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn in 2015. With investment from DJ Charlie Sloth it enjoyed rapid growth before being formally acquired by one of the world's largest spirits companies. Financial terms have not been disclosed, but the Reuters news agency reported the deal values Au Vodka at about £300m ($405m). Sazerac chief executive Jake Wenz said Au had enjoyed a "phenomenal growth trajectory" since it was founded in Swansea. "Au Vodka is a brand we've long admired," he said. "What Charlie, Jackson, and Charlie have achieved in just over a decade is spectacular and rare, and we have big plans for Au as we welcome the brand into the Sazerac family." Viral vodka brand Au set to sell for £500m to BuzzBallz owner It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable' He said that the deal would strengthen Sazerac's position in the UK while creating "a path for continued global growth" for the vodka maker. Au Vodka was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn, with broadcaster and DJ Charlie Sloth later joining as an investor. Known for its distinctive bottles and cans, the company built a large following through social media marketing and celebrity collaborations. It has grown into one of the UK's best-known premium vodka brands, and employs more than 80 people in south Wales. International DJ Charlie Sloth was an early investor in Au Vodka Morgan said the founders had started the business with "nothing but an idea and a belief that vodka didn't have to be boring". "We are proud to have built it into one of the most disruptive brands of this generation," he said. "With Sazerac, Au can be offered to more people, in more markets, faster than we ever could alone." The acquisition adds Au Vodka to a portfolio of more than 500 brands owned by Sazerac, including BuzzBallz and Southern Comfort. title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules
description: The home secretary wants to double the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for permanent residence.
body: The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood Trade unions are putting pressure on the government to soften proposed changes to immigration rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK. If the plans are approved, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for permanent residence, rather than five years, while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait. The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, who has kept the same role under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn. A government spokesperson said ministers had received 200,000 responses to a consultation on the proposals, which was launched under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, and they were carefully considering them. Mahmood has previously defended the plans, saying the "unprecedented" number of people arriving in the UK demands an answer from the government. Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years. People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years. Indefinite leave to remain gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanent residence in the coming months. Some Labour MPs have also criticised plans for the changes to apply to migrants already in the UK. Earlier this year, when she was a backbench MP and not a government minister, Angela Rayner, herself a former care worker, labelled the proposals "un-British". Rayner, who has since been appointed housing secretary by Burnham, warned that "moving the goalposts undermines our sense of fair play". At the time, Burnham, who was still Greater Manchester mayor, said he understood where Rayner was "coming from" and that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say". Don't change rules for migrants already in UK, Labour MPs tell Mahmood Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants The UK's biggest union, Unison, called on delegates to agree they were "alarmed at sweeping attacks on migrant workers which render them second-class citizens in the UK". Unison senior vice president Debbie Rowden said the plans would drive away international staff despite shortages in critical roles, including in the care sector, where the qualification period would treble. "The government wants to give bankers a three-year route to settlement, but social care workers will be kept waiting for 15 years," she said. "The same for nursing auxiliaries, theatre nurses, health care assistants, children's residential care workers, probation service workers and more. "What does this say about how public service workers are valued? What does this say about the soul of the country, when health and social care is seen as being a low contributor, but bankers as the highest?" The Society of Radiographers seconded the motion, setting out how international technician numbers had plugged major gaps in NHS workforces, but that numbers had fallen 12% by more than 1,500 between January and March this year because "the goalposts had moved" on settlement. The motion, which also called for the five-year route to settlement to be retained for workers, was passed unanimously by delegates. title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
description: It comes after Reform received donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad.
body: Reform leader Nigel Farage says the donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne comply with the current law The government is planning to tighten residency rules for political donors to ensure that those giving significant amounts of money reside in the UK. The announcement follows a row over two donations totalling £72m to Reform UK from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad. Reform leader Nigel Farage said the donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are "100% compliant with the law today" but he was unable to say they would be permissible under proposed rule changes. The government wants to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet It also wants to introduce a minimum residency period of at least 12 months in which the cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK. It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK. Under the current rules, foreign donations are illegal in the UK, but British voters living abroad can give as much as they want to political parties. MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords. Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy." Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the £100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK. Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year. Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues". He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain. "That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain." Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough". She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain." On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal. He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way. "We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'." Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public. Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees. Since the 2024 election, the Conservative Party has raised £37m, Reform has raised £35m before Delo and Harborne's large donations, Labour had raised £21m, the Liberal Democrats £17m and the Green Party £1.9m Union leaders agreed a statement on political donations on Tuesday, following discussions at the Trades Union Congress in Brighton. It called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super-rich" and pledge to work with policymakers to "clean up our politics". They also argued that trade union funding is the "cleanest money in politics" which is "heavily regulated". But there was no explicit call for a cap on individual donations in the UK. There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties. The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this. Unite - the country's second biggest union - has called for a cap of between £500,000 and £1m on individual donations but this would not apply to trade union donations. Other smaller unions favour a cap across the board but some bigger unions are wary in case this would threaten donations to Labour. Before the joint statement was issued, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham told the BBC that "we're talking about apples and pears" when asked about the donations to Reform and those from trade unions. She told Today: "Individual donations from very, very wealthy people, from billionaires, the Americanisation of our democracy is very, very different from everyday people, workers putting 10p-a-week into a political fund that fights on a whole range of things." Graham added: "If there's an ick feeling, a yucky feeling about something then it's probably wrong. "I think most people will think two crypto billionaires giving £72m to Reform in two days is a problem for British politics and if it's wrong then deal with it." Delo and Harborne each gave £36m to Reform in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party. Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings

title: Rodon absent as Ashford earns first Wales call-up
description: Craig Bellamy hands a first call-up to Cardiff City forward Cian Ashford for Wales' Nations League A campaign but is without key defender Joe Rodon.
body: Joe Rodon was injured in Leeds' third game of the season while Cian Ashford has featured in all nine Cardiff matches Craig Bellamy has handed a first call-up to Cardiff City forward Cian Ashford for Wales' return to the top flight of the Nations League but is without key defender Joe Rodon to take on Erling Haaland and Cristiano Ronaldo. Wales face Portugal, Denmark and Norway in League A of the competition, but will do so without first-choice centre-back Rodon who has been ruled out with a hamstring injury. Defensive partner Dylan Lawlor is also missing from the 28-man squad - he is yet to appear this season because of a knee problem - as is fellow Cardiff defender Ronan Kpakio. Leeds United's Harry Wilson and Wolves midfielder Jordan James return to the squad after missing June's friendlies with Ghana and Romania through injury, as does Swansea City defender Ben Cabango. As well as returns for Mark Harris and Liam Cullen, there is a recall for 10-cap winger Wes Burns, now of Leicester City, who could make his first international appearance since 2024. Wales travel to face Portugal on 24 September in the first of four fixtures in this newly extended international break, with a home match against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway sandwiched by two games with Denmark. Captain Ben Davies retains his place having been named in the squad for the summer games without featuring. The 33-year-old defender had not played since a serious ankle injury suffered with Tottenham in January, but has since returned to action for Spurs and is in contention for his first international appearance since October 2025 when he won his 100th cap. Ashford, 21, gets his chance having impressed in the early stages of the Championship season, as part of attacking options that also include Liverpool's Lewis Koumas. Fellow Cardiff forwards Isaak Davies and Rubin Colwill are unavailable for selection because of injury, while there is no place for midfielder Kai Andrews despite his impressive start at Aaron Ramsey's Oxford United on loan from Coventry City. Cian Ashford has featured in all nine Cardiff City games this season, scoring twice Wales' opponents are yet to name their squads, although Cristiano Ronaldo is expected to be selected for Portugal in their first games under his former Saudi Pro League club boss, Jorge Jesus. The games are the first since manager Bellamy was close to leaving his national post after holding talks with Championship club Burnley. The 78-cap former striker has seen two key members of his backroom staff leave their roles in the meantime, with number two Piet Cremers taking a job in Belgium and assistant coach James Rowberry opting to focus on club duties as assistant manager at Stoke City. They will be replaced on Bellamy's coaching staff by former captain Ashley Williams and ex-Swansea City boss Alan Sheehan in what is expected to be a challenging period for Wales. Without a win in their past four games, these are the first competitive fixtures since a penalty shoot-out defeat by Bosnia-Herzegovina in March's play-offs cost Wales a place in the World Cup. Wales have not beaten a side in the top 20 of the world rankings since a 2-1 win over Croatia in October 2023 - and are yet to beat a side ranked higher than themselves under Bellamy. Now they face that challenge in quick succession, starting with prospect of current Nations League holders Portugal. Wales - who are 38th in the world rankings, their lowest position since August 2014 - then travel to Copenhagen to take on a Denmark side ranked 21st in the world before the visit of World Cup quarter-finalists Norway to Cardiff (1 October) and the return game with Denmark (4 October). Goalkeepers: Karl Darlow (Manchester United), Danny Ward (Wrexham), Tom King (Everton). Defenders: Jay DaSilva (Coventry City), Jayden Lienou (Leeds United), Ben Davies (Tottenham Hotspur), Rhys Norrington-Davies (Sheffield United), Chris Mepham (West Bromwich Albion), Ben Cabango (Swansea City), Neco Williams (Nottingham Forest), Connor Roberts (Burnley). title: Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport, sprinter Hunt says
description: British sprinter Amy Hunt says she is concerned the controversial advert starring Sydney Sweeney is a part of a "barrier" to girls' participation in sport.
body: This video can not be played 'Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like!' - Hunt on controversial ad British sprinter Amy Hunt says she is concerned about the controversial advert starring Sydney Sweeney being part of a "barrier" to girls' participation in sport. The advert for a sports betting company features the American actress naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment. After running a season's best 22.10 seconds in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday, Hunt said: "This is what women in sport look like." Hunt, 24, is among several female athletes who have spoken out against the advert's messaging. "When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like," Hunt told Good Morning Britain. "When we see the stats of 64% of young girls dropping out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don't need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like - professional or kind of just going to do a Parkrun with your friends. "So it's about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there, and you don't have to worry what you look like. You don't have to worry about what you're wearing." Hunt has enjoyed a breakthrough season, winning four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month. She said "sport is not pretty", describing how she is often sick during sessions or in tears if something does not go to plan. Hunt said the responses to Sweeney's advert had eclipsed the controversy. "The reaction has almost outweighed the moment because the first thing I saw was all of the positive compilations of women in sport," she said. title: Spurs' Richarlison posts crying emoji after being left out of Liverpool tie
description: Richarlison publicly expresses his displeasure at Roberto de Zerbi's decision to leave him out of Tottenham's squad for Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie against Liverpool.
body: Tottenham signed Richarlison from Everton for £60m on a five-year deal in 2022 Richarlison has publicly expressed his displeasure at Roberto de Zerbi's decision to leave him out of Tottenham's squad for Tuesday's Carabao Cup tie against Liverpool. The Brazil striker shared a screenshot of a social media post about his omission and accompanied it with the message "Why?" and a tearful sad-faced emoji. Richarlison's future in north London has become increasingly uncertain after a proposed transfer to Brazilian side Vasco da Gama fell through last week. Sources suggested the Premier League club had agreed a fee with with Vasco for the 29-year-old, but personal terms were not agreed before the Brazilian transfer window closed on Friday. "At the start of this season, I spoke to him many times to convince him to stay and he didn't want to," De Zerbi said in his pre-match news conference on Monday. "I can't go every day to pray for him to stay. "What I have done at the beginning of this season has been to speak with him and to propose an extension of the contract. If he said, 'no thank you,' I finished my job. "I know what happened in the last 45 days. It's not right if I explained. It's not my behaviour. The relationship, the problem is between the player and the club." This video can not be played Tottenham's wait for league goal continues after Everton draw Richarlison also had a proposed £35m deadline-day transfer to Everton collapse after the forward failed to agree personal terms with the Toffees. He was left out of Spurs' Premier League squad amid a dispute between him and the club over the remaining nine months of his contract. Richarlison is understood to be exploring his options, with sources indicating he is keen to be released from the remainder of his current deal, which runs out next summer, although Spurs have the option of triggering a 12-month extension. His exile comes at a difficult time for Spurs, who are still searching for their first win of the new Premier League season under De Zerbi. They have not scored in their opening four league matches - the first time they have failed to do so in their history. Their underwhelming start comes despite the club spending more than £300m in the summer to strengthen De Zerbi's squad after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes. Richarlison was Spurs' leading scorer last season with 12 goals in all competitions - five more than centre-back Micky van de Ven and defensive midfielder Joao Palhinha. He also has four goals in seven matches against Tuesday's opponents Liverpool during his time at Tottenham. The striker joined Spurs from Everton in 2022 after spells with Watford and Everton and has won 54 caps for Brazil. title: Police commissioner may cancel tour after backlash
description: Colin Sutton is due to perform his true crime show on-stage 127 times between January and November.
body: Colin Sutton said he was "absolutely" reconsidering his UK-wide tour after the backlash Norfolk's police commissioner is considering scrapping his 127-date theatre show after a backlash from local people, he has told the BBC. Since announcing his UK-wide true crime tour, Colin Sutton said constituents had emailed him with concerns about his ability to perform his day job. He was elected to the £79,000-a-year post on a Reform UK ticket in July and announced the gig two months later. Steffan Aquarone, the Liberal Democrat MP for North Norfolk, accused Sutton of acting more like pop star Taylor Swift than a politician. Police and crime commissioners (PCCs) are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account. Sutton, who led the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield, has priced tickets for his "Makings of a Murderer" show at about £40. Sutton was elected as Norfolk's police and crime commissioner in July Asked if he was now reconsidering the theatre run, Sutton said: "Absolutely. I'm in talks with the people who promote it to see how we can curtail it or, if necessary, just cut it completely. "I don't want anything to interfere with the job that I've got to do." One of the solutions he proposed was stripping the tour back to venues only local to Norfolk. Sutton is due to appear at a Norfolk police and crime panel on 2 February, before being on stage in Leeds that evening. "There are lots of people who do meetings like that by [Microsoft] Teams or across the internet now, which might be an option," the ex-detective said. "But it may well be that it's a moot point now, because I've listened and I think I should make sure the people of Norfolk still have the confidence that I would do the job properly." Sutton admitted the reaction from constituents on social media and via emails sent to his office had caught him off-guard. "That's made me think about it again," he conceded. However, the PCC said the theatre tour was not something he needed to mention to voters during the election campaign and he denied letting them down. Steffan Aquarone accused Sutton of taking voters for granted The role of PCCs in England and Wales is due to be scrapped by the government by the end of Parliament, with their powers to be transferred to newly directly elected mayors. Aquarone said Sutton had taken the voters of Norfolk for granted by not telling them about the tour. "Either the job is serious and requires somebody full time paying attention, or it's not and it's OK to go off and do nearly as many tour dates as Taylor Swift," he said. A spokesperson for Reform said the party was supportive of "celebrity detective" Sutton and pointed out half of his shows would take place at weekends. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
description: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.
body: Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway operator has said. ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while several level crossings were also malfunctioning. Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action". It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating. The BBC has contacted police for comment. The network's website showed that 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected. ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved". Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands. title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
description: But other factors, including developments in the Middle East, may also be playing a role.
body: The number of small boat crossings is down more than 40% this year Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says. The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show. The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role. However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals. While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline. "It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues. He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact. The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium. NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before". "However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued. "We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel." The NCA said organised crime groups had been affected by "supply constraints" on vital equipment used in crossings. More than 1,600 boats or engines have been seized by the authorities since late 2023, it said. The wholesale cost of these items has gone up as a result, according to an NCA spokesperson. The NCA said a "number of key suppliers" had also been targeted, including the jailing of Adem Savas who reportedly supplied equipment used in about half of all crossings in 2023. However, the NCA also admitted the war in the Middle East had also made it harder for criminals to source dinghies. It added it could not publish its report on small boats in full because it contained sensitive intelligence. Between 1 January and 7 September 2026, a total of 17,281 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 8 September 2025 to 7 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. The NCA also pointed to activity targeting people smugglers reducing small boat crossings. In the year to April 2026, arrests linked to organised immigration crime involving the NCA increased by more than 55%, it said. The agency added it had also worked with social media networks to have more than 40,000 posts pages or accounts linked to immigration crime removed. "We are making it more difficult and costlier for people smuggling networks to source equipment, more difficult to get it to the beaches and in the water, more difficult to communicate with potential customers, and more likely smugglers will be confronted by law enforcement," said Jones. "Our message to the gangs is clear – moving people in small boats and supplying equipment gets riskier for you by the day," he continued. However, the Migration Observatory said "most notably" there had been a sharp decline in detected unauthorised border crossings into the EU. It said arrivals fell 26% in 2025, before declining another 37% in the first half of 2026. "This is likely to lead, with a lag, to fewer unauthorised crossings to the UK, since most small boat migrants travel through the EU before reaching beaches in northern France," it added. Adem Savas is thought to have supplied equipment used in about half of all small boat crossings in 2023 In August, the Home Office credited police in France with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques. Many migrants come from some of the poorest parts of the world and almost all ask to claim asy

title: State pension likely to rise by £488 a year in April
description: The increase has reignited the debate about the state pension's long-term affordability and generational fairness.
body: The state pension is expected to top £13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness. The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday. The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest. Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age. The triple lock was designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. Although the state pension age is rising to 67, the cost to the government has risen considerably too. Forecasts suggest state pension spending, already at £154bn this year, could go up by a further £600m a year by 2029-30. The policy is "crazy," Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation think tank, told the BBC. The triple lock is creating a "ratchet effect" where "pensioners' living standards grow even faster than just a typical worker," she added. "Pensioners have seen living standards grow three times more than typical workers over the last 20 years." Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank, said: "Each increase in spending builds upon the last, and so the long-run cost is substantial but very uncertain." The state pension is expected to match wage growth in the next calculations. Average wage growth, including bonuses, stood at 3.9% between May and July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), external. That is likely to be the key figure to determine April's rise in the state pension, although it could be revised, as it is likely to be higher than the rate of inflation. the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year. That would be an increase of £488 the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, an increase of £374.40 Pensioner groups have said older people face significant cost of living pressures, such as high energy bills, and the state pension itself remained relatively small compared with state provision across Europe. Almost 13 million people receive the state pension in the UK. If it does rise by 3.9%, it would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and therefore be liable for income tax. The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - promised that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay. However, when asked by the BBC on Tuesday, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds refused to confirm that pensioners reliant on the state pension will be exempted from paying income tax. Asked by BBC Breakfast whether he could reiterate that commitment, he said: "The vast majority of people in Britain have their own private pension provision alongside the state pension so this wouldn't be a substantial change for them, they'd already certainly be receiving an income in that case above the personal allowance. "Any changes to personal allowances, to tax rates, take place in the Budget, that's on October 28." He was repeatedly asked to confirm the previous pledge, but again pointed to the Budget. Analysis by consultants LCP suggested that only one in 16 pensioners would benefit if the government kept to its previous pledge, saving about £91 each a year. The majority of pensioners have additional pension income and so pay income tax already. "The government's plans to address this point are a mess," said Sir Steve Webb, a partner at LCP and a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister. The ONS also published figures on the UK labour force. While the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.9%, the number of vacancies and employees on payrolls fell in recent months. Will the increase see you pay tax for the first time? title: Assembly to debate bill aimed at banning conversion practices
description: The bill contains provisions that could see a two-year jail sentence imposed on people who conduct conversion practices.
body: A bill aimed at banning sexuality and gender conversion practices will be debated by assembly members for the first time at Stormont later on Tuesday. It contains provisions, external that could see a two-year jail sentence imposed on people who conduct conversion practices. Alliance's deputy leader Eóin Tennyson proposed the private member's legislation, but it has been criticised by the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) which said the bill "presents a real threat to freedom". Unionist parties are expected to oppose the bill, but it is believed to have support from Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP). Advocates say the legislation is about protecting LGBT people from harmful attempts to change or suppress who they are. Critics contend it is a legislative overreach which limits freedom of choice for gay and trans people, and risks criminalising important conversations around sexual orientation and gender. 'They wanted me to repent': Inside the push to ban conversion practices What is conversion therapy and will it be banned? Jail time and unlimited fines planned under conversion practices ban Ahead of the debate, Tennyson said Northern Ireland had lagged behind on equality for too long. "No-one should face coercion, abuse or harm because of who they are or who they love. This is balanced legislation which protects LGBT+ people from harm whilst also upholding freedom of speech and freedom of religion," he added. But DUP leader Gavin Robinson has said the legislation is vague and that Northern Ireland already has laws to deal with abuse and coercive behaviour. "We can protect people from mistreatment without creating vague new offences that reach into homes, churches and private conversations," he added. Conversion practices - sometimes called "reparative therapy" or "gay cure therapy" - try to change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity, according to the British Psychological Society (BPS). In practice, it means trying to stop or suppress someone from being gay or from identifying as a different gender to their sex recorded at birth. It often includes talking therapies and prayer but more extreme forms can exist. The BPS and other professional bodies, including NHS England and the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said all types of conversion practices were "unethical and potentially harmful". The bill would make it a criminal offence to provide conversion therapy, or to engage in coercive conversion behaviour, with the goal of changing a person's sexual orientation or gender identity. It would also make it an offence to remove a person from Northern Ireland for the purposes of subjecting them to conversion practices. The definition for coercive behaviour is borrowed from the Domestic Abuse and Civil Proceedings Act (Northern Ireland) 2021. It includes violent or threatening behaviour, humiliating the victim, or controlling their to day activities. In a summary of legal advice, the Christian Institute - a nondenominational charity that states that it is opposed to abortion, homosexuality and "transgender ideology" - said Aidan O'Neill KC's critique of Tennyson's bill was "devastating". "O'Neill argues that the proposals are fundamentally illiberal, poorly drafted, and pose a severe threat to basic civil liberties," the charity said. "He ultimately concludes that the bill likely exceeds the legislative competence of the Northern Ireland Assembly." James Kennedy, the Christian Institute's Northern Ireland policy officer, said that "existing law offers strong safeguards against coercion in the home and verbal or physical abuse anywhere else, too". He called on assembly members (MLAs) to oppose the bill. Meanwhile, the Ban Conversion Practices Coalition has urged MLAs to take a "historic opportunity" to pass the bill and become "the first jurisdiction on these islands to pass a ban on these harmful, abusive practices". Scott Cuthbertson, CEO of The Rainbow Project, said "politicians have the opportunity to buck that unfortunate trend, and deliver real protections for LGBTQIA+ people in Northern Ireland". Patrick Corrigan, head of nations and regions at Amnesty UK, said the draft bill "sends a clear message that everyone has the right to be safe and live openly and fully". "LGBT+ people are not broken and do not need fixing - protection from harm is long overdue." The bill was brought to the assembly floor by Alliance Party MLA Eóin Tennyson, but Stormont politicians have debated the issue of gay conversion practices before. In 2021, MLAs passed an Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) motion calling for it to be banned in all forms, however it was not binding. However the UUP has now changed its position under new leader Jon Burrows and has said it would vote against the bill, saying it was "excessively broad, legally uncertain and potentially damaging". The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) is also expected to vote against the legislation. The private member's bill has been brought forward by Alliance Party MLA Eóin Tennyson When Sinn Féin held the communities brief in the executive, several of its ministers advocated banning the practice - with Deirdre Hargey at the time saying her officials were drafting a bill, but a subsequent collapse of power-sharing meant this got no further. DUP assembly member Gordon Lyons became communities minister in 2024 when devolution was restored. He is expected to respond to Tennyson during the debate. Unionist parties cannot use a veto mechanism known as a petition of concern at this stage but they could seek to use it in future, if the bill passes its second stage on Tuesday. In England, the government has published its own plans to legislate to ban the practice there, which could carry jail time and fines for those found to have carried out "abusive acts" aiming to change someone's sexual orientation or transgender identity. title: We must heed warnings of AI tech developers, says UK minister
description: Louise Haigh is set to address growing concerns over AI safety in a speech at the TUC Congress.
body: Protesters warning about AI in London earlier this year The UK government must "heed the warnings" of "those who are at the forefront" of developing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, a senior minister will say later. First Secretary of State Louise Haigh will address the growing anxiety over AI safety when she speaks at the TUC congress on Tuesday. She is expected to say the government is "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security. Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity. On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the recent discussion of the risks, with his spokesperson saying: "It's a good thing that the companies developing the most advanced AI systems are now talking openly about the risks as well as the opportunities." Speaking at the TUC congress later on Tuesday, Haigh is also expected to acknowledge the benefits, saying: "AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs." In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should "never be complacent" about the impact AI might have but "we've got to be careful not to get hyperbolic about this either". "Of course there are risks but, let's be frank, there are some tremendous upsides, whether it's public services, healthcare, the contribution to the economy," he added. The UK First Secretary of State Louise Haigh is due to speak at the TUC Congress, a federation of trade unions It comes as MPs in the UK are seeking new laws on AI after a report found the technology was responsible for numerous abuses of human rights. "Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel said. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? One Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, made headlines after he said he believed there is a greater than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade. Hubinger's claim came after a researcher who quit Anthropic went viral for sounding the alarm on the "fate of humanity in the next two years" from AI. "If we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic employee, told the BBC. Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei has since called for the pace of development on AI models, such as Claude or ChatGPT, to slow down and be closely monitored. Amodei said risks associated with it were "serious" and that companies and governments must be given time to address them. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk backed him. However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may even be designed to generate hype. This video can not be played AI "more powerful by the day", Anthropic co-founder tells BBC An AI "kill switch" has also been floated by an Anthropic co-founder as a way to shut down AI software that becomes too dangerous. Jack Clark, one of seven founders of the AI company, told the BBC "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said MPs may need to enforce having one. Asked about the idea of a "kill switch", Reynolds told the BBC: "I don't think that's a particularly helpful way to think about how we manage the risks - I'm not really sure what that would mean in practice." He warned that overregulation could risk the UK losing access to models developed abroad, which he argued would make the country "less safe". The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency was brought to Parliament by Lords and MPs. But the Cabinet Office said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off". "Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News. Meanwhile, the US President Donald Trump has dismissed the idea of AI taking over the world, saying on social media that AI "destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX". In a more recent Truth post, Trump said the AI Hoax was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats" and likened it to what he describes as the "Global Warming Scam" by the left. The president, who frequently shares AI content on his platform Truth Social, has lauded the benefits of AI and has been public about his desire for the US to win "the AI race". title: What is the triple lock and how much is the state pension worth?
description: The triple lock guarantees that the state pension is not overtaken by inflation or wage increases.
body: The new state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year, as a result of the triple lock arrangement. The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest. The age at which millions of people can claim their state pension has started to increase from 66 to 67. The state pension is a payment made every four weeks by the government, to people who have reached the qualifying age and have paid enough National Insurance (NI) contributions. the new flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a year the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week, or £9,614.80 a year Many people on the old basic state pension may also receive the additional state pension, external. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension. Some people may have gaps in their NI record if, for example, they have lived abroad or taken time off to care for children. It is possible to make voluntary payments to boost your contribution history. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. Data suggested that the state pension will increase in April 2027, meaning: the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now The government will confirm the rise, possibly in October's Budget. Check your state pension age Check your state pension forecast and whether you can increase it Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest: inflation in the September of the previous year, using a measure called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) the average increase in total wages, including bonuses, across the UK for May to July of the previous year The rise in wages of 3.9% is likely to determine the April 2027 state pension increase. The triple lock was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010. It was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. The Labour government has previously said it would keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament. But since that commitment, there has been intense debate over the cost of the triple lock and whether it is justified. In July 2025, the government's official forecaster said the cost of the triple lock guarantee was set to be three times higher by the end of the decade than was originally anticipated when it began. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the annual cost is set to reach £15.5bn by 2030. It said the cost of the state pension has risen steadily over the past eight decades, and now equates to £138bn, or around half the total amount the government spent on benefits. Earlier in July, the influential Institute for Fiscal Studies think-tank suggested that the triple lock should be scrapped as part of a wider pensions overhaul. The expected increase in April 2027 would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and so liable to pay about £91 next year in income tax. The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - pledged that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay. However, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds was non-committal, saying that it was a decision for the new chancellor, John Healey, in the Budget. The majority of pensioners are already income taxpayers owing to the addition of other pension income, on top of the state pension. More than 12 million people currently receive the state pension. Men and women born between 6 October 1954 and 5 April1960 start receiving their pension at the age of 66. But for people born after this date, the state pension age is increasing in two phases: a gradual rise to 67 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1960 a gradual rise to 68 between 2044 and 2046 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1977 The rise from 66 to 67 began in April 2026. The first affected are those born between 6 April and 5 May 1960, who will have to wait an extra month. The increase is expected to save the Treasury about £10bn a year by 2030. But charities have warned that it will disproportionately affect areas of the UK where life expectancy is lower, and those on lower incomes. A government review is considering whether to delay the second phase, which would currently take the state pension age to 68 between 2044 and 2046. State pension age starts rising to 67 - here's how much you get and when Future pensioners to be worse off, government warns Depending on their overall income, those above retirement age may also be entitled to pension credit, external in addition to the basic state pension. Pension credit increased by 4.8% in April 2026. If your income is above the stated limits, you may still be eligible for pension credit if you have a disability or care for someone. Anyone who qualifies for pension credit may also be entitled to other financial support, including housing benefit, a reduction in council tax, help with heating costs and the warm home discount scheme.
